entries.rq_with_context: Despite evidence of gender disparities in leadership across professional domains, prior studies of U.S. elections have found little evidence of gender bias in electoral outcomes, leading to the claim that 'when women run, women win.' This creates a puzzle: why would politics be an exception? The authors argue that past research overlooks the role of power in moderating gender bias. Specifically, they test whether power—operationalized as incumbency status—alters the impact of gender on election outcomes. They propose the 'power shield' hypothesis: women in high-power roles (incumbents) will achieve parity with men, while women in low-power roles (challengers) will face disadvantages. Using a comprehensive dataset of all U.S. senator and governor elections since 1920 and a novel bootstrapping method to address dependency in candidate-level data, they examine how gender and incumbency interact to predict election success. Their findings challenge the conventional wisdom by revealing that gender disparities exist but are concentrated among challengers, not incumbents.

title: “Fully recharged” evenings? The effect of evening cyber leisure on next-day vitality and performance through sleep quantity and quality, bedtime procrastination, and psychological detachment, and the moderating role of mindfulness.

entries.rq_with_context: Evening cyber leisure—using electronic devices for nonwork purposes like entertainment—is increasingly common, yet its impact on employee recovery and subsequent work outcomes remains unclear. While cyber-device use for work is known to harm sleep and next-day functioning, leisure use may offer psychological detachment, a key recovery process. However, it may also lead to bedtime procrastination, delaying sleep. This creates a paradox: cyber leisure could simultaneously support and undermine recovery. The study addresses this gap by proposing a dual-path model in which evening cyber leisure differentially affects next-day psychological vitality and performance through psychological detachment (positive path) and bedtime procrastination (negative path), which in turn affect sleep quantity and quality. Trait mindfulness is examined as a boundary condition. The research uses an experience sampling method with R&D employees to test these daily processes, contributing to recovery, sleep, and mindfulness research by clarifying when and how cyber leisure aids or hinders workplace outcomes.

title: Hot, cold, or both? A person-centered perspective on death awareness during the COVID-19 pandemic.

entries.rq_with_context: The COVID-19 pandemic serves as an ongoing mortality cue that heightens employees' awareness of death. While prior research has examined death anxiety and death reflection as separate constructs, little is known about how they coexist within individuals over time or how their combined experiences affect work-related outcomes. This study addresses that gap by identifying distinct profiles of death awareness during the pandemic. Using a person-centered approach, it investigates whether employees differ in their joint levels of death anxiety and death reflection, what health, work, and community factors predict membership in these profiles, and how the profiles relate to well-being (depression, emotional exhaustion) and prosocial behaviors (organizational citizenship, pro-diversity actions). The research uses latent profile analysis across two studies to uncover patterns not detectable through traditional variable-centered methods.

title: Can good followers create unethical leaders? How follower citizenship leads to leader moral licensing and unethical behavior.

entries.rq_with_context: While leadership research has traditionally focused on leaders' influence on followers, less is known about how follower behaviors affect leaders. Recent calls emphasize the need to reverse this lens and examine follower-to-leader effects. This study addresses that gap by exploring whether followers’ organizational citizenship behaviors (OCB) can trigger unethical behavior in leaders through moral licensing. Drawing on moral licensing theory, the authors suggest that leaders may psychologically claim credit for their followers' moral actions, freeing them to act unethically. Using multiple studies—pilot, experiments, and field data—they test this mechanism and its boundary conditions. The key contribution is demonstrating a counterintuitive pathway whereby followers’ positive behaviors can promote leader unethicality, advancing understanding of reciprocal leader-follower dynamics and vicarious moral licensing in organizations.

title: The psychological implications of COVID-19 on employee job insecurity and its consequences: The mitigating role of organization adaptive practices.

entries.rq_with_context: The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread job insecurity, but most research has focused on economic and organizational factors rather than how employees psychologically perceive the pandemic itself. This study addresses this gap by applying event system theory to examine how three dimensions of perceived event strength—novelty, disruption, and criticality—influence job insecurity. It further explores how this insecurity leads to negative outcomes (emotional exhaustion, organizational deviance, and saving behavior) and investigates whether organization adaptive practices can mitigate these effects. Using a two-wave survey of Chinese employees, the authors test a moderated mediation model. The study contributes by identifying psychological antecedents of job insecurity during a global crisis and offering timely insights on organizational practices that may protect employee well-being.

title: The COVID-19 pandemic and new hire engagement: Relationships with unemployment rates, state restrictions, and organizational tenure.

entries.rq_with_context: Starting a new job is inherently uncertain, but the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic introduced additional macro-level stressors, including health risks and economic instability. While prior research has explored individual and organizational influences on new hire engagement, there is little understanding of how broader societal stressors—such as pandemics or economic downturns—shape newcomer experiences. This study addresses that gap by examining how the pandemic and unemployment rates relate to new hire engagement, how the effect varies with organizational tenure, and whether state-level restrictions buffer these impacts. Using a large U.S. sample of quick service restaurant employees hired within 90 days, the study employs multilevel modeling to test these relationships. The findings contribute by highlighting the role of macro stressors in socialization and suggesting that health-related concerns may outweigh economic ones in influencing engagement.

title: Can becoming a leader change your personality? An investigation with two longitudinal studies from a role-based perspective.

entries.rq_with_context: Personality research in organizations has traditionally assumed that traits influence work outcomes, not the reverse. However, emerging evidence suggests personality can develop through adult role transitions. This study addresses a gap by examining whether becoming a leader—a significant work role change—shapes personality development, specifically conscientiousness and emotional stability. Prior research has not clearly established if leadership emergence causes personality change or how this might occur. Using a role-based perspective grounded in transactional theory, the authors test whether assuming leadership roles leads to personality growth, with job role demands as a mediating mechanism. The research contributes by providing longitudinal, quasi-experimental evidence on causal pathways in personality development at work.

title: Leveraging age diversity for organizational performance: An intellectual capital perspective.

entries.rq_with_context: The global trend of increasing workplace age diversity has sparked research on its organizational consequences, but mechanisms linking age diversity to performance remain understudied. Prior work has focused on direct statistical relationships without probing how age-diverse workforces create value. This study addresses that gap by adopting an intellectual capital perspective, investigating how age diversity influences performance through human and social capital. The authors use a large U.S. manager-report survey (N = 3,888) and test whether functional diversity and age-inclusive management moderate these effects. The research contributes by identifying specific mechanisms and boundary conditions through which age diversity can enhance organizational performance.

title: The self-sacrificial nature of leader identity: Understanding the costs and benefits at work and home.

entries.rq_with_context: Leader identity is traditionally viewed as beneficial, but the daily demands of leadership suggest it may have both positive and negative consequences. Existing research largely assumes strong leader identity improves outcomes without considering potential costs for leaders themselves. This study addresses this gap by investigating how daily fluctuations in leader identity lead to self-sacrificial behaviors that simultaneously enhance work outcomes and impair home life. Using an experience sampling method with 80 leaders over 10 days, the authors test a model integrating leader identity, self-sacrificial leadership, and self-regulation theories. They find that daily leader identity increases self-sacrifice, which boosts task performance and prosocial impact while also increasing depletion and home conflict, especially for work-addicted leaders. The key contribution is demonstrating the dual consequences of leader identity, challenging the assumption that strong identity is universally beneficial.

title: Prompt-specificity in scenario-based assessments: Associations with personality versus knowledge and effects on predictive validity.

entries.rq_with_context: Scenario-based assessments are widely used in personnel selection and training, but there is ongoing debate about whether prompts should be general or specific. While general prompts may reveal spontaneous trait-related behaviors, specific prompts clarify performance expectations and may better elicit relevant knowledge. However, it remains unclear how prompt-specificity affects which constructs (personality vs. knowledge) are tapped by these assessments and how this influences their predictive validity. This study addresses this gap by testing how prompt-specificity moderates the relationships between openness to experience, perspective taking, and cultural knowledge with scenario-based scores, and how these differential relationships affect validity for intercultural, in-role, and extrarole performance. Drawing on situation construal and situational strength theory, the authors propose that prompt-specificity systematically shifts the underlying constructs being assessed. The research uses a randomized design with intercultural scenarios and finds that lesser prompt-specificity strengthens the role of personality traits in predicting intercultural performance, whereas greater prompt-specificity increases the role of knowledge in predicting in-role performance.

title: Are you sick? Understanding the effects of coworker presenteeism on workplace mistreatment.

entries.rq_with_context: As organizations resume in-person work during the COVID-19 pandemic, employees are increasingly exposed to coworkers who attend work while ill—a practice known as presenteeism. While presenteeism is recognized as a controversial act with well-documented productivity costs, little is known about how it influences interpersonal treatment by coworkers. Existing research has not clarified whether employees respond to sick colleagues with self-protective (self-concern) or altruistic (coworker-orientation) motives. This study addresses this gap by proposing a dual-mechanism model in which coworker presenteeism simultaneously triggers both self-concern and coworker-orientation, which in turn shape behaviors like avoidance and incivility. The study uses a stressful event framework and draws on social motives and self-construal theory, testing the model across two field studies during the pandemic. The authors claim the study advances understanding by identifying opposing social mechanisms and establishing workload as a key boundary condition.

title: Risks and rewards of conscientiousness during the COVID-19 pandemic.

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates how the work context changes caused by the COVID-19 pandemic—specifically the shift to remote work with less supervision and role clarity—alter the well-established positive relationships between conscientiousness and employee well-being and performance. Although conscientiousness is typically linked to higher performance, greater satisfaction, and lower strain, the authors argue that the pandemic-induced weakening of situational strength may disrupt these patterns. The gap lies in understanding how contextual shifts can fundamentally alter trait-outcome relationships. Using a two-wave field study of 474 employees surveyed before and during the pandemic, the authors test a moderated mediation model based on situational strength theory. Their key contribution is demonstrating that conscientiousness can become a liability under low situational strength, increasing strain and reducing satisfaction despite boosting performance.

title: Investing for keeps: Firms’ prepandemic investments in human capital decreased workforce reductions associated with COVID-19 financial pressures.

entries.rq_with_context: The economic crisis caused by the COVID-19 pandemic led many firms to reduce costs through workforce reductions, but we know little about the conditions under which firms are more or less likely to resort to layoffs during such crises. While existing research links financial pressures to downsizing, it does not adequately explain how prior resource investments shape firms' responses. This study addresses this gap by investigating how firms' prepandemic investments in human capital—specifically in employee training, salaries, and development—affect their use of workforce reductions when facing pandemic financial pressures (PFPs). Drawing on resource orchestration theory, the authors argue that higher human capital investment (HCI) makes workforce reductions less attractive because they threaten valuable, firm-specific employee knowledge and motivation. Moreover, this effect is expected to be stronger when HCI is paired with greater physical capital investment (PCI), as co-specialization increases employee value or provides alternative cost-cutting options. The study analyzes data from 1,364 U.S. banks using FDIC reports, WARN filings, and news sources. Its primary contribution is demonstrating that firms’ prior investments in human capital can protect jobs during crises, especially when aligned with broader resource strategies.

title: Class advantage in the white-collar labor market: An investigation of social class background, job search strategies, and job search success.

entries.rq_with_context: The phenomenon under study is job search effectiveness among new white-collar job seekers, focusing on how social class background influences outcomes. While job search intensity is known to predict success, less is understood about why individuals from different class backgrounds may vary in their effectiveness. Existing research highlights class-based disparities in access to education and social networks but provides limited insight into how class shapes job search behaviors directly. This study addresses the gap by testing whether upper-class job seekers achieve more interviews and offers not just due to resources but because they use more focused, less haphazard strategies. Using two studies—one time-lagged multisource and one longitudinal—the authors examine parental income, education, and subjective class as indicators of background. The key contribution is demonstrating that class background strengthens the link between search intensity and success, partly through reduced reliance on haphazard strategies, and identifying psychological capital as a factor that may help working-class job seekers become more strategic over time.

title: Words that hurt: Leaders’ anti-Asian communication and employee outcomes.

entries.rq_with_context: With the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, public figures—including U.S. political leaders—used racially charged terms to refer to the virus, contributing to a rise in anti-Asian harassment. Although organizational research has examined racial harassment, it has largely overlooked the experiences of Asian employees and novel forms of prejudice like stigmatizing disease labeling. This study investigates whether and how leaders' use of such language harms workplace outcomes. Drawing on organizational justice theories, the authors propose that these labels reduce employees' perceptions of interpersonal justice, leading to higher emotional exhaustion and lower work engagement. They test this model using a survey and an experiment, examining both direct effects and psychological mechanisms. The study contributes by identifying a new form of racial harassment in organizations and showing its adverse effects on both targeted and non-targeted employees.

title: The effects of blue-light filtration on sleep and work outcomes.

entries.rq_with_context: The workforce widely suffers from sleep deprivation, which negatively impacts work engagement, task performance, and nontask performance such as organizational citizenship and counterproductive behaviors. While prior research has explored organizational interventions like flexible scheduling, these are often impractical in settings requiring round-the-clock staff, such as hospitals. Recent findings in circadian science suggest that exposure to blue light from electronic devices delays sleep onset by suppressing melatonin, and that filtering blue light may improve sleep. However, this intervention has not been studied in relation to workplace outcomes. This paper asks whether wearing blue-light filtering glasses at night improves sleep and, in turn, work-related attitudes and behaviors. Using theory from chronobiology, the authors test a mediation model in which blue-light filtration enhances sleep, which then improves daily work outcomes. They further propose chronotype as a boundary condition, suggesting the intervention is more effective for those with later sleep preferences. The key contribution is demonstrating a cost-effective, employee-controlled means to improve both sleep and work outcomes.

title: Referents or role models? The self-efficacy and job performance effects of perceiving higher performing peers.

entries.rq_with_context: The phenomenon under study is how employees are affected by their perceptions of higher performing peers at work. While existing research recognizes that upward comparisons can either motivate learning or provoke threat, there is little consensus on when these effects occur or what determines their direction. This study addresses the gap by examining individual differences in information processing, specifically performance-prove goal orientation (PPGO), as a key moderator. The research question is whether PPGO determines if observing higher performers enhances or undermines observer self-efficacy and performance. Drawing on social comparison theory, social–cognitive theory, and goal orientation theory, the authors propose a conditional indirect effects model tested through one field and one experimental study. The key contribution is identifying PPGO as a dispositional mechanism that explains inconsistent findings in prior research on peer performance effects.

title: Transformed by the family: An episodic, attachment theory perspective on family–work enrichment and transformational leadership.

entries.rq_with_context: Transformational leadership is critical for organizational success, yet many managers struggle to consistently display these behaviors. While workplace factors have been studied, less is known about non-work antecedents, particularly daily family experiences. Although prior research links family–work enrichment (FWE) to leadership, findings are inconsistent, and the mechanisms and boundary conditions remain unclear. Drawing on attachment theory, this paper explores how daily FWE acts as a within-person prime of promotion focus—motivating leaders to pursue ideal future goals—which in turn fosters transformational leadership. Using experience-sampling methods across two studies, the authors test whether this mediated effect varies by supervisor attachment styles. The study contributes by identifying promotion focus as a key mechanism and offering an explanation for mixed prior findings through the moderating role of attachment avoidance and anxiety.

title: Out of sight and out of mind? Networking strategies for enhancing inclusion in multinational organizations.

entries.rq_with_context: Employees in multinational corporations (MNCs) are often dispersed across different countries and subsidiaries, making it difficult for them to feel included. While prior research has focused on top-down diversity and inclusion policies, such approaches are hard to apply consistently across global units. This study investigates how professional advice networks—specifically, being central as a source of advice to HQ contacts—can enhance employees’ perceived inclusion. We examine two agentic strategies—engaging in cross-border work and having well-connected site leaders—that may help employees, particularly those outside HQ countries, build such ties. Using social capital theory and MNC literature on status differences, we test how these strategies vary by employee location. The findings clarify which network ties promote inclusion and offer accessible, location-sensitive strategies for fostering inclusion across MNCs.

title: How critical activities within COVID-19 intensive care units increase nurses’ daily occupational calling.

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses how occupational calling—typically viewed as stable—may fluctuate in crisis situations like the COVID-19 pandemic. While prior research treats calling as a long-term trait, qualitative evidence suggests it may shift in extreme contexts where societal needs intensify. This research investigates whether daily exposure to code blue events (i.e., emergency resuscitations) increases nurses’ daily occupational calling in a Wuhan ICU. Using a daily diary design with 66 nurses over five days, it examines both within-person fluctuations and between-person differences. The study also tests how nurses’ prosocial motivation shapes their calling patterns and how calling variability and average level affect job performance. The authors aim to advance calling research by demonstrating its dynamic nature and performance implications in crisis contexts.

title: How CEOs respond to mortality salience during the COVID-19 pandemic: Integrating terror management theory with regulatory focus theory.

entries.rq_with_context: The tragic scale of the COVID-19 pandemic, with hundreds of thousands of deaths in the U.S., created an unprecedented crisis that brought mortality to the forefront of public awareness. As chief strategists responsible for vast stakeholder networks, CEOs face unique psychological pressures during such crises. While prior research has examined corporate social responsibility through CEO traits or institutional pressures, little is known about how CEOs psychologically respond to large-scale mortality. This study addresses that gap by applying terror management theory (TMT) and regulatory focus theory to understand how salient death awareness influences CEO decision-making. The research question is how mortality salience affects CEOs’ other-orientation and self-orientation, and whether these responses vary based on their prevention or promotion focus. Using text analysis of earnings calls from S&P 500 firms, the study finds that mortality salience increases other-orientation among prevention-focused CEOs and reduces self-orientation among promotion-focused CEOs. The work contributes by revealing the psychological mechanisms behind CEO responses to existential threats.

title: When helping hurts: COVID-19 critical incident involvement and resource depletion in health care workers.

entries.rq_with_context: Healthcare workers are on the frontlines of the COVID-19 pandemic and face intense physical and psychological demands. While prior research has focused on the benefits of prosocial motivation, less is known about its potential negative consequences in high-stress, high-risk contexts where helping goals are difficult to achieve. This study investigates whether critical incident involvement during the pandemic is linked to emotional exhaustion and depression among doctors and nurses, and how individual differences in prosocial motivation and perceived prosocial impact shape these relationships. Drawing on ego depletion theory, the authors examine resource depletion as a mechanism linking crisis involvement to negative outcomes. The study uses longitudinal data collected before and during the pandemic. The key contribution is in identifying how a typically beneficial trait—prosocial motivation—can intensify strain during crises, offering new insight into the 'dark side' of helping behavior.

title: When passions collide: Passion convergence in entrepreneurial teams.

entries.rq_with_context: While passion is recognized as crucial in entrepreneurship, research has largely focused on individual-level dynamics, with limited attention to how passion evolves within teams. Most existing team-level studies adopt static approaches, failing to capture the temporal dynamics inherent in team processes. This study addresses this gap by examining passion convergence—the increasing similarity in passion levels among team members over time. Drawing on multilevel theory of emergence and using the consensus emergence model (CEM), the authors investigate how team progress and setbacks influence this convergence and its impact on team performance. Using longitudinal data from 314 individuals in 82 new venture teams, the study tests whether team experiences shape passion convergence and whether convergence, in turn, predicts performance. The main contribution is introducing and testing a dynamic model of passion at the team level, offering new insights into affective dynamics in entrepreneurial teams.

title: This job is (literally) killing me: A moderated-mediated model linking work characteristics to mortality.

entries.rq_with_context: Research has established that job demands affect employee health, but less is known about how these demands connect to mortality through physiological and psychological pathways. A key gap lies in understanding the mechanisms—particularly how job control and individual cognitive ability might buffer the stress process. This study addresses when and for whom job demands lead to death by testing a moderated-mediation model. Drawing from the job demands-control and allostatic load theories, the authors examine whether job control and cognitive ability moderate the effects of job demands on allostatic load and depression, which in turn influence mortality. The study uses a 20-year longitudinal dataset from the MIDUS survey. Its key contribution is identifying divergent pathways linking work characteristics to death, while integrating individual and job-level buffers.

title: Job search self-regulation during COVID-19: Linking search constraints, health concerns, and invulnerability to job search processes and outcomes.

entries.rq_with_context: The COVID-19 pandemic has increased job loss and introduced new constraints—such as childcare, financial strain, and health concerns—that interfere with job search efforts. Prior research on job search constraints shows inconsistent findings, often assuming direct negative effects, yet self-regulation theory suggests both negative and adaptive responses may occur depending on situational factors. This study addresses the gap by exploring how job search constraints during the pandemic simultaneously affect job search distress and effort, contingent on individuals' sense of invulnerability to COVID-19—a novel protective cognition. Drawing on self-regulation theories, the authors test a model linking constraints to job search outcomes through hope and metacognitive activities, moderated by invulnerability, which in turn is shaped by personal and interpersonal health risk factors. The study uses three-wave survey data from 228 unemployed U.S. job seekers. The authors argue this approach advances understanding of job search under extreme conditions and highlights inequities in vulnerability.

title: The fatiguing effects of camera use in virtual meetings: A within-person field experiment.

entries.rq_with_context: With the rise of remote work during the COVID-19 pandemic, virtual meeting fatigue—commonly called 'Zoom fatigue'—has become a widespread concern, yet little empirical research has identified its specific causes. While some suggest fatigue stems from meeting length or volume, recent evidence shows actual meeting time has decreased, pointing instead to features of virtual platforms themselves. This study focuses on camera use as a potential fatiguing element, drawing on self-presentation theory to argue that being on camera increases cognitive load due to heightened self-awareness and impression management. The research question is whether being required to use a camera in virtual meetings increases daily fatigue, which then reduces employee voice and engagement in meetings. Using a 4-week within-person field experiment with daily surveys, the study tests this model while controlling for number and duration of meetings. It contributes by isolating the causal effect of camera use on fatigue and performance, and by identifying gender and organizational tenure as key moderators.

title: The influence of COVID-induced job search anxiety and conspiracy beliefs on job search effort: A within-person investigation.

entries.rq_with_context: New labor market entrants face significant challenges in their job search, which were intensified during the economic and social disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic. While prior research has examined the effects of negative affect on job search, less is known about how context-specific anxiety—such as anxiety tied directly to pandemic-related job market stress—impacts job seekers’ cognitive and behavioral responses. The authors identify a gap in understanding whether such anxiety leads to adaptive (e.g., proactive planning) or maladaptive (e.g., distressing rumination) processes, and how it subsequently shapes the quality of job search effort. They also explore how stable beliefs, such as belief in conspiracy theories or the severity of the pandemic, shape these dynamics. Using a weekly diary study, they ask how COVID-induced job search anxiety influences rumination and job search behaviors over time, particularly in the context of stable individual beliefs. The study applies control theory and affect-as-information theory to examine within-person fluctuations. The authors claim their work contributes by distinguishing types of job search effort and identifying boundary conditions shaped by conspiratorial beliefs.

title: Understanding the relationship between prior to end-of-workday physical activity and work–life balance: A within-person approach.

entries.rq_with_context: While employee physical activity is often studied as a postwork recovery behavior, little is known about how physical activity prior to the end of the workday affects nonwork outcomes like work–life balance. Existing research has largely ignored within-day physical activity and its potential to influence energetic resources that span work and nonwork domains. This study addresses this gap by testing whether prior to end-of-workday physical activity improves daily satisfaction with work–life balance through increased vigor at the end of the workday. Using a daily diary design with objective step measurements from actigraphs, the authors apply Hirschi et al.'s (2019) action regulation model and the work–home resources model to trace the process by which physical activity generates vigor, enabling employees to meet both work recovery and family goals after work. The study claims to extend theorizing on physical activity by demonstrating its boundary-spanning benefits before the workday ends.

title: Getting worse or getting better? Understanding the antecedents and consequences of emotion profile transitions during COVID-19-induced organizational crisis.

entries.rq_with_context: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many organizations faced crisis conditions marked by threats to survival, time pressure, and inadequate resources, triggering complex emotional responses in employees. While prior research has examined emotions during crises, little is known about how discrete positive and negative emotions co-occur and change over time, particularly in response to leadership behaviors. There is also limited understanding of how transitions in emotional profiles—rather than static emotional states—affect employee outcomes. This study addresses these gaps by using a person-centered approach to identify monthly emotional profiles and their transitions among university employees from August to November 2020, a period marked by significant organizational changes. The research examines how perceptions of leader ability, benevolence, integrity, and pandemic handling predict movement between emotional profiles, and how these transitions are linked to well-being, performance, and preventive health behaviors. The key contribution lies in advancing a dynamic, profile-based understanding of emotions during organizational crises.

title: Making daily decisions to work from home or to work in the office: The impacts of daily work- and COVID-related stressors on next-day work location.

entries.rq_with_context: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many organizations allowed employees to choose daily whether to work from home or in the office, creating a unique context for studying work location decisions. While prior research has focused on long-term telework arrangements, little is known about the factors driving day-to-day work location choices under dynamic, high-stress conditions. Existing literature typically assumes stable personal or job characteristics drive such decisions, but in a fast-evolving crisis like the pandemic, proximal stressors may play a more immediate role. This study fills that gap by examining how five categories of daily stressors—work–family boundary, technology, work coordination, workload, and COVID-19 infection-related stressors—impact next-day work location. Using a daily diary design with data from 127 IT workers in China over five workdays, the study applies a social ecological perspective, framing work location choice as a coping strategy. The key contribution is revealing how employees use daily work location decisions to manage different types of stressors, including the moderating role of health-related concerns.

title: When there is a will there is a way: The role of proactive personality in combating COVID-19.

entries.rq_with_context: Frontline healthcare professionals faced unprecedented uncertainty, high workloads, and personal risk during the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic. While existing research points to organizational and leadership responses in crisis management, less is known about how individual differences, such as proactive personality, help healthcare workers navigate such chaos. This study investigates whether a proactive disposition enables doctors and nurses to maintain performance and well-being by actively using their personal strengths. Drawing on proactive behavior theory and conservation of resources (COR) theory, the authors use a multiwave, multisource design with 408 healthcare workers in Wuhan, China. They aim to show how proactive personality indirectly contributes to job performance, resilience, and thriving via perceived strengths use, and how this process is shaped by crisis-related contextual factors. The study claims to extend proactive personality research into extreme crisis contexts and demonstrate the mechanism through which personal agency leads to positive outcomes.

title: Gaining perspective: The impact of close cross-race friendships on diversity training and education.

entries.rq_with_context: Diversity education aims to improve skills needed to work in diverse environments, with perspective taking being a key skill. However, it remains unclear whether such training actually improves perspective-taking abilities and what factors influence its effectiveness. The research identifies a gap in understanding how pretraining relational experiences—particularly close cross-race friendships—impact training outcomes. The study tests whether these friendships increase the efficacy of diversity education in boosting perspective taking. Using longitudinal data from organizational and academic settings, the authors apply a relational model integrating intergroup contact and disequilibrium theories. The key contribution is demonstrating that close cross-race friendships, but not other forms of interracial contact, uniquely enhance perspective-taking development through diversity education.

title: Robots at work: People prefer—and forgive—service robots with perceived feelings.

entries.rq_with_context: Service robots are increasingly used in customer-facing roles, but their frequent failures can frustrate customers and harm organizations. While research shows people often dislike automated service, it remains unclear how to improve human-robot interactions in real-world settings. Drawing from mind perception and anthropomorphism theories, this paper explores whether making robots seem more humanlike—specifically, capable of thinking and feeling—affects customer satisfaction. The authors test whether attributing agency (thinking) and experience (feeling) to robots changes how customers respond, particularly when service failures occur. They propose a moderated mediation model tested in a robot-staffed hotel and a lab experiment. The key contribution is identifying that perceived experience, not agency, drives more forgiving responses to robot failures, offering insight into how organizations can humanize robots effectively.

title: Changes in perceptions of ethical leadership: Effects on associative and dissociative outcomes.

entries.rq_with_context: Ethical leadership research has traditionally focused on static levels of leadership behavior, but recent observations suggest that leadership can change over time. Despite this, little is known about how changes in perceived ethical leadership affect employee attitudes and behaviors beyond the current level of ethical leadership. This study addresses this gap by exploring whether changes in ethical leadership perceptions influence employees' pride and contempt, and whether these emotions mediate behavioral outcomes such as functional/dysfunctional voice and turnover. Guided by social exchange theory, the study uses both experimental and longitudinal data to test these dynamics. It contributes by showing that changes in ethical leadership perceptions are meaningful in their own right and help explain shifts in employee emotions and behaviors.

title: The regulating role of mindfulness in enacted workplace incivility: An experience sampling study.

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace incivility—low-intensity deviant behavior violating norms of mutual respect—is a prevalent issue with negative consequences for individuals and organizations. While prior research has largely focused on victims of incivility, less is known about what drives individuals to engage in such behavior or how they respond to their own transgressions. The authors adopt a self-regulation perspective, arguing that enacted incivility often results from self-regulatory failures. They propose that trait mindfulness, defined as a tendency to bring attention and awareness to present-moment experiences, may serve as a protective factor by enhancing self-regulation. Using an experience-sampling design over five workdays, the study investigates how trait mindfulness relates to the average level and day-to-day variability of enacted incivility, as well as to guilt following uncivil acts. The paper’s primary contribution is advancing understanding of dynamic, within-person processes in workplace mistreatment by integrating mindfulness research with theories of self-regulation and moral emotion.

title: The costs of mindfulness at work: The moderating role of mindfulness in surface acting, self-control depletion, and performance outcomes.

entries.rq_with_context: While mindfulness is typically seen as beneficial for employee well-being and performance, especially through enhanced self-control, researchers have suggested it may also have a 'dark side.' Prior studies show mindful employees are less likely to engage in surface acting—a form of emotional labor involving emotional dissonance and resource depletion. However, when they do engage in surface acting, their heightened awareness may make the experience more taxing. This paper investigates whether, for mindful employees, surface acting leads to greater self-control depletion and poorer performance. Using six field studies with multi-wave, multi-source data, the authors test a first-stage moderated mediation model. They find that mindfulness intensifies the negative indirect effects of surface acting on performance via self-control depletion. This work contributes to mindfulness and emotional labor research by revealing a potential cost of mindfulness under certain workplace conditions.

title: Pay communication, justice, and affect: The asymmetric effects of process and outcome pay transparency on counterproductive workplace behavior.

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing interest in pay transparency, research has focused narrowly on performance outcomes, leaving gaps in understanding its effects on contextual behaviors like counterproductive workplace behavior (CWB). While some studies suggest transparency improves employee behavior, others find mixed or negative effects, potentially due to unexamined distinctions between forms of transparency. This study addresses that gap by distinguishing between process pay transparency (information about how pay is determined) and outcome pay transparency (disclosure of actual pay levels). Grounded in uncertainty management theory, it investigates how these forms differentially impact CWB through procedural and distributive justice perceptions. The research question is whether and how process versus outcome transparency influences CWB-O and CWB-I, particularly under varying pay comparison conditions. The approach tests these mechanisms using both a two-wave field study and an experimental simulation. The key contribution is clarifying when and why pay transparency can yield beneficial or harmful behavioral outcomes.

title: The dynamics of gender and alternatives in negotiation.

entries.rq_with_context: A well-documented gender gap in negotiation performance has been attributed either to women being less assertive (the 'tameness' account) or to social backlash when women act assertively (the 'backlash' account). Prior research has struggled to distinguish between these explanations. This paper uses a dataset of over 2,500 negotiators to test how the strength of one’s alternative—commonly seen as empowering—interacts with gender to affect negotiation outcomes. The research examines both value extraction and impasse rates. Findings show that the gender gap in performance emerges only when negotiators have strong alternatives, and impasses are more frequent when at least one woman has a strong alternative. These results support the backlash account, not the tameness account, as women with strong alternatives do not differ from men in aspirations or reservation values, yet still perform worse.

title: Team leader coaching intervention: An investigation of the impact on team processes and performance within a surgical context.

entries.rq_with_context: Effective teamwork in healthcare, especially in surgical settings, is critical due to its life-or-death implications, yet team-level effects of leadership coaching remain understudied. While prior research confirms individual benefits of coaching leaders, scholars have called for evidence on whether such interventions extend to team functioning. This study addresses that gap by testing whether coaching surgeons (as team leaders) enhances team processes and performance in operating rooms. Guided by Marks, Mathieu, and Zaccaro’s (2001) theory of episodic team processes, we employed an interrupted time series quasi-experimental design with 223 surgeries across 40 surgeons. We test whether coaching improves team transition processes and how these influence action and interpersonal processes, ultimately affecting two performance outcomes—delays and distractions. Our contribution lies in providing direct, longitudinal field evidence linking leader coaching to team-level outcomes in a high-stakes context.

title: Does manager servant leadership lead to follower serving behaviors? It depends on follower self-interest.

entries.rq_with_context: Servant leadership is theorized to foster serving behaviors in followers, yet it remains unclear whether follower characteristics influence this process. Existing research has not clarified if all followers respond similarly to servant leadership or if certain individuals are more susceptible. This study investigates whether follower dispositional self-interest moderates the relationship between manager servant leadership and follower serving behaviors. Using social learning theory, the authors test if servant leadership strengthens serving behaviors more among self-interested followers by enhancing their serving self-efficacy. The research employs three studies—two experiments and one field study—to examine this moderated mediation model, claiming a contribution by identifying a boundary condition and underlying mechanism in the transference of servant leadership behaviors.

title: Is maternal labor market re-entry after childbirth facilitated by mothers’ and partners’ flextime?

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses how national-level work–life balance policies shape the relevance of organizational flextime arrangements for maternal labor market re-entry after childbirth. While prior research shows such policies influence employers' provision of flextime, less is known about how they affect workers' use of these arrangements. In Germany, significant family policy reforms occurred in 2007, including paid parental leave and expanded childcare. Using longitudinal data from 2003–2013, the research asks whether mothers' and partners' pre-birth flextime use affects return-to-work timing and work hour maintenance. Event history analysis is applied to German Socio-Economic Panel data. The study contributes by showing that generous state policies may diminish the effectiveness of organizational-level flextime arrangements.

title: The dialectics of spatial performances: The interplay of tensions in activity-based organizing

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly adopt flexible workspace designs like activity-based working, yet research reveals inconsistent outcomes—such as improved accessibility alongside difficulties in locating colleagues—suggesting inherent tensions in these environments. Existing studies often treat space as fixed or focus on macro-level changes, leaving unclear how tensions arise and are managed in everyday interactions. This study addresses that gap by asking how tensions emerge from the dialectical interplay among conceived (designed), perceived (rules and norms), and lived (practiced) spaces in an activity-based office. Using a process-based, constitutive lens, the research examines how employees manage these tensions through responses that involve ordering and disordering practices. The authors claim their contribution lies in rethinking space as performative and fluid, showing how embracing tensions—not resolving them—leads to adaptive, creative spatial practices.

title: Who says there’s a problem? Preferences on the sending and receiving of prohibitive voice

entries.rq_with_context: Employees often possess critical information about organizational threats, but may hesitate to speak up due to perceived risks, and leaders may not attend to such messages even when they are shared. While prior research has examined general voice behavior, less is known about the specific factors influencing prohibitive voice—communication aimed at preventing harm. This study investigates how employee hierarchical rank, leader-member exchange (LMX), and work prevention regulatory focus affect both the likelihood of employees sending threat-related messages and leaders’ interest in those messages. Drawing on power theories, the authors test hypotheses using a two-wave field study with 55 leaders and 214 employees. The key contribution is identifying asymmetries in voice transmission: certain employee traits predict sending prohibitive voice, while leader attention depends on different, and sometimes counterintuitive, combinations of rank and relationship quality.

title: Engaged yet excluded: The processual, dispersed, and political dynamics of boundary work

entries.rq_with_context: Efforts to create 'boundaryless' organizations often assume that inclusion automatically follows from openness, but real-world boundary processes are more complex. Existing research tends to treat boundaries as either stable or fluid but underestimates the ongoing, multi-site negotiations that shape who participates, on what issues, and with what influence. This paper investigates how attempts to include local citizens in a care home's decision-making triggered unexpected rounds of boundary re-drawing across different organizational platforms. The research asks: How do actors’ disparate boundary enactments interact across time and space, and how do these sequences reshape power relations? Using ethnographic data, the study analyzes the unfolding negotiations around actor inclusion, issue scope, and authority. It reveals that inclusion efforts paradoxically intensify boundary work and that non-hierarchical engagement still depends on hierarchical support—a finding that challenges assumptions about decentralized participation.

title: The influence of supervisor bottom-line mentality and employee bottom-line mentality on leader-member exchange and subsequent employee performance

entries.rq_with_context: Supervisors who prioritize financial outcomes over employee well-being may negatively influence workplace dynamics. While prior research links supervisor BLM to unethical or undermining behaviors, little is known about how employees perceive these supervisors and how such perceptions shape performance. The gap lies in understanding the relational mechanism—specifically, the quality of the leader-member exchange (LMX)—through which supervisor BLM might harm performance. Drawing on social exchange theory, the authors propose that high-BLM supervisors are seen as low-quality exchange partners, leading employees to reciprocate with lower performance. They test this mediated model using data from two multi-source, time-lagged field studies. The key contribution is identifying LMX as a mechanism linking supervisor BLM to reduced task performance, especially when employees themselves do not share a BLM.

title: Organizing the sensory: Ear-work, panauralism and sonic agency on a forensic psychiatric unit

entries.rq_with_context: This article investigates how sound organizes care and security relations in a medium-secure forensic psychiatric unit. While prior research in organization studies focuses on visual modes of control (e.g., panopticism), auditory dynamics remain underexplored despite their immersive, inescapable nature. The authors address this gap by exploring how the acoustic environment—shaped by both managed and unmanaged sounds—mediates staff-patient interactions. Drawing on a qualitative study involving interviews and photoproduction with staff and patients, they analyze how listening practices, or 'ear-work', enable orientation to shifting ward atmospheres. Key concepts include the contested management of sound (panauralism) and patients’ attempts to reclaim sonic agency. This research contributes to sensory organizational studies by demonstrating how sound, as a diffuse and relational medium, reconfigures power and belonging within institutional space.

title: Emotional expression at work: The effects of strategically expressing anger and positive emotions in the context of ongoing relationships

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace interactions often involve emotional expressions, including anger, which has traditionally been viewed as disruptive. However, recent theories suggest anger may serve functional roles when expressed appropriately. Existing research largely examines discrete emotional expressions in isolation, often in one-off interactions, neglecting the complex, ongoing patterns of emotional exchange in real workplace relationships. This paper addresses that gap by investigating how the strategic expression of anger—defined as expressing irritation or frustration in response to norm violations—interacts with the strategic expression of positive emotions to affect cooperation and work effectiveness. Drawing on the dual threshold model and emotions-as-social-information theory, the authors test a moderated mediation model across four field studies. They propose that strategic anger enhances perceived cooperation and effectiveness only when paired with strategic positive emotions, offering a more nuanced understanding of emotional expression at work.

title: The Other side of ‘us’: Alterity construction and identification work in the context of planned change

entries.rq_with_context: The paper explores how people use constructions of the Other to make sense of who they are during planned organizational change. While identity research typically focuses on self-construction or on othering as a hierarchical, demeaning process, this study highlights that alterity construction is varied, fluid, and reciprocal. The gap it addresses is the lack of attention to how othering unfolds situationally in interaction and how it co-constitutes identities. Based on an ethnographic study of a lean management change project in a Danish hospital, the authors analyze how nurses, surgeons, consultants, and administrators construct Others. They use a relational identity and ethnographic interactionist approach to show the multiplicity of othering practices. The key contribution is a conceptualization of four varieties of othering—horizontal and vertical differentiation, and boundary-crossing and boundary-collapsing appropriation—demonstrating that othering is integral to identification work.

title: Position taking and field level change: Capability Brown and the changing British landscape

entries.rq_with_context: This study investigates how a socially disadvantaged actor can drive institutional change within a field, a phenomenon underexplored in institutional theory. While existing research acknowledges agency in field change, it often portrays change agents as heroic figures acting against structural constraints, overlooking how such actors gradually shift their social positions to gain influence. The gap lies in understanding how movements in social position—shaped by capital accumulation and context—enable actors to reshape institutions over time. Our research question asks: How does an actor’s transition from a peripheral to a central social position enable them to influence field-level change? Drawing on Bourdieu’s Theory of Practice and the underexplored concept of ‘position taking’, we analyze the longitudinal case of Capability Brown, who rose from humble origins to transform British landscape design. Our contribution is to show that position taking is not merely reproductive but can be a conscious, agentic process central to institutional change.

title: Navigating the gender structure in information technology: How does this affect the experiences and behaviours of women?

entries.rq_with_context: Despite early hopes that information technology (IT) would be a gender-neutral field, it remains overwhelmingly male-dominated, with only one in six IT specialists in the UK being female. This stark imbalance creates a gendered social structure that shapes workplace norms, assumptions, and career trajectories. While prior research has focused on women’s underrepresentation or departure from IT, less is known about how women who remain navigate their gender identities within this male-dominated context. This study addresses two research questions: how male dominance in IT influences women’s gender identity, and how women use agency to challenge structural constraints and maintain their fit in the profession. Drawing on gender structure theory and interviews with 57 female IT professionals in the UK, the paper examines women’s experiences of being perceived as less technical, pressure to conform to masculine norms, and strategic responses to these challenges. It contributes by revealing how women assert femininity, reinterpret 'female strengths,' and engage with 'geek culture' to sustain their careers, offering insight into retention strategies for gender-diverse workplaces.

title: Shifting focus: Antecedents and outcomes of proactive feedback seeking from peers

entries.rq_with_context: In team-based work environments, peer feedback seeking is an understudied form of proactive behavior despite its potential value. While existing research focuses on feedback seeking from supervisors, this study addresses a gap by exploring why employees seek feedback from peers—particularly in task-interdependent settings—and what individual and collective benefits may result. The authors ask how task interdependence and psychological safety shape peer feedback inquiry, whether such seeking positively affects supervisors’ evaluations of employees (cross-source effect), and whether team-level peer feedback seeking boosts team creativity. Using a cost-value framework, the study tests these relationships in two samples: employee-supervisor dyads in consulting teams (Study 1) and self-managed MBA teams (Study 2). The authors claim contributions by identifying contextual antecedents of peer feedback seeking and demonstrating its dual value for individuals and teams.

title: ‘It’s not all it’s cracked up to be’: Narratives of promotions in elite professional careers

entries.rq_with_context: Promotions are widely recognized as important career events for both organizations and individuals, yet little research explores how they are subjectively experienced. While existing literature focuses on promotion systems, fairness, and career success, it often treats promotions as rational, positive, and unambiguous processes. This study addresses a gap by investigating the lived emotional experiences of both decision-makers and candidates during promotions in elite professional careers—specifically, partnership promotions in law firms. Using a narrative approach that combines spoken interviews and visual drawings, the authors explore how these groups make sense of the promotion process. The research reveals that while decision-makers describe promotions in detached, objective terms, candidates' experiences vary widely—from joy to frustration to anxiety. The study contributes by proposing an emotion-based understanding of promotions, challenging the assumption that promotions are inherently positive, and demonstrating the value of multimodal methods in capturing nuanced, contradictory experiences.

title: Making up leaders: Reconfiguring the executive student through profiling, texts and conversations in a leadership development programme

entries.rq_with_context: Leadership development programmes (LDPs) commonly use tools like personality profiling and coaching to shape leader identities, often framed as either regulatory or agentic processes. However, the micro-level, situated processes through which these identities are formed remain undertheorized. Drawing on a focused ethnography of a university-based LDP, this study investigates how leader identities are reconfigured through everyday interactions involving texts and conversations. Using a communicative constitution of organizations (CCO) lens, it analyzes how participants and instructors ventriloquize personality profiles and other figures in dialogue, thereby authorizing new versions of the self. The research contributes by showing how identity reconfiguration emerges through epistemic negotiations, revealing the performative role of texts and the distributed nature of authority in shaping who counts as a leader.

title: How social networks facilitate collective responses to organizational paradoxes

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations frequently face paradoxical demands, such as balancing scientific rigor and commercial viability, which create tensions experienced differently by individuals based on their roles and identities. While existing research recognizes that paradox responses are socially co-constructed, less is known about how these individual responses aggregate into collective organizational outcomes. This gap is critical because organizational responses depend on diverse perspectives and interactions. The study addresses this by investigating how the composition of individuals’ social networks—specifically heterogeneity in advice and friendship ties—affects their alignment with either an organization-wide consensus or polarized subgroup responses. Using a two-stage mixed-method design in a Taiwanese research institute that merged basic and applied science divisions, the authors employ cultural consensus theory to map individual views and test network effects. The key contribution is revealing that different types of social networks (instrumental vs. expressive) play distinct roles in shaping collective responses to paradoxes.

title: Becoming upbeat: Learning the affecto-rhythmic order of organizational practices

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational practices are known to be both rhythmic and affective, yet how rhythms and affects interrelate in practice remains poorly understood. Existing research often treats them separately, neglecting their reciprocal dynamics and the consequences for collective action. This study addresses this gap by asking: How are rhythms and affects connected in organizational practice, and how do members learn and embody them? Using a sociomaterial practice perspective, the authors conduct an ethnographic study of a Nordic startup accelerator. They introduce the concept of 'affecto-rhythmic order' to capture the entanglement of rhythm and affect. The study's primary contribution is theorizing this entanglement and showing how it regulates participation and shapes capacity to act in fast-paced organizational contexts.

title: Team familiarity in cardiac surgery operations: The effects of hierarchy and failure on team productivity

entries.rq_with_context: Surgical teams are high-stakes, short-term, and hierarchical, making team productivity crucial for patient outcomes. While prior research shows that team familiarity improves performance, it largely treats familiarity as a uniform construct based on average past interactions. This paper identifies a gap by questioning whether the structure of those interactions—specifically, whether they occur horizontally (among same-status members) or hierarchically (across status levels)—leads to different productivity outcomes. It further investigates whether shared experiences of failure have a different (potentially stronger) effect than shared successes. Using a dataset of 6,206 cardiac surgeries and transactive memory system (TMS) theory, the authors analyze how familiarity at different levels and from different types of past experiences affects surgery duration. The study contributes by showing that not all familiarity is equally beneficial—horizontal familiarity and failure-gained familiarity have stronger positive effects on productivity.

title: Egoistic norms, organizational identification, and the perceived ethicality of unethical pro-organizational behavior: A moral maturation perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Unethical pro-organizational behavior (UPB) involves actions that benefit the organization but violate ethical standards. While prior research has explored individual traits and social influences on UPB, it remains unclear whether employees genuinely perceive these behaviors as ethical rather than merely rationalizing them. The study addresses this gap by examining how egoistic organizational norms—those emphasizing self-interest—affect employees’ ethical judgments of UPB. Drawing on moral maturation theory, the authors propose that such norms limit moral knowledge, leading to faulty ethical appraisals. They test this through three field studies using multi-source and time-lagged data. The key contribution is identifying ethical judgments as a central cognitive mechanism linking organizational context to UPB, challenging the assumption that UPB is driven only by moral disengagement.

title: The use of mobile technologies for work-to-family boundary permeability: The case of Finnish and Canadian male lawyers

entries.rq_with_context: Despite family-friendly policies in Finland and Quebec, male lawyers in both countries face tensions between shifting cultural ideals of involved fatherhood and entrenched professional norms that prioritize work over family. Existing research has not fully explored how mobile technologies (MTs) intersect with these dynamics, especially among high-status professionals. This study fills that gap by investigating how male lawyers use MTs to navigate work–family boundaries across different national and organizational contexts. Drawing on shifting ideals of fatherhood and work–family boundary theory, the authors analyze 34 interviews to understand men’s strategies for managing spatial, temporal, and psychological permeability. The study contributes by identifying distinct boundary management styles and showing how senior lawyers’ behaviors model expectations that reinforce gender inequalities in promotion and career advancement.

title: ‘Same, but different’: A mixed-methods realist evaluation of a cluster-randomized controlled participatory organizational intervention

entries.rq_with_context: Participatory organizational interventions (POIs) are recommended for improving the psychosocial work environment, but their outcomes vary due to context-specific implementation. Existing research has not fully explained how different mechanisms are triggered in different contexts. This study addresses this gap by investigating how collective efficacy and transformational leadership function as mediational mechanisms in a POI across three industrial production plants. Using a mixed-methods realist evaluation approach, the study tests whether these mechanisms are activated differently across contexts and identifies which contextual factors influence their activation. The contribution lies in demonstrating that POI outcomes are not uniform but depend on how mechanisms interact with specific organizational settings.

title: Coming home: Why veterans with disabilities withhold workplace accommodation requests

entries.rq_with_context: Many veterans with disabilities struggle to reintegrate into the civilian workforce and often do not request needed workplace accommodations, despite legal rights to do so. Existing research identifies individual and organizational factors influencing accommodation requests among people with disabilities broadly, but little is known about how veterans' unique military identities interact with disability-related factors. This study addresses this gap by exploring how veteran identity strain—the conflict between military and civilian identities—shapes psychological safety and accommodation decisions. Drawing on social identity and disability help-seeking theories, the authors test a moderated mediation model using survey data from employed veterans with disabilities. The study contributes by identifying psychological safety as a key mechanism and highlighting the role of identity and inclusion in accommodation decisions.

title: Holding on to let go: Identity work in discontinuous and involuntary career transitions

entries.rq_with_context: This study investigates identity work among severely disabled soldiers undergoing involuntary career transitions after traumatic injuries. Existing research shows that individuals facing such disruptions often attempt to build bridges between past and future identities or adopt new identity standards. However, less is known about identity work when returning to the original profession is impossible and no clear aspirational identity exists. The study focuses on soldiers in a military-affiliated rehabilitation facility, where they remain embedded in a familiar, military-aligned context alongside peers with similar experiences. The research question is: how do these individuals perform identity work during career transition? Using a discursive approach to identity, the study analyzes narrative accounts from 30 soldiers in vocational training. It contributes by showing how narrative continuity—rather than identity replacement—is central to identity work in this context, even when forward movement is the goal.

title: Trust in teams: A taxonomy of perceived trustworthiness factors and risk-taking behaviors in face-to-face and virtual teams

entries.rq_with_context: Trust is crucial for team effectiveness, especially in virtual teams where uncertainties are greater, yet little is known about the specific mechanisms of trust emergence in team contexts. While existing research offers models of dyadic trust, such as Mayer et al.'s (1995) model focusing on ability, benevolence, and integrity, there is no integrative taxonomy of trust antecedents and consequences tailored to teams, particularly when team virtuality is considered. Moreover, most studies rely on student samples, limiting generalizability. This study addresses these gaps by exploring experienced professionals’ perceptions using qualitative interviews. The research questions are: (1) Which perceived trustworthiness factors predict team trust? (2) Which risk-taking behaviors result from team trust? (3) Do these factors and behaviors differ in virtual versus face-to-face teams? The study uses the critical incident technique and grounded theory to develop a taxonomy. It contributes a comprehensive, empirically derived model of team trust with distinct categories of antecedents and consequences applicable across team types.

title: Sandwiched: Exploring role and identity of middle managers in the genuine middle

entries.rq_with_context: Middle managers play a critical role in organizations but are often studied either as leaders or subordinates, with less attention to their dual, relational position. This study focuses on academic heads in UK business schools—middle managers in a professional context—where tensions are heightened due to growing managerialism and bureaucracy in higher education. Despite the literature on middle management, few studies seriously examine the 'genuinely middle' experience. The authors explore what it means to be in this sandwiched position by analyzing interviews with heads and their subordinates. They identify three subject positions—'umbrella–protector', 'performance driver', and 'impotent'—with a focus on how managers enact identity and role, especially through protective behaviors. The study uses a hermeneutical approach to interpret narratives and behaviors, offering a nuanced understanding of middle-levelness.

title: Organizational form and pro-social fantasy in social enterprise creation

entries.rq_with_context: Social entrepreneurship is marked by persistent tensions between commercial and social goals, raising questions about why founders persevere despite challenges. Existing research highlights these tensions but does not fully explain the psychological and affective dynamics that sustain entrepreneurs' commitment. This study asks how and why social entrepreneurs continue their efforts in the face of uncertainty, anxiety, and the risk of failure. Drawing on Lacanian psychoanalysis, we examine how fantasy operates in the context of organizational form choice, specifically the Community Interest Company (CIC) in the UK. We find that the CIC functions as a fantasmatic object that supports founders’ desires for pro-social change. Our contribution is twofold: we show how fantasy helps neutralize both present and future anxieties, and we highlight the role of organizational form as a concrete anchor for such fantasies, shaping the very process of social enterprise creation.

title: Examining the inverted U-shaped relationship between workload and innovative work behavior: The role of work engagement and mindfulness

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates whether workload fosters or hinders employee innovation, a critical issue given organizations' need for innovation amid increasing work demands. While some research suggests workload can be motivating, meta-analyses show inconsistent effects, possibly because workload contains both challenging and hindering aspects. The paper identifies a gap in understanding the curvilinear relationship between workload and innovation, particularly the psychological mechanisms involved. Using the job demands–resources (JD-R) model and activation theory, it examines whether work engagement mediates an inverted U-shaped relationship between workload and innovative behavior, and whether mindfulness moderates this indirect effect. The contribution lies in clarifying how and when workload can be beneficial for innovation.

title: Should I stay or should I go? Multi-focus identification and employee retention in post-acquisition integration

entries.rq_with_context: Retaining employees is critical during post-acquisition integration, yet many employees reconsider their commitment when their firm is acquired. While prior research emphasizes organizational identification as a driver of retention, the role of occupational identification remains unclear, and findings on both are inconsistent. This study addresses the gap by exploring how organizational and occupational identification—alongside the professionalization of the occupation and employees’ disappointment with integration—affect exit intentions. Using a longitudinal configurational study in two acquired hospitals, it investigates combinations of conditions that lead to staying or leaving. The authors argue that identification effects depend on these contingencies and propose attention as a mediating mechanism, contributing to theories of multi-focus identification and post-acquisition integration.

title: From job crafting to home crafting: A daily diary study among six European countries

entries.rq_with_context: Many employees proactively shape their jobs through job crafting to find more meaning. But it is unclear whether such proactive behaviors extend beyond work into non-work domains like home life. Existing research has not examined whether daily job crafting is linked to home crafting, or under what conditions such spillover occurs. This study addresses that gap by exploring daily links between job and home crafting, drawing on spillover and compensation theories. Using a daily diary design with employees from six European countries, the study tests whether job crafting predicts home crafting and whether home workload and autonomy moderate these relationships. The findings suggest that expansion-oriented job crafting does spill over to home crafting under certain conditions, contributing to understanding how proactive behaviors transcend life domains.

title: ‘There is a crack in everything’: An ethnographic study of pragmatic resistance in a manufacturing organization

entries.rq_with_context: Resistance is a pervasive feature of organizational life, yet existing research often frames it as episodic opposition to corporate rationality. This study addresses a gap by exploring how resistance may instead emerge from organizational disorder and irrationality—conditions long documented but underexamined in resistance literature. Drawing on ethnographic research in a manufacturing firm undergoing a poorly implemented change initiative (STS), the authors investigate how such disordered conditions foster a distinct form of resistance. They introduce the concept of 'pragmatic resistance'—a pervasive, under-the-radar form of resistance that simultaneously undermines and enables organizational processes. The study uses an ethnographic framework to analyze everyday employee and managerial behaviors, arguing that pragmatic resistance reflects an attempt to manage irrational demands while sustaining core work activities. The key contribution is reframing resistance not as anti-work, but as a complex, ambivalent response to the cracks in corporate rationality.

title: Respectful leadership and followers’ knowledge sharing: A social mindfulness lens

entries.rq_with_context: Knowledge sharing is critical for organizational success but remains challenging because employees may be reluctant to share their valuable knowledge. While prior research has linked broad leadership styles to knowledge sharing, the individual-level motivational mechanisms—particularly those emphasizing other-oriented behavior—are not well understood. This paper addresses this gap by focusing on respectful leadership as a specific, unidimensional leadership style and proposing that it enhances followers' knowledge sharing through social mindfulness, defined as the cognitive (perspective taking) and affective (empathic concern) willingness to support others. Using a two-study design—one a three-wave field study with 275 employees and another a multi-source dyadic study with 83 leader-follower pairs—the authors test a mediation model. The research contributes by identifying social mindfulness as a theoretically aligned mechanism linking respectful leadership to knowledge sharing and by examining potential synergies between its components.

title: Identity work by a non-white immigrant business scholar: Autoethnographic vignettes of covering and accenting

entries.rq_with_context: Non-white immigrants in the Global North often face misidentification and ethno-racial stigmatization in organizational settings, leading to identity tensions. While existing research acknowledges identity work in organizational contexts, there is limited understanding of how multiple-identified immigrants manage these tensions through understudied self-presentational strategies like covering and accenting. This study addresses that gap by exploring how a non-white immigrant business scholar engages in identity work in response to being misidentified.
