However, realizing this potential depends on how the mission is connected to employees' daily work, with performance measurement practices playing a critical but poorly understood role. While prior research has explored sensegiving and leader-led rituals in shaping meaningfulness, less is known about how formal, standardized measurement practices influence employees’ perceptions of work worthiness. This study investigates how performance measurement practices—such as KPIs, social return on investment, and case studies—shape employees' sense of work as worthy through day-to-day encounters. Drawing on a qualitative, inductive study of two U.K. social enterprises, the authors develop a model that identifies practical, existential, and relational pathways through which measurement can expand or contract work worthiness. The study contributes by revealing how measurement is not merely a technical or controlling tool but can dynamically influence meaningfulness in organizational life.

title: There Is a Time to Be Creative: The Alignment between Chronotype and Time of Day

entries.rq_with_context: Creativity is essential for innovation and effectiveness in organizations, yet little research has examined how the human body's biological rhythms influence creative performance during the workday. While prior work has explored creativity in relation to external factors like leadership and work environment, the internal, embodied aspects—such as circadian rhythms—remain understudied. A key gap exists in understanding how within-person fluctuations in creativity throughout the day may be driven by chronobiological factors. This study addresses that gap by testing whether chronotype moderates the effect of time of day on creativity. Based on the two-process model of sleep regulation and an embodied cognition perspective, we propose a synchrony effect: people are more creative when external time matches their internal biological clock. The study uses three complementary methods to examine this effect and investigates positive mood and creative self-efficacy as affective and cognitive mechanisms. Our contribution lies in demonstrating that bodily states grounded in circadian rhythms systematically influence creative functioning at work.

title: Valuing Spanners: Why Category Nesting and Expertise Matter

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations that span categories face valuation challenges because they must balance differentiation with audience expectations. While prior research treats category spanning uniformly, this paper argues that the level of category nesting—whether firms span basic or subordinate categories—matters for valuation. Existing studies often assume audience homogeneity in processing categorical information, but this study contends that expertise shapes how investors assess the congruence of mixed cues. The research investigates whether subcategory spanning is valued less than basic category spanning and whether more expert investors perceive such combinations as more congruent. Using a mixed-methods approach in venture capital, the study tests these relationships through observational data and experiments, contributing to understanding when and why spanners are valued differently based on categorization level and evaluator expertise.

title: Learning Down to Train Up: Mentors Are More Effective When They Value Insights from Below

entries.rq_with_context: Mentorship is widely recognized as crucial for individual success, yet potential mentors often see it as a costly burden that hinders their productivity. While prior research has focused on barriers faced by mentees, this paper identifies a critical but overlooked barrier: mentors’ reluctance to engage because they do not perceive personal learning benefits. Existing research assumes knowledge flows top-down, leading mentors to overlook insights from less powerful individuals. This study addresses the gap by introducing 'learning direction'—the belief about who in a hierarchy is a valuable source of knowledge. The research asks whether mentors who value learning from below (downward learning) are more engaged and effective. Using multiple studies—including surveys, a field study, and an experiment—the authors test this using mentor engagement (time and effort invested) and mentee outcomes (skills and hireability) as key measures. The primary contribution is demonstrating that beliefs about the direction of learning significantly influence mentor motivation and effectiveness, shifting the focus from mentorship as obligation to mutual development.

title: Bridge Supervision: Correlates of a Boss on the Far Side of a Structural Hole

entries.rq_with_context: Traditional network research focuses on a manager’s ego network but overlooks how the structural relationship between a manager and their boss—specifically, whether their networks overlap—shapes behavior and performance. The authors identify a gap in understanding 'bridge supervision,' where manager and boss lack shared contacts, creating structural separation. They ask whether this form of supervision affects how managers play their role and whether it impacts performance. Drawing on Bott’s classic work on conjugal role segregation, they propose that bridge supervision leads to behavioral isolation—such as excluding the boss from discussions and suppressing emotional expression—but argue that core performance indicators remain tied to the manager’s own network brokerage. The study uses survey and personnel data from 455 supply chain managers to test these predictions, measuring network structure, communication patterns, and performance outcomes like salary and idea value.

title: How Leaders with Divergent Visions Generate Novel Strategy: Navigating the Paradox of Preservation and Modernization in Swiss Watchmaking

entries.rq_with_context: The phenomenon under study is how leaders with divergent strategic visions respond to technological discontinuities, such as the quartz crisis in Swiss watchmaking. While existing research emphasizes either preserving legacy practices or embracing modernization as separate strategic paths—often framed as a defender-prospector dichotomy—this paper identifies a gap in understanding how opposing visions can be integrated rather than resolved. The research question is: How do leaders with divergent visions for their organization come together to create a novel strategy? The authors employ paradox theory as a lens to analyze the sustained tensions between preservation and modernization, using a qualitative historical case study of Nicolas G. Hayek and Jean-Claude Biver at SMH. Their key contribution is a process model outlining individual, relational, and structural mechanisms that allow leader dyads to productively sustain paradox rather than eliminate it, thus enabling strategic reorientation.

title: Lay Theories of Instrumental Relations: Explaining Individual Differences in Dispositional Similarity-Attraction

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the growing diversity in workplaces, research has largely treated similarity-attraction as a universal tendency, paying limited attention to individual differences in how people respond to deep-level dissimilarity in values, attitudes, and personality. This gap is critical because building cohesive yet diverse teams requires understanding why some individuals are more willing than others to engage with dissimilar others. The paper addresses this by investigating how lay theories of instrumental relations—personal beliefs about whether workplace compatibility is fixed or malleable—influence dispositional similarity-attraction. Using both survey and experimental methods, the authors test whether fixed theorists show stronger avoidance of dissimilar partners and lower satisfaction with them compared to growth theorists. Their approach combines theory from mindset research with network and similarity-attraction literature, offering a novel psychological mechanism—expected compatibility—to explain variation in tie formation and satisfaction.

title: The Impact of Communist Ideology on the Patenting Activity of Chinese Firms

entries.rq_with_context: Although the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has shifted from Maoist ideology to a more pragmatic Dengist approach over the past four decades, Maoist beliefs appear to persist among Party members. The puzzle is how these ideological imprints endure, especially among younger members who did not experience the Maoist era firsthand. While existing research suggests ideological imprinting during formative periods, it does not explain how such beliefs are transmitted across generations when direct environmental exposure is absent. This study addresses the gap by investigating whether 'secondhand imprinting'—ideological transmission from older to younger Party members—explains continued resistance to innovation. Using data from 1,298 non-state-owned Chinese firms (2000–2017), the authors examine how board chairs’ Party membership relates to patenting activity and how age, education, and regional presence of older Party members moderate these effects. The study contributes by identifying a mechanism—cross-generational social interaction—that sustains ideological persistence even as official doctrine evolves.

title: Ruminating on What You Think of Me: A Grounded Model of Construed Image Work

entries.rq_with_context: The paper addresses a gap in research on professional self-concept by focusing on construed image—individuals’ internal sense of how others define them—rather than identity alone. While identity research has explored how people maintain or reconstruct who they believe they are, little attention has been paid to how people make sense of how they are seen by others after a major career disruption. This is significant because professional roles, especially highly visible ones like professional athletics, shape not only identity but also how individuals expect to be perceived. The authors investigate what happens to construed image when a career ends abruptly, how individuals adapt, and what explains differences in adaptation outcomes. Using a grounded theory approach and data from former professional athletes, they develop a process model of "construed image work." Their contribution is introducing and theorizing construed image as a foundational, yet overlooked, dimension of the professional self-concept.

title: What Changes after Women Enter Top Management Teams? A Gender-Based Model of Strategic Renewal

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses the unresolved question of how female executives entering top management teams (TMTs) influence firm strategy, moving beyond static analyses of gender representation to examine dynamic, within-firm mechanisms. While prior research shows associations between female TMT representation and firm outcomes, it lacks explanatory models showing how and when these changes unfold. A key theoretical tension exists between arguments that women increase innovation (change orientation) and those suggesting they reduce risk-taking—seemingly contradictory effects. This paper resolves this by proposing a time-dependent model linking female TMT appointments to strategic renewal through cognitive shifts. Using dynamic OLS on panel data from 163 multinationals, the authors test whether female, but not male, TMT appointments shift TMT cognitions toward greater change orientation and lower risk-taking, which then redirect strategic renewal from acquisition (M&A) to internal development (R&D). The study's primary contribution is providing causal, temporal evidence of the mechanisms connecting gender diversity in top teams to strategic change.

title: Do I Dare? The Psychodynamics of Anticipated Image Risk, Leader-Identity Endorsement, and Leader Emergence

entries.rq_with_context: Although organizations value leadership at all levels, many individuals are reluctant to step up. The paper investigates psychological barriers to leader-identity endorsement, focusing on anticipated image risk—individuals’ fears that leading will damage how others see them. While prior research has highlighted relational and situational factors in leadership emergence, less attention has been paid to internal, psychodynamic obstacles such as ego defense. The authors argue that when people anticipate image risks, they may avoid endorsing a leader identity to protect their self-concept. They also examine whether beliefs about leadership ability (as fixed or malleable) moderate this process. Using multiple studies across diverse samples, the research tests how anticipated image risk reduces leader-identity endorsement and leadership emergence, particularly among those who believe leadership ability is fixed. The study contributes by identifying specific image concerns and showing how identity dynamics can suppress leadership even when structural opportunities exist.

title: Joining Forces: How Can Founding Members’ Prior Experience Variety and Shared Experience Increase Startup Survival?

entries.rq_with_context: Research has long debated whether startup success stems from founders' diverse experiences or their shared industry background, offering conflicting guidance for assembling founding teams. While prior work has treated these two perspectives separately—focusing either on the benefits of experience variety or the advantages of spinout teams with common origins—little is known about how these forms of experience might work together. This paper addresses this gap by asking whether and how within-founder experience variety and across-team shared experience jointly affect startup survival. Drawing on organizational knowledge and social cognition theory, the study proposes that these two types of experience are complementary: shared experience enables the integration of varied knowledge brought by individual founders. Using a sample of technological manufacturing startups from U.S. Census data, the study tests this interaction effect, with the key contribution being the reconciliation of two previously disconnected literatures by demonstrating their joint effect on survival.

title: Here Comes the Sun: The Impact of Incidental Contextual Factors on Entrepreneurial Resource Acquisition

entries.rq_with_context: Seed-stage startups face intense uncertainty and limited information, making investment decisions highly challenging. While prior research has focused on startup characteristics or investor traits to explain funding patterns, this paper investigates factors outside the investor–startup pair—specifically, incidental contextual factors like weather. The authors argue that in the presence of uncertainty, ambient conditions such as sunshine may influence investors’ mood and thereby affect funding outcomes. Drawing on affect-as-information theory, they propose that increased sunshine on Demo Day positively impacts investment likelihood. Using archival data from European accelerators and an experimental study, the paper tests this hypothesis and explores boundary conditions related to startup maturity and founder human capital. The study contributes by highlighting the role of non-task-relevant environmental cues in entrepreneurial resource acquisition.

title: A Trojan Horse Inside the Gates? Knowledge Spillovers During Patent Litigation

entries.rq_with_context: Patent litigation is typically viewed as a mechanism to protect firms’ proprietary knowledge and prevent spillovers. However, the litigation process may unintentionally expose valuable, non-patented knowhow from the patent-holding firm to the accused firm. Despite strong appropriability regimes, it remains unclear whether this exposure translates into tangible learning and improved innovation outcomes for accused firms. This study addresses that gap by asking whether knowledge spillovers during litigation enhance accused firms’ subsequent innovation. Using data from over 3,000 patent litigation cases in the U.S. pharmaceutical industry (1998–2015), we analyze whether accused firms introduce more novel drugs post-litigation. We find that litigation not only fails to fully contain knowledge but can actually boost innovation in accused firms, especially when the litigated patents are built on recent, heterogeneous, or broad-knowledge bases. This demonstrates that litigation can act as a double-edged sword, simultaneously protecting and disseminating knowledge.

title: The Role of Discernment and Modulation in Enacting Occupational Values: How Career Advising Professionals Navigate Tensions with Clients

entries.rq_with_context: Expert professionals rely on enacting occupational values to maintain solidarity and demonstrate their distinctive worth to audiences. However, when clients hold incongruent values and possess growing power through market-based logics and review systems, value enactment can threaten professionals’ jurisdictional control—their legitimacy and autonomy over tasks. Existing research suggests experts either abandon value enactment, rely on structural advantages, or use rhetorical tactics, but often treats clientele as monolithic. This study addresses the gap by asking how experts can navigate value tensions without jeopardizing their jurisdictional control, particularly by recognizing intraclientele heterogeneity. Drawing on ethnographic and interview data from career advisers in business schools, the authors examine how advisers discern student values and modulate their practices accordingly. The study contributes by revealing how practitioners use discernment and modulation to navigate relational tensions, enabling them to mask, moderate, or magnify value enactment depending on client alignment.

title: The Role of Attribution in Learning from Performance Feedback: Behavioral Perspective on the Choice between Alliances and Acquisitions

entries.rq_with_context: Firms use performance feedback to guide strategic decisions, but existing research largely overlooks how managers attribute causes to performance outcomes. This omission is critical because attribution shapes learning—managers may credit success to internal capabilities and blame failure on external factors. The paper addresses this gap by investigating how attribution following alliance performance affects a firm’s subsequent choice between alliances and acquisitions. While prior work assumes performance directly drives behavior, this study argues that attribution processes significantly alter that link. Using Fortune 500 data from 1994–2017, the authors test how three factors—diffusion of responsibility, partner capability, and performance ambiguity—influence attribution and thereby moderate the effect of performance feedback. The study contributes by integrating attribution theory into performance feedback research and offering a behavioral explanation for governance mode choices.

title: Paradoxical Leadership and Innovation in Work Teams: The Multilevel Mediating Role of Ambidexterity and Leader Vision as a Boundary Condition

entries.rq_with_context: Innovation in work teams involves inherent paradoxes such as balancing exploration and exploitation, flexibility and control, or individuality and collectivity. While leadership is recognized as crucial for innovation, how leaders manage these paradoxical tensions remains understudied. Existing research has not fully explained the mechanisms through which leadership affects both individual and team innovation simultaneously, nor the conditions under which such effects are stronger. This paper proposes that paradoxical leadership—leaders’ use of seemingly contradictory yet interrelated behaviors—promotes innovation by enhancing ambidexterity at both individual and team levels. It further suggests that leader vision clarifies the rationale behind paradoxical behaviors, strengthening their impact. Using multilevel mediation models tested across three studies, the authors analyze survey and multisource data to identify these pathways. The key contribution is a multilevel model that explains how and when paradoxical leadership drives innovation through ambidexterity.

title: Appraising and Reacting to Perceived Pay For Performance: Leader Competence and Warmth as Critical Contingencies

entries.rq_with_context: While pay for performance (PFP) is widely used to boost employee performance, its effects are inconsistent—sometimes motivating, sometimes causing stress or withdrawal. Existing research often focuses on PFP systems rather than individual perceptions, overlooking why reactions vary. This study addresses that gap by examining how employees' perception of PFP based on individual performance (PFP-I) is appraised either as a challenge or a threat, depending on leader characteristics. Drawing on transactional theory of stress and role engagement theory, the authors propose that leader competence strengthens challenge appraisals and subsequent engagement, while leader warmth reduces threat appraisals and withdrawal. Using two three-wave survey studies, they test these mechanisms. The contribution lies in reframing PFP effectiveness through employee perception and leader influence, offering a more nuanced understanding of when and why PFP works.

title: Losing Control: The Uncertain Management of Concealable Stigmas When Work and Social Media Collide

entries.rq_with_context: Employees with concealable stigmas traditionally manage disclosure through controlled, face-to-face interactions, assuming social contexts can be separated. However, social network sites (SNSs) like Facebook and Instagram create a context collapse—blurring boundaries between work and personal life by merging audiences. This raises uncertainty about who can access stigma-related information and when. The gap lies in understanding how this collapse disrupts established assumptions of control in stigma management. The research asks how context collapse impacts the everyday dynamics of concealable stigma management among gay male employees. Using qualitative data from observations and interviews at a Latin American organization, the study develops a grounded model of employee responses. The key contribution is showing that SNSs destabilize the assumption of controlled disclosure and challenge the notion of online platforms as safe spaces for stigmatized individuals.

title: Leveraging Knowledge Diversity in Hierarchically Differentiated Teams: The Critical Role of Hierarchy Stability

entries.rq_with_context: Knowledge diversity in teams is a double-edged sword: it can enhance performance by broadening perspectives, yet often fails to do so because teams struggle to share unique knowledge. Prior research suggests that status hierarchies may either hinder this process by privileging high-status members or help by incentivizing low-status members to contribute unique insights. However, these opposing predictions remain unresolved. This paper addresses that gap by proposing that hierarchy stability—the extent to which status positions are fixed over time—determines whether status hierarchies constrict or amplify information sharing in diverse teams. Using data from 156 teams across 110 organizations, the authors test this moderated moderation model. Their key contribution is identifying hierarchy stability as a critical contingency that clarifies when status differences help or harm knowledge sharing in diverse teams.

title: Mixed Messages: Crisis Communication–Dismissal (In)Coherence and Shareholder Trust Following Misconduct

entries.rq_with_context: Following financial misconduct, firms use crisis communication and executive dismissal to rebuild shareholder trust, but existing research largely examines these tactics in isolation. This approach fails to explain inconsistent shareholder reactions, suggesting that the interplay between words and actions may matter more than any single tactic. This study investigates how the coherence between a firm’s communication about misconduct and its subsequent dismissal of an executive (CEO or CFO) shapes shareholder trust. Using a mixed-methods design—fsQCA of 51 real-world cases and a policy-capturing experiment with investors—we examine whether consistent messaging and action lead to more favorable reactions. The key contribution is identifying crisis management coherence as a central mechanism in trust repair, challenging the prevailing focus on isolated tactics.

title: The Relational Dynamics of Issue-Selling: Enacting Different Genres for Dealing with Discontent

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational change often begins with actors without formal power who voice concerns about current practices through issue-selling. While prior research emphasizes rational persuasion and emotional regulation to avoid fear-driven paralysis, this study explores the paradox that discontent—often seen as inhibiting—can also energize change efforts. The gap lies in understanding how issue-sellers and recipients co-create relational dynamics that either enable or suppress the expression of discontent. Based on a longitudinal field study of middle managers across six manufacturing firms, the paper asks: How do issue-sellers and -recipients jointly shape how discontent is enacted or circumvented over time? The authors use a relational process lens to analyze in vivo interactions, identifying recurring patterns in how issues are framed, mobilized, and pursued. Their key contribution is revealing that discontent can motivate productive change when embedded in collective interaction patterns characterized by mutual perspective-taking and low power distance.

title: When Do Novel Business Models Lead to High Performance? A Configurational Approach to Value Drivers, Competitive Strategy, and Firm Environment

entries.rq_with_context: While novelty in business models is widely seen as a key driver of firm performance, this paper challenges the assumption that it is universally beneficial. Prior research has often treated novelty as sufficient for high performance, especially in technology-driven contexts like e-businesses during the dotcom era. However, it remains unclear whether these findings generalize to more mature technological environments or account for the interdependence between novelty and other value drivers such as efficiency, lock-in, and complementarity. This study addresses this gap by asking: under what configurations of value drivers, competitive strategy, and firm environment does novel business model design lead to high performance? Using a configurational approach (fsQCA) on two samples of Internet-enabled firms—one from the late 1990s and one from 2014—it analyzes how combinations of factors produce high performance. The authors claim their contribution lies in showing that novelty’s effectiveness depends on its alignment with other elements, offering a more nuanced understanding of business model innovation.

title: Addressing Performance Tensions in Multiteam Systems: Balancing Informal Mechanisms of Coordination within and between Teams

entries.rq_with_context: Multiteam systems (MTSs) face coordination challenges due to their hierarchical goals and structural differentiation, requiring integration both within and across teams. While informal coordination mechanisms like interpersonal interactions are known to aid knowledge-based work, their effects in MTSs remain ambiguous, with prior studies yielding conflicting results. This study addresses the gap by examining how the balance between intrateam and interteam interactions influences MTS outcomes. Drawing on MTS and team boundary spanning theories, it proposes that imbalance in these interactions creates tension, affecting conflict and performance differently at team and system levels. The research uses a multimethod design with wearable sensors to measure interactions in 44 MTSs, testing how interaction balance shapes effectiveness. Its contribution lies in clarifying when and how informal mechanisms help or hinder MTS functioning, resolving contradictions in prior research.

title: Structuring the Start-Up: How Coordination Emerges in Start-Ups through Learning Sequencing

entries.rq_with_context: Start-ups must establish coordination mechanisms—such as roles, routines, rules, and plans—to integrate team efforts and scale effectively. However, unlike established firms, early-stage start-ups often lack such structures and face unique challenges due to their small size, peer-based leadership, and dynamic environments. While prior research has highlighted the importance of coordination, it has largely offered static explanations or focused on mature organizations with existing scaffolds. We know less about how coordination emerges from scratch in nascent start-ups. To address this gap, the authors conducted a longitudinal qualitative multiple-case study of five start-ups. They ask: (a) How do start-ups develop coordination over time? and (b) How does successful coordination affect organizational performance? The study uses an emergent-coordination lens combined with organizational learning theory to trace the processual development of coordination. The key contribution is identifying a learning sequence—anticipatory, vicarious, experimental, and trial-and-error learning—that explains how start-ups build coordination deliberately and adaptively.

title: Leader Perfectionism—Friend or Foe of Employee Creativity? Locus of Control as a Key Contingency

entries.rq_with_context: Leader perfectionism—setting exceptionally high standards and demanding flawless outcomes—is increasingly common in workplaces and may influence employee creativity. However, it remains unclear whether this trait enhances or undermines creativity, as it could either motivate employees to innovate or overwhelm them with pressure. Existing research has not sufficiently explained this inconsistency, particularly how individual differences might shape these effects. This study addresses this gap by examining how employees' locus of control (belief in personal control over outcomes) moderates the relationship between leader perfectionism and creativity. Using a self-regulation perspective, the authors propose that leader perfectionism influences two regulatory states—engagement and emotional exhaustion—differently depending on whether employees are internals or externals. The research uses an experimental and a field study to test these mechanisms. The study contributes by clarifying the contingent effects of leader perfectionism on creativity, highlighting the importance of employee characteristics in leadership processes.

title: “Who Are You Going to Call?” Network Activation in Creative Idea Generation and Elaboration

entries.rq_with_context: Creativity involves multiple phases, particularly idea generation and elaboration, each with distinct social needs. While theory suggests weak ties benefit idea generation by fostering cognitive flexibility and strong ties aid elaboration through supportive feedback, little empirical evidence confirms these effects or examines whether individuals actually activate the right ties at the right time. This paper addresses this gap by testing the causal impact of weak and strong ties on creativity across phases, and explores barriers to optimal activation. Using experimental studies, the authors investigate how network size and perceived risk affect individuals’ tendency to activate weak ties and switch ties between phases. They also examine downstream consequences—false positives (pursuing uncreative ideas) and false negatives (abandoning creative ones)—resulting from suboptimal activation. The research contributes by moving beyond static network structures to analyze dynamic cognitive activation processes in creativity.

title: Receiving Service from a Person with a Disability: Stereotypes, Perceptions of Corporate Social Responsibility, and the Opportunity for Increased Corporate Reputation

entries.rq_with_context: Despite advocacy for hiring people with disabilities, employers often avoid doing so due to concerns about negative customer reactions, particularly in service roles. Prior research has suggested both potential reputational risks and benefits, but empirical evidence on customer responses is limited. This paper addresses this gap by investigating whether receiving service from employees with disabilities—specifically those with a hearing disability or who use a wheelchair—affects corporate reputation. Drawing on signaling theory, stereotype content, and stigma-by-association logic, the authors propose that such employment signals corporate social responsibility (CSR), leading to improved reputation. Using a field study in a Lithuanian supermarket chain and an online experiment with video vignettes, they test CSR perceptions as a mediator and examine the influence of contact quality and CSR motives. The key contribution is demonstrating that employing people with disabilities can enhance corporate reputation through perceived CSR, countering managerial fears of customer backlash.

title: The Downside of CFO Function-Based Language Incongruity

entries.rq_with_context: Corporate executives are expected to behave in ways that align with their functional roles, and prior research has focused on demographic-based role incongruity (e.g., gender and leadership). This study addresses a gap by exploring within-role, function-based incongruity—specifically how CFOs' language in public disclosures may violate bankers’ expectations of appropriate CFO behavior. The authors examine how such linguistic incongruity increases perceived hazards and affects debt contract design, manifested by the number of covenants. Drawing on role congruity theory and communication expectation research, they test whether social context (CEO language) and media sentiment moderate this effect. The study contributes by identifying language as a novel trigger of role incongruity and advancing understanding of individual-level influences on interorganizational contracts.

title: Overcoming Conflict Between Symmetric Occupations: How “Creatives” and “Suits” Use Gender Ordering in Advertising

entries.rq_with_context: In knowledge-based organizations, interdependent yet symmetric occupations often face unresolved jurisdictional conflict due to the absence of formal hierarchy. This conflict is increasingly shaped by horizontal gender segregation, as women enter some male-dominated roles (like account management) but not others (like creative design), creating same-level but gender-divided occupational pairs. While workplace demography affects intergroup conflict, the role of gender in symmetric relationships—as opposed to hierarchical ones—remains understudied. This paper investigates how "creatives" (mostly men) and "suits" (mostly women) in advertising agencies manage such conflict. Drawing on 16 months of observation across five agencies and 116 interviews, the authors explore how gender-based practices are used to negotiate authority, legitimacy, and knowledge claims. They identify "gender ordering"—the enactment of essentialist gender roles and stereotypes—as a key mechanism for resolving conflict. The study contributes by showing how gender functions not just as a demographic difference but as a shared status hierarchy that organizes occupational cooperation, even as it reinforces women’s disadvantage through unequal performance of scut work.

title: Forming Entrepreneurial Teams: Mixing Business and Friendship to Create Transactive Memory Systems for Enhanced Success

entries.rq_with_context: Entrepreneurial success in early-stage ventures depends heavily on the founding team's composition and dynamics. Prior research identifies two main team formation strategies: interpersonal attraction (choosing cofounders based on friendship, family, or closeness) and resource-seeking (selecting partners for complementary skills). While some studies suggest a dual strategy may be beneficial, little is known about how these strategies impact the team's ability to develop learning systems crucial for navigating uncertainty. This study addresses that gap by investigating whether forming teams using both strategies from the onset enhances early venture performance through the development of transactive memory systems. Using data from crowdfunding, entrepreneurial competitions, and a controlled field experiment, the authors test if dual strategy use leads to stronger transactive memory systems, which in turn improve success. The work contributes by linking formation strategies to micro-level team learning mechanisms, offering a novel explanation for early entrepreneurial performance.

title: Enabling Rapid Financial Response to Disasters: Knotting and Reknotting Multiple Paradoxes in Interorganizational Systems

entries.rq_with_context: Market-based solutions are increasingly proposed for large-scale societal issues such as disaster response, yet they inherently produce contradictory tensions between market logic and development goals, immediate needs and long-term planning, and individual versus collective interests. While paradox theory offers insights into managing such tensions, most research focuses on single paradoxes within organizations, not on how multiple paradoxes interact in interorganizational systems. This study addresses that gap by analyzing multi-country risk pools that provide rapid disaster relief funding. Drawing on a longitudinal qualitative study, the authors investigate how actors maintain dynamic equilibrium despite constant threats of disequilibrium. They introduce the concepts of 'paradox knotting'—where tensions are mutually reinforcing—and 'reknotting'—a response to crisis when tensions cluster and unravel the system. The framework reveals how iterative cycles of knotting and reknotting enhance the viability of interorganizational responses to grand challenges, contributing new insights into paradox multiplicity and systemic resilience.

title: The Social Aftershocks of Voice: An Investigation of Employees’ Affective and Interpersonal Reactions after Speaking Up

entries.rq_with_context: Speaking up at work involves risks and rewards, yet research offers conflicting views on whether voice leads to pride or anxiety for employees. While both promotive and prohibitive voice aim to improve outcomes, it remains unclear how each type uniquely affects the speaker’s emotional experience and social interactions afterward. This study addresses this gap by proposing that promotive voice fosters pride due to a sense of social accomplishment, whereas prohibitive voice triggers anxiety due to social uncertainty. Using cognitive-motivational-relational theory, the authors test how these emotions influence interpersonal avoidance and, subsequently, interpersonal citizenship behavior. They also explore how voice reception moderates these affective appraisals. The key contribution is a within-person model that unpacks the divergent emotional and relational consequences of speaking up.

title: “I Go Here…But I Don’t Necessarily Belong”: The Process of Transgressor Reintegration in Organizations

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational transgressions are common, yet most transgressors are retained rather than terminated, leaving them in a liminal state: formally affiliated (structural insiders) but judged as morally outside the community. While prior research has examined reintegration from victims' or third-party perspectives, little is known about how transgressors themselves experience reintegration. This gap is critical because transgressors' integration affects engagement and performance. Drawing on longitudinal data from a military academy, this study asks: How do transgressors attempt to reintegrate, and what makes them feel more or less reintegrated? Using a qualitative, inductive approach, the research develops a process model showing that transgressors work to restore both membership (via compliance and institutional endorsements) and belonging (through relational investment), but belonging is more vulnerable. The key contribution is revealing that membership and belonging are distinct and necessary for full reintegration—making it rare even in supportive environments.

title: The Highs and Lows of Hierarchy in Multiteam Systems

entries.rq_with_context: Multiteam systems are increasingly used to manage complex tasks, yet they often fail due to coordination challenges and system complexity. While existing research assumes hierarchical structures—with a central leadership team—are superior, this paper challenges that view by proposing a more balanced understanding. The research question is: how do hierarchical versus egalitarian arrangements affect multiteam system learning through horizontal coordination and cognitive depletion? The authors use an experimental design with 76 multiteam systems observed over three performance episodes. They argue that hierarchy reduces cognitive depletion initially but harms horizontal coordination, and these effects change over time. The key contribution is demonstrating that hierarchy has both benefits and drawbacks, and that its advantages diminish as teams gain experience.

title: Gains and Losses: Week-To-Week Changes in Leader–Follower Relationships

entries.rq_with_context: Leader–member exchange (LMX) theory has long emphasized the differentiation and assumed stability of leader–follower relationships, yet little research has examined how these relationships change over time and what impact such fluctuations have. While prior work treats LMX as relatively stable after initial development, recent evidence suggests within-person variation exists but remains underexplored. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how short-term gains and losses in LMX—assessed through weekly comparisons to the previous week—affect followers’ emotional states. The authors argue that because relationships are difficult to evaluate in absolute terms, individuals use their own past experiences as a salient referent. Using two longitudinal studies with weekly assessments, they test whether week-to-week LMX changes predict affective responses. Their approach integrates social comparison and affect theories to model dynamic relationship evaluations. The key contribution is demonstrating that LMX is not only differentiated between individuals but also meaningfully fluctuates within individuals, with distinct implications for PA and NA.

title: Surging Underdogs and Slumping Favorites: How Recent Streaks and Future Expectations Drive Competitive Transgressions

entries.rq_with_context: Competitive transgressions—behaviors that violate accepted rules within a contest—are a significant concern in workplaces and sports, as they can undermine motivation and damage reputations. While prior research has focused on underdogs and favorites as distinct motivational states, it has largely treated competitions as isolated events, neglecting the influence of past performance streaks. This paper addresses the gap by investigating how past outcomes (winning or losing streaks) and future expectations (underdog vs. favorite status) interact to influence transgressive behaviors. Drawing on mental time travel theory, the authors propose that streaks amplify outcome uncertainty, which then triggers strong emotions—excitement for underdogs on winning streaks and anxiety for favorites on losing streaks—leading to transgressions. The proposed model is tested across four diverse studies using both field and experimental data. The main contribution is a temporally embedded framework that integrates past performance and future expectations to better predict when and why people break competitive rules.

title: It’s Not Always Sunny in Relationally Rich Jobs: The Influence of Negative Beneficiary Contact

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research highlights the motivational benefits of positive contact with beneficiaries, less is known about how employees make sense of negative interactions with those they aim to help. Such negative contact may threaten perceived social worth, yet individuals might simultaneously interpret these experiences as self-sacrifice for a meaningful cause. This study investigates this dual effect using social information processing theory, testing how negative beneficiary contact influences both low social worth and high perceived self-sacrifice across three studies. We also examine boundary conditions, including coworker emotional support, attributions for contact, and affective commitment. The research contributes by revealing when and how negative contact can be cognitively reframed in ways that sustain motivation and performance.

title: The Grand Tour: The Role of Catalyzing Places for Industry Emergence

entries.rq_with_context: While research has traditionally linked industry emergence to geographic clusters, some industries originate in iconic places yet emerge distantly from their birthplace. This paper investigates why certain renowned locations act as catalysts for industries that do not locally cluster. The gap lies in understanding non-clustered industry emergence, as existing literature focuses on agglomeration economies and anchor firms within clusters. The study asks: 'What are the mechanisms by which certain places catalyze the emergence of industries, but not their local clustering?' Using a longitudinal case study of Arco, Italy and its RockMaster event in the sport climbing industry, the authors develop a process model. Their approach identifies centripetal, catalyzing, and centrifugal forces that explain how places support global industry emergence. The key claimed contribution is the concept of 'catalyzing places' and the introduction of 'portable economies' and 'springboard firms' as alternatives to traditional cluster-based mechanisms.

title: Polishing the Gilt Edge: Elite Category Endurance and Symbolic Boundaries in U.S. Luxury Hotels, 1790–2015

entries.rq_with_context: Elite market categories are prestigious, exclusive, and symbolically valuable, yet their endurance is puzzling given serious challenges from competitors and shifting societal values. While prior research observes that status hierarchies tend to be self-sustaining, less is known about the dynamic cultural processes that allow elite categories to persist over centuries. This study investigates how the U.S. luxury hotel category has maintained its elite status from 1790 to 2015 despite disruptions. Using historical discourse analysis, interviews, and observations, the authors model the category’s symbolic boundary as a semiotic code of opposition that is periodically redefined. They find that endurance results not from stability but from adaptive redefinitions balancing exclusivity with cultural consonance. The contribution lies in showing that elite endurance is an ongoing cultural accomplishment shaped by discursive boundary work.

title: Does Power Protect Female Moral Objectors? How and When Moral Objectors’ Gender, Power, and Use of Organizational Frames Influence Perceived Self-Control and Experienced Retaliation

entries.rq_with_context: Moral objection—speaking out against unethical behavior—is a critical organizational behavior, and scholars suggest that higher-power individuals should lead such efforts because they are assumed to face less retaliation. However, research is unclear about whether this protection extends equally to women. While some studies suggest power can free women from constraining role expectations, others indicate that women may still face backlash due to gender role violations. This paper addresses this gap by investigating whether and how gender moderates the protective effect of power during moral objection. Drawing on power role theory, gender role theory, and expectancy violation theory, the authors examine perceived self-control as a key mechanism and test whether using an organizational frame (emphasizing group benefits) can mitigate retaliation. Their approach combines archival data and multiple experiments to assess both the phenomenon and a potential intervention.

title: Does Job Satisfaction Rise and Fall with the Economy? Cross-Sectional, Longitudinal, and Experimental Evidence That Job Satisfaction Increases during Recessions

entries.rq_with_context: While recessions typically worsen workplace conditions, this paper investigates the counterintuitive possibility that they may increase job satisfaction. Existing research focuses on internal organizational factors affecting job satisfaction, leaving unclear how broader economic contexts influence workers' evaluations of their jobs. The authors identify a gap in understanding how external societal conditions—specifically economic downturns—affect workplace attitudes. Their research question asks whether job satisfaction rises during recessions and why. They test this using cross-sectional, longitudinal, and experimental data across three studies. The key contribution is demonstrating that macroeconomic conditions outside the organization can positively shape job satisfaction through psychological mechanisms related to perceived job alternatives.

title: Creating and Sustaining Stakeholder Emotional Resonance with Organizational Identity in Social Mission-Driven Organizations

entries.rq_with_context: Social mission-driven organizations depend heavily on stakeholder support for survival but face ongoing threats from economic pressures that can lead to mission drift. While research has examined identity maintenance and cognitive aspects of stakeholder relations, little is known about how organizations sustain emotional resonance with stakeholders over long periods amid repeated existential threats. This study addresses this gap by asking: How do senior managers of social mission-driven organizations build and sustain stakeholders’ emotional resonance with organizational identity beliefs over time in the face of repeated existential threats? Drawing on a 20-year ethnographic study of Solidum, a philanthropic organization, we develop a process model of emotional resonance work. The findings reveal how emotional resonance must be actively maintained through practices that respond to ongoing challenges, offering insight into the dynamic processes that allow mission-driven organizations to survive.

title: Stranger Leaders: A Theory of Marginal Leaders’ Conception of Learning in Organizations

entries.rq_with_context: Marginal leaders, such as chief learning officers (CLOs), occupy senior roles but lack clear professional or organizational mandates, making their leadership identity ambiguous. While existing research examines leader identity in contexts with dominant templates, little is known about how leaders develop identities when central aspects of their role are contested. This study addresses that gap by asking how marginal leaders navigate defining dualities in organizations. Drawing on a systems psychodynamic lens and an inductive study of 69 L&D executives, it explores how these leaders respond to conflicting instrumental and humanistic views of learning. The key contribution is a theory of 'conception of learning'—a process involving finding a place, taking a stance, and building learning spaces—that explains how marginal leaders craft identities that resolve or sustain duality.

title: Balancing “Protective Disguise” with “Harmonious Advocacy”: Social Venture Legitimation in Authoritarian Contexts

entries.rq_with_context: Social ventures in authoritarian regimes face unique legitimacy challenges due to political repression and cultural conservatism, yet existing research predominantly focuses on democratic contexts. In authoritarian settings, advocacy for social change can lead to censorship, crackdowns, or imprisonment, making traditional legitimation strategies risky. This study addresses a critical gap by exploring how social ventures can gain legitimacy under such constraints. Using a case study of a disability rights organization in post-revolutionary Egypt, it asks: How do new social ventures gain legitimacy in authoritarian contexts? The authors employ a qualitative, process-tracing approach to examine the organization’s strategic evolution over time. Their key contribution is a theoretical model of 'optimal assimilation,' where ventures balance 'protective disguise'—downplaying their activist agenda—with 'harmonious advocacy'—gradually promoting their cause in ways aligned with state interests.

title: Inside-Out, Outside-In, or All-in-One? The Role of Network Sequencing in the Elaboration of Ideas

entries.rq_with_context: Individuals developing novel ideas in organizations face a dilemma: they need feedback and support to refine their ideas, but early exposure to the wrong people can lead to dismissal of promising yet ill-defined concepts. While prior research has focused on network structure, this paper explores how the timing and order of network mobilization matter. The authors identify a gap in understanding how sequencing—rather than just structure—influences idea elaboration. They ask: how does the order in which R&D scientists and engineers involve inner- versus outer-circle network contacts affect their innovation performance? Using survey and archival data from 301 R&D professionals, they test whether inside-out sequencing (inner-circle first) outperforms alternative approaches. Their contribution is to show that network behavior—specifically, the strategic timing of engagement—matters for innovation outcomes.

title: Intersectionality in Intractable Dirty Work: How Mumbai Ragpickers Make Meaning of Their Work and Lives

entries.rq_with_context: Many individuals performing dirty work face intersecting sources of stigma related to their occupation, social class, and living conditions, making meaning-making especially challenging. While prior research has examined how workers manage taint through positive reframing, less is known about cases where escape from dirty work is nearly impossible due to entrenched structural, familial, and cultural forces—a condition termed 'intractable dirty work.' The study focuses on ragpickers in Mumbai who experience the compounded burden of doing physically degrading work, belonging to India’s lowest caste, and living in slums. The research question asks: How do people engaged in intractable dirty work at the intersection of multiple sources of taint make and manage meanings of their work and lives? The authors analyze interview and observational data through an intersectional lens and a sensemaking framework. They identify a dual process of meaning-making and propose the concept of 'functional ambivalence' as a key contribution, highlighting that such work need not lead to despair but can instead be a site of resilience.

title: How Global Leaders Gain Power through Downward Deference and Reduction of Social Distance

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations rely on positional power to achieve goals, but global expansion creates conditions where leaders from headquarters lack local knowledge, networks, and influence relative to their in-country subordinates. While theory suggests power leads to social distance and reduced empathy, this study identifies a countervailing behavior—'downward deference'—where leaders submit to lower-power workers to bridge expertise gaps. The gap lies in understanding when and why individuals with formal authority choose to reverse traditional power dynamics. The research asks: Why do leaders defer to subordinates? What behaviors constitute downward deference? And what role does social distance play? Drawing on interviews with 115 global leaders and archival data, the authors use power and social distance theories to examine these questions. They find that leaders who recognize their local shortcomings engage in downward deference, which correlates with prior deep international experience and leads to better job performance and promotions.

title: How Do Investors Evaluate Past Entrepreneurial Failure? Unpacking Failure Due to Lack of Skill versus Bad Luck

entries.rq_with_context: Most entrepreneurial ventures fail, and many founders launch multiple ventures, meaning that past failure is increasingly common. Existing research typically assumes symmetry between past success and failure, where success signals skill and failure implies lack thereof, but empirical findings on the impact of past failure are mixed. This study addresses the gap by questioning whether past failure is inherently detrimental or merely a 'noisy' signal that may result from bad luck rather than lack of skill. The research asks whether investors rationally incorporate additional information about entrepreneurial skill when evaluating previously failed entrepreneurs, or whether they exhibit failure aversion by dismissing them regardless of skill cues. The study uses experiments in equity crowdfunding to test these possibilities. Its key contribution is providing evidence that investors do not treat failure as a definitive negative signal but instead update their beliefs based on credible skill cues, challenging the assumption of failure aversion.

title: How Work Orientation Impacts Objective Career Outcomes via Managerial (Mis)perceptions

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research has established that a calling orientation improves subjective well-being and life satisfaction, its link to objective career outcomes like income and promotion remains unclear and contested. Some argue calling leads to better performance and success, while others suggest it may undermine organizational compliance and hurt performance. The unresolved debate stems from focusing exclusively on internal pathways—how work orientation affects individual effort and job performance. This study addresses the gap by proposing an external pathway: managerial (mis)perceptions. Drawing on signaling theory, cognitive biases, and reciprocity, the authors suggest managers interpret calling-oriented behaviors as signals of better performance and stronger commitment, even when actual performance is equivalent. They test whether these perceptions explain why calling-oriented employees receive better career outcomes. The research uses longitudinal survey data and a controlled experiment to demonstrate that managerial perceptions—though potentially inaccurate—mediate the relationship between work orientation and outcomes. The contribution lies in identifying a novel, perception-based mechanism that explains career disparities beyond direct performance effects.

title: Going Viral or Growing Like an Oak Tree? Towards Sustainable Local Development Through Entrepreneurship

entries.rq_with_context: Despite widespread promotion of high-growth, venture capital–backed entrepreneurship as a solution for local development in economically challenged regions, its impact has been limited and often short-lived. This paper identifies a critical gap: the lack of understanding about how different resourcing modes lead to varying spatiotemporal patterns of venture growth and their implications for sustainable local development. Drawing on ethnographic and archival data from Detroit, the authors investigate how ventures developed through financing (scaling up) versus local bricolage (scaling deep) grow differently in time and space, and how these growth trajectories generate distinct contributions to their communities. The study employs a time–space lens to frame venture growth not just in terms of size but as a process unfolding across spatial and temporal scales. The key contribution is revealing that sustainable local development requires not only explosive, widespread growth but also enduring, locally anchored growth that keeps benefits within the community.

title: When Helping Hurts Helpers: Anticipatory versus Reactive Helping, Helper’s Relative Status, and Recipient Self-Threat

entries.rq_with_context: Research has generally shown that workplace helping leads to positive outcomes for helpers due to social exchange norms. However, this view may overlook important distinctions between types of helping. The authors identify a critical gap: most studies treat helping as reactive (in response to requests), while anticipatory helping (offering help without being asked) may provoke different reactions. They argue that anticipatory helping, especially from higher-status individuals, can threaten recipients' sense of competence and status, leading to defensive responses. The research uses social exchange and self-affirmation theories to explore when and why anticipatory helping backfires. The studies employ experimental and field methods across varied work contexts to test these ideas, examining help acceptance, performance evaluations, and relational evaluations as outcomes.

title: When Do Outside CEOs Underperform? From a CEO-Centric to a Stakeholder-Centric Perspective of Post-Succession Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Appointing an outside CEO is common but often associated with underperformance and high performance variance compared to inside CEOs. Prior research has focused on CEO-centric explanations, such as the value of external experience or information asymmetry, but these have not fully explained performance differences. A key gap is the lack of attention to stakeholders’ reactions to CEO appointments and how these sociocognitive responses might undermine performance. This study addresses that gap by investigating how corporate misfit and negative sentiment—especially toward outside CEOs—affect post-succession performance. We use an integrative framework combining CEO-centric (experience and fit) and stakeholder-centric (sentiment) perspectives, analyzing 1,275 U.S. public firm appointments from 2001–2014. Our central contribution is showing that while CEO experience does not explain performance differences, corporate misfit and negative sentiment do—particularly for outside CEOs.

title: When and Why Bias Suppression Is Difficult to Sustain: The Asymmetric Effect of Intermittent Accountability

entries.rq_with_context: The justice literature suggests that adhering to procedural rules like bias suppression should be self-reinforcing, yet evidence shows debiasing efforts often fail over time. A key unresolved question is why sustained bias suppression remains challenging despite external controls like accountability. The authors identify a gap in understanding how fluctuating accountability affects consistency in decision-making. They propose that when decision-makers suppress bias under high accountability, it generates internal tension that leads to counterfactual thinking and regret, which then undermines future consistency if accountability drops. However, this process does not occur when accountability rises. Using a multi-study design—archival analysis of CEOs, a field study of Supreme Court judges, and two experiments—the authors test this asymmetric effect. Their main contribution is showing that intermittent accountability shapes decision consistency through internal self-regulatory processes, challenging the assumption that accountability uniformly promotes fairness.

title: Fast or Slow: How Temporal Work Design Shapes Experienced Passage of Time and Job Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Employees experience work time as either fast or slow, which affects their well-being and performance, yet little is known about how work design shapes this experience. While existing research focuses on enriching job characteristics like autonomy and variety, this paper identifies two novel, time-specific features—temporal predictability (reducing uncertain waiting times) and task segmentation (dividing work time with distinct markers)—that may shift attention away from time itself. Drawing on the attentional gate theory, the authors propose that these characteristics speed up experienced time, which then enhances job performance. The research tests this model across five studies using experiments, field data, and surveys. Its key contribution is introducing a new, attention-based mechanism in work design that applies even to simple, routine jobs where traditional enrichment strategies are hard to implement.

title: Glue or Gasoline? The Role of Interorganizational Linkages in the Occurrence and Spillover of Competitive Wars

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the severe performance consequences of competitive wars, research on their causes and dynamics remains limited, especially regarding the role of interorganizational linkages. Existing work focuses on day-to-day competition or economic triggers like demand fluctuations, but neglects how social embeddedness shapes war dynamics. This study addresses this gap by investigating how relational and structural embeddedness—through strategic alliances, common ownership, and common analyst ties—affect both the initiation and spillover of competitive wars. Drawing on social embeddedness theory, we propose that while all three linkages reduce the likelihood of war initiation (acting as 'glue'), they differ in their effects on spillover: alliances amplify spillover (like 'gasoline') whereas indirect ties continue to inhibit it. Using 20 years of U.S. airline industry data, we test these dual roles. Our contribution lies in revealing how a competitive war fundamentally shifts the function of interorganizational linkages, offering new insights into the social mechanisms underlying extreme competition.

title: Longing for the Road Not Taken: The Affective and Behavioral Consequences of Forgone Identity Dwelling

entries.rq_with_context: The literature on identity construction assumes that employees move forward in creating coherent and distinctive work identities, eventually leaving behind past career decisions and alternative paths. However, this paper challenges that assumption by proposing that some employees continue to reflect on forgone professional identities long after those paths were abandoned. The gap this research addresses is the lack of attention to these 'identity echoes' and their emotional and behavioral consequences. Specifically, it asks how dwelling on such identities affects employees' feelings and behaviors at work. Drawing on cognitive-motivational-relational theory, the study tests whether forgone identity dwelling triggers longing, which in turn leads to both withdrawal and job crafting. The primary contribution is demonstrating that past identity decisions remain psychologically salient and have dual behavioral implications, thereby challenging forward-progress models of identity construction.

title: Painting a Clear Picture while Seeing the Big Picture: When and Why Leaders Overcome the Trade-Off Between Concreteness and Scale

entries.rq_with_context: Leaders who think concretely—by visualizing vivid, image-based futures—are theorized to be more effective at inspiring organizational change. However, research shows that concrete thinkers typically focus on short-term, narrow problems rather than long-term strategic visions, creating a paradox: those best equipped to communicate compelling visions may be least likely to formulate them. This gap raises the question of how concrete-oriented leaders can overcome this limitation. The authors propose that organizational hierarchy acts as a structural condition that redirects the attention of concrete-thinking leaders away from operational details and toward large-scale strategic issues. Using an archival study of CEOs and a preregistered experiment, they test whether hierarchical strength (e.g., multiple management layers, concentrated authority) enables concrete-oriented leaders to shift their focus and drive change. The key contribution is identifying a boundary condition under which concrete cognition leads to large-scale action, advancing theory on leadership, attention, and construal.

title: Regulating Top Managers’ Emotions during Strategy Making: Nokia’s Socially Distributed Approach Enabling Radical Change from Mobile Phones to Networks in 2007–2013

entries.rq_with_context: Strategy making in large organizations can be highly emotional, especially when facing disruptive changes or crises, yet little is known about how top managers' emotions are regulated in such contexts. Existing research has focused on individual-level emotion regulation or interpersonal dynamics in non-strategic settings, leaving a gap in understanding how emotion regulation operates collectively during complex, long-term strategic decisions. This study addresses two research questions: (a) Whether and how are strategic decision makers’ emotions regulated during strategy making in large organizations? (b) How does this regulation influence the strategy-making process? Using a longitudinal case study of Nokia from 2007 to 2013, the authors develop a process model of socially distributed emotion regulation. The study contributes by showing how multiple organizational groups—such as the board, advisory teams, and external partners—collectively regulate top managers’ emotions through complementary mechanisms that enable radical strategic change.

title: Advancing Reform: Embedded Activism to Develop Climate Solutions

entries.rq_with_context: As corporations increasingly express support for sustainability goals, social movement organizations are shifting toward collaborative tactics rather than contentious challenges to drive internal organizational change. However, little is known about how activists operate through coordinated efforts that span both movement and partner organizations—what the authors call 'embedded activism.' Furthermore, organizations vary significantly in their prior experience with activist issues, creating different 'opportunity structures' for collaboration that are not well understood. This study asks how embedded activists create new solutions to advance climate reforms across organizations with differing levels of prior issue development. Drawing on data from the Environmental Defense Fund's Climate Corps program, which placed graduate students in 99 host organizations, the authors use fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine how organizational context and movement resource use combine to enable solution creation. The findings reveal how activists navigate the tension between organizational support (which provides resources to act) and issue ambiguity (which provides opportunities to act), offering a new framework for understanding collaborative activism.

title: OMG! My Boss Just Friended Me: How Evaluations of Colleagues’ Disclosure, Gender, and Rank Shape Personal/Professional Boundary Blurring Online

entries.rq_with_context: As online social networks blur personal and professional lives, employees face new decisions about connecting with colleagues online. While past research focused on individual boundary management strategies, this paper highlights a gap: how the characteristics of relational partners—such as their self-disclosure, gender, and rank—influence boundary-blurring decisions. Existing work has overlooked how employees evaluate *whom* they connect with, instead focusing on personal preferences or tactics. The authors investigate how these colleague characteristics shape warmth perceptions and connection decisions using a multi-study design across archival, survey, and experimental data. They propose a relational boundary-blurring framework that shifts attention from the focal employee to the relational partner. Their key contribution is demonstrating that boundary management is not just about personal preferences but is critically dependent on social evaluations of others.

title: Paradox Peers: A Relational Approach to Navigating a Business–Society Paradox

entries.rq_with_context: Individuals in CSR-related occupations, such as corporate grantmakers, often face persistent paradoxical tensions between social and business goals that are central to their role but not prioritized by organizational leaders. While existing research highlights individual cognitive strategies and internal organizational practices for managing paradox, less is known about how individuals sustain engagement with paradox when such tensions are not organizationally supported. This study addresses this gap by exploring how grantmakers navigate a business–society paradox through external peer relationships. Drawing on interview and observational data from 40 grantmakers across 32 firms, the paper identifies a peer-based model that reveals how 'paradox peers'—external colleagues who share similar challenges—offer key relational support. The findings contribute by showing that relational mechanisms outside the organization are critical to enabling individuals to manage internal paradox.

title: Who Will Stay When Crisis Strikes? Venture Capitalist Threat-Defiant Learning Response to Ventures in Crisis

entries.rq_with_context: Interfirm relationships are often strained when one firm faces a crisis, as indirect threats like reputational spillover can trigger threat-rigidity responses—conservative, risk-averse actions such as withdrawal. While existing research has focused on how organizations respond to direct threats, less is known about how firms react to crises affecting their partners. This study investigates why some venture capitalists (VCs) defy the expectation to abandon ventures involved in lawsuits, a form of crisis that poses indirect threats. Drawing on experiential learning and Oliver’s defiance theory, the authors propose that VCs develop 'threat-defiant learning' from three relational experiences: general investment experience, prior ties to the focal venture, and their own past lawsuit experiences. Using a dataset of 435 VC investment decisions across 105 ventures facing lawsuits, the study tests how these experiences influence follow-on investments. The key contribution is showing how experiential learning enables organizations to defy threat rigidity in interfirm relationships, offering a novel explanation for continued relational investment during external crises.

title: Ritual Work and the Formation of a Shared Sense of Meaningfulness

entries.rq_with_context: A shared sense of meaningfulness—when organizational members collectively experience their work as significant—is not innate but forms through social processes. While prior research emphasizes leaders’ deliberate communication and rhetoric as key triggers, this study identifies a gap in understanding how such meaning emerges without top-down messaging, particularly through embodied, experiential practices. Drawing on a 21-month field study of an athletic apparel company, the paper asks how a shared sense of meaningfulness forms when leaders do not initially articulate a higher purpose. Using interaction ritual chain (IRC) theory as a sensitizing lens, the study investigates the role of leaders’ actions and member interactions in triggering and propagating meaning. The key contribution is a three-step process model that explains how meaningfulness forms through ritual work, emotional sharing, and symbolic articulation.

title: The Impostor Phenomenon Revisited: Examining the Relationship between Workplace Impostor Thoughts and Interpersonal Effectiveness at Work

entries.rq_with_context: The impostor phenomenon is widely viewed as harmful, linked to low self-esteem and self-handicapping behaviors. However, hints in the literature suggest those experiencing it may also be seen as socially skilled or likable, pointing to unexplored interpersonal benefits. This study addresses the gap by introducing the construct of workplace impostor thoughts—the belief that others overestimate one’s competence—and theorizing how it may positively relate to interpersonal effectiveness. Drawing on contingencies of self-worth theory, the author proposes that these thoughts trigger an other-focused orientation as a defensive response to protect self-esteem. Using survey, video, and preregistered experimental data from four samples (n = 3,603), the study tests whether workplace impostor thoughts enhance interpersonal effectiveness through this mechanism. The key contribution is rebalancing scholarly understanding by demonstrating a positive, interpersonal upside to a phenomenon typically seen as wholly detrimental.

title: The Push and Pull of Attaining CEO Celebrity: A Media Routines Perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Despite extensive research on the consequences of CEO celebrity, far less is known about its antecedents. While prior assumptions suggest celebrity accrues to high-performing CEOs due to the 'romance of leadership,' evidence shows firm performance is only weakly linked to celebrity. This gap raises the central question: why do some CEOs become celebrities while others with seemingly equal accomplishments do not? Drawing on media routines theory, the authors propose a push–pull framework. Journalists (pull) are drawn to CEOs who stand out—either through firm strategic nonconformity or demographic atypicality—because these characteristics create compelling, newsworthy narratives. Simultaneously, CEOs (push) actively promote themselves through press releases and social media, facilitating journalists’ work. The study tests how these factors independently and jointly shape CEO celebrity, conceptualized as an ordinal construct: noncelebrity, B-list, or A-list. The key contribution is a novel, multimedia measure of celebrity and a theory explaining how both structural media processes and individual agency shape unequal attention among CEOs.

title: The Use of Strategic Noise in Reactive Impression Management: How Do Market Reactions Matter?

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often engage in impression management (IM) to shape stakeholders' perceptions of strategic decisions. While prior research has focused on anticipatory IM—using strategic noise (i.e., unrelated news) before or during an announcement to offset potential negative reactions—this study explores reactive IM, where the market reaction is already known. The gap lies in understanding how firms use both positive and negative strategic noise *after* a focal event, such as an M&A announcement, when stakeholders’ initial reactions have been revealed. The authors ask: How do firms adjust their release of strategic noise reactively based on the direction (positive/negative) and magnitude of the market reaction? Drawing on expectancy violations theory, they propose a model where firms tailor their noise—offsetting small negative reactions with positive news, confirming large negative ones with more bad news (big-bath effect), amplifying small positive reactions, or hiding negative news during strong positive reactions (hiding effect). They test this using a sample of 7,575 M&A deals. The key contribution is shifting the strategic noise literature from purely anticipatory to include reactive, targeted use, showing that firms strategically time unrelated news based on observed market feedback.

title: Network Stability: The Role of Geography and Brokerage Structure Inequity

entries.rq_with_context: While brokerage relationships are known to vary in stability, existing research has primarily focused on the broker's perspective, overlooking the role of alter firms in shaping brokerage persistence. This study addresses a critical gap by examining how structural inequity—defined as the broker's superior opportunity to recombine knowledge from alters compared to vice versa—affects the stability of brokerage triads. Drawing on an altercentric view, the paper argues that perceived inequity triggers efforts by alters to neutralize disadvantages, increasing the likelihood of brokerage decay.
