Furthermore, the study introduces geographic distance as a key contingency, proposing that greater spatial separation reduces alters' tendency to view brokers as rivals, thereby increasing tolerance for structural inequity. Using a discrete time survival model on 53,377 triad-year observations from the global biopharmaceutical industry (1985–2005), the study tests these arguments. Its key contribution lies in advancing network stability research by integrating structural and spatial embeddedness perspectives to explain brokerage decay.

title: Investing In Communities: Forging New Ground in Corporate Community Codevelopment through Relational and Psychological Pathways

entries.rq_with_context: Corporate community investment (CCI) is widely promoted as a form of corporate social responsibility, yet community development scholars argue it often fails to achieve meaningful, lasting change and can even reinforce corporate power at the expense of vulnerable communities. While management research emphasizes business value from CCI, it largely overlooks the implementation processes that determine social impact. This gap limits understanding of how CCI can achieve mutual benefit. This study addresses that gap by asking: How does the implementation of CCI contribute to mutual development in corporations and communities? Drawing on a longitudinal qualitative study of 35 CCI programs involving Indigenous Australian communities, corporations, and a nonprofit, the research develops a process model grounded in relational and psychological pathways. The study contributes by identifying concrete mechanisms—such as mutual perspective-taking and communal advocacy—that bridge management and community development discourses and enable sustainable development.

title: The Policy–People Gap: Decision-Makers Choose Policies That Favor Different Applicants than They Select When Making Individual Decisions

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often fail to implement their espoused diversity and inclusion policies in actual selection decisions, leading to persistent inequality. While prior research has attributed such gaps to abstract principle endorsement or moral temptation in concrete contexts, this paper identifies a novel organizational problem: a systematic divergence between policy and individual selection decisions, even when consequences are identical. The gap persists across college admissions and workplace hiring contexts among admissions officers, tech industry professionals, and laypeople. The research questions are whether decision-makers favor disadvantaged applicants more when choosing policies than individuals, and whether shifting standards of fairness—prioritizing microjustice (individual fairness) in individual decisions and macrojustice (aggregate fairness) in policy decisions—explain this gap. The study uses a combination of within- and between-subjects experimental designs across 16 preregistered studies. The key contribution is identifying and explaining a robust policy–people gap in selection decisions, offering a new account for why organizational policies often fail to translate into equitable outcomes.

title: “Am I Next?” The Spillover Effects of Mega-Threats on Avoidant Behaviors at Work

entries.rq_with_context: Mega-threats—negative, identity-relevant societal events like police killings or mass shootings that receive widespread media attention—frequently affect racial minority communities, yet their impact on workplace behavior remains understudied. While prior research shows these events harm mental health for identity group members, less is known about how they influence work behaviors. This paper addresses that gap by investigating how mega-threats lead to avoidant behaviors such as work withdrawal and reduced social engagement among racial minority employees. Drawing on the theory of racialized organizations, the authors propose a three-stage model: shared identity with victims triggers 'embodied threat' (a heightened sense of personal vulnerability to identity-based harm), which leads to threat suppression at work due to constrained emotional expression in racialized workplaces, ultimately depleting psychological resources and increasing avoidant behaviors. The study tests this model across two empirical studies involving different mega-threats and racial groups. The key contribution is uncovering the spillover mechanism through which societal trauma translates into workplace disengagement and identifying psychological safety in identity discussions as a buffering factor.

title: From Sheltered to Included: The Emancipation of Disabled Workers from Benevolent Marginalization

entries.rq_with_context: Disabled workers in sheltered workshops often experience benevolent marginalization—being treated with well-meaning paternalism that subtly reinforces their dependency and limits their autonomy. While research has explored overt forms of marginalization and resistance, less is known about how individuals who implicitly accept their subordinated status can achieve collective emancipation, especially when there is no overt conflict. The gap lies in understanding emancipation in contexts where power operates through care and solidarity rather than coercion. This study addresses that gap by asking how benevolently marginalized individuals, whose self-concept is regulated by an organizational identity, can collectively achieve emancipation. Drawing on a six-year longitudinal study of a German sheltered workshop, the authors analyze identity work processes over time. They argue that emancipation occurs not through confrontation but through collaborative identity work, revealing how insider activists leverage support from select allies in power to shift organizational identity toward inclusion.

title: Upward Mobility, the Cleft Habitus, and Speaking Up: How Class Transitions Relate to Individual and Organizational Antecedents of Voice

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates the organizational experiences of upwardly mobile employees, who move from lower to higher social class positions, particularly in elite 'gateway organizations' like prestigious companies. While prior research has emphasized how lower-class backgrounds instill a persistent sense of reduced personal initiative (a 'sticky habitus'), this paper challenges that view by exploring the 'cleft habitus'—where upward mobility may foster a stronger internal sense of efficacy. However, despite potentially greater willingness to speak up, these individuals may still face barriers because managers may prefer input from those with elite backgrounds. The research asks whether upward mobility increases self-efficacy and voice, and whether managers are less likely to solicit voice from the upwardly mobile due to perceived differences in competence and cultural fit. Drawing on a dual-pathway model of voice, the study uses a field survey, archival data analysis, and a preregistered experiment. It contributes by showing that structural inequities in voice opportunities persist even when individuals overcome internal barriers, highlighting how class background shapes organizational inclusion.

title: Living Up to the Hype: How New Ventures Manage the Resource and Liability of Future-Oriented Visions within the Nascent Market of Impact Investing

entries.rq_with_context: Hype—defined as a collective vision and promise of a possible future around which attention, excitement, and expectations grow—presents a dual challenge for entrepreneurs in nascent markets. While hype can mobilize early stakeholder support and resources, it also creates mounting temporal and categorical expectations that constrain entrepreneurial flexibility. Existing research has highlighted the tension between hype and legitimacy but has largely overlooked how entrepreneurs actively manage these expectations through relational and cultural work. Drawing on an inductive, longitudinal study of three social stock exchanges in the impact investing market, this paper asks: How do entrepreneurs in nascent markets engage with and manage hype to retain temporal and categorical flexibility? The study uses field theory and the sociology of expectations to trace how ventures employ cultural and relational organizing practices to convert hype into social proof. The key contribution is an emergent theory of hype management that reveals how different forms of social proof—salient versus proximate—enable distinct pathways for sustaining flexibility and opportunity.

title: Prosocial Occupations, Work Autonomy, and the Origins of the Social Class Pay Gap

entries.rq_with_context: Despite decades of research, a puzzle remains in social mobility literature: individuals from lower-class families earn less than their upper-class peers, even when they attain similar levels of education and occupational prestige. Existing research has focused on advantages in education and access to prestigious jobs as mechanisms behind the class pay gap, but these factors do not fully account for income disparities. This study addresses a missing piece by exploring whether people from different class origins sort into different types of occupations—specifically, whether those from upper-class backgrounds are more likely to work in autonomous jobs (with greater freedom and control), while those from lower-class origins are more likely to work in prosocial jobs (focused on helping others). Using a sociocultural perspective, the authors argue that these occupational differences, which are shaped by childhood experiences, contribute to the pay gap because autonomous jobs pay more than prosocial ones. By analyzing two large U.S. datasets (GSS and NLSY), the study tests whether this pattern of occupational sorting explains part of the unexplained income disparity. The findings reveal that class origin predicts both occupational type and income, offering a new explanation for the class pay gap that goes beyond education and prestige.

title: When Conscientious Employees Meet Intelligent Machines: An Integrative Approach Inspired by Complementarity Theory and Role Theory

entries.rq_with_context: Conscientiousness has long been seen as the key predictor of work performance, particularly because orderly employees complement traditional technology that requires user input and direction. However, 21st-century intelligent machines can autonomously make decisions, creating a non-complementary overlap with the systematic tendencies of conscientious employees. This raises uncertainty about whether the established benefits of conscientiousness still apply. The study addresses this gap by investigating how working with intelligent machines affects role breadth self-efficacy and role ambiguity for conscientious employees. Drawing on complementarity theory and role theory, the authors use three studies—experience sampling, a field experiment, and an online experiment—across Malaysia, Taiwan, and the U.S. They find conscientious employees benefit less from intelligent machines, showing reduced self-efficacy and increased ambiguity. The contribution is showing that the long-standing consensus on conscientiousness may need to be revised in the context of modern technology.

title: “Invisible” Discrimination: Divergent Outcomes for the Nonprototypicality of Black Women

entries.rq_with_context: Black women face both racial and gender discrimination, yet their experiences are often overlooked compared to those of White women and Black men. This phenomenon, termed 'intersectional invisibility,' suggests that Black women’s dual-subordinated identities render them less prototypical members of both their racial and gender groups. While prior research has shown that prototypicality affects recognition as a victim of discrimination, it remains unclear how nonprototypicality influences post-allegation treatment, particularly financial remedy. This paper investigates whether Black women’s discrimination claims are less believed than those of White women (for gender discrimination) and Black men (for racial discrimination), and whether their nonprototypical attributes lead to differing financial outcomes. Drawing on the intersectional invisibility hypothesis and the BIAS map framework, the authors test these predictions across six experimental studies and two archival analyses of EEOC data. The authors claim to contribute the first empirical demonstration of how intersectional invisibility shapes both the recognition and treatment of Black women in workplace discrimination contexts, revealing when their nonprototypical status leads to disadvantage or advantage.

title: Remaking Capitalism: The Strength of Weak Legislation in Mobilizing B Corporation Certification

entries.rq_with_context: Many initiatives aim to remake capitalism through sustainability reforms, but it remains unclear how different governance efforts—such as weak legislation and strong voluntary certification—interact. Prior research often assumes legislation is strong and certifications are weak, overlooking the prevalence of ambiguous and poorly enforced laws. This study addresses the gap by asking how weak sustainability legislation, such as benefit corporation laws, influences the adoption and retention of more rigorous certifications like B Corp certification. Drawing on organizational values and the sociology of law, the authors propose that weak legislation increases both immediate values authentication needs and ongoing material authentication needs. They test this using longitudinal data on B Corp certification across U.S. states, finding that weak legislation increases initial certification and recertification—especially when legislation is broad in scope—and that these effects depend on regional sustainability norms.

title: “I” Am Affirmed, but Are “We”? Social Identity Processes Influencing Refugees’ Work Initiative and Community Embeddedness

entries.rq_with_context: Refugees face significant challenges in integrating into host societies due to marginal status and societal stigmatization, which create social identity threats. While workplaces are seen as potential 'social bridges' for integration, there is limited understanding of the psychological processes through which treatment at work affects refugees’ broader social engagement. The authors address this gap by investigating how perceived insider status—feeling personally affirmed at work—encourages work initiative and community embeddedness. They propose that this occurs via organizational identification, but these effects depend on the broader social context. Specifically, a favorable diversity climate and lower perceived societal stigma reduce the salience of the stigmatized refugee identity, allowing personal affirmations to more strongly influence identification. The study uses self-categorization theory to explain how identity salience moderates the translation of personal treatment into organizational and societal engagement. The key contribution is identifying boundary conditions under which personal recognition leads to broader integration, offering insight into when and how employers can support refugee inclusion.

title: Big Fish versus Big Pond? Entrepreneurs, Established Firms, and Antecedents of Tie Formation

entries.rq_with_context: Entrepreneurial firms often rely on established partners to access resources such as development help and market access, especially in technology-intensive industries like video games. While existing research highlights mutual resource dependence as a driver of collaboration, it largely treats tie formation through static lenses, overlooking how dynamic factors shape partner choice. A key dilemma entrepreneurs face—termed the 'big fish versus big pond' trade-off—revolves around choosing between a partner that offers more attention and development support or one that provides broader market reach. Despite its prevalence, the conditions under which each option is preferred remain unclear. This study examines how entrepreneurs’ changing internal resource needs and external competitive pressures moderate this choice. Drawing from resource dependence theory and analyzing tie formation between video game developers and publishers, the authors test whether anticipated development help and market access drive partnerships, and how two moderators—resource need evolution and resource uncertainty due to competition—influence this decision. The authors claim the study advances understanding of dynamic resource dependence and reveals when entrepreneurs prioritize being a 'big fish' versus joining a 'big pond.'

title: Too Much on the Plate? How Executive Job Demands Harm Firm Innovation and Reduce Share of Exploratory Innovations

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research has focused on top executives' cognition and individual attributes in shaping innovation, this study addresses a gap by examining how the objective job environment—specifically executive job demands—influences innovation outcomes. Despite theoretical recognition of job demands as central in upper echelons theory, their impact on innovation remains untested, and their boundary conditions are underdeveloped. The research asks how executive job demands affect overall firm innovation and the balance between exploratory and exploitative innovations, and how factors like TMT variety, climate, and human capital moderate these relationships. Drawing on job demands theory and psychological research, the study uses survey data from 243 Chinese firms. It contributes by shifting focus from individual executive traits to their job environment and by empirically validating and extending executive job demands theory into the domain of innovation management.

title: No Change Is an Island: How Interferences between Change Initiatives Evoke Inconsistencies That Undermine Implementation

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational change research has largely focused on isolated initiatives, neglecting how multiple concurrent changes interact. This gap is critical because real-world strategic change typically involves several overlapping initiatives that may interfere with one another. Despite growing recognition of 'change turbulence,' little is known about the underlying mechanisms—particularly cognitive and emotional processes—through which one initiative undermines another. Drawing on a longitudinal study of a multinational tech firm, this paper asks: How do interferences between change initiatives emerge, and what mechanisms link them to implementation outcomes? Using an interpretive sensemaking lens and consistency theory, the authors analyze real-time data on two interfering initiatives. They reveal how inconsistency judgments provoke collective emotions that erode engagement, offering a novel process model of change interference.

title: How Other- and Self-Compassion Reduce Burnout through Resource Replenishment

entries.rq_with_context: Burnout is a multidimensional state of depletion affecting employees across industries, yet most interventions focus on organizational or passive recovery strategies, leaving individuals as recipients rather than active agents in their recovery. Existing research has largely overlooked how employees might self-initiate recovery through their own actions. This paper addresses this gap by investigating whether compassionate actions—directed toward oneself or others—can serve as agentic strategies to reduce burnout. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory, the authors propose that compassion reduces specific burnout dimensions by generating corresponding psychological resources: self-compassion replenishes self-control to reduce exhaustion, other-compassion fosters belonging to reduce cynicism, and both enhance self-esteem to reduce inefficacy. The study tests this model using two complementary designs: a longitudinal field survey and an experiential sampling study with business students. The key contribution is identifying the conditions under which compassion functions as a self-sustaining recovery mechanism, emphasizing the importance of matching compassion type to burnout dimension.

title: To Catch a Predator: The Lived Experience of Extreme Practices

entries.rq_with_context: In response to growing societal alarm over online child sexual exploitation, volunteer pedophile hunting teams have emerged globally, conducting livestreamed confrontations with suspected predators. Police and researchers are deeply concerned about the ethical and practical consequences of these extreme practices, especially public shaming and the trauma inflicted on suspects and their families, yet lack insight into hunters’ motivations beyond their stated aim of protecting children. This gap persists because existing research relies on social-psychological models that essentialize vigilantes through individual dispositions, neglecting the deeper phenomenological experience that drives their actions. To address this, the authors conducted a three-year phenomenological ethnography of a U.K. hunting team, asking: How do hunters’ lived experiences shape and sustain their use of extreme practices? Drawing on Heideggerian phenomenology, they deploy the concept of "way-of-being" to explain how multiple existential orientations—including pragmatic, moralistic, narcissistic, traumatic, and heroic—suffuse hunters' practices with layered affectivity that constitutes their identity and reinforces persistence. The study advances theoretical understanding of lived experience in organizational action while offering practical insight for law enforcement seeking more constructive engagement with such civic interventions.

title: Identity–Society (Mis)Alignment and the Instrumentalization of Firm Creation: Creative Destruction and Creative Reconstruction

entries.rq_with_context: Research on founder identity has advanced our understanding of entrepreneurship, yet it typically assumes that a founder's identity is aligned with their sociocultural context—treating this alignment as a background condition. This study challenges that implicit assumption by exploring what happens when founders' identities are misaligned with their perceived social structures. The gap lies in understanding how such (mis)alignment influences venture creation, especially with regard to ventures that challenge or seek to reconstruct sociocultural norms. The research asks: How does the alignment or misalignment between an entrepreneur’s identity and their perceived sociocultural context influence new venture creation? Drawing on 49 qualitative interviews with founders in Taiwan—a context of traditional and modern coexistence—the study uses identity theory and structural analysis to examine how tensions or reinforcement from (mis)alignment shape venture outcomes. The authors identify a mechanism linking identity and society that explains variation in venture types, especially those with sociopolitical missions.

title: Pumping the Brakes: Examining the Impact of CEO Political Ideology Divergence on Firm Responses

entries.rq_with_context: Research on CEO political ideology has shown its influence on various firm outcomes, but it remains unclear how a mismatch between a CEO’s ideology and the national political climate impacts strategic decision-making. While prior work treats political ideology as a static value system, this study addresses the gap by exploring how ideological divergence creates a perceived threat that alters CEO behavior. The authors propose that when the national political climate diverges from a CEO’s ideology, it triggers threat responses in the form of reduced R&D spending and increased retained earnings. Drawing on upper echelons theory and threat response theory, the study further examines two boundary conditions: CEO vested stock options as an amplifier of threat sensitivity and industry regulation as a constraint on threat response. The key contribution is demonstrating that ideological divergence—not ideology alone—drives strategic shifts, advancing understanding of how political context interacts with executive cognition.

title: The Fragility of Experts: A Moderated-Mediation Model of Expertise, Expert Identity Threat, and Overprecision

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations rely on experts for critical decisions, particularly in uncertain contexts, yet research on expert judgment reveals mixed and sometimes contradictory findings about accuracy and overconfidence. While experts are expected to be more accurate and self-aware, evidence shows they are often no better than novices—and sometimes worse—especially in complex, unpredictable domains. A key unresolved issue is how experts respond to negative feedback, which is common in high-stakes settings. Existing work emphasizes cognitive factors and task structure, but overlooks social and identity-based responses. This paper investigates how disconfirming feedback triggers identity threat among experts, leading to greater overprecision in judgments. Using a moderated-mediation model tested across lab and field studies, the authors explore the mechanisms linking expertise, identity threat, and judgment bias. The research contributes by identifying expert identity threat as a key factor that can undermine decision quality, offering insight into when experts may become less reliable despite their knowledge.

title: Divergent Market Reactions to Abstract Language: A Multicountry Event Study of European Central Bank Communications

entries.rq_with_context: Global leaders increasingly communicate with diverse international audiences, but we know little about how strategic communication affects markets in economically unequal settings. While prior research shows abstract language can build consensus within homogeneous markets, it overlooks how audience heterogeneity—especially along core-periphery lines—might lead to divergent interpretations. This paper investigates whether ECB presidents’ use of abstract language produces different market reactions in core versus peripheral eurozone countries. Drawing on world systems theory, the authors argue that due to differing levels of trust and preferences for status quo change, core country markets will react more positively to abstract language, while peripheral countries will prefer concreteness. Using a multicountry event study of 548 ECB speeches from 1998–2015, they analyze cumulative abnormal returns in 11 eurozone countries. The study contributes by revealing how global communication strategies can backfire when audiences have divergent interests.

title: Perceived Firm-Specific Human Capital: Mobility Constraint or Enhancer?

entries.rq_with_context: This study investigates the relationship between workers' perceptions of firm-specific human capital (FSHC) and their likelihood of turnover. While existing resource-based theory assumes actual FSHC limits mobility because skills are less valuable elsewhere, this rests on assumptions of labor market efficiency that may not hold. There is little evidence that actual FSHC constrains mobility, and it is difficult to measure. In contrast, supply-side theories emphasize workers' perceptions and agency in mobility decisions. We therefore examine whether perceived FSHC—workers' beliefs about the specificity of their skills—is linked to higher turnover. Using four datasets from South Korea and the U.S., we test whether this relationship is mediated by job satisfaction and embeddedness and moderated by job autonomy importance. Our contribution is showing that perceived FSHC increases mobility, challenging dominant demand-side assumptions in human capital theory.

title: Top Management Team Experiential Variety, Competitive Repertoires, and Firm Performance: Examining the Law of Requisite Variety in the 3D Printing Industry (1986–2017)

entries.rq_with_context: The law of requisite variety (LRV) suggests that organizational survival depends on matching internal variety with external environmental variety, but prior research has oversimplified this principle by focusing only on absolute levels of behavioral variety rather than calibrated fit. Studies have typically assumed that more diverse top management teams (TMTs) automatically lead to better performance through increased competitive action variety, without testing the mediating role of calibration. This paper addresses three key gaps: the lack of clear metrics for assessing repertoire calibration, the narrow focus on complexity alone, and the absence of empirical verification of the full LRV chain from TMT diversity to performance via calibrated repertoires. The research asks whether TMT industry experience variety enables firms to calibrate both the complexity and consistency of their competitive repertoires to match those of top performers, and whether this calibration improves performance. Using hand-collected data from the 3D printing industry (1986–2017), the study applies a longitudinal panel design to model the indirect effects of TMT variety through calibrated repertoires. The key contribution is providing empirical validation of the LRV's core thesis in strategic management by demonstrating that performance benefits come not from variety per se, but from its role in achieving calibrated behavioral fit with the environment.

title: CEO Attentional Vigilance: Behavioral Implications for the Pursuit of Exploration

entries.rq_with_context: Firms often struggle to maintain exploration due to organizational inertia favoring exploitation. While prior research emphasizes the amount of CEO attention as critical for strategic outcomes, this paper identifies a gap: sustained attention (vigilance) may matter more than sheer quantity for exploration, which is vulnerable to interruptions. The study asks whether CEO attentional vigilance positively impacts a firm’s exploration rate, even when controlling for attention quantity. Using longitudinal data from software firms, it applies text analysis to earnings calls to measure vigilance and tests the role of performance feedback and employee satisfaction. The key contribution is showing that consistency of attention, not just volume, drives exploration, advancing the attention-based view by introducing temporal stability as a critical dimension.

title: Strategic Nepotism in Family Director Appointments: Evidence from Family Business Groups in South Korea

entries.rq_with_context: Family firms often appoint family members to leadership positions to preserve socioemotional wealth (SEW), such as family identity and control, but this can come at the expense of financial performance if appointees lack managerial competence. While prior research recognizes this trade-off, it has not adequately explained how controlling families might actively manage it. This paper addresses that gap by investigating whether family appointments to boards are used not just for SEW preservation but also as a strategic tool to develop managerial resources. Using data from South Korean family business groups, the authors examine whether family members are preferentially placed in firms with high market performance, strong reputations, and central network positions, while being shielded from distressed firms or boards already dominated by family. The study also explores whether these patterns are stronger for later-generation members, who face greater challenges in proving their merit. The approach combines socioemotional wealth theory with board capital and stigma avoidance literatures. The key contribution is introducing 'strategic nepotism' as a proactive mechanism through which families shape the SEW–financial wealth trade-off in their favor.

title: More than a Feeling: How Board Member Displays of Anger and Happiness Influence Strategic Decisions

entries.rq_with_context: Board members play a key role in shaping strategic decisions, yet little is known about how their interpersonal behaviors—specifically emotional expressions—affect influence during meetings. While research has moved beyond viewing boards solely as monitoring bodies, there remains limited understanding of the micro-level dynamics that enable some directors to shape decisions more than others. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how nonverbal emotional displays impact influence. Drawing on the Emotions as Social Information (EASI) model, the authors propose that peak displays of anger enhance focused influence (direct persuasion of top managers), while peak displays of happiness increase diffuse influence (gaining board-wide support). They test these ideas using video data from 68 board meetings across four Dutch water management organizations. The study contributes by revealing distinct pathways through which emotions operate in corporate governance settings, offering empirical evidence on how affect shapes strategic leadership interactions.

title: The Past Is Prologue? Venture-Capital Syndicates’ Collaborative Experience and Start-Up Exits

entries.rq_with_context: Prior research on interorganizational collaboration presents conflicting findings about whether prior relationships between organizations enhance or hinder collective performance. Some studies suggest that relational embeddedness improves collaboration through trust and coordination, while others warn of rigidity and overembeddedness. This study addresses the unresolved question of when prior collaboration leads to collaborative success by distinguishing between two types of outcomes: focused and broadcast successes. The authors argue that the effect of relational embeddedness depends on the nature of the success being pursued. Using a sample of nearly 11,000 U.S. start-ups funded by VC syndicates, they test whether prior coinvestment experience among VCs predicts the likelihood of a start-up exiting via acquisition or IPO. Their approach uses longitudinal data and competing-risks hazard models to isolate the impact of relational embeddedness. The key contribution is resolving contradictions in the literature by showing that relational embeddedness promotes different kinds of success depending on the outcome type.

title: Custodianship across Generations: Preserving the Practice of Vinyl Record Manufacturing

entries.rq_with_context: The phenomenon of declining practices—such as film photography, typewriter production, and violin making—raises the question of how some manage to survive long after market relevance fades. While practice studies have focused on emergence, growth, and diffusion, the work involved in preserving practices in decline remains understudied. Existing custodianship literature emphasizes symbolic meanings and institutional guarding but pays less attention to how materials and competences are regenerated and transferred across generations. This leaves a gap in understanding how declining practices avoid extinction. The authors address this by asking: How can custodians preserve a declining practice across generations? Using a longitudinal case study of vinyl record manufacturing, they adopt Shove et al.’s (2012) practice framework—comprising meanings, materials, and competences—to trace preservation efforts. The study identifies distinct custodian roles and processes that sustain the practice through diversification and intergenerational support. Its key contribution is a process model showing how preservation hinges not on defending uniformity but on enabling multiple, resilient variants through inclusive custodianship.

title: Which Ideas for Change Are Endorsed? How Agentic and Communal Voice Affects Endorsement Differently for Men and for Women

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates which ideas for change are endorsed and how this depends on the speaker's gender and the nature of their voice. While prior research has examined idea endorsement based on content or presentation in isolation, this study highlights a gap in understanding how speaker gender interacts with voice characteristics. The authors argue that idea endorsement is shaped by whether the speaker’s voice positively violates gender expectations—termed 'positive counter-stereotypical voice'—such as agentic (task-oriented, assertive) voice by women and communal (relational, polite) voice by men. Drawing on expectancy violations theory, they propose that such violations lead to higher endorsement because they trigger stronger attributions of competence for women and benevolence for men. The research uses one field study and two experiments to test these claims, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of gender dynamics in voice evaluation.

title: The Interactive Effects of Abusive CEOs and Philanthropic Corporate Social Responsibility on Organizational Innovation and Performance

entries.rq_with_context: CEO abusive leadership is a pervasive yet understudied phenomenon at the organizational level, particularly in how it undermines team processes and firm outcomes. While prior research has explored positive CEO leadership styles or other negative traits like narcissism, less is known about how direct, sustained abusive behaviors from CEOs affect top management teams and organizational performance. Furthermore, CEOs often engage in philanthropic CSR, which may signal inconsistent treatment when paired with internal abuse. We address this gap by investigating how CEO abusive leadership diminishes TMT behavioral integration, thereby reducing organizational innovation and performance, and whether philanthropic CSR strengthens this indirect negative effect. Drawing on upper echelons theory and the CEO–TMT interface perspective, we use data from two studies involving SMEs in China. We contribute by revealing the interactive harm of abusive leadership and outwardly positive CSR when internal treatment is poor.

title: Constructing Envelopes: How Institutional Custodians Can Tame Disruptive Algorithms

entries.rq_with_context: As algorithms increasingly disrupt organizational fields—transforming practices, destabilizing expertise, and challenging norms—actors often respond defensively. One important but poorly understood response is the construction of 'envelopes,' or boundaries that constrain how algorithms interact with their environments without altering the algorithms themselves. While prior research highlights the opacity and speed of algorithms as barriers to regulation, less is known about the collective processes through which such envelopes emerge. This study addresses that gap by focusing on institutional custodians—actors motivated to preserve valued elements of fields. Using the rise of high-frequency trading in U.S. securities markets (2009–2016) as a case, the authors explore how custodians constructed an envelope around this disruptive technology. The study employs inductive analysis of interviews, hearings, and media to develop a process model. It contributes by theorizing envelope construction as a layered, conjunctive process involving multiple types of custodians, thereby advancing understanding of algorithmic governance and custodial work.

title: Hiding and Seeking Knowledge-Providing Ties from Rivals: A Strategic Perspective on Network Perceptions

entries.rq_with_context: Rivalry in organizations, often fueled by structural equivalence—where individuals share similar network connections—is linked to heightened competition and strategic behavior. While prior research has theorized that structural equivalence can lead to rivalry, the assumption that individuals act strategically by hiding their own knowledge sources and detecting those of rivals has not been empirically tested. This paper addresses this gap by asking whether people perceive structurally equivalent colleagues as rivals and whether such perceptions lead them to hide their knowledge-providing relationships and seek out those of their rivals. Using two experiments and a field study, the authors test these propositions. They find that perceived structural equivalence does induce rivalry and leads to intentions and behaviors related to hiding and seeking. The main contribution is providing first evidence that rivalry based on network perceptions drives strategic manipulation of social network visibility, with implications for understanding covert competition in organizations.

title: Revving Up or Backing Down? Cross-Level Effects of Firm-Level Tournaments on Employees’ Competitive Actions

entries.rq_with_context: Employees often compete for career advancement within individual-level tournaments, but these are typically nested within firm-level tournaments where organizations vie for market position, contracts, or rankings. While prior research has focused on individual tournament characteristics (e.g., reward spread) as drivers of competitive behavior, little attention has been paid to how firm-level competitive dynamics might shape employees’ actions. This paper addresses that gap by investigating how a firm’s competitive threats (risk of losing standing) and opportunities (chance to gain standing) influence employees’ decisions to engage in internal versus external competitive actions. Drawing on reputational incentives theory, the authors propose that employees adjust their behavior based on how firm-level dynamics may affect their personal reputation. Using panel data from MotoGP riders (2004–2020), they measure internal and external overtakes as competitive actions. The key contribution is demonstrating that firm-level tournament conditions—not just individual-level ones—shape employee competition, offering a multilevel extension to tournament theory.

title: Credentials or Chemistry? Entrepreneur Gender and Cofounder Selection

entries.rq_with_context: Research on entrepreneurial networking suggests women may prioritize resource-rich cofounders to counter investor bias, while research on gender in networking suggests women prefer cofounders based on personal chemistry and trust. These competing predictions create a puzzle about how women actually choose cofounders. This paper addresses this gap by asking: How, when, and why do women differ from men in cofounder selection? The authors propose that women generally favor interpersonal attraction due to higher interdependent self-construal but shift toward resource seeking when legitimacy is low. Using an interactionist model integrating gender, self-construal, and legitimacy, the study tests this framework across three studies. The key contribution is reconciling conflicting predictions by showing that women’s cofounder selection is flexible and context-dependent, shaped by both internal preferences and external pressures.

title: Fairness Judgments in the Context of Structural Sexism: The Role of Beliefs in Individual and Structural Causes of Success

entries.rq_with_context: Women often face lower performance ratings due to structural sexism, creating tension between merit-based allocations and fairness. While equity theory suggests outcomes should match contributions, it's unclear whether observers view adjustments for structural barriers as fairer or less fair than relying on raw performance indicators. Prior research offers conflicting predictions and often fails to account for how people interpret causal information about structural barriers. This study addresses this gap by proposing that beliefs about the causes of success—specifically whether success stems from individual effort or structural advantages—influence how observers weigh performance data when judging fairness. Using experimental studies, the authors examine how these beliefs shape fairness judgments when information about structural sexism is present versus absent. The research contributes by showing how meritocratic beliefs interact with contextual information to shape fairness perceptions, helping reconcile equity principles with social justice concerns.

title: Screening Theory and Its Boundaries: Investigation of Screen Credibility, Necessity, and Salience in the Context of Corporate Venture Capital

entries.rq_with_context: Corporate venture capital (CVC) decisions in unfamiliar industries are fraught with uncertainty, prompting decision-makers to rely on external cues to guide funding termination. While screening theory explains how actors use information to reduce information asymmetry, it lacks clarity on when and under what conditions such screens are effective. This paper identifies three boundary conditions—screen credibility, screen necessity, and screen salience to the screener—that determine when a screen influences decision-making. The research question is whether and when CVC decision-makers use their firm’s quality shareholders’ (QSs) industry investment patterns as a screen for funding termination decisions. Using archival data and a policy-capturing study, the authors test these ideas within diversifying CVC contexts. Their contribution is extending screening theory by specifying boundary conditions that clarify its applicability and efficacy in strategic decision-making.

title: Linguistic Inclusiveness in Organizations: A Russophone Bank in Post-Soviet Kazakhstan

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly face pressure to provide multilingual services externally while relying on a common corporate language internally. Language is both a skill and a source of identity, and low-status language speakers may experience identity-based exclusion even when fluent in the corporate language. While prior research treats language mainly as a skill, it often overlooks how linguistic identity intersects with other marginalized identities. This gap is especially salient in post-colonial or multilingual societies where societal changes elevate the status of previously marginalized languages. We thus investigate: How can linguistic inclusiveness emerge among tensions between the demands for multilingual services and the need for a lingua franca in organizations? Drawing on a qualitative study of a Russophone bank in post-Soviet Kazakhstan, we analyze how actors from different linguistic backgrounds engage in sociolinguistic work—everyday actions that shape language practices. Our findings reveal how inclusiveness develops through interactions involving a marginalized group (Kazakhophone language workers), a dominant group (Russophone monolingual bankers), and an in-between group (receptive bilingual bankers), highlighting the process by which recognition of linguistic identity unfolds.

title: Balancing Professional Autonomy and Managerial Goals amid Broad Technology Adoption Pressures: Intraprofessional Segmentation at a Finnish School

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often face tension between managerial desires for technology adoption and professionals' resistance due to their autonomy. While prior research has explored this tension in the context of specific technologies, less is known about how it plays out under broad technology adoption pressures—expectations to adopt from wide technological categories without clear prescriptions, success criteria, or sanctions. This study investigates how a Finnish school navigated this challenge through a 16-month ethnography. It asks how professional communities respond when pressured to embrace broad technological change without concrete directives. The authors use qualitative data to trace the emergence of intraprofessional segmentation as a response. Their key contribution is showing how such segmentation can serve as a middle ground that accommodates both managerial goals and professional autonomy in ambiguous technological environments.

title: How Much Inequity Do You See? Structural Power, Perceptions of Gender and Racial Inequity, and Support for Diversity Initiatives

entries.rq_with_context: Despite substantial investments in diversity initiatives, these efforts often fail due to lack of managerial support. While existing research attributes resistance to managers' demographic or ideological characteristics, anecdotal evidence shows even equity-minded leaders like Marc Benioff initially deny inequity in their own organizations. This suggests a gap in understanding how the managerial role itself may contribute to resistance. The authors propose that structural power fosters organizational identification, which motivates a positive view of the organization and thus reduces perceived inequity. Using archival data and surveys across multiple studies, they test whether structural power leads to lower perceptions of inequity via organizational identification, resulting in less support for diversity initiatives. Their key contribution is shifting the explanation of resistance from individual traits to the psychological effects of holding power within an organization.

title: Intra-Individual Conflict and Task Performance in a Multiteam Context: Examining the Structural Elements of Conflict Experience

entries.rq_with_context: Conflict is a common phenomenon in team settings, yet research on individual conflict experiences has yielded inconsistent results regarding their impact on performance. This inconsistency may stem from treating conflict as an inter-individual or aggregated construct, thereby overlooking its inherently intra-individual nature. The authors argue that prior research fails to account for the structural elements of conflict: its direction (whether one sends or receives conflict) and its boundary (within-team or between-team). To resolve this, they propose a cognitive process framework grounded in attentional self-regulation theory. They investigate how these two structural elements shape task performance via mechanisms of on-task attentional pull and off-task attentional demands. Using behavioral data from emergency response simulations and experimental scenarios, the study tests when and why certain conflict configurations help or harm performance, offering a more nuanced understanding of conflict dynamics in multiteam systems.

title: How Do Fieldworkers in Poverty Craft Meaningful Roles to Achieve Social Impact? Female Teachers in Slums in India

entries.rq_with_context: Fieldworkers such as teachers, health workers, and microfinance agents are crucial for achieving social impact in impoverished communities, yet little is known about how they navigate extreme challenges like low pay, household responsibilities, and limited autonomy. While job-crafting theory suggests employees proactively shape their roles to find meaning, it remains unclear whether this applies in contexts of poverty where resources like time and energy are severely depleted. This paper studies female para-teachers in Indian slums to explore how they engage in relational job crafting—extending interactions with students and parents beyond formal duties—and how stressors related to financial dependence and lack of family support affect this behavior. Using a mixed-methods approach, the authors test whether community identification buffers these challenges and enables social impact. The study contributes by contextualizing job-crafting theory in an under-researched, high-stress setting and linking employee behavior directly to beneficiary outcomes.

title: Firm–Stakeholder Dialogue and the Media: The Evolution of Stakeholder Evaluations in Different Informational Environments

entries.rq_with_context: Scholarship on stakeholder evaluations has largely focused on reputational damage and remedial responses following corporate scandals or accidents, while under-examining how ongoing, proactive interactions—like firm–stakeholder dialogue—shape stakeholder perceptions. Moreover, most research assumes stakeholders operate in information-rich, reliable media environments, despite growing global concerns about misinformation, media censorship, and uneven coverage. This study identifies a key gap: we lack understanding of how the broader informational environment influences the effectiveness of firm–stakeholder dialogue. The research question is whether proactive dialogue's effect on stakeholder evaluations depends on three dimensions: how much information is available about the firm, what kind of information (particularly ESG-related content) is circulating, and how reliable the media is perceived to be. Using stakeholder-level data from 26 global mining projects, the authors analyze media-reported interactions and evaluation patterns through a multilevel model. Their contribution lies in showing that dialogue’s effectiveness is not uniform but highly contingent, challenging assumptions that stakeholder engagement always improves evaluations.

title: Faking It with the Boss’s Jokes? Leader Humor Quantity, Follower Surface Acting, and Power Distance

entries.rq_with_context: Most research concludes that leader humor benefits follower well-being by inducing positive emotions. However, this view is incomplete because prior studies often conflate humor expression (quantity) with humor quality (effectiveness) and overlook how followers regulate their emotions. This paper addresses these gaps by investigating the emotional costs of frequent leader humor expression, regardless of whether the jokes are funny. The authors argue that frequent humor from leaders creates pressure for followers to display positive emotions, prompting surface acting—faking or exaggerating amusement. They propose this is especially true for followers with high power distance, who are more inclined to comply with authority. Using three studies (a field experiment, a lab experiment, and a multi-wave field study), the paper applies emotional regulation and power theory to explore these dynamics. The key contribution is demonstrating that while leader humor is often seen as beneficial, its mere frequency can harm follower well-being through increased emotional labor.

title: The Outcomes of Cross-Category Career Moves: How Cross-Industry Mobility and Industry Prestige Jointly Impact Executive Compensation

entries.rq_with_context: Executives frequently move across industries, but it remains unclear how such cross-category moves impact their compensation. Prior research has produced conflicting findings—some suggesting a generalist premium, others a specialist advantage—yet most studies focus on accumulated experience rather than specific job moves. This study addresses that gap by analyzing the immediate compensation effects of voluntary cross-industry mobility. It further considers how industry-status differences shape these outcomes, proposing that both audience evaluations (demand side) and executives’ willingness to trade pay for status (supply side) depend on relative industry prestige. Using longitudinal data on S&P 1500 executives, the study tests whether industry-changing moves lead to different compensation outcomes than within-industry moves, and how this effect is moderated by status differences. The findings contribute to category and status-attainment research by showing how categorical mobility and vertical status hierarchies jointly shape labor-market outcomes.

title: Avoidance and Aggression in Stakeholder Engagement: The Impact of CEO Paranoia and Paranoia-Relevant Cues

entries.rq_with_context: CEOs may view stakeholders through a lens of paranoia, characterized by suspicion, mistrust, and belief in external malevolent influence. While prior research has linked CEO traits to strategic actions, little attention has been paid to how subclinical paranoia influences stakeholder engagement strategies, or why these strategies might shift over time. Existing upper echelons theory assumes relative stability in trait effects, but does not account for situational triggers that may activate certain tendencies. This paper addresses this gap by asking how CEO paranoia influences engagement with powerful stakeholders (government and competitors), and how paranoia-relevant cues alter this relationship. Drawing on trait activation theory, the authors propose that CEOs high in paranoia initially avoid engagement but shift to aggressive behaviors when cues signal that avoidance has failed. The key contribution is demonstrating that CEO traits can dynamically manifest depending on environmental triggers, advancing both upper echelons and stakeholder theories.

title: Performance Shortfalls, Response Directions, and Belief in the Effectiveness of Responses

entries.rq_with_context: When firms face performance shortfalls, they may respond in various ways, but existing research has largely focused on abstract decision rules—like proximity, time horizon, and risk-taking—to predict search directions, implicitly assuming all considered responses are effective. This paper challenges that assumption by asking how decision-makers’ beliefs about a response’s actual effectiveness shape their choices. Specifically, it explores whether shared beliefs within top management teams regarding the effectiveness of R&D or corporate social responsibility (CSR) influence how firms adjust these investments after poor performance. The authors argue that when decision-makers collectively believe a response works, they are more likely to adopt it, especially if supported by evidence like past performance correlations. Using panel data from Chinese listed firms (2009–2018), they test this via textual analysis of management discussions and financial data. The key contribution is showing that belief in action–outcome linkages—not just abstract response characteristics—shapes problemistic search.

title: Turning Work into a Refuge: Job Crafting as Coping with Personal, Grief-Inducing Events

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates how work can serve as a refuge for employees experiencing personal grief from events like bereavement or breakup—among the most stressful life experiences. While prior research has framed work either as a burden or a passive source of distraction during grief, it largely overlooks the active role employees play in shaping their work experience. This study addresses that gap by asking: How, and with what consequences, can work become a refuge from grief-inducing experiences? Using an inductive, qualitative approach based on 68 in-depth interviews, the author develops a model grounded in job crafting theory. The key contribution is revealing that grieving employees actively turn work into a refuge through promotion-oriented job crafting, challenging the assumption of passivity and highlighting agency in grief management.

title: Coevolutionary Lock-In in External Search

entries.rq_with_context: While external search is often seen as a way for organizations to access diverse, novel ideas from outside, it frequently results in a narrow set of similar suggestions. Existing research has not fully explained why this narrowing occurs, especially in ongoing crowdsourcing contexts. This paper identifies a coevolutionary lock-in process where organizational selection shapes contributor behavior: contributors infer preferences from past selections and either stop submitting (self-select out) or adjust their ideas to align with perceived preferences. The central research question is: How does an organization’s selection consistency affect the future variety of ideas submitted by external contributors? Using longitudinal data from 1,218 organizations engaged in crowdsourcing, the authors analyze idea content via natural language processing and network methods. They find that higher selection consistency reduces subsequent idea variety, with effects moderated by contributor churn and cohesion. The study contributes by redefining external search as a two-way interaction rather than a passive reception of ideas.

title: Happy Talk: Is Common Diversity Rhetoric Effective Diversity Rhetoric?

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the prevalence of diversity initiatives, organizations often fail to achieve diversity and inclusion goals, partly because these initiatives do not consistently motivate employees to support them. Prior research has focused on value-in-diversity rhetoric, which emphasizes the benefits of diversity, and found it often effective but potentially disconnected from the reality that diversity can have both positive and negative outcomes. This paper investigates a new form of rhetoric—contingent-diversity rhetoric—that acknowledges diversity's challenges while asserting its benefits if those challenges are overcome. Drawing on self-presentation theory and goal-setting theory, the authors examine whether this rhetoric is less common due to leaders' fear of appearing prejudiced, and whether it is more effective because it increases perceptions of goal difficulty. The research uses archival, experimental, and survey methods. The key contribution is identifying a descriptive–prescriptive paradox in diversity rhetoric: contingent rhetoric is underused but more effective than the dominant value-based rhetoric.

title: Bricks without Straw: Overcoming Resource Limitations to Architect Ecosystem Leadership

entries.rq_with_context: While much research focuses on how focal firms lead ecosystems, less attention has been paid to how peripheral complementors with limited resources can rise to leadership positions. Unlike dominant firms, these complementors cannot set participation rules or access critical supply-side assets. This gap is especially relevant given that most ecosystem participants are small, resource-constrained actors. The paper asks: How does a resource-disadvantaged complementor architect ecosystem leadership? Drawing on a nine-year longitudinal study of Xiaomi, which began as a software complementor in the Android ecosystem, the authors trace how the firm used community-driven innovation and user mobilization to transition into a hardware leader and eventually an orchestrator of its own derivative ecosystem. The approach combines demand-side engagement with strategic supply-side orchestration. The key contribution is revealing how firms without superior resources can build power by integrating demand mobilization with resource coalescing.

title: Tick Off the Gender Diversity Box: Examining the Cross-Level Effects of Women’s Representation in Senior Management

entries.rq_with_context: Firms under pressure to improve gender diversity often increase women's representation in senior roles, which can enhance legitimacy and stakeholder trust. However, this external progress may lead organizations to reduce attention to internal diversity initiatives, potentially harming junior women's hiring outcomes. While prior research has documented adverse spillover effects of top management diversity, it remains unclear how this affects lower-level hiring and what mechanisms drive these effects. This paper investigates whether firms with relatively higher gender diversity at the top extend fewer job offers to junior women due to decreased engagement with internal diversity practices. Using panel data from U.S. law firms, the authors employ an attention-based perspective to analyze cross-level effects. They propose that women's substantive representation on diversity and hiring committees can mitigate these adverse spillovers by maintaining organizational focus on diversity issues.

title: Collaborating on the Edge of Failure: Frame Alignment across Multiple Interaction Arenas in Multi-Stakeholder Partnerships

entries.rq_with_context: Multi-stakeholder partnerships (MSPs) face significant challenges in sustaining collaboration due to conflicting agendas and symbolic commitments. While framing theory explains how shared understanding is built among partners, little attention has been paid to how negotiated frames must also gain acceptance from stakeholders' constituents—a challenge known as the 'two-table problem.' This paper investigates how participants in the German Partnership for Sustainable Textiles navigated this issue over six years, especially when public pressure had waned. The research asks: How do multiple interaction arenas affect frame alignment, and how can it be navigated across these arenas? Using a longitudinal process study and interactional framing theory, the authors trace how frame alignment unfolded through relational, issue, and process framing. They show that sustained collaboration required stretching frames across arenas through reciprocal, integrative, and bilateral processes, contributing a dynamic model of frame alignment that explains how partnerships survive near collapse.

title: Coherence within and across Categories: The Dynamic Viability of Product Categories on Kickstarter

entries.rq_with_context: Product categories are central to market organization, yet their viability—whether they remain in active use—fluctuates over time. While prior research has focused on single categories in isolation, it remains unclear how related categories influence a focal category’s fate. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how both intra-category dynamics (a category’s internal heterogeneity) and inter-category dynamics (its distinctiveness relative to related categories) jointly shape category viability. Drawing on classification and valuation benefits, we propose that the effect of heterogeneity on viability shifts depending on a category’s distinctiveness. Using longitudinal data from 170 Kickstarter categories over 11 years, we test these dynamics. Our contribution lies in showing how category viability emerges from the interaction between internal variation and external positioning, offering a more nuanced model of category evolution.

title: The Social Structure of Insiders and Outsiders: Toward a Network Community Perspective on Firm Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Prior research on interorganizational networks has emphasized connections, positions, and cliques as key drivers of firm performance. However, a theoretical tension remains between the need for cohesive networks and openness to new ideas. This paper addresses this gap by introducing the concept of network communities—overlapping, cohesive structures that balance closure and access. The authors investigate whether VC firms affiliated with network communities (insiders) perform better than those not affiliated (outsiders), when the benefits of multiple affiliations decline, and how institutional development moderates these effects. Using community-detection algorithms and longitudinal data from China’s VC industry, they test these relationships. The study contributes by isolating the effect of network communities, revealing their performance implications, and integrating social network and institutional perspectives.

title: External Disruption Following CEO Succession: How Human and Social Capital Changes May Attract Competitive Attacks

entries.rq_with_context: CEO succession is known to cause internal disruption due to changes in strategic direction and organizational relationships, but little research explores how such internal changes affect the external competitive environment. While prior studies focus on performance outcomes within the firm, this paper addresses a gap by examining how competitors may perceive CEO succession as an opportunity to exploit or a future threat to preempt. The research question is: How do internal disruptions due to human or social capital changes in the CEO position lead to external disruption by attracting competitors’ attacks? Drawing from executive capital theories, the authors use a sample of S&P 500 firms from 2010–2018 to test the effects of predecessor–successor professional experience differential (PSPED) and insider–outsider status on competitive attacks. The key contribution is introducing a theory of disruption that links internal governance events to external competitive dynamics.

title: When and How Artificial Intelligence Augments Employee Creativity

entries.rq_with_context: Employee creativity is vital for organizational performance, and industry leaders suggest AI can enhance it by freeing workers to focus on creative tasks. However, there is limited theoretical and empirical evidence on whether AI actually boosts creativity and under what conditions. The study addresses this gap by analyzing a sequential division of labor in which AI performs well-codified, repetitive tasks and human employees handle higher-level problem-solving. Using a field experiment and interviews in a telemarketing company, the authors investigate whether this setup increases creativity and how employee job skills moderate the outcome. They find that AI assistance increases creativity on average, but significantly more so for higher-skilled employees, contributing causal evidence and theoretical insight into skill-biased AI-augmented creativity.

title: When the Symphony Does Jazz: How Resourcefulness Fosters Organizational Resilience during Adversity

entries.rq_with_context: The COVID-19 pandemic created unprecedented adversity for organizations, especially in the performing arts, where traditional operations became impossible. While research has shown that resources are critical for resilience, less is known about how organizations generate and reconfigure resources under extreme constraints. Existing studies often focus on survival or bouncing back, but do not explain the processes through which some organizations not only survive but transform. This paper addresses the gap by asking: How do established organizations use resourcefulness to act resiliently during a crisis? Drawing on a grounded theory study of two orchestras, the authors analyze how resourcefulness unfolds over time. They develop a process model showing how initial responses lead to divergent trajectories of resilience. The key contribution is unpacking the mechanisms—such as crisis agency, trust, and identity expansion—that determine whether organizations adjust weakly or strongly to adversity.

title: Dirty Heroes? Healthcare Workers’ Experience of Mixed Social Evaluations during the Pandemic

entries.rq_with_context: Healthcare workers faced a paradox during the pandemic: they were publicly praised as heroes for their frontline service, yet privately stigmatized as contamination risks by the same society. While research on stigma has traditionally focused on uniformly negative evaluations, and studies on moralization on uniformly positive ones, this binary approach overlooks the reality of mixed social evaluations increasingly common in polarized contexts. The gap lies in understanding how workers process and respond to such contradictory judgments—both celebration and stigma—especially in high-legitimacy professions. This study asks: How do stigmatized workers experience, evaluate, and respond to mixed social evaluations, such as being called a 'dirty hero'? Using grounded theory and interviews with 98 healthcare workers, the authors explore the conditions under which workers accept or reject these evaluations. They highlight criteria like proximity, informedness, and authenticity in shaping responses. The authors claim a theoretical contribution by introducing 'dirty heroes' and 'hero-washing,' showing how mixed evaluations disrupt identity and generate complex internalization outcomes.

title: Left Behind? Understanding the Career Consequences of Collaborator Exits

entries.rq_with_context: Prior research on career interdependence has focused on how colleague exits create job vacancies that lead to vacancy-driven promotions. However, less is known about other ways these exits affect employees' careers, especially in collaborative knowledge work. This paper addresses this gap by investigating whether colleague exits create relational 'vacancies' that open new collaboration opportunities and enhance learning, thereby increasing the likelihood of competency-driven promotion—advancement based on skill development rather than job openings. Using longitudinal data from a scientific research organization, the study tests whether collaborator exits (but not noncollaborator exits) increase such promotions, particularly when the exiting collaborator is at a higher job grade. The approach draws on vacancy chain theory applied to collaboration networks. The key contribution is identifying a novel mechanism—relational vacancies—through which colleague mobility shapes intraorganizational careers beyond traditional job structures.

title: Media Coverage of Firms in the Presence of Multiple Signals: A Configurational Approach

entries.rq_with_context: Firms face competing pressures to appear both legitimate through conformity and competitive through distinctiveness, leading them to orchestrate mixed signals to achieve 'optimal distinctiveness.' However, it remains unclear how external audiences like the media interpret these multiple, potentially conflicting signals and what combinations lead to positive evaluations. While optimal distinctiveness theory suggests that balancing conformity and distinctiveness is beneficial, signaling theory predicts that incongruent messages will be penalized. This paper addresses this puzzle by investigating how the media assess firms based on various signal combinations in the context of environmental sustainability. Using a configurational approach (fsQCA) on data from 118 firm-year observations in the energy utility industry, the authors analyze how different mixes of six types of signals—varying by content (conformity vs. distinctiveness) and source (firm, relationship, third-party)—relate to media coverage outcomes. The study's main contribution is uncovering the conditions under which mixed signals are rewarded or punished, highlighting the critical role of signal credibility in shaping audience perceptions of congruence.

title: Echoes from the Past: The Impact of Racial Transference on Leader Selection during Succession

entries.rq_with_context: Leader selection during succession is a critical process that can perpetuate racial inequality. While leader categorization theory (LCT) dominates explanations of racial bias—arguing that evaluators prefer White leaders due to prototypical traits or minority leaders during crises (e.g., Glass Cliff effect)—this framework may not apply when a predecessor exists. During succession, evaluators compare candidates to the predecessor, shifting focus from abstract stereotypes to concrete comparisons. This paper argues that LCT is insufficient in this context and introduces 'racial transference' as an alternative bias: evaluators falsely assume that candidates share personality traits with racially similar predecessors and judge them accordingly. The research question is whether predecessor performance moderates the effect of racial similarity between predecessor and candidate on leader selection. Using an archival study, a preregistered experiment, and supplementary studies, the authors test this model across sports, business, and political contexts. Their contribution is a new theoretical lens—racial transference—that better explains racial bias in succession by focusing on dyadic comparisons rather than categorical thinking.

title: How Founder Human Capital and Founding Conditions Shape New Firm Performance: A Study of Necessity Entrepreneurship during Times of Economic Crisis

entries.rq_with_context: Economic crises push many unemployed individuals into necessity entrepreneurship—starting firms out of need rather than opportunity. These entrepreneurs typically lack resources beyond their human capital, yet it remains unclear whether generalist or specialist skills are more valuable for new firm success during crises. Prior theory offers conflicting predictions: Lazear’s balanced skills theory favors generalists, while evidence on domain-specific expertise suggests specialists may thrive. This paper identifies a key gap: existing research treats crises as uniform shocks, ignoring variation in how industries are affected. The authors argue that founding conditions—specifically industry growth or decline during a crisis—moderate the value of human capital. Using survey data from 500 Greek founders during the Great Recession, combined with official industry statistics, they test how general and specific human capital influence firm performance across different industry contexts. Their approach reconciles conflicting theories by showing that the value of human capital depends on industry-level crisis severity.

title: Job Insecurity and Well-Being: Integrating Life History and Transactional Stress Theories

entries.rq_with_context: Job insecurity is increasingly common in modern work environments and generally harms employee well-being. However, prior research has not fully considered how individual differences rooted in early life experiences might shape these effects. Drawing on life history theory and transactional stress theory, this study investigates whether childhood financial standing shapes adults’ psychological responses to job insecurity. The research asks whether employees from poorer backgrounds suffer greater declines in engagement and higher emotional exhaustion when facing job insecurity compared to those from wealthier backgrounds, even when current job and financial conditions are similar. Using a longitudinal field study during the COVID-19 crisis and a quasi-experiment across India and the U.S., the study tests a model where sense of control mediates these differential effects. The key contribution is revealing that job insecurity acts as a mechanism that reproduces childhood inequalities in adulthood through stratified well-being outcomes.

title: Becoming a Right-Hand Partner: How Lower-Power Employees Heedfully Challenge Organizational Leaders

entries.rq_with_context: Powerful leaders often struggle to consider others' perspectives due to the psychological effects of power, yet they need diverse viewpoints to make effective decisions. While lower-power employees are better positioned to provide these perspectives, relational barriers like fear of speaking up and leader skepticism about motives prevent honest communication. Existing research focuses on self-interested or transactional relationships, leaving unclear how a lower-power employee can credibly challenge a leader. This study asks: How does a lower-power employee become a right-hand partner and influence a high-power organizational leader? Using qualitative data from 74 individuals (61 chiefs of staff and 13 leaders), the authors develop a process model of 'heedful challenging.' The key contribution is revealing how loyalty and a three-phase process enable influence in unequal-power relationships.

title: The Publicization of Organizational Misconduct: A Social Structural Approach

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational misconduct often remains hidden for years despite widespread private knowledge, but we know little about the contextual factors that determine whether such wrongdoing becomes public. While prior research focuses on whistleblowers or external shocks as triggers, this paper investigates how the social-structural features of communities shape the likelihood of misconduct being publicized. The authors argue that community homogeneity and the embeddedness of the offending organization increase the social cost of speaking up, while social connectedness facilitates broader information dissemination. Using data on sex abuse in the U.S. Catholic Church (1980–2010), they test whether these community-level factors explain variation in media coverage of misconduct across dioceses. The study contributes by re-conceptualizing scandal emergence as a socially embedded process shaped by community dynamics rather than isolated individual or institutional actions.

title: Responding to Professional Knowledge Disruptions of Unmitigable Uncertainty: The Role of Emotions, Practices, and Moral Duty among COVID-19 Physicians
