entries.rq_with_context: Servant leadership is widely advocated for its positive impact on followers and organizations, yet critiques suggest it may come at a personal cost to leaders, potentially leading to strain and diminished performance. While existing research acknowledges both benefits and costs, there is limited clarity on the specific mechanisms and conditions under which these opposing effects occur. This study addresses that gap by investigating the dual psychological processes—energizing through need satisfaction and draining through role conflict—through which servant leadership impacts leaders. Drawing on the demands–resources model, it proposes a dual-path model and examines how LLX acts as a critical resource that can strengthen the energizing effect and buffer the draining effect. The research uses five-wave, multisource data to test these mechanisms, aiming to clarify when and how servant leadership is beneficial or harmful for leaders themselves.

title: The benefits of cognitive style versatility for collaborative work.

entries.rq_with_context: While research has established that cognitive styles—such as object visualization, spatial visualization, and verbalization—affect how individuals process information and influence team dynamics, less attention has been paid to individuals who exhibit strength in multiple styles, known as cognitive style versatility. These versatile individuals may uniquely enhance team collaboration by improving information sharing and group cohesion. However, their specific contribution to team performance remains underexplored. This study examines whether the presence of cognitively versatile individuals improves team performance and identifies the mechanisms—such as reduced task and process conflict and increased social integration—through which this effect occurs. Using data from two team studies involving 452 participants, the authors test their hypotheses using regression and mediation analyses. The findings contribute to team composition research by highlighting the value of intra-individual diversity in cognitive styles beyond traditional measures of team diversity and ability.

title: Cannabis use does not increase actual creativity but biases evaluations of creativity.

entries.rq_with_context: Many people believe cannabis enhances creativity, and some employees use it for this purpose, yet empirical evidence is mixed. Prior research has not clearly distinguished between actual creativity and subjective evaluations of creativity, nor has it rigorously tested the affective mechanisms—particularly joviality—that may explain this lay belief. This study addresses this gap by experimentally testing whether cannabis use enhances actual creativity and evaluations of creativity through increased joviality. Using two experiments with diverse creativity tasks and raters, the authors examine both self- and other-evaluations of creativity. They find that while cannabis use increases joviality and leads to more favorable evaluations of creativity, it does not improve actual creativity. The study contributes by clarifying that the perceived creativity-boosting effects of cannabis are due to biased evaluations, not real creative gains.

title: The impact of supportive leadership on employee outcomes during organizational mergers: An organizational-level field study.

entries.rq_with_context: Mergers are often assumed to harm employee well-being, but past research shows mixed findings, partly due to a lack of control groups and insufficient attention to organizational-level dynamics. This study addresses these gaps by investigating whether mergers lead to declines in job satisfaction and increases in absenteeism compared to nonmerging organizations. It further explores whether supportive leadership from midlevel managers can buffer these negative effects. Using a quasi-experimental design across multiple NHS primary care trusts in England, the study tests a compensation model based on organizational support theory and conservation of resources theory. The key contribution is demonstrating that increases in supportive leadership during mergers can reduce adverse employee outcomes, highlighting the role of midlevel management in change processes.

title: Perceived misalignment of professional prototypes reduces subordinates’ endorsement of sexist supervisors.

entries.rq_with_context: Despite efforts to promote gender diversity, many organizations still have sexist supervisors who define their profession through stereotypically masculine traits and view it as a 'man’s job.' These supervisors risk transmitting gender bias to subordinates who endorse them as leaders. While top-down interventions exist, this research explores a bottom-up strategy to reduce endorsement of sexist supervisors by manipulating subordinates’ professional prototypes. The study investigates whether encouraging subordinates to adopt a more balanced professional prototype—one that values both masculine and feminine traits equally—reduces their perceived professional prototype alignment (PPPA) with sexist supervisors, thereby lowering supervisor endorsement. Using two experiments in the context of the U.S. fire service, the authors test this mechanism against alternative pathways like value congruence and leader prototypicality. The research contributes a novel psychological lever—PPPA—for curbing the spread of gender bias by targeting followership dynamics.

title: Do you see me? An inductive examination of differences between women of color’s experiences of and responses to invisibility at work.

entries.rq_with_context: Women of color frequently experience workplace invisibility—an intersectional phenomenon rooted in their nonprototypicality in both gender and race. While prior research has established this broad pattern, it treats women of color as a homogenous group and overlooks the variation in their experiences. This study addresses that gap by asking how differences in racial identity, immigration status, age, and organizational rank shape the types of invisibility women of color experience and how they respond to it. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 65 women of color in the U.S. and Canada, the authors use an inductive grounded theory approach to examine how social power influences both visibility and response strategies. The study identifies four forms of invisibility and three response pathways, showing how social power shapes both the experience and the consequences of invisibility. The key contribution is advancing intersectionality theory by highlighting intracategorical complexity and offering a response pathway model that illustrates how repeated experiences of invisibility lead to different coping strategies.

title: Preventing success: How a prevention focus causes leaders to overrule good ideas and reduce team performance gains.

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the recognized benefits of leader promotion focus, leaders in resource-constrained or high-threat environments are often trained to adopt a prevention focus, emphasizing error avoidance and routine compliance. However, it remains unclear how this focus shapes leaders’ own actions—particularly their potential to overrule correct team decisions—and how it affects team processes and performance. While regulatory focus theory suggests such leaders may overcorrect and suppress innovation, prior work has not directly examined these leader-focused behaviors or identified specific team-level mechanisms. We address this gap by testing whether leader prevention focus leads to harmful overruling (i.e., rejecting correct decisions) and indirectly impairs team performance through increased risk avoidance, reduced prospecting, and lower positive team affective tone. Using an experimental simulation with 84 teams, we manipulated leader prevention focus. Our findings identify harmful overruling as a novel mechanism and reveal that team performance suffers mainly through reduced team prospecting and lower positive affective tone.

title: What makes you proactive can burn you out: The downside of proactive skill building motivated by financial precarity and fear.

entries.rq_with_context: Proactivity at work is typically viewed as positive, driven by intrinsic motivation and leading to beneficial outcomes like career success. However, emerging research suggests negative states like fear may also motivate proactivity, and that such behavior can be depleting. A key gap remains in linking these ideas—specifically, whether fear-driven proactive skill building has negative consequences. This study addresses that gap by investigating how financial precarity triggers fear, which in turn motivates proactive skill development, and whether this process ultimately leads to burnout. Using a four-wave study of 1,315 university employees during the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic, the authors test a moderated serial mediation model. The key contribution is showing that proactive behavior, when driven by financial fear and image concerns, can harm employee well-being.

title: Motivational drivers for serial position effects: Evidence from high-stakes legal decisions.

entries.rq_with_context: Serial position effects—where the order of cases in a sequence influences decisions—are commonly attributed to decision-maker fatigue. However, such effects also occur in contexts where fatigue is unlikely, suggesting alternative explanations. The authors propose that motivation to appear or be consistent may drive these effects, particularly in legal contexts where decisions face scrutiny. They analyze U.S. immigration judges' asylum decisions and 18th-century London jury verdicts to test whether serial position effects align with motivational versus fatigue-based predictions. Using field data and theoretical modeling, they examine whether leniency increases with serial position, persists over breaks, and is stronger among experienced decision-makers. The study’s main contribution is demonstrating that motivational factors, especially the desire to avoid scrutiny, better explain serial position effects than fatigue in high-stakes settings.

title: Above the law? How motivated moral reasoning shapes evaluations of high performer unethicality.

entries.rq_with_context: Recent high-profile cases have revealed that high-performing employees often face fewer career consequences for unethical behavior, despite organizational expectations for ethical conduct. While research has explored antecedents of unethical behavior, less is known about why and how employee performance distorts moral evaluations. The gap lies in understanding how performance biases supervisors' punitive judgments of misconduct and how supervisors' bottom-line mentality shapes whether those moral judgments factor into promotion decisions. This study investigates the research question: How do employee performance and supervisor bottom-line mentality interact to shape moral evaluations and promotion outcomes for unethical behavior? Drawing on motivated moral reasoning theory, it tests a model in which performance leads to leniency in judgment, and supervisor orientation toward performance outcomes determines whether that leniency translates into advancement. The contribution lies in revealing a moral double standard in organizational decision-making and clarifying when ethical violations are overlooked based on employee and supervisor characteristics.

title: Self-selection as an explanation for general mental ability test score differences between mobile and nonmobile devices in observational studies.

entries.rq_with_context: Past research reports inconsistent findings on whether mobile device use affects general mental ability (GMA) test scores, with operational studies showing large disadvantages for mobile users (average d = 0.79) while experimental studies show little to no effect (d = 0.05). This discrepancy may stem from selection bias in observational studies, where applicants self-select their testing device. The gap lies in whether these observed score differences reflect true measurement differences or are artifacts of systematic differences between mobile and nonmobile users. The research question asks whether controlling for selection bias reduces the observed GMA score gap between device types. The study uses propensity score weighting and poststratification methods on a large operational dataset of 76,948 job applicants. The key contribution is demonstrating that selection bias substantially inflates mobile device effects in observational studies, clarifying contradictory findings in the literature.

title: No reason to leave: The effects of CEO diversity-valuing behavior on psychological safety and turnover for female executives.

entries.rq_with_context: Despite extensive research on barriers that lead female leaders to leave organizations, less is known about factors that mitigate their turnover. This study addresses this gap by investigating how CEOs’ diversity-valuing behaviors may reduce turnover among female executives. Drawing on the push model of turnover and psychological safety theory, we propose that perceptions of CEO diversity-valuing behavior enhance psychological safety for female executives, which in turn lowers their likelihood of exiting. Using a unique dataset combining survey responses and archival turnover data from 365 executives in large U.S. firms, we examine this mediated relationship while controlling for individual, CEO, and firm-level factors. The study contributes by shifting focus from barriers to retention mechanisms and identifying a psychological pathway through which CEO behavior influences female executive turnover.

title: The costs of insecurity: Pay volatility and health outcomes.

entries.rq_with_context: Pay volatility is increasingly common as organizations shift risk to employees through performance-based pay systems like tips, commissions, and gig work. While such systems are linked to higher performance, their impact on employee health remains unknown. Prior research has largely focused on pay levels rather than volatility, and lacks theoretical grounding on why fluctuating pay might harm health. This study addresses this gap by proposing that pay volatility creates resource insecurity, which harms health. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, the research examines whether volatile pay leads to physical symptoms, insomnia, and poor sleep through the mechanism of scarcity mindset. Using three studies across tipped, gig, and salaried workers, the paper tests this model while controlling for income level. The findings contribute to theory by identifying pay volatility as a distinct stressor and suggest practical strategies for reducing its health costs.

title: How well can an AI chatbot infer personality? Examining psychometric properties of machine-inferred personality scores.

entries.rq_with_context: Personality assessment is widely used in organizational settings, but self-report measures face challenges such as faking, low criterion validity, and respondent burden. An emerging alternative uses AI chatbots to infer personality from free-text responses through machine learning. While such approaches offer efficiency and reduced tedium, there is limited empirical evaluation of their psychometric properties. The present study fills this gap by examining the reliability, validity, and generalizability of machine-inferred personality scores. Using data from over 1,400 undergraduates who completed self-report inventories and interacted with a chatbot, the authors test whether these AI-derived scores are psychometrically sound. They employ a multi-faceted validation approach—including internal consistency, test–retest reliability, factorial structure, convergent and discriminant validity, and criterion-related validity—using both self-report and peer- and performance-based outcomes. The study’s contribution lies in providing one of the most comprehensive validations of chatbot-based personality inference to date.

title: Revisiting Sackett et al.’s (2022) rationale behind their recommendation against correcting for range restriction in concurrent validation studies.

entries.rq_with_context: Sackett et al. (2022) recommend against correcting for range restriction (RR) in concurrent validation studies, arguing that indirect RR is typically so minimal (ux ≥.90) that correction is unnecessary unless two conditions hold: the unrestricted true-score correlation (rzx) between the predictor and the actual selection variable is at least .90 and the selection ratio is .30 or lower—conditions they deem unlikely. This commentary challenges that rationale by reevaluating the plausibility of these thresholds. The research question is whether rzx values of .90 or higher are implausible, whether selection ratios of .30 or below are extreme, and whether RR in concurrent studies is as negligible as claimed. Using reanalysis of Sackett et al.’s tables and empirical evidence from personnel selection literature, the study applies psychometric correction methods (Case IV and Case V) to assess the severity of RR. The authors claim their findings undermine the empirical basis for Sackett et al.’s recommendation, suggesting that RR correction remains meaningful even under common conditions.

title: Performance pressure amplifies the effect of evening detachment on next-morning shame: Downstream consequences for workday cheating behavior.

entries.rq_with_context: Psychological detachment from work is generally seen as beneficial for employee recovery and well-being. However, in organizations with high performance pressure—where employees face strong expectations to perform—detaching may violate normative expectations, leading to feelings of shame. Research has not adequately explored when detachment might carry negative consequences. Drawing on social self-preservation theory, this paper investigates whether evening detachment increases next-morning shame in high (vs. low) performance pressure contexts, and whether this shame leads to unethical cheating behaviors aimed at protecting one’s image. Using a 2-week experience sampling study and two experiments, our approach isolates within-person fluctuations in detachment and tests causal mechanisms through complementary designs. We claim that our work reveals a previously unrecognized trade-off of detachment in high-pressure environments, contributing to the literatures on recovery, performance pressure, and unethical behavior.

title: Benefits of leaders’ pleasurable recovery activities on follower performance via emotional contagion.

entries.rq_with_context: While employee recovery research has traditionally focused on individual benefits, less is known about how one person's recovery affects others at work. This study addresses that gap by examining leader-follower dyads, focusing on how leaders' pleasurable recovery activities at home impact followers' work outcomes. The research question is whether these activities influence followers' performance by affecting leaders' positive affect displays at work and transferring positive emotions to followers through emotional contagion. Using conservation of resources and emotional contagion theories, the study uses experience sampling methods across multiple workdays to test this spillover-crossover model. The authors claim this advances understanding of interpersonal recovery effects in leadership contexts.

title: When narcissists exemplify ethics: Contingent consequences of ethical leadership.

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations promote ethical leadership to prevent misconduct, yet leadership roles are often filled by individuals high in narcissism. While ethical leadership is generally seen as beneficial, its impact on leaders themselves—particularly those high in narcissism—remains unclear. The paper identifies a gap in understanding how individual differences shape the personal costs and benefits of ethical leadership. Drawing on self-concordance theory, the authors ask: How does leader narcissism moderate the effects of ethical leadership on leadership effectiveness through motivational (i.e., leader self-efficacy) and social (i.e., leader social admiration) pathways? They test this model using a field study and two experiments. The key contribution is revealing that ethical leadership can carry hidden costs for narcissistic leaders, challenging the assumption that it uniformly enhances leadership effectiveness.

title: On the asymmetry of losses and gains: Implications of changing work conditions for well-being.

entries.rq_with_context: Prior research suggests work conditions affect employee well-being, with deteriorations impairing and improvements enhancing it, typically assuming symmetric effects. However, Hobfoll's conservation of resources (COR) theory posits that losses have a stronger psychological impact than equivalent gains. Despite this, little empirical work has tested this asymmetry in organizational settings. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether changes in work quality affect well-being asymmetrically—specifically, whether deteriorations in job stressors and resources harm well-being more than corresponding improvements help. Using longitudinal data from three large samples, the authors apply multilevel modeling to examine these dynamics. The findings suggest that losses generally have a stronger impact than gains, particularly for certain stressors like social stressors, advancing understanding of how temporal changes in work conditions influence well-being.

title: Using wearable technology (closed loop acoustic stimulation) to improve sleep quality and work outcomes.

entries.rq_with_context: Employees often face time constraints that limit their ability to get sufficient sleep, making it difficult to improve sleep duration. While sleep quality is equally important, few practical interventions exist to enhance it. Closed loop acoustic stimulation—a neuroscience-based wearable technology—has shown promise in improving sleep quality by enhancing slow-wave activity during deep sleep. This study tests whether using this technology during sleep improves next-day work outcomes (work engagement, task performance, OCB, and counterproductive behavior) in a sample of full-time employees. Using a within-subjects field experiment with 81 participants, the authors examine the intervention’s effect and test age as a boundary condition. The study contributes by identifying a low-cost, non-invasive method to improve sleep quality and work outcomes without requiring more sleep time.

title: Humane orientation, work–family conflict, and positive spillover across cultures.

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing cross-national work–family research, studies have been limited by narrow geographical scope and a focus on well-represented regions, leading to insufficient variance in cultural dimensions and restricted generalizability. Notably, Southern Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa—regions with high humane orientation—are underrepresented. Humane orientation, reflecting societal encouragement of kindness and support, is key to understanding social support dynamics but has been overlooked. This study addresses these gaps by analyzing data from 10,307 employees across 30 countries, including underrepresented regions, and directly measuring humane orientation. Using fit theory, it explores whether humane orientation strengthens support effects (congruence) or makes support more impactful where it is lacking (compensation). The research reveals that humane orientation has a mostly compensatory role in reducing work–family conflict and an amplifying role in enhancing positive spillover, particularly for coworker and instrumental family support.

title: When does paternalistic control positively relate to job satisfaction and citizenship behavior in Taiwan? The role of follower expectation.

entries.rq_with_context: Paternalistic control—leaders asserting authority and demanding obedience—is commonly found in Confucian Asian contexts but is often linked to lower job satisfaction and reduced citizenship behavior. While previous research assumes followers generally reject such control, this study challenges that view by proposing that follower expectations may vary by context. Using connectionist models of implicit leadership theory, the authors argue that it's not the level of control per se, but the match between what followers expect and perceive that determines outcomes. Through two daily experience sampling studies in Taiwan, they test whether alignment in expectations and perceptions leads to better job satisfaction and citizenship behaviors. The key contribution is shifting focus from leader behavior alone to the dynamic follower expectation model, offering a more nuanced understanding of when and why paternalistic control may be effective.

title: Meetings and individual work during the workday: Examining their interdependent impact on knowledge workers’ energy.

entries.rq_with_context: Knowledge workers spend significant time in meetings and individual work, both of which can impact their energy levels, yet little research has examined how these activities interact to influence daily energy. Prior studies have either treated work as uniform or focused on single activities in isolation, missing potential interdependencies between different types of work. This study addresses this gap by investigating how the time allocation between meetings and individual work, as well as the complementarity of their performance pressure levels, jointly shape energy. Drawing on workday design and event system theory, the authors use two experience sampling studies with 245 and 167 knowledge workers to test these dynamics. The key contribution is demonstrating that both time allocation and pressure complementarity between meetings and individual work have interdependent effects on energy, advancing a more nuanced understanding of workday design.

title: Consistent and low is the only way to go: A polynomial regression approach to the effect of abusive supervision inconsistency.

entries.rq_with_context: The literature on abusive supervision typically assumes employees respond to current levels of abuse without considering past experiences. This creates a 'clean slate' view that may overlook how temporal comparisons influence reactions. A critical gap exists in understanding how changes in abusive supervision over time—what the authors term 'inconsistent' abuse—affect employees, despite recognition that people mentally compare past and present experiences. The study addresses this by asking whether inconsistent levels of abusive supervision (e.g., high then low, or low then high) produce worse outcomes than consistent patterns. Drawing on temporal comparison and stress appraisal theories, the authors use polynomial regression and experience sampling data from two studies with different time lags (monthly and weekly) to examine anxiety and turnover intentions as outcomes. Their key contribution is demonstrating that inconsistency itself—regardless of direction—is harmful and that employee status can buffer this effect.

title: Is it just me or am I the people’s choice? The stress and performance implications of (in)congruence between self- and other-identification as a leader or follower.

entries.rq_with_context: Informal leadership is increasingly recognized as critical to team effectiveness, with leader identity construction theory suggesting that individuals claim leadership identities and others grant them. However, little research has examined what happens when self-identification as a leader or follower differs from how others identify the individual. This study addresses this gap by investigating the individual-level consequences of such (in)congruence. Drawing on stress appraisal theory, the authors propose that incongruence creates stress that undermines performance, particularly when individuals identify as leaders but are seen as followers. They test this using a two-study design: a field study with coworker dyads and a controlled experiment with full-time employees. The key contribution is demonstrating that leader identity (in)congruence meaningfully affects stress appraisals and performance, advancing understanding beyond the assumption of identity consensus.

title: Emotional exhaustion across the workday: Person-level and day-level predictors of workday emotional exhaustion growth curves.

entries.rq_with_context: Although emotional exhaustion (EE) is recognized as a dynamic state, most research has treated it as static or examined long-term trends, leaving short-term within-day changes poorly understood. The workday is a psychologically salient period shaped by resource expenditure and recovery, yet no study has empirically modeled EE growth curves across a single workday. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory and the Work–Home Resources (W-HR) framework, this study develops and tests hypotheses about the linear increase of EE during the workday and how both stable (between-person) and fluctuating (within-person) factors predict the starting level (intercept) and rate of increase (slope) of EE. Using experience sampling data from 114 service employees across 925 days, it examines predictors including prior detachment, social interactions, customer mistreatment, supervisor support, and autonomous and controlled motivation. The study’s contribution is establishing workday EE trajectories and identifying multi-level, multi-source predictors that shape them, informing both theory and workplace interventions.

title: The importance of leader recovery for leader identity and behavior.

entries.rq_with_context: Leader identity—seeing oneself as a leader—is important for daily leadership effectiveness, yet little is known about how leaders can strengthen this identity on a day-to-day basis. Given that leadership is cognitively taxing and often depleting, the authors explore how off-work recovery experiences may shape leaders' daily sense of self as leaders. They focus on two key after-hours experiences: psychological detachment (mentally disconnecting from work) and affect-focused rumination (repetitive negative thoughts about work). These are theorized to differentially impact morning depletion, which in turn may affect how strongly leaders identify with their role and behave at work. Using experience sampling methods across two studies, the authors test a serial mediation model linking recovery experiences to leader behaviors via depletion and leader identity. The study contributes to understanding how daily nonwork experiences shape leadership processes.

title: Who needs nature? The influence of employee speciesism on nature-based need satisfaction and subsequent work behavior.

entries.rq_with_context: While research in fields like environmental psychology suggests nature exposure benefits well-being, it remains unclear whether these effects meaningfully impact employee work outcomes, especially given that nature is often at the periphery of employees' jobs. A key gap exists in understanding how and for whom nature exposure influences work behavior. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study asks whether exposure to nature at work satisfies employees' basic psychological needs (autonomy, relatedness, competence), thereby improving task performance and prosocial behavior, and whether these effects are weaker for employees high in speciesism—the belief that humans are superior to other life forms. The research uses a mixed-method approach across four studies to test this model. Its key contribution is demonstrating that workplace nature exposure can impact performance through psychological need satisfaction, but that this benefit depends on employees' underlying speciesist beliefs.

title: Crossing the domain: Unintended consequences of safety and service climates.

entries.rq_with_context: Service and safety climates are well-established in their respective domains, but little is known about their cross-domain effects. In health care settings like hospitals, nurses face competing demands of delivering high-quality service while adhering to strict safety protocols. The coexistence of strong service and safety climates may lead to unintended consequences, yet research has largely ignored how one climate affects outcomes in the other's domain. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether service climate negatively affects safety performance and whether safety climate negatively affects service performance. Using an exploration–exploitation framework, the authors examine team exploration and team exploitation as mediating mechanisms. The research uses two multiwave, multisource field studies with nursing teams to test these relationships. The key contribution is uncovering the conflicting cross-domain roles of service and safety climates, advancing climate theory beyond domain-specific assumptions.

title: COVID-19 and the great resignation: The role of death anxiety, need for meaningful work, and task significance.

entries.rq_with_context: The 'Great Resignation' during the COVID-19 pandemic presents a paradox: employees expressed high turnover intentions despite economic uncertainty and job insecurity. To understand this, the authors draw on terror management theory (TMT), which suggests that awareness of mortality triggers existential concerns that lead individuals to seek meaning in life. While prior research links death anxiety to various workplace outcomes, little has examined its role in turnover decisions. The study proposes that death anxiety increases employees’ need for meaningful work, which in turn raises their turnover intentions. Furthermore, it tests whether task significance—the degree to which one’s job impacts others—buffers this effect. Using multiple studies (including longitudinal and experimental designs), the research investigates this indirect pathway and its conditional nature. The authors claim their work offers one of the first empirical tests of TMT's self-transcendent mechanism in explaining turnover during a global health crisis.

title: No person is an island: Unpacking the work and after-work consequences of interacting with artificial intelligence.

entries.rq_with_context: As AI becomes more integrated into daily work, employees increasingly interact with machines rather than human coworkers, potentially leading to social disconnection. While prior research has examined benefits or drawbacks of AI separately, little is known about simultaneous adaptive and maladaptive outcomes from a social perspective. This study addresses this gap by asking how employee interactions with AI relate to both increased helping behavior (adaptive) and negative after-work outcomes like insomnia and alcohol consumption (maladaptive), and whether attachment anxiety strengthens these effects. Drawing on the social affiliation model and attachment theory, the authors use four studies with diverse samples and methods. The research contributes a dual-path model showing how AI interactions can simultaneously trigger both prosocial workplace behaviors and impairments in employee well-being.

title: Within-person personality variability in the work context: A blessing or a curse for job performance?

entries.rq_with_context: While personality traits are well-established predictors of job performance, recent research highlights that personality also varies within individuals over time. However, it remains unclear whether such within-person variability benefits or harms performance, with prior findings being inconsistent. This study addresses gaps regarding the role of rater source (self vs. others) and whether mean-level personality shapes the impact of variability. Drawing on socioanalytic theory, it investigates how self- and other-rated within-person personality variability predict self- and other-rated job performance, and whether mean-level personality moderates these links. Using experience sampling data from teachers, supervisors, and students, the study employs the relative variability index (RVI) to assess variability while accounting for situational factors. The key contribution is demonstrating that the desirability of personality variability depends on who perceives it and the individual’s underlying trait level.

title: Comparing forced-choice and single-stimulus personality scores on a level playing field: A meta-analysis of psychometric properties and susceptibility to faking.

entries.rq_with_context: Personality assessments are commonly used in hiring but are vulnerable to faking, especially in high-stakes settings. Forced-choice (FC) formats—where respondents compare statements—are thought to be more faking-resistant than traditional single-stimulus (SS) formats—where items are rated independently. However, past comparisons of FC and SS measures often rely on different samples or contexts, making it hard to isolate the effect of format. This study addresses this gap by conducting a meta-analysis that only includes studies using matched FC and SS assessments in the same context, allowing for a fair comparison. The research examines three key areas: the correlation between FC and SS scores (construct validity), differences in score inflation due to faking (mean shifts), and criterion-related validity in both honest and faked conditions. The authors use this more rigorous, level-playing-field approach to clarify whether FC formats offer real advantages over SS formats in real-world settings, particularly in reducing faking and maintaining predictive validity.

title: The forgotten side of empowering others: How lower social structural empowerment attenuates the effects of empowering leadership on employee psychological empowerment and performance.

entries.rq_with_context: Empowering leadership is widely seen as a key driver of employee psychological empowerment, with extensive research supporting its positive effects on motivation, creativity, and performance. However, this focus may overlook critical organizational constraints that limit its effectiveness. The authors argue that social structural empowerment—reflecting employees’ access to resources, information, and sociopolitical support—acts as a crucial boundary condition often neglected in the literature. While theory suggests both leadership behavior and structural context jointly shape empowerment, prior research has largely treated them in isolation. This study addresses that gap by asking whether and how social structural empowerment shapes the impact of empowering leadership on psychological empowerment and performance. Drawing on empowerment theory, the authors propose an interaction model: empowering leadership enhances psychological empowerment only when structural conditions support it. Their four-study approach tests this moderating effect across diverse samples and methods, offering a more nuanced understanding of when empowerment initiatives succeed or fail.

title: Wearing different hats enriches “outside the box” thinking: Examining the relationship between personal life activity breadth and creativity at work.

entries.rq_with_context: Employees engage in various personal life activities outside of work and family, but how this participation affects workplace creativity remains underexplored. Prior research has largely focused on time spent in specific leisure activities and emphasized affective recovery over cognitive gains. This study addresses the gap by examining the cognitive mechanisms through which diverse personal life activities contribute to creativity. Drawing on enrichment theory and construal level theory, the authors investigate whether broader engagement in personal life generates nonwork cognitive developmental resources (e.g., skills, knowledge, perspectives) that enhance creativity at work. They also explore how the way people think about their activities—concretely (how) versus abstractly (why)—affects both the generation and application of these resources. The primary contribution is demonstrating a cognitive instrumental path from personal life to work creativity, moving beyond traditional stress-recovery frameworks.

title: Progressive or pressuring? The signaling effects of egg freezing coverage and other work–life policies.

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly offer diverse work–life policies to attract talent, with existing theory suggesting these policies uniformly signal personal-life support and generate positive employee attitudes. However, novel policies like egg freezing coverage—framed as supporting employees' fertility needs—may instead signal that career prioritization and personal-life sacrifice are expected. This raises uncertainty about whether such policies elicit favorable reactions. The research investigates whether egg freezing coverage leads to more negative employee attitudes compared to other work–life policies and explores the underlying signaling mechanisms. Using a signaling theory framework, the study tests whether perceptions of encouraged personal-life sacrifice, work prioritization, employee benefits, and organizational costs explain differential reactions. The key contribution is demonstrating that employee reactions to work–life policies are more variable and driven by multiple factors beyond simple personal-life support signals.

title: Does taking charge help or harm employees’ promotability and visibility? An investigation from supervisors’ status perspective.

entries.rq_with_context: Taking charge—employees' proactive efforts to improve their work environment—is recognized as beneficial for organizations, but it remains unclear how supervisors evaluate such behavior in terms of career outcomes like promotability and visibility. Prior research has focused mainly on performance ratings and overlooked supervisors' personal orientations as a determining factor. This study addresses this gap by exploring how supervisors' motivation to achieve higher status (status goal striving) shapes their assessments of employees who take charge. Using dyadic complementary fit theory, the authors propose that taking charge enhances the status of supervisors who are striving for greater recognition, making them more likely to view these employees as promotable and visible. The study uses multiple methods across different cultural settings to test this idea.

title: Biting the hand that feeds: A status-based model of when and why receiving help motivates social undermining.

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational research typically assumes that receiving help leads to positive reciprocity due to social exchange norms. However, this paper identifies a gap in understanding when and why help recipients may respond negatively—specifically by socially undermining the help giver. The study addresses this by proposing that perceptions of relative competence influence whether help is seen as a status threat. When help comes from a more competent coworker, it increases status threat and evokes envy, which may prompt social undermining. The paper tests this via four studies using different designs. The core contribution is identifying a previously underexplored negative consequence of receiving help by revealing the psychological mechanism and boundary conditions of 'biting the hand that feeds.'

title: A recipe for success? Sustaining creativity among first-time creative producers.

entries.rq_with_context: Sustaining creativity over time is a challenge, particularly for first-time producers. While some individuals go on to produce multiple creative works, others abandon further production despite initial success. Existing research has explored how creativity evolves over time but has not sufficiently examined what determines whether producers continue at all. This paper identifies a paradoxical effect: the very factors that enhance the success of a creative work—its novelty and recognition through awards—may reduce the likelihood of follow-up production. Using data from first-time cookbook authors and experimental studies, the authors test whether award-winning producers of novel work are less likely to create a second work due to a heightened threat to their creative identity. The study contributes by revealing how early success can undermine sustained creativity, offering both theoretical and practical insights into supporting long-term creative productivity.

title: Status acuity: The ability to accurately perceive status hierarchies reduces status conflict and benefits group performance.

entries.rq_with_context: Informal status hierarchies are central to group functioning, yet individuals vary in their accuracy when perceiving these hierarchies. While prior research has shown that accurate status perception benefits individual performance, the existence of a general individual ability to perceive status across different groups—and its implications for group dynamics—remains unexplored. This study addresses that gap by introducing and validating 'status acuity' as a dispositional ability. The research questions are whether status acuity is a reliable individual trait distinct from emotional intelligence, cognitive ability, and network perception accuracy, and whether groups with higher levels of status acuity experience less status conflict and perform better. The authors use a multimethod approach, including experiments with face-to-face groups, and compositional models to analyze group-level outcomes. The key claimed contribution is identifying status acuity as a novel individual ability that enhances group performance by reducing conflict.

title: Am I motivated to share knowledge for better innovative performance? An approach and avoidance framework.

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research has examined approach and avoidance motivation in relation to creativity, results—especially for avoidance motivation—have been mixed, suggesting multiple underlying mechanisms. This study addresses the gap by investigating knowledge-sharing (KS) as a behavioral mechanism linking motivation to innovative performance. It differentiates between explicit and implicit KS and proposes distinct pathways: approach motivation enhances both types of KS, while avoidance motivation increases explicit KS but reduces implicit KS. The study also considers contextual moderators—perceived organizational support (POS) and psychological contract breach (PCB)—to explain when these motivational orientations influence KS. Using survey data from 331 Chinese employees and their supervisors, the authors test a moderated mediation model. The research contributes by offering a behavioral explanation for mixed findings on avoidance motivation and highlighting the importance of context in motivational processes.

title: Getting unstuck: The effects of growth mindsets about the self and job on happiness at work.

entries.rq_with_context: Employees often struggle to sustainably improve their happiness at work, despite having the autonomy to shape their roles. While prior research highlights the benefits of a growth mindset about the self—believing one’s abilities can change—this may not be enough if employees see their jobs as fixed. The authors identify a gap: mindset research has largely ignored beliefs about job malleability. They propose dual-growth mindset—viewing both the self and job as changeable—as critical for lasting happiness. Using two experiments, they test whether fostering this dual mindset leads to more durable happiness gains than focusing on either mindset alone. They argue that only when both mindsets are present can employees make substantial agentic changes through job crafting. The claimed contribution is identifying dual-growth mindset as a novel driver of sustained happiness at work.

title: Too good to be true? Are supervisor-perspective ratings a valid substitute for actual supervisor ratings?

entries.rq_with_context: Researchers often use supervisor-perspective ratings—where employees estimate how their supervisor would rate their job performance—as a substitute for actual supervisor ratings due to practical challenges in collecting the latter. While prior research suggests this method improves validity over traditional self-ratings, findings on its effectiveness vary widely. The gap lies in the lack of a comprehensive meta-analytic evaluation of whether supervisor-perspective ratings are sufficiently correlated with and close in mean to actual supervisor ratings. This study addresses that gap by meta-analyzing correlations, mean differences, and nomological network similarities. Using a three-level meta-analytic model across 26 studies, it tests whether these ratings can be a viable proxy. The authors conclude they generally cannot, especially for citizenship performance, in collectivistic cultures, or when all data come from one source.

title: A cross-lagged longitudinal investigation of the relationship between stigma and job effectiveness among employees with HIV.

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing attention to workplace inclusion, little is known about how employees with stigmatized medical conditions like HIV manage job demands. HIV stigma is particularly dehumanizing due to its moral condemnation, yet how it undermines job effectiveness remains unclear, especially the emotional mechanisms involved. While prior research has focused on stigma disclosure and third-party reactions, this study addresses the gap by examining how PLHIV themselves experience stigma and its impact on work outcomes. Drawing on stigma and appraisal theory, the authors test a dual-path model examining fear (external threat) and shame (internal damage) as mediators between HIV stigma and job effectiveness. They further investigate whether CSE (psychological resource) and CD4 cell count (physiological resource) moderate the mediation paths. The key contribution is identifying shame—not fear—as the central emotional mechanism and showing how personal resources buffer its damaging effects.

title: Crossover effects of parent work-to-family experiences on child work centrality: A moderated mediation model.

entries.rq_with_context: Work-to-family conflict (WFC) and enrichment (WFE) are common experiences for working parents, with research showing their crossover effects on spouses, but limited understanding of how they influence children's emerging work beliefs like work centrality. While parents are recognized as key socializers of work values, there is little empirical research on how parental work-family experiences specifically relate to adolescent work centrality, including the mechanisms and boundary conditions involved. This study addresses this gap by proposing that parental WFC and WFE relate to child work centrality through two paths: an instrumental path via perceived parental career support and a sociocognitive path via perceived parental job satisfaction. It also investigates whether parental intrinsic work motivation moderates these effects. Using a moderated mediation model tested with time-lagged data from parent-child dyads, the research aims to uncover how and when parental work experiences cross over to shape adolescent work beliefs. The study's main contribution is providing new insights into the crossover processes from parents to children and identifying early predictors and outcomes of work centrality during adolescence.

title: Are gossipers looked down upon? A norm-based perspective on the relation between gossip and gossiper status.

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace gossip is ubiquitous yet its impact on gossiper status remains unclear, with conflicting views suggesting it either enhances status by clarifying norms or reduces status by violating them. Existing research lacks integration of these perspectives and fails to distinguish between positive and negative gossip. This study addresses this gap by proposing that negative gossip increases perceptions of norm violation but also clarifies norms, while positive gossip clarifies norms without violating them. The research question is whether and how these dual mechanisms explain the relationship between gossip and gossiper status. Using a norm-based framework across three studies with experimental and field data, the authors test these mechanisms and their interactions. The key contribution is clarifying the contradictory literature by showing how both types of gossip concurrently influence status through countervailing pathways.

title: Retaining retirement-eligible older workers through training participation: The joint implications of individual growth need and organizational climates.

entries.rq_with_context: As the workforce ages, organizations face challenges in retaining retirement-eligible workers to maintain knowledge and avoid labor shortages. While prior research has focused on socioemotional factors like organizational commitment and social needs, little is known about how human capital development—specifically training participation—can support retention. The study addresses this gap by investigating how individual motivation (growth need) and organizational contexts (climates for developing older workers and age-inclusive climate) jointly influence training participation and, in turn, decisions to stay. Using the motivated choice framework, the authors test hypotheses across two Dutch datasets. The main contribution is identifying training participation as a retention pathway and clarifying how organizational climates shape this process, both directly and by amplifying individual motivations.

title: Matches measure: A visual scale of job burnout.

entries.rq_with_context: Job burnout is a widespread occupational syndrome with significant personal and economic costs, yet existing measurement tools are often lengthy and proprietary, making rapid assessment difficult. While researchers sometimes shorten these scales, such adaptations raise validation concerns. This study addresses the need for a brief, reliable burnout measure by developing and validating a visual scale that uses progressively burned matches as a metaphor for burnout severity. The research question is whether this single-item visual measure can demonstrate strong convergent validity, criterion-related validity, and reliability compared to established burnout measures like the Maslach Burnout Inventory. The approach combines multiple preregistered studies using Bayesian comparisons with meta-analytic effect sizes and direct convergence tests. The claimed contribution is a validated, efficient tool for assessing burnout that is easier to deploy than current instruments.

title: When new talent scores: The impact of human capital and the team socialization context on newcomer performance in professional sports teams.

entries.rq_with_context: Newcomers joining existing teams face challenges in translating their human capital into performance, and the team environment may either support or hinder this process. Prior research offers conflicting findings on whether team characteristics like prior performance or cohort size help or harm newcomer adjustment. This study addresses this gap by investigating how the socialization context—specifically, the amount of time available for integration—shapes the impact of team-level factors on newcomer performance. Using data from European football leagues, it tests how individual human capital, prior team performance, and the number of simultaneously joining newcomers affect performance when time for socialization is high (preseason) versus low (mid-season). The study applies conservation of resources theory to explain when team attributes act as resources or demands. It contributes by clarifying contradictory findings and identifying boundary conditions under which human capital and team context jointly shape newcomer success.

title: Collective turnover response over time to a unit-level shock.

entries.rq_with_context: Collective turnover—turnover at the unit level—has effects on unit performance, but existing research does not adequately explain why or how it occurs over time. While individual-level turnover models exist, such as the unfolding model, they do not capture the collective response to shocks experienced by entire units. This study addresses this gap by theorizing and testing how a unit-level shock affects collective turnover over time. Using event systems theory, the authors propose a model with two novel temporal dimensions: a delay phase before turnover response begins, and a disruption phase marked by cumulative abnormal voluntary turnover. The study tests this model using data from 239 general manager departures in a large U.S. retailer from 2012 to 2014. The authors aim to improve understanding of the temporal dynamics of collective turnover responses and provide insight into how shock strength, timing, and spatial characteristics shape these patterns. The contribution lies in advancing collective turnover theory by introducing time-sensitive phases and modeling social mechanisms that drive turnover beyond individual decision-making.

title: Turning words into numbers: Assessing work attitudes using natural language processing.

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often collect open-ended employee comments to understand work attitudes, but manually analyzing such narrative data is time-consuming and costly. While Likert scales are standard for measuring constructs like job satisfaction and engagement, qualitative text offers richer, contextual insights. However, current natural language processing (NLP) tools lack validated, off-the-shelf algorithms for scoring a broad range of work-related constructs from text. The gap lies in both the availability of comprehensive NLP scoring systems and the understanding of their psychometric properties. This study addresses this by developing the Text-Based Attitude and Perception Scoring (TAPS) dictionaries—publicly available algorithms that generate theme and valence scores for 28 organizational constructs. Using a large employee sample, the research examines the reliability and validity of these scores, comparing transformer-based models to traditional bag-of-words approaches. The key contribution is the creation and validation of TAPS, which enables researchers and practitioners to automatically assess employee attitudes from text with documented psychometric support.

title: New strategies for addressing the diversity–validity dilemma with big data.

entries.rq_with_context: The diversity–validity dilemma in personnel selection refers to the challenge of using assessments that are both predictive of job performance and fair across demographic groups, as high-validity tools often show adverse impact. While traditional strategies exist, new big data and machine learning (ML) advancements offer innovative approaches to address this issue. However, many existing methods are not well-suited to high-dimensional data common in modern selection systems. To address this gap, the authors propose and evaluate two analytical techniques—iterative predictor removal and multipenalty optimization—for reducing group differences while preserving validity in big data contexts. Using a real-world sample of asynchronous video interviews, they apply these methods to natural language processing-derived predictors. The study contributes by introducing scalable, legally compliant techniques that simultaneously optimize for diversity and validity, offering practical solutions for organizations facing equal employment opportunity constraints.

title: My boss is younger, less educated, and shorter tenured: When and why status (in)congruence influences promotion system justification.

entries.rq_with_context: Status incongruence—where subordinates have older, more educated, or more tenured bosses—is increasingly common, challenging traditional assumptions that such status markers naturally justify higher positions. While prior research links status markers to competence and rank, this paper argues that in ongoing relationships, subordinates rely less on traditional status cues and more on observed competence when judging supervisors. The central question is whether and when status (in)congruence affects subordinates’ perceptions of promotion system fairness, particularly when supervisors appear less competent. Drawing on system justification theory, the authors predict that when supervisor competence is low, subordinates use status congruence as a basis to rationalize the system and perceive it as fairer—especially under conditions that heighten system justification motivation (e.g., low power or low escapability). The studies test this interaction across field and experimental settings, using both direct and implicit measures.

title: Adverse impact reduction and job performance optimization via pareto-optimal weighting: A shrinkage formula and regularization technique using machine learning.

entries.rq_with_context: In personnel selection, the Pareto-optimal weighting approach helps balance job performance and diversity by generating trade-off curves that show optimal predictor weight combinations. However, recent research shows these solutions suffer from shrinkage when applied to new samples, meaning both validity and diversity gains are overstated in practice. While shrinkage is well-known in single-criterion regression, its dual impact in multiobjective optimization—especially in diversity–performance trade-offs—remains less addressed. This study asks how to reduce shrinkage in Pareto-optimal solutions to produce more accurate estimates of job performance and diversity outcomes. The authors propose two approaches: a formula-based shrinkage adjustment and a regularization technique adapted from machine learning (elastic net/ridge regression). The primary contribution is providing practical tools to mitigate shrinkage in multiobjective selection systems, enabling more realistic predictions of hiring outcomes.

title: An empirical taxonomy of leadership situations: Development, validation, and implications for the science and practice of leadership.

entries.rq_with_context: Leadership situations play a crucial role in shaping leader behavior and outcomes, yet existing frameworks for understanding these situations are fragmented, incomplete, and lack empirical validation. Prior taxonomies of leadership situations are either too broad, too narrow, idiosyncratic, or conceptual rather than empirically derived, limiting their utility for systematic research. This study addresses the gap by developing and validating an empirically based taxonomy of psychological leadership situation characteristics—the way leaders subjectively perceive situations. Using natural language processing and factor analyses on ratings from 1,159 leaders, the research identifies core dimensions of perceived situations and develops the Leadership Situation Questionnaire (LSQ) to measure them. The study tests the nomological network of these characteristics by examining their relationships with structural cues, leader behavior, and outcomes, providing a foundation for future situational leadership research.

title: The definition and measurement of human capital resources: A content and meta-analytic review.

entries.rq_with_context: Human capital resources (HCR) are considered important for organizational performance, but researchers have defined and measured them inconsistently. This lack of standardization makes it unclear whether existing measures provide valid inferences about HCR or their relationships with performance. While some recent frameworks define HCR as collective knowledge, skills, abilities, and other characteristics (KSAOs), many studies still use proxies like education or tenure that may be antecedents rather than HCR themselves. The study addresses three key issues: how HCR is defined across research, how it is measured, and whether measurement quality affects predictive validity for performance. Using a three-study design involving content analysis and meta-analysis, the authors examine definitions (k=84), measures (k=127), and criterion-related validity (k=94). The key contribution is identifying widespread contamination and deficiency in HCR measures and showing how these measurement issues impact conclusions about HCR's role in organizational effectiveness.

title: Losing sleep over speaking up at work: A daily study of voice and insomnia.

entries.rq_with_context: Insomnia is a widespread sleep disorder with serious consequences for health and work performance, and prior research has largely focused on organizational and stable individual factors as its antecedents. However, little is known about how malleable employee behaviors—particularly prosocial yet psychologically costly behaviors like voice—affect sleep. This study addresses this gap by investigating the daily relationship between two forms of voice—promotive (suggesting improvements) and prohibitive (expressing concerns)—and insomnia. Using a daily diary design with 113 employees over 10 workdays, the study tests whether affect and detachment mediate the voice-sleep link and whether insomnia impairs next-day voice via depletion. The research contributes by identifying employee-controlled behaviors as key predictors of sleep, thus extending models of sleep and voice beyond workplace outcomes.

title: Self-promotion in the structured interview—No evidence of differential effects for men and women.

entries.rq_with_context: Previous research suggests that self-promotion may be more effective for men than women in job interviews, potentially due to gender stereotypes that view assertive behavior as more appropriate for men. This could lead to hiring discrimination against women, especially in male-dominated, high-status roles. The current study addresses whether this gender-based disparity in the effectiveness of self-promotion replicates in a structured interview setting. Using an experimental design with 831 participants, the study examines the interaction between candidate gender, level of self-promotion, and rating process (structured vs. unstructured) on hireability ratings. The approach uses audio-recorded mock interviews with manipulated self-promotion levels. The key claimed contribution is testing whether structured rating processes—such as behaviorally anchored rating scales—can eliminate gender bias in interview evaluations.

title: An alternative procedure for subgroup analyses in the think manager–think male paradigm.

entries.rq_with_context: The think manager–think male (TMTM) paradigm consistently observes that leader stereotypes are more similar to male than female stereotypes, and that male participants perceive greater similarity between men and leaders than female participants. However, the traditional method—using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs)—cannot reveal how participant characteristics drive these differences because ICCs conflate variance across categories and are sensitive to mean differences and unequal variances. This study addresses the gap by applying a regression framework (Edwards, 1995) that models category congruence as a function of participant characteristics while analyzing effects on individual categories (e.g., men, women, managers) separately. The research question is: how do participant sex, agency (masculinity), and communion (femininity) relate to the congruence between gender and leader categories in emotional expression stereotypes? The approach uses difference-score regression on ratings from a between-subjects design. The key claimed contribution is a methodological demonstration that regression provides clearer, more interpretable insights into subgroup effects than ICCs.

title: Does the interplay of diversity and inclusion buffer the impairment of health and well-being in a STEM organization?

entries.rq_with_context: STEM organizations are becoming more diverse, yet remain challenging environments for underrepresented groups, where stressors like work–self conflict, discrimination, and unclear procedures may impair well-being and commitment. While research recognizes the importance of both diversity and inclusion, less is known about how they jointly influence employee responses to stress. This paper addresses that gap by testing whether perceived diversity and experienced inclusion interact to moderate the impact of hindrance stressors on exhaustion and affective commitment. Using survey data from 1,187 employees at a technical university, the study applies a moderated moderation model grounded in inclusion and stressor frameworks. The authors claim their work connects diversity and inclusion research with occupational health, offering insight into how inclusion may protect employees in diversifying STEM workplaces.

title: The impact of interviewees’ anxious nonverbal behavior on interview performance ratings.

entries.rq_with_context: Interview anxiety is consistently correlated with lower interview performance ratings, but the causal mechanism is unclear. It is unknown whether this link is due to verbal content, nonverbal behavior, or other factors. This study isolates the effect of anxious nonverbal behavior—specifically fidgeting, reduced eye contact, and limb movements—on interview performance ratings by using scripted videos where verbal content is held constant. The research addresses a gap in understanding how nonverbal cues alone influence evaluative judgments. Using a between-subjects experimental design with 823 participants rating simulated interviews, the study tests whether anxious nonverbal behavior leads to lower performance ratings and whether this effect varies by job type (high vs. low interpersonal interaction) or interviewee gender. The authors claim this clarifies a key mechanism in the interview anxiety–performance link.

title: Making job candidates more honest with a theory-based form: A field study.

entries.rq_with_context: Resume fraud is a widespread problem in hiring, with studies showing high rates of embellishment, omission, and fabrication in job applications. Current methods to detect or deter deception, such as personality assessments or background checks, are either time-consuming, costly, or rarely implemented. This study addresses the gap by testing a novel, cost-effective intervention: a customized application form designed using the General Theory of Deception (GTD). The research asks whether incorporating dissonance, punishment, and risk factors into the form reduces deception in candidates’ self-reported information. Using a field study with real job applicants, the authors compare information accuracy between initial free-form resumes and the theory-based form. They claim the method not only reduces deception but also generates cues (e.g., missing contact details) that help identify remaining dishonesty, offering a practical solution for recruiters.

title: Scale mean and variance differences in MTurk and non-MTurk samples: A meta-analysis.

entries.rq_with_context: The use of Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (MTurk) has grown rapidly in organizational and psychological research, raising concerns about data quality and generalizability. While prior research has examined demographic differences and bivariate relationships, little is known about whether MTurk samples differ systematically from non-MTurk samples in terms of scale means and variances—key distributional properties that affect effect sizes and comparability. This meta-analysis addresses this gap by comparing MTurk samples to the original non-MTurk validation samples of 120 scales (N = 110,090). The study investigates whether mean and variance differences exist overall and whether they are moderated by construct domain, valence, sample characteristics, or data cleaning procedures. The approach uses random-effects meta-analysis to estimate standardized mean differences (d) and log ratios of variances (LRV). The authors claim this work contributes to understanding when MTurk samples yield comparable psychometric properties and under what conditions differences may arise.

title: Improving employee mental health through an internet-based job crafting intervention: A randomized controlled study.

entries.rq_with_context: Modern work environments increasingly require employees to proactively shape their jobs, and job crafting has been proposed as a way to improve well-being. While prior studies suggest job crafting interventions (JCIs) can enhance well-being, evidence remains limited and inconsistent, particularly in experimental settings with randomized control groups. This study addresses this gap by testing a web-based JCI in a randomized controlled trial with 208 participants. The research question is whether a four-week, self-guided online intervention focused on task crafting affects irritation and job satisfaction. Using a repeated-measures mixed model, the study compares outcomes at pre, post, and follow-up measurements. The authors claim the study contributes by being the first theory-driven, web-based JCI tested in a randomized design and by introducing irritation as a novel indicator of psychological ill-being.

title: Social undermining and three forms of organizational commitment: The moderating role of employees’ attachment style.

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace mistreatment, particularly social undermining (SU), is widely believed to reduce organizational commitment, especially affective commitment. However, it remains unclear how SU affects normative and continuance commitment, and whether individual differences shape these relationships. Drawing on attachment theory, this study investigates how SU is linked to all three forms of commitment and whether employees’ attachment styles—specifically anxious and avoidant attachment—moderate these relationships. Using time-lagged survey data from 626 employees, the authors test hypotheses about SU’s differential effects on commitment types. The study contributes by showing that SU’s impact is not uniformly negative and depends on employees’ relational orientations.

title: Telepressure and recovery experiences among remote and onsite workers.

entries.rq_with_context: Telepressure—the urge to respond quickly to work-related messages—is known to hinder employee recovery and well-being by blurring work–life boundaries. Prior research has established its negative impact on recovery experiences, but has not considered how work context might shape these associations. This study addresses a gap by testing whether the negative links between telepressure and recovery (i.e., psychological detachment, relaxation, control, and mastery) differ for employees working remotely versus those working onsite. Using conservation of resources theory, the study proposes that remote work may buffer these negative associations by enabling greater psychological distance from job pressures. The study uses an online survey with Prolific participants (n = 442), testing moderated structural equation models to assess these relationships. It contributes by showing that work context plays a critical moderating role in how telepressure affects recovery.

title: Measuring employees’ communication for innovation: The Employee Innovation Potential Scale.

entries.rq_with_context: Employees contribute to innovation not only by generating ideas but also through early-stage mental and communicative processes that precede actual innovation behavior. Existing scales mostly focus on observable innovative behaviors or organizational climates, neglecting the internal cognitive, affective, and conative processes that drive idea formation and communication. This study addresses the gap by developing and validating a new measure, the Employee Innovation Potential Scale (EIPS), which captures employees’ insights, interest, communication ability, and perceptions of organizational responsiveness. Using exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis on two Serbian employee samples (N = 723), the research tests the structure and criterion validity of the EIPS. The authors claim the EIPS offers a more nuanced understanding of the precursors to innovation by focusing on employees’ self-reported potential rather than enacted behavior.

title: Congruence in perceived employee–peer overqualification and organizational citizenship behavior: The mediating role of perceived insider status.

entries.rq_with_context: Overqualification is common and linked to both negative and positive employee outcomes, yet findings on its relationship with organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) are inconsistent. Prior research largely focuses on individual employees, neglecting peer influence in team contexts. This study addresses this gap by examining how congruence between an employee’s and their peers’ perceived overqualification influences OCB through perceived insider status. Drawing on equity theory and person–group fit theory, it proposes that alignment in overqualification perceptions fosters fairness and belonging, enhancing insider status and subsequent OCB. Using multilevel polynomial regression with data from 211 employees in 55 teams, the study analyzes congruence effects beyond simple individual or peer levels. The findings aim to clarify mixed results in the literature and highlight the relational dynamics shaping overqualification outcomes.

title: Agreeable supervisors promoting the organization—Implications for employee commitment and retention.

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates how supervisors' active promotion of the organization (SPO) influences employee affective organizational commitment (AOC) and voluntary turnover. While prior research emphasizes social exchange processes in shaping commitment, this paper explores an alternative mechanism: supervisors as internal employer brand advocates who proactively shape employee attitudes through persuasive communication. A key gap is understanding when such promotional efforts are most effective. The research asks whether perceived supervisor agreeableness strengthens the link between SPO and AOC, and indirectly, reduces turnover. Using social information processing theory, the study employs two studies—one cross-sectional (N = 910) and one time-lagged (N = 272)—to test these relationships. The authors claim the study advances understanding by identifying SPO as a distinct construct and showing how supervisor traits condition its impact.

title: Performance feedback during a pandemic—(Social) distancing from feedback? A qualitative study.

entries.rq_with_context: The shift to teleworking during the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted many organizational practices, including performance management (PM) and feedback processes. While prior research debates the merits of formal versus continuous informal feedback systems, little is known about how these systems hold up during rapid, large-scale shifts to remote work. This study investigates how HR managers experienced disruptions to PM and feedback practices when employees moved to working from home. Drawing on interviews with 45 HR managers, the research identifies how pre-pandemic PM approaches—categorized as formal, informal, or combined—affected organizational resilience. The study uses grounded theory to analyze qualitative data. It contributes by revealing that organizations combining formal and informal practices adapted most effectively, maintaining feedback continuity during crises.

title: The “perfect storm”—Perfectionists’ perceptions and experiences of abusive supervision.
