title: When and Why Narcissists Exhibit Greater Hindsight Bias and Less Perceived Learning

entries.rq_with_context: The phenomenon under investigation is hindsight bias—people's tendency to exaggerate what they knew in foresight after an outcome is known—and how it varies with narcissism and prediction accuracy. While existing research links narcissism to overconfidence and poor decision-making, less is known about the underlying cognitive mechanisms, particularly how narcissists process feedback after accurate versus inaccurate predictions. The gap lies in understanding why narcissists may fail to learn from experience. The research questions are: (1) Does prediction accuracy moderate the relationship between narcissism and hindsight bias? (2) Is this effect mediated by should counterfactual thinking (SCT)? (3) How does this chain affect perceived learning? The authors use a motivational framework centered on self-enhancement and self-protection, testing a moderated mediation model across four studies. The key claimed contribution is identifying SCT as a critical mechanism explaining when and why narcissists distort hindsight and fail to learn.

title: Unemployed Needn’t Apply: Unemployment Status, Legislation, and Interview Requests

entries.rq_with_context: This research investigates whether unemployed job applicants—particularly those long-term unemployed—are discriminated against in hiring, and whether antidiscrimination laws mitigate such bias. Prior research shows mixed evidence about employer discrimination based on unemployment status, with some studies finding lower callback rates for the unemployed while others do not. A key gap is the lack of research on how legal protections influence hiring outcomes. Using a field experiment across Los Angeles (without legislation) and New York City (with legislation), the study tests whether unemployment status affects interview request rates and whether legislation reduces disparities. The authors use a resume audit design and supplement findings with survey data from hiring personnel. The contribution is to provide empirical evidence on both the presence of unemployment-based discrimination and the real-world efficacy of antidiscrimination legislation.

title: The Effects of Rule Complexity on Organizational Noncompliance and Remediation: Evidence From Restaurant Health Inspections

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational noncompliance with legal rules is a widespread problem with serious consequences, yet prior research has treated all rules as if they were the same, either studying compliance with specific rules or aggregating across rules. This study challenges that assumption by arguing that rules vary in complexity, which systematically influences compliance and correction. The authors identify a gap in the literature: no prior work has examined how rule-level features shape variation in noncompliance and remediation across rules within the same system. Drawing on theories of routines and bounded rationality, they investigate how two sources of rule complexity—components and connections—affect noncompliance and remediation using data from 81,266 health inspection observations of restaurants. They find that both components and connections increase noncompliance, but only connections increase repeated noncompliance. The key contribution is advancing noncompliance as a rule-level phenomenon, urging scholars to consider rule features as central to understanding regulatory outcomes.

title: Transformational Leadership, High-Performance Work System Consensus, and Customer Satisfaction

entries.rq_with_context: Strategic HR research shows that high-performance work systems (HPWS) improve firm performance, but less is known about how leadership contributes to their realization. While HPWS are designed centrally, their success depends on employee perceptions and alignment, which may vary within units. The concept of HR system strength emphasizes employee consensus as a key mechanism, yet empirical research linking leadership to consensus and downstream outcomes is limited. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether transformational leadership fosters consensus on the HPWS, reduces job satisfaction dispersion, and improves customer satisfaction in 255 DIY stores. Using a 4-year linked employee–customer panel dataset, the authors test a model based on HR system strength theory. The study contributes by demonstrating how leadership strengthens HR systems through consensus, thereby enhancing strategic alignment and unit-level performance.

title: Legacy of the State: Prior Shared Experience and Survival of Spin-Offs From Restructured State Enterprises

entries.rq_with_context: Many organizations in emerging economies originate from restructured state enterprises, yet the implications of this origin for adaptation to environmental change remain understudied. While prior research highlights advantages of organizational origins through spin-offs, less is known about spin-offs created through government-driven restructuring rather than entrepreneurial initiative. This study addresses this gap by exploring how prior shared experience among managers and employees in state enterprises shapes strategic activity choices and post-reform survival. Drawing on transactive memory systems (TMS) theory, the authors compare spin-offs from restructured Soviet-era banks with de novo banks in Russia before and after a 1995 regulatory regime shift. The central research question is how prior shared experience influences activity selection and survival in changing institutional environments. The paper contributes by showing that while prior shared experience aids initial survival, it can hinder adaptation unless spin-offs proactively engage in new activities before regulatory change.

title: When Staying Is Dissatisfying: Examining When and Why Turnover Cognitions Affect Stayers’ Career Satisfaction

entries.rq_with_context: Many employees consider leaving their organization but end up staying, forming a group known as 'reluctant stayers.' While prior research has focused on predictors of turnover cognitions or their link to actual turnover, little is known about the longer-term consequences of these cognitions for those who stay. This study addresses this gap by examining how initial turnover thoughts influence subsequent career satisfaction among stayers over time. Drawing on the insufficient justification perspective and regret theory, the authors test whether the effect of turnover cognitions on career satisfaction is moderated by contextual factors (internal job transitions, lack of external opportunities, on- and off-the-job embeddedness) and mediated by internal processes (justifiability and regret). Using two longitudinal studies with Belgian employees, the research identifies conditions under which turnover cognitions harm career satisfaction and reveals the psychological mechanisms involved. The study contributes to a more dynamic understanding of turnover and retention by showing that turnover cognitions can negatively impact well-being even when employees remain in their jobs.

title: You’re Fired! Gender Disparities in CEO Dismissal

entries.rq_with_context: Despite increasing numbers of women in CEO roles, there is limited understanding of whether they face different outcomes once in these positions. Media reports and some studies suggest female CEOs may be more likely to be fired, especially when firms face challenges, yet rigorous academic evidence is lacking. A key unresolved question is whether gender bias affects CEO dismissal decisions, particularly when firm performance is strong and evaluation is more subjective. This study investigates whether female CEOs are more likely to be dismissed than male CEOs and whether the relationship between firm performance and dismissal differs by CEO gender. Using a sample of 641 CEO dismissals from 2000–2014 and multiple econometric approaches, we analyze dismissal patterns with regard to gender and performance. We contribute evidence of significant gender disparities in CEO dismissal, highlighting a previously underexamined form of bias in corporate governance.

title: Perceived Overqualification at Work: Implications for Extra-Role Behaviors and Advice Network Centrality

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses conflicting views on whether employees who feel overqualified are more or less likely to engage in beneficial behaviors at work and become central in advice networks. While some suggest overqualified employees can be valuable knowledge sources, others find they may disengage or feel cynical. The gap is that no research has tested how perceived overqualification relates to advice network centrality, or under what conditions (like P-O fit) it might lead to more or less extra-role behaviors. The research question is whether P-O fit moderates the effects of perceived overqualification on organizational citizenship behaviors toward others (OCBI) and voice, and indirectly on advice network centrality. The authors use person-environment fit theory and network generation theory to frame the model, testing it with multi-source, time-lagged data. The claimed contribution is integrating overqualification and social network literatures by identifying when and how overqualification affects social integration.

title: Do Group and Organizational Identification Help or Hurt Intergroup Strategic Consensus?

entries.rq_with_context: Many organizations struggle with silo thinking that undermines strategic implementation, yet research has largely ignored how teams develop shared understanding with other interdependent teams—known as intergroup strategic consensus. While existing studies focus on within-team consensus, little is known about what drives alignment between teams. Drawing on social identity theory, this paper investigates how team members’ identification with their own group versus the broader organization affects intergroup strategic consensus. The authors hypothesize that organizational identification promotes consensus, but group identification hinders it, particularly when both are strong. They test these hypotheses using dyadic data from interdependent teams in two organizations, analyzing survey responses with MRQAP. Their key contribution is revealing that high group identification can undermine the benefits of organizational identification for cross-team strategic alignment.

title: Line Managers as Paradox Navigators in HRM Implementation: Balancing Consistency and Individual Responsiveness

entries.rq_with_context: While HRM research has traditionally focused on intended HR practices designed by executives, less is known about how line managers actually implement these practices—specifically, the 'how' rather than just the 'what.' A key gap exists in understanding how managers navigate the tension between treating employees consistently and responding to individual differences. This study addresses that gap by investigating the process of HRM implementation in a global professional services firm. Drawing on paradox theory, the authors explore how consistency and individual responsiveness in line managers’ HRM practices jointly influence individual job performance and team viability. Using multilevel data from 171 employees across 60 project teams, they test both main and interactive effects. The study contributes by showing that how HRM is implemented—through balancing competing demands of fairness and individualization—matters for individual outcomes, even if not for team viability.

title: Toot Your Own Horn? Leader Narcissism and the Effectiveness of Employee Self-Promotion

entries.rq_with_context: Employees often use self-promotion to create a positive impression on their leaders, hoping it will lead to better performance evaluations and career outcomes. However, research shows mixed results about whether self-promotion actually works, suggesting its success may depend on the observer. This study addresses the gap by examining leader narcissism as a factor that may influence how self-promotion is received. The research question is whether narcissistic leaders respond more positively to employee self-promotion compared to less narcissistic leaders. The authors test a moderated mediation model using two scenario experiments and a multisource field study with 311 leader-follower dyads. They claim the study contributes by identifying leader narcissism as a key contingency in impression management effectiveness.

title: How Do Prior Ties Affect Learning by Hiring?

entries.rq_with_context: Research shows that hiring R&D scientists from competitors helps firms access external knowledge and boost innovation. However, less is known about how preexisting collaborative ties between the incoming scientist and the hiring firm shape what kind of learning occurs. This study addresses a gap by investigating whether scientists with many prior ties (e.g., through copatenting) generate different learning outcomes compared to those with few or no such ties. The research question is whether prior ties promote exploitative learning—focusing on shared, firm-familiar knowledge—or explorative learning—drawing on unique, novel knowledge. The authors use patent data from the Electronics and Electrical Goods industry and apply organizational learning theory, particularly March’s (1991) exploration-exploitation framework, to analyze knowledge flows before and after mobility. The key claimed contribution is showing that prior ties steer learning toward exploitation, with implications for how firms design hiring strategies to match their learning goals.

title: Killing Me Softly: Organizational E-mail Monitoring Expectations’ Impact on Employee and Significant Other Well-Being

entries.rq_with_context: The proliferation of mobile technology has blurred work–nonwork boundaries, creating norms of constant connectivity that may harm employee well-being. While research has explored general technology use and personal urges to stay connected, little attention has been paid to organizationally driven expectations around email monitoring outside work hours. This study fills that gap by investigating organizational expectations for e-mail monitoring (OEEM) as a distinct job stressor. It proposes that OEEM triggers e-anxiety through persistent attention allocation dilemmas, which in turn harms employee and significant other health and relationship satisfaction. Using resource-based theories and interruption research, the study tests this model across three studies with diverse samples. The authors claim it advances understanding of how normative technology expectations, beyond actual usage, impact employee and family well-being.

title: The Role of Firm Size and Knowledge Intensity in the Performance Effects of Collective Turnover

entries.rq_with_context: High collective turnover is generally seen as harmful to firm performance due to disruptions in human and social capital and operational inefficiencies. However, empirical findings show wide variation in turnover effects, suggesting that organizational context plays a crucial role. Firm size has been proposed as a key contingency, but prior research offers conflicting evidence—some studies suggest larger firms are better equipped to manage turnover, while others indicate they suffer more. This study addresses this inconsistency by proposing that knowledge intensity moderates the moderating role of firm size. Drawing on the resource-based view, the authors argue that firm size determines the resources available to cope with turnover (e.g., financial, human, organizational), while knowledge intensity determines the type of resources needed (e.g., dense social networks, specialized knowledge). The study uses longitudinal data from 6,913 Belgian firms to test a three-way interaction. Its key contribution is reconciling opposing perspectives on firm size by showing that its effect depends on knowledge intensity, advancing context-emergent turnover theory.

title: Performance Feedback Persistence: Comparative Effects of Historical Versus Peer Performance Feedback on Innovative Search

entries.rq_with_context: Firms use performance feedback—based on peer or historical referents—to guide strategic decisions like innovative search, but research has largely treated these feedback sources as equivalent. However, conflicting findings suggest they may differ fundamentally. This paper addresses a gap by introducing 'persistence'—the likelihood that performance feedback endures over time—as a key distinguishing feature. Drawing on profit persistence literature, the authors argue that peer feedback is more persistent than historical feedback due to interfirm mobility barriers. They propose that this leads to more pronounced effects on innovative search: positive peer feedback reduces R&D more than positive historical feedback, while negative peer feedback increases it more. The study uses panel data from U.S. manufacturing firms (1974–2018) and fixed-effects models. It contributes by empirically validating persistence as a critical characteristic that differentiates feedback types and shapes search behavior.

title: Knowledge Recombination and Inventor Networks: The Asymmetric Effects of Embeddedness on Knowledge Reuse and Impact

entries.rq_with_context: Inventors recombine knowledge to create innovations, but the reuse of technologically similar components may have mixed effects—enhancing absorptive capacity while limiting novelty. While prior research has explored inventor networks and knowledge reuse separately, less is known about how network structures interact with reuse patterns and firm-level search strategies. This paper addresses this gap by asking: How do internal embeddedness and network centrality influence the curvilinear relationship between internal knowledge reuse and invention impact? And do these effects vary for firms with inward- versus outward-looking search orientations? Using patent data from 39,785 semiconductor inventions, the authors test hypotheses grounded in embeddedness theory. They find that reuse has an inverted U-shaped relationship with impact, as predicted, and that internal embeddedness steepens this curve—especially in inward-looking firms—while network centrality flattens it in such firms, countering standard network arguments.

title: Punishing the Perpetrator of Incivility: The Differential Roles of Moral Identity and Moral Thinking Orientation

entries.rq_with_context: Witnessing interpersonal mistreatment often motivates third parties to restore justice, yet their responses can be unethical, creating a paradox in deontic justice theory. Prior research has not clearly explained why third-party punitive reactions vary in ethicality, especially in subtle forms of mistreatment like peer-to-peer incivility. This study addresses this gap by differentiating destructive punitive reactions (e.g., retaliating with incivility) from constructive ones (e.g., reporting or correcting behavior) and testing how moral identity and moral thinking orientation moderate these outcomes. Using a three-study design across cultures, it employs a justice framework emphasizing moral outrage as a mediator. The research contributes by identifying conditions under which moral motivation leads to ethical or unethical third-party actions, refining understanding of deonance in justice processes.

title: How Do Authoritarian Leadership and Abusive Supervision Jointly Thwart Follower Proactivity? A Social Control Perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Authoritarian leadership and abusive supervision are two distinct yet related forms of leader control—formal and informal—that both aim to maintain organizational order. While prior research has treated them separately, this study integrates them using a social control perspective to understand their combined influence on employee proactivity. The authors argue that when one form of control is low, the other may compensate, suggesting a substituting effect. The research question is whether these leadership behaviors interact to reduce follower proactivity through increased perceived powerlessness. The study uses three field samples with different operationalizations of proactivity. It claims to advance theory by proposing a unified control-based model that explains how formal and informal controls jointly shape employee behavior through a shared psychological mechanism.

title: CEO Greed, Corporate Social Responsibility, and Organizational Resilience to Systemic Shocks

entries.rq_with_context: Top executives' motives may significantly impact stakeholder well-being and long-term organizational outcomes, yet empirical evidence on how CEO greed affects these areas remains limited. While greed has been linked to negative shareholder outcomes, its influence on CSR and organizational resilience during systemic shocks is understudied. This paper addresses this gap by examining how CEO greed shapes firms' CSR stances and subsequent resilience during the 2008 GFC. Drawing on the upper-echelons perspective and agency theory, it investigates whether greedy CEOs, driven by short-term wealth accumulation, reduce CSR investment, thereby weakening stakeholder relationships and organizational resilience. The study uses panel data on 301 U.S. public firms to test these relationships, contributing an integrative view of how intrinsic and extrinsic motives jointly affect CSR and long-term performance.

title: Mind Your Language: The Effects of Linguistic Ostracism on Interpersonal Work Behaviors

entries.rq_with_context: As workplaces become increasingly linguistically diverse, employees may experience linguistic ostracism when colleagues use non-mutually understood languages, even unintentionally. While prior research has focused on macro-level language policies, less is known about the micro-level consequences of such everyday language-based exclusion. This paper identifies a gap in understanding how perceived linguistic exclusion affects employee behavior, particularly through identity processes. Drawing on ethnolinguistic identity theory, the authors ask how linguistic ostracism influences interpersonal citizenship and deviance behaviors. They test a model using multisource and longitudinal data across three countries. The study contributes by introducing linguistic ostracism as a distinct form of workplace exclusion and identifying disidentification and social self-efficacy as key explanatory mechanisms.

title: A Dynamic Model of the Effects of Feedback-Seeking Behavior and Organizational Commitment on Newcomer Turnover

entries.rq_with_context: Newcomers typically reduce their feedback-seeking behavior (FSB) as they adjust to new roles, a pattern assumed to reflect successful task mastery. However, this decline may undermine social integration and acculturation—key aspects of organizational adjustment. Despite extensive research on FSB and job performance, little is known about its longitudinal impact on commitment and turnover. This study addresses that gap by investigating how within-person changes in FSB influence affective organizational commitment and subsequent turnover outcomes. Using sensemaking theory, the authors propose that declining FSB disrupts newcomers’ understanding of organizational norms and values, weakening commitment. The research uses latent growth modeling across two longitudinal studies with new graduates. It contributes by revealing the potential downside of reduced FSB, linking behavioral dynamics during socialization to long-term retention.

title: Ties That Bind and Grind? Investor Reactions to Politician Appointments to Corporate Boards

entries.rq_with_context: The appointment of politicians to corporate boards is a widespread corporate political strategy, yet empirical evidence on its value for shareholders remains inconsistent—showing positive, negative, and nonsignificant effects. This ambiguity suggests a need to unpack the conditions under which such appointments are viewed favorably or unfavorably by investors. Drawing on director role theory, the authors propose that politician-directors offer resource-provisionary benefits but pose governance-based costs. Investors, therefore, assess their value based on the firm's need for political resources versus governance oversight, and the institutional context in which the firm operates. Specifically, the study asks how firm regulatory and financial dependencies, board political connectedness, and country-level perceived corruption influence investor reactions to politician appointments. Using an event study of 345 appointments across 14 OECD countries, the research applies a multilevel regression model to analyze cumulative abnormal returns. The key contribution is a contingent, integrative framework that explains when and why politician appointments are seen as value-enhancing or value-diminishing, reconciling conflicting findings in the literature.

title: Received Respect and Constructive Voice: The Roles of Proactive Motivation and Perspective Taking

entries.rq_with_context: Despite extensive research on voice antecedents like personality and job conditions, social-relational factors—especially peer dynamics—remain underexplored. While leadership-related variables have been studied, peer-level drivers such as received respect are less understood. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how employees’ perception of being respected by coworkers affects their likelihood to engage in constructive voice. It proposes that received respect enhances two forms of proactive motivation—"can-do" (via control beliefs) and "energized-to" (via positive mood)—which in turn promote voice. Additionally, it explores perspective taking as a precursor to received respect. Using a multimethod design across four studies, including experiments and longitudinal field data, the authors test this model. Their key contribution is advancing a social-relational view of voice by highlighting received respect and perspective taking as critical, yet overlooked, mechanisms shaping employee voice behavior.

title: Abusive Supervision Differentiation and Employee Outcomes: The Roles of Envy, Resentment, and Insecure Group Attachment

entries.rq_with_context: The phenomenon of abusive supervision—where supervisors engage in sustained hostile behaviors toward subordinates—is well-documented in its negative effects on employee well-being and organizational outcomes. However, less is known about how employees are affected when they perceive that this abuse is distributed unevenly within their workgroup, a phenomenon termed abusive supervision differentiation (ASD). While employees typically rely on their workgroup for emotional support during distress, ASD may disrupt this function by triggering negative social comparisons. Existing research has not adequately explained the psychological mechanisms through which ASD influences employee outcomes. Grounded in attachment theory, this paper examines how ASD perceptions lead to two forms of insecure attachment to the group—attachment anxiety and avoidance—and whether these mediate effects on distress, deviance, and turnover. The authors propose and test a model in two studies, demonstrating that ASD undermines the employee–group bond in distinct ways, offering a more nuanced account than social identity theory alone.

title: CEO Gender-Based Termination Concerns: Evidence From Initial Severance Agreements

entries.rq_with_context: Women remain underrepresented at the CEO level despite progress in breaking the glass ceiling, prompting questions about why women may 'opt out' of top leadership roles. Prior research has suggested that gender biases and male-typed leadership schemas lead female executives to anticipate biased evaluations and greater professional risks in CEO positions. However, little is known about what specific concerns female candidates have when considering CEO roles or how firms might address them. This study addresses this gap by asking whether female CEO candidates perceive higher termination vulnerability than male candidates, using initial severance agreement value as an indicator of this perception. It further investigates how firm-level signals of organizational distress (declining performance, early prior CEO dismissal) and the presence of female leaders (on the board or in the industry) shape these concerns. The study uses upper echelons and gender role theory to frame severance agreements as termination insurance and applies regression analysis to new CEO appointments from 2007–2014. The key contribution is providing empirical evidence that women negotiate higher initial severance due to perceived termination vulnerability, highlighting contextual factors that amplify or reduce this concern.

title: The Influence of Bondholder Concentration and Temporal Orientation on Investments in R&D

entries.rq_with_context: Although innovation is critical for long-term competitive advantage, prior research suggests debt financing can reduce managerial willingness to invest in R&D due to bondholders' presumed preference for short-term returns. However, this view treats bondholders as homogeneous and overlooks variation in their investment horizons and influence based on ownership concentration. This study addresses the gap by examining how the presence of bond blockholders—bondholders with concentrated stakes—and their temporal orientation (short-term vs. long-term) shape firm-level R&D investments. Drawing on stakeholder bargaining power theory, the authors argue that concentrated bondholdings increase investor influence, but the effect depends on whether these bondholders are transient or dedicated. Using a unique dataset of institutional bond holdings, the study tests whether dedicated bond blockholders support higher R&D intensity and quality compared to transient ones and whether investor time horizon outweighs the debt-equity distinction in shaping innovation outcomes. The key contribution is challenging the assumption that bondholders uniformly constrain innovation by highlighting the importance of investor type and time horizon.

title: Opportunity/Threat Perception and Inertia in Response to Discontinuous Change: Replicating and Extending Gilbert (2005)

entries.rq_with_context: Existing research on organizational adaptation to discontinuous change emphasizes threat perceptions as necessary to overcome resource rigidity—incumbents' failure to change investment patterns—while simultaneously exacerbating routine rigidity—failure to change internal processes (Gilbert, 2005). This view relies on framing opportunity and threat as a single dimension. However, theoretical work in psychology suggests that evaluations involve primary appraisals (e.g., gain or loss) and secondary appraisals (e.g., perceived control), which may not covary. Contrary to Gilbert’s model, evidence reveals anomalies: some firms commit resources under opportunity perceptions, while others fail to act despite perceiving threats. Our research addresses this gap by replicating Gilbert's study in book retailing and mobile telecommunications, and extending it by unbundling opportunity/threat perception into gain/loss framing and perceived control. Using qualitative case analysis, we examine how these dimensions jointly shape resource and routine rigidity. We show that moderate perceived control is essential to relax resource rigidity under threat, and that opportunity can drive action when firms perceive control and strategic relevance.

title: Customer Injustice and Employee Performance: Roles of Emotional Exhaustion, Surface Acting, and Emotional Demands–Abilities Fit

entries.rq_with_context: Research has established that customer mistreatment negatively affects employee attitudes and behaviors, such as increasing counterproductive work behaviors and reducing organizational citizenship behaviors. However, the underlying psychological processes explaining why and how customer injustice impacts different forms of employee performance are not well understood. This study addresses this gap by proposing a sequential mediation model in which emotional exhaustion and surface acting link customer injustice to in-role performance, OCBC, and CWBC. Drawing on organizational justice and emotional labor theories, the authors test whether customer injustice leads to emotional exhaustion, which in turn increases surface acting, ultimately affecting employee performance. The model is tested across two studies using both cross-sectional and time-lagged data. The research contributes by elucidating a specific psychological mechanism and identifying ED-A fit as a boundary condition, particularly in the prediction of CWBC.

title: Can Firms Be Both Broad and Deep? Exploring Interdependencies Between Horizontal and Vertical Firm Scope

entries.rq_with_context: Firms can be horizontally broad, operating across multiple markets or project types, or vertically deep, integrating upstream or downstream activities. While prior research has separately examined horizontal diversification and vertical integration, less is known about how these two dimensions interact and influence each other. Existing studies present conflicting findings—some suggest positive interdependencies, others negative—but all treat the relationship as unidirectional and fail to account for simultaneity. This study fills that gap by analyzing the bidirectional interdependence between horizontal breadth and vertical depth. Using the resource-based view, the authors theorize that scope-specific capabilities drive each dimension independently, but that constrained executive capabilities—due to coordination demands—create a negative trade-off between breadth and depth. The study further considers how organizational centralization can mitigate this trade-off. The context is the Chilean construction industry, leveraging detailed project-level data from 355 firms. The approach uses a simultaneous equations model with instrumental variables to account for endogeneity. The key contribution is demonstrating the conditional nature of the breadth–depth relationship, showing that negative interdependencies emerge only under high coordination demands and can be moderated by structural centralization.

title: Platform Development: Emerging Insights From a Nascent Industry

entries.rq_with_context: Innovation platforms are increasingly central to value creation across industries, yet most research focuses on established platforms rather than their emergence in nascent industries. There is limited empirical understanding of how platforms initially develop when industry structures, participant roles, and technological standards remain unclear. This study addresses this gap by examining platform development in the U.K.’s nascent tele-rehabilitation through gaming (TRTG) industry. Guided by a dynamic capabilities perspective, it explores two research questions: (1) What capabilities enable business ventures to develop innovation platforms in nascent industries, and how? (2) How do firms deploy these capabilities for platform development? Using longitudinal, inductive case study methods, the research identifies four key capabilities—innovation leverage, market exploration, quality control, and appropriation—and explains how they interact to facilitate platform development. The study contributes by offering a holistic, process-based framework that advances theoretical understanding of platform emergence in uncertain, evolving contexts.

title: When Is a Governmental Mandate not a Mandate? Predicting Organizational Compliance Under Semicoercive Conditions

entries.rq_with_context: Governmental mandates are traditionally viewed as coercive pressures that generate homogeneous organizational compliance, but in institutional settings with enforcement uncertainty—such as emerging economies—compliance may be more varied. The paper identifies a gap in institutional theory by questioning the assumed uniformity of responses to governmental regulations when rule of law is weak and enforcement is inconsistent. The research investigates why approximately one-quarter of Chinese listed firms failed to comply with a clear regulatory mandate to appoint independent directors, despite its high visibility and public support. Using a sociopolitical framework, the authors analyze how regional rule of law, state ownership, and public exposure influence firms’ differential sensitivity to sanctions. The study contributes by redefining such pressures as 'semicoercive' and showing that compliance heterogeneity can be predicted based on firm-specific contextual factors.

title: The Curse of Extremes: Generalist Career Experience and CEO Initial Compensation

entries.rq_with_context: Research on CEO compensation has produced conflicting views: some argue that generalist CEOs with diverse career experiences receive higher pay due to their broader skill sets, while others contend that specialization and deep expertise are more valuable. This study addresses the unresolved debate by examining whether the relationship between CEO career generalism and initial compensation is curvilinear rather than linear. Drawing on both generalism and specialization perspectives, the authors propose an inverted U-shaped relationship, suggesting that while some breadth of experience increases market value, too much mobility leads to a lack of depth and lower pay. Using hierarchical linear modeling on data from 197 CEO appointments, they test this hypothesis and explore how organizational and environmental factors—such as firm diversification, prior performance, and industry complexity—moderate this relationship. The study contributes by challenging the assumption that more generalist experience is always better and highlights the contingent nature of CEO human capital valuation.

title: More Than Meets the Eye: The Role of Immigration Background for Social Identity Effects

entries.rq_with_context: The number of immigrants worldwide has grown rapidly, yet management research has paid little attention to how immigration background influences workplace interactions. While prior research focuses on race and gender in relational demography, immigration status may be a more salient identity marker in many global contexts. This study addresses the gap by investigating whether employee-customer congruence in immigration background affects customer complaints in service interactions. Using multi-study data from a Swiss logistics firm and a UK-based experiment, the authors test if shared migration experiences create a common identity that reduces complaints. They apply social identity theory and find that both high-high and low-low congruence in immigrant status are linked to fewer complaints, suggesting that migrants identify with each other across national lines. The key contribution is identifying immigration background as a critical social identity factor in organizational settings.

title: Following an Uneven Lead: Trickle-Down Effects of Differentiated Transformational Leadership

entries.rq_with_context: Despite extensive research on transformational leadership, less is known about how leaders treating followers differently (i.e., differentiated leadership) propagates across organizational hierarchies and affects lower-level outcomes. While prior work shows such differentiation harms team functioning, it remains unclear whether and how differentiated leadership behaviors at higher levels influence similar behaviors at lower levels. This study addresses this gap by proposing a trickle-down model rooted in conservation-of-resources (COR) theory. Using data from a large multisource field study across three hierarchical levels, the authors test whether manager-level differentiated transformational leadership negatively impacts team helping behavior via increased department stress, supervisor differentiation, and team stress. The study contributes by offering an alternative to social learning explanations, demonstrating a stress-based mechanism for leadership cascades in the context of differentiated leadership.

title: Welcome Back? Job Performance and Turnover of Boomerang Employees Compared to Internal and External Hires

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations are increasingly rehiring former employees (‘boomerang’ employees), often assuming they perform well and adjust quickly due to existing organizational knowledge. However, research on this practice is scarce, and existing findings come largely from atypical contexts like professional sports. This study addresses this gap by examining boomerang managers in a large retail organization, comparing their performance and turnover to internal promotions and external hires. The research asks whether boomerang employees perform better, worse, or similarly after being rehired and how they compare to other hire types over time. Using longitudinal data and behavioral consistency and human capital theories, the study analyzes performance ratings, promotion rates, and turnover across hire types. The authors claim the findings challenge assumptions about the benefits of rehiring and suggest organizations should consider initial turnover reasons and performance trajectories when making staffing decisions.

title: Trust Consensus Within Culturally Diverse Teams: A Multistudy Investigation

entries.rq_with_context: While existing research on team trust focuses primarily on the average level of trust (trust magnitude), little attention has been paid to how similarly team members perceive trust (trust consensus), despite evidence of widespread variation. This gap limits understanding of how trust functions in teams, especially culturally diverse ones. The paper addresses this by investigating what affects trust consensus and how it independently influences team performance. It proposes a contingency model in which team virtuality and collective leadership moderate the impact of national culture diversity on trust consensus. Using a multi-study design with data from work and MBA teams, the study tests hypotheses about the antecedents and outcomes of trust consensus. Its key contribution is positioning trust consensus as a theoretically relevant and empirically impactful team property in its own right.

title: Jump-Starting the Socialization Experience: The Longitudinal Role of Day 1 Newcomer Resources on Adjustment

entries.rq_with_context: New employee onboarding is a critical process influencing long-term success, yet little is known about how different types of resources available on the first day shape adjustment patterns over time. While research recognizes the importance of socialization, there is limited understanding of how specific newcomer resources—such as having a workstation ready or possessing proactive personality—affect both initial adjustment and the trajectory of change. This study addresses this gap by using conservation of resources (COR) theory to examine how early resources predict adjustment levels and growth rates across the first nine months. The authors analyze data from 985 new hires in a Fortune 500 tech company, tracking self-reported adjustment and manager evaluations. The research question is whether and how different resource types relate to distinct adjustment indicators over time, offering insight into how organizations can better support newcomer integration.

title: Whatever It Takes: How and When Supervisor Bottom-Line Mentality Motivates Employee Contributions in the Workplace

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses a gap in the literature by moving beyond the dominant view that supervisor bottom-line mentality (BLM) is primarily dysfunctional. While prior research links BLM to negative outcomes like abusive supervision and social undermining, less is known about its potential positive effects on employee performance. The authors examine whether BLM can also motivate constructive outcomes like task performance, alongside unethical pro-organizational behaviors (UPB), through a mechanism of felt obligation toward the bottom line. Drawing on social exchange theory, they propose that BLM supervisors provide clear guidance that employees feel obligated to reciprocate. Using three-wave, multisource data from the Nigerian financial sector, the study tests this mediated model and the moderating role of employee ambition. The contribution lies in offering a more balanced view of BLM as a double-edged sword that can both enhance performance and promote unethical behavior depending on employee characteristics.

title: Unit-Level Counterproductive Work Behavior (CWB): A Conceptual Review and Quantitative Summary

entries.rq_with_context: Counterproductive work behavior (CWB) has been widely studied, but most research focuses on individual-level CWB despite the assumption that it harms organizational outcomes. There is a notable gap in understanding CWB at higher levels of analysis, such as teams or departments, even though many theoretical antecedents (e.g., leadership, HR practices) and outcomes (e.g., profit, customer satisfaction) are inherently unit-level constructs. This study addresses this gap by defining and examining unit-level CWB as a distinct construct. The research questions are: (1) What factors are associated with the emergence of unit-level CWB? (2) How is unit-level CWB related to unit-level performance? The authors use social information-processing (SIP) theory as a framework and test their hypotheses via meta-analysis across 7,110 units. The study contributes by verifying the detrimental strategic consequences of CWB and clarifying its nomological network at the unit level.

title: Decentralized Governance of Digital Platforms

entries.rq_with_context: Digital platforms have become central to economic and social activity, but concerns are growing about the concentration of power among platform owners. While existing research focuses on centralized governance, decentralized models—particularly in blockchain—offer alternative structures. This study investigates the performance implications of varying governance models by examining the tradeoffs between centralization and decentralization. Using mechanism design theory, the authors identify semi-decentralization as a potentially optimal structure that balances incentive compatibility and informational efficiency. The research question is whether decentralization has a nonlinear (inverted U-shaped) relationship with platform performance. The authors use empirical data from blockchain platforms to test this, measuring performance through market capitalization, developer engagement, and activity. The study contributes by identifying semi-decentralization as a higher-performing governance model and by revealing how platform type and leadership influence governance design.

title: Disciplining Role of Short Sellers: Evidence From M&A Activity

entries.rq_with_context: Prior research has focused on long investors, such as institutional shareholders, in shaping corporate M&A decisions, but little is known about the impact of short sellers who profit from stock price declines. Given that managers' wealth and job security are tied to stock prices, they may avoid M&A activity when short interest is high to prevent short sellers from spreading negative information that could drive down stock prices. This paper asks how short sellers influence the intensity and quality of firm M&A decisions. Building on agency theory and external governance, we argue that short sellers discipline managers by increasing the cost of value-destroying acquisitions. We test this using S&P 1500 firms from 2002 to 2014. Our contribution is to show that short sellers—despite not being traditional shareholders—serve as an external governance force by curbing excessive M&A and improving deal quality.

title: Gritty Leaders Promoting Employees’ Thriving at Work

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates how leaders' grit influences employee thriving, a state characterized by vitality and learning. While prior research highlights the importance of thriving, less is known about leadership's role in fostering it, particularly through noncognitive traits like grit. The authors aim to clarify whether it is the leader's self-perceived grit or the grit perceived by employees (conveyed grit) that matters, and under what conditions this effect occurs. Drawing on social embeddedness theory, they propose a model in which conveyed leader grit enhances employee self-attributed grit, which in turn supports thriving, especially when leaders are perceived as supportive. The contribution lies in distinguishing between self-attributed and conveyed grit and identifying leader support as a key boundary condition, thereby refining both leadership and grit research.

title: Reducing Customer-Directed Deviant Behavior: The Roles of Psychological Detachment and Supervisory Unfairness

entries.rq_with_context: Customer mistreatment is a common stressor in service jobs and can lead employees to engage in deviant behaviors toward customers. Prior research using conservation of resources (COR) theory suggests emotional exhaustion mediates this relationship, but lacks precision on how resource loss unfolds over time and in combination with individual and contextual factors. The paper addresses this gap by investigating the daily-level process linking customer mistreatment to next-day deviant behavior, with emotional exhaustion as a mediator. It proposes that employees’ tendency to psychologically detach from work and their perceptions of supervisory unfairness combine to shape this process. Using a daily diary design with call-center employees in South Korea, the study tests a moderated mediation model grounded in both COR theory and the person-situation interactionist perspective. The key contribution is revealing how home-based (psychological detachment) and work-based (supervisory unfairness) factors jointly intensify or weaken the spillover of daily mistreatment into future deviant behavior.

title: Incorporating Job Demand Variability Into Job Demands Theory: A Meta-Analysis

entries.rq_with_context: Research on job demands has traditionally treated demands as stable, average levels experienced by individuals, focusing on between-person differences. However, daily experiences show that job demands fluctuate within individuals over time, yet the implications of this variability remain underexplored. This paper identifies a gap in the literature: while existing work considers average demand levels or within-person changes separately, it does not examine how the degree of within-person variability shapes the impact of average job demands on outcomes like strain and engagement. Drawing on arousal theory, the authors propose that variable demands amplify the effects of challenge and hindrance demands because fluctuating demands require more attention and cognitive resources. Using a meta-analytic path analysis of experience sampling studies, they test whether higher variability strengthens the relationships between overall demand levels and employee outcomes. The study contributes by offering a new integrated perspective that treats job demand variability as a key contingency in job demands theory.

title: Serving You Depletes Me? A Leader-Centric Examination of Servant Leadership Behaviors

entries.rq_with_context: Research has shown that servant leadership benefits followers, but less is known about its implications for leaders themselves, especially on a daily basis. Drawing on resource allocation theories of self-control, this study explores whether engaging in servant leadership behaviors depletes leaders' mental resources, potentially leading to withdrawal from active leadership (i.e., increased laissez-faire behavior) the next day. It tests whether perspective taking—a cognitive ability to understand others' viewpoints—acts as a key boundary condition. Using two experience sampling studies, the authors examine within-person fluctuations in servant leadership behavior and test a moderated mediation model. The findings contribute to leadership and self-regulation research by showing that the impact of servant leadership on leaders depends on individual differences in perspective taking, revealing a dynamic process where daily behaviors influence subsequent leadership actions.

title: Team Decision Making: The Dynamic Effects of Team Decision Style Composition and Performance via Decision Strategy

entries.rq_with_context: The phenomenon under study is team decision making, specifically how team composition of individual rational decision styles affects team decision processes and performance over time. Although team processes are conceptualized as dynamic, prior research has treated them as static, leaving a gap in understanding how decision strategies evolve. The authors address this by investigating the reciprocal relationship between team rational strategy and performance, and how the effect of team composition changes over time. They draw on the IMOI and episodic performance frameworks to model team rational strategy as both shaped by and shaping team performance. The key contribution is demonstrating the dynamic, reciprocal nature of team decision strategy and performance, and showing that team composition matters early on while outcome feedback dominates later.

title: Thriving at work but insomniac at home: Understanding the relationship between supervisor bottom-line mentality and employee functioning

entries.rq_with_context: Supervisor bottom-line mentality (BLM) — a singular focus on financial outcomes — has been predominantly studied for its negative workplace effects, such as unethical behavior and social undermining. However, existing research largely overlooks both potential positive effects on employee functioning and the spillover into non-work domains. This paper addresses these gaps by examining how supervisor BLM influences thriving at work and insomnia at home. Drawing on social information processing theory and person–environment fit, the authors propose that BLM increases employees’ perception of a competitive climate, which in turn boosts thriving at work but also contributes to insomnia. The study further tests whether employee trait competitiveness moderates these indirect effects. Using two field studies from China and the U.S., the research identifies both beneficial and harmful consequences of BLM, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of its organizational and personal impacts.

title: Mitigating the psychologically detrimental effects of supervisor undermining: Joint effects of voice and political skill

entries.rq_with_context: Supervisor undermining—destructive leadership behavior such as criticism and anger—is common and harms employee well-being. While voice is seen as a constructive way employees might counteract such harm, its effectiveness remains unclear and may depend on social competencies. Existing research has not examined the boundary conditions under which voice mitigates or exacerbates the negative effects of undermining. This study addresses this gap by testing whether political skill determines whether voice buffers or worsens the impact of undermining. Using a three-wave field study with nurses in China, we examine the joint moderating role of voice and political skill on the relationship between supervisor undermining and work engagement, job satisfaction, and turnover intention, with psychological empowerment as a mediating mechanism. We contribute by identifying political skill as a key boundary condition and psychological empowerment as the mechanism through which voice either helps or harms employees.

title: The interactive effects of socialization tactics and work locus of control on newcomer work adjustment, job embeddedness, and voluntary turnover

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational newcomers face uncertainty during onboarding, and companies use socialization tactics to help them adjust and reduce turnover. While prior research has identified general best practices, less is known about how individual differences shape responses to these tactics. This study addresses the gap by asking: for whom are certain socialization tactics more or less beneficial? Focusing on work locus of control (WLOC), the authors examine whether newcomers who believe they control their outcomes (internals) versus those who attribute outcomes to external forces (externals) respond differently to institutionalized (structured) versus individualized (unstructured) socialization approaches. Using longitudinal data from 676 newcomers over 12 months, the study tests whether WLOC moderates the effects of tactics on adjustment, embeddedness, and turnover. The authors claim their work extends socialization research by identifying a key individual difference that conditions the effectiveness of onboarding strategies.

title: Who’s Hiding in the Shadows? Organized Crime and Informal Entrepreneurship in 39 Economies

entries.rq_with_context: Informal entrepreneurship—starting and operating a business without legal registration—is widespread globally, yet the motivations behind it remain poorly understood. While prior research emphasizes formal institutions, this paper identifies a gap in understanding how informal institutions, particularly organized crime, shape registration decisions. The authors pose the central question: How does the prevalence of organized crime affect entrepreneurs’ choice to operate nonregistered new ventures? Drawing on institutional theory, they argue that institutionalized extortion leads entrepreneurs to avoid formal registration as a buffering strategy. Using data from over 8,000 new ventures across 39 economies, the study tests this mechanism and its contingencies. The key contribution is identifying organized crime as a novel antecedent of informal entrepreneurship and advancing a multilevel theory of organizational form choice.

title: Omitted Variable Bias: Examining Management Research With the Impact Threshold of a Confounding Variable (ITCV)

entries.rq_with_context: Omitted variable bias is widely regarded as a major threat to causal inference in management research, often prompting scholars to use instrumental variable (IV) techniques to correct for it. However, these methods come with tradeoffs, including inefficiency and potential for introducing new biases. Despite widespread concern, there is little systematic evidence on how prevalent or impactful omitted variables actually are in published work. This paper addresses this gap by asking: (1) To what extent is omitted variable bias an issue in management research? (2) Can scholars quantify the effect of omitted variables? and (3) When should scholars seek to address them? Using the ITCV technique across two studies—content analysis of published articles and simulations—the authors evaluate the robustness of causal inferences to potential confounders. Their key contribution is showing that most causal inferences in top journals are unlikely to be invalidated by omitted variables unless those variables have implausibly high correlations with both independent and dependent variables.

title: How and when does top management team regulatory focus influence firm environmental misconduct?

entries.rq_with_context: Firm environmental misconduct (FEM) remains prevalent despite its harmful consequences, and existing research has called for greater attention to the psychological traits of top managers as antecedents. While prior studies focus on individual CEO characteristics or demographic traits of top management teams (TMTs), they overlook the motivational psychological traits of the TMT as a collective. This study addresses this gap by investigating how TMT regulatory focus—a key motivational trait—impacts FEM. Drawing on upper echelons theory and regulatory focus theory, it explores both the direct effects of promotion and prevention focus and the moderating roles of external and internal environmental dynamism through regulatory fit. The study uses computer-aided content analysis of Chinese firm disclosures to measure TMT regulatory focus and conducts longitudinal analysis. Its contribution lies in linking TMT regulatory focus to FEM for the first time, emphasizing collective rather than individual traits, and examining both internal and external environmental contingencies.

title: Lost Control Driving Home: A Dual-Pathway Model of Self-Control Work Demands and Commuter Driving

entries.rq_with_context: Daily work experiences may negatively spill over into commuter driving safety, but theoretical explanations for this spillover are lacking. While self-control depletion theory suggests that self-control demands at work impair subsequent self-regulation, empirical evidence is limited, particularly regarding distinct forms of self-control demands and their unique pathways to behavioral outcomes. This study addresses gaps by examining whether resisting-distractions and impulse-control demands at work uniquely predict speeding behavior through separate self-control failure mechanisms. Using a dual-pathway model tested across two daily studies, the authors analyze both self-report and objective telematics data. They claim their work provides one of the most comprehensive field-based tests of multidimensional self-control demands, offering new insights into how specific workplace demands translate into real-world safety risks.

title: Underemploying highly skilled migrants: An organizational logic protecting corporate ‘normality’

entries.rq_with_context: Highly skilled migrants often face underemployment in host countries, even when labor shortages exist. While prior research emphasizes individual-level barriers or societal discrimination, this study shifts focus to the organizational level. It asks why organizations might actively underemploy such migrants, challenging the common assumption that firms are willing to hire them. Drawing on qualitative data from a mentorship program in Sweden, the study uses the relational theory of risk to analyze narratives from mentors, mentees, and program staff. It identifies an organizational logic that protects internal 'normality' from perceived disruptions associated with migrant employees. The contribution lies in revealing how organizational risk perception, rather than mere bias or structural limitation, helps explain underemployment.

title: Does Performance Breed Slack? Ownership as a Contingency to the Performance Feedback and Slack Relationship

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational slack is a key construct in strategic management, yet its antecedents remain underexplored despite its influence on firm adaptability and performance. While Cyert and March’s behavioral theory of the firm (BTF) suggests that performance relative to aspirations affects slack, this relationship has not been thoroughly tested, especially across different institutional contexts. Moreover, ownership structure—particularly the distinction between domestic (communitarian) and foreign (contractarian) owners—may shape decision-making norms and thus influence how firms adjust slack in response to performance feedback. This paper investigates how domestic ownership in Japanese firms moderates the relationship between performance feedback and three types of slack: unabsorbed, absorbed, and potential. Using a longitudinal sample of Japanese manufacturing firms, the authors employ dynamic panel models to test their hypotheses. The study contributes by empirically examining slack as an outcome, highlighting the role of ownership as a contingency, and showing how the location of slack (internal vs. external) shapes its responsiveness to performance.

title: Be smart, play dumb? A transactional perspective on day-specific knowledge hiding, interpersonal conflict, and psychological strain

entries.rq_with_context: Employees often hide knowledge despite awareness of its negative consequences for coworkers and relationships, suggesting there may be personal benefits that motivate such behavior. Existing research has largely focused on knowledge hiding as a counterproductive work behavior with detrimental outcomes, overlooking potential short-term intrapersonal benefits. This study addresses the gap by investigating whether employees use deceptive knowledge hiding (playing dumb and evasive hiding) as a day-to-day coping strategy to manage psychological strain resulting from interpersonal conflict. Drawing on the transactional model of stress and coping, the authors test if these behaviors mediate the relationship between daily relationship conflict and end-of-work exhaustion and negative affect. The study uses a diary design with multilevel analysis of 615 workdays from 101 employees. It contributes by showing that knowledge hiding—particularly playing dumb—may serve instrumental, adaptive functions in the short term, offering a more nuanced understanding of 'negative' workplace behaviors.

title: Rivals or Collaborators? Relational Ambidexterity and Absorption Speed

entries.rq_with_context: In technology-intensive industries like pharmaceuticals, the speed at which firms absorb external knowledge (absorption speed) is critical for competitive advantage. While prior research has focused on overall interfirm knowledge flows or dyadic alliances, it often overlooks the temporal dimension and fails to distinguish between rival and collaborative relationships within a firm’s broader alliance portfolio. This study addresses these gaps by investigating how the configuration of rivals and collaborators—termed relational ambidexterity—affects absorption speed. Drawing on interorganizational learning theory, the authors propose that balancing rivals and collaborators accelerates learning by increasing receptivity and partner transparency. The study further examines boundary conditions: internal knowledge variety (an inward-looking factor) and common third parties (an outward-looking factor). Its key contribution is shifting focus from static knowledge flows to dynamic absorption speed and offering a firm-controllable strategy—portfolio configuration—to enhance learning.

title: Unlearning and consent in the UK Fire and Rescue Service

entries.rq_with_context: Organisational unlearning is often framed as a 'clean slate' process where obsolete knowledge is discarded to make way for the new. However, this view overlooks the role of people who must actually unlearn. In the UK Fire and Rescue Service, firefighters face ongoing changes due to fewer fires and new technologies, requiring them to adapt practices. Existing research has not explored how they remember, forget, or consent to unlearning. This study addresses that gap by asking: how do firefighters unlearn, and what is the role of trust and consent in that process? Drawing on qualitative data from observations, interviews, and focus groups, it uses a human-centred approach to examine unlearning as a social, iterative process. It contributes by showing that unlearning does not require forgetting, and that consent—shaped by trust in innovations—is essential for successful implementation.

title: Survey response rates: Trends and a validity assessment framework

entries.rq_with_context: Survey response rates are commonly used as a benchmark for assessing sample quality in social science research, yet there is limited understanding of how response rates have evolved over time and what factors influence them. While prior research has examined response rates, recent technological advances, the rise of online panels, and changes in researcher behavior suggest that response rates may have shifted significantly. There is also no comprehensive framework for evaluating whether a given response rate is valid for supporting generalizable inferences. This study analyzes response-rate data from 1014 surveys in 703 articles across 17 journals from 2010 to 2020 to understand trends and predictors of response rates. It then proposes a validity assessment framework to move beyond simple benchmarking. The key contribution is both empirical—documenting rising response rates and their predictors—and theoretical—introducing a framework to assess when a response rate is functionally valid despite being high or low.

title: Hybrid (un)freedom in worker hostels in garment supply chains

entries.rq_with_context: Worker hostels in global supply chains, especially in the garment industry, are commonly associated with exploitative practices and restrictions on freedom, often framed as modern slavery. However, binary understandings of freedom versus unfreedom overlook the complex realities migrant women face. This study addresses a gap in the literature by exploring how freedom is simultaneously restricted, protected, and enabled in hostels within a garment cluster in Tamil Nadu, India. Drawing on qualitative interviews with workers, employers, and stakeholders, we ask how freedom is experienced in these hostels and how suppliers respond to conflicting pressures from global brands and local socio-cultural norms. Using a grounded approach, we analyze how hostels embody a mixture of control and opportunity. The study contributes by introducing the concept of 'hybrid (un)freedom' to capture the interwoven nature of restriction, protection, and liberation, challenging dominant binaries in modern slavery discourse.

title: Racialised professionals’ experiences of selective incivility in organisations: A multi-level analysis of subtle racism

entries.rq_with_context: Despite decades of equality legislation, workplace racism persists, particularly in subtle forms that are hard to identify and challenge. Existing research often focuses on individual or structural levels in isolation, failing to capture the layered complexity of subtle racism. This paper addresses this gap by exploring how racialised professionals experience selective incivility across individual, organisational and societal levels. Using Cortina’s multi-level framework of selective incivility, the study draws on 22 in-depth interviews with racialised professionals in the UK. It aims to show how subtle racism operates through interlocking dynamics across these levels. The authors claim their multi-level analysis advances understanding of how racism is reproduced in ways that evade traditional anti-discrimination measures.

title: Management without morals: Construct development and initial testing of amoral management

entries.rq_with_context: Leadership plays a key role in shaping ethical behavior in organizations, yet little research has examined what happens when leaders routinely fail to address ethical concerns—a phenomenon termed amoral management. While unethical and ethical leadership have been widely studied, amoral management remains underexplored despite its reportedly common occurrence. The gap lies in the lack of an empirical measure and understanding of its consequences for employees. This study addresses this by developing and validating a measure of amoral management and testing its impact on employees’ moral courage and unethical behavior. Drawing on moral conation theory, the authors propose that amoral management reduces moral courage, which in turn increases unethical behavior. They also examine how an ethical organizational environment influences this relationship. The key contribution is establishing amoral management as a distinct, measurable construct with negative employee outcomes, even in otherwise ethical contexts.

title: Up to No Good? Gender, Social Impact Work, and Employee Promotions

entries.rq_with_context: Firms increasingly sponsor social impact initiatives to benefit both society and employees, with expectations of career advancement for participants. However, prior research has not fully explored whether these benefits are realized or if biases exist. A key gap is understanding how gender—both of employees and evaluators—affects the evaluation of social impact work, which is often stereotyped as more appropriate for women. This study investigates whether participating in such initiatives hinders promotion, especially for men, due to lowered perceptions of fit and commitment. Using longitudinal field data and a vignette experiment, the authors test how participant and evaluator gender moderate promotion outcomes. The key contribution is revealing that male participants face a promotion penalty due to gender-based biases, particularly from male evaluators.

title: Doing More With Less: Interactive Effects of Cognitive Resources and Mindfulness Training in Coping With Mental Fatigue From Multitasking

entries.rq_with_context: Modern work environments are characterized by increasing challenge stressors—such as workload, time pressure, and responsibility—that simultaneously enhance engagement and produce mental fatigue. While prior research has linked challenge stressors to fatigue, less is known about the behavioral mechanisms involved, particularly how people respond through multitasking. Furthermore, it remains unclear why some individuals experience greater mental fatigue than others when multitasking. This study addresses these gaps by testing a model in which multitasking mediates the link between challenge stressors and mental fatigue, with cognitive resources moderating this effect. It further investigates whether mindfulness training can mitigate fatigue for those with fewer cognitive resources. Using an experience sampling design across two studies—including a field experiment with mindfulness training—the authors test these hypotheses. The study contributes by identifying multitasking as a key behavioral mechanism linking stressors to subjective fatigue and demonstrating that mindfulness can help individuals with lower cognitive resources manage multitasking demands.

title: A Configurational Exploration of How Female and Male CEOs Influence Their Compensation

entries.rq_with_context: The paper addresses two prominent societal issues: excessive CEO compensation and gender pay gaps. While prior research has explored these topics separately, little attention has been paid to whether the mechanisms through which CEOs influence their compensation are the same for women and men. Given that board decisions about CEO pay are inherently ambiguous and subject to social influence, and considering role congruity theory suggests female leaders face higher scrutiny, the authors investigate whether female and male CEOs achieve high compensation through different configurations of influence. Using a configurational approach (fsQCA) on a matched-pair sample of U.S. public company CEOs from 2010–2016, they identify sufficient causal combinations. The study's key contribution is revealing distinct gendered pathways to high pay, advancing understanding of how influence operates differently for female and male CEOs despite similar outcomes.

title: How Idealized Professional Identities Can Persist through Client Interactions

entries.rq_with_context: New professionals often experience 'reality shock' when their idealized expectations of a profession clash with the actual demands of their first job. While existing theory suggests they adapt their identities to align with organizational and professional goals, this ethnographic study of first-time hospital nurses reveals otherwise. It explores how romanticized, identity-related dreams formed early in life can persist despite negative work conditions. The paper identifies a gap in understanding how identity mismatches are resolved when formal socialization from senior professionals or organizations is weak. The central research question is: how and when can a professional identity persist when it is mismatched with modern work demands? Using ethnographic data, the study analyzes identity enactments through interactions with patients. The key contribution is showing that idealized identities can be sustained not through institutional support, but through client interactions that allow nurses to claim and occasionally be granted these identities.

title: Social Performance Feedback and Firm Communication Strategy

entries.rq_with_context: As corporate social responsibility becomes a key performance metric, understanding how firms respond to social performance feedback is increasingly important. While prior research has focused on financial performance feedback and substantive strategic responses, little is known about how firms manage impressions in response to social performance gaps. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how firms adjust the use of visual expressions in CSR reports following positive or negative social performance discrepancies. Drawing on the behavioral theory of the firm and impression management literature, the authors propose that firms use fewer visuals when outperforming aspirations (to avoid appearing inefficient) and more visuals when underperforming (to restore legitimacy). The study uses a sample of Chinese listed firms from 2009 to 2017 and finds support for these hypotheses, contributing new insights into non-financial performance feedback and symbolic communication strategies.

title: Federal employees or rogue rangers: Sharing and resisting organizational authority through Twitter communication practices

entries.rq_with_context: Following the Trump administration's 2017 social media blackout of federal science agencies, 'rogue rangers' created alternative National Park Service Twitter accounts to disseminate scientific information. This case reveals a gap in understanding how authority and resistance are communicatively performed in social media contexts, particularly when organizational members operate outside official channels. The study asks how these employees use Twitter practices to simultaneously claim organizational authority while resisting censorship. Using a communicative constitution of organizations (CCO) framework, the authors analyze how actors attribute their communication to organizational figures (like logos, mission statements, and identities) or disattribute to alternative movements (like #resist). The key contribution is demonstrating that authority and resistance are not opposites but are co-constituted through the same communicative practices of dis/attribution, creating strategic ambiguity that enables organizational members to speak authoritatively while evading official sanction.

title: Perceived Overqualification and Collectivism Orientation: Implications for Work and Nonwork Outcomes

entries.rq_with_context: Perceived overqualification—having more skills and education than required for a job—affects many workers globally, often leading to negative outcomes like disengagement and withdrawal. However, individuals may react differently based on cultural values. This research investigates whether collectivism orientation shapes how overqualified employees experience their work situation by testing two competing explanations: person-environment (P-E) fit (a cognitive mismatch with the job or group) and relative deprivation (an affective sense of deserving better). The study asks whether collectivism reduces the negative impact of overqualification on positive outcomes (OCB, personal initiative, work engagement, life satisfaction) by lessening misfit or deprivation. Using a moderated mediation model across two studies, the authors test which mechanism explains the buffering effect. Their key contribution is identifying P-E fit—but not relative deprivation—as the primary pathway, clarifying when and why overqualification leads to poorer outcomes.
