title: Frenemies: Overcoming Audiences’ Ideological Opposition to Firm–Activist Collaborations

entries.rq_with_context: Collaborations between firms and social movement organizations (SMOs) are seen as valuable for addressing societal challenges like climate change, enabling firms to improve their social and environmental practices while allowing SMOs to influence corporate behavior. However, despite their potential benefits, such collaborations remain rare in many cases, raising the question of what prevents their formation. Existing research emphasizes resource complementarity but overlooks how the need for social approval from different audiences may inhibit collaboration. Firms seek collaborations to gain legitimacy from their stakeholders, but SMOs risk backlash from their own supporters and peers who define their identity in opposition to firms. This study identifies 'oppositional audiences'—those who define themselves against corporate actors—as a key constraint. It asks how and when these constraints are overcome. Drawing on 25 years of archival data on environmental movements and Fortune 500 firms, the study uses panel data models to examine how audience dynamics and movement structures influence collaboration. The key contribution is identifying countervailing audience effects that suppress collaboration when SMOs face strong opposition from within their movements, especially when firms seek partnerships after being publicly targeted.

title: Both a curse and a blessing? A social cognitive approach to the paradoxical effects of leader narcissism

entries.rq_with_context: Leader narcissism has been shown to have both positive and negative effects on organizational outcomes, yet the mechanisms and contingencies underlying these paradoxical effects remain unclear. While existing research acknowledges the dual nature of narcissism, few studies have explained when and how it leads to beneficial or harmful results. This paper fills that gap by investigating the role of leader effectiveness as a key contingency that shapes followers’ collective leadership perceptions—either as narcissistic supervision or charismatic leadership—in response to leader narcissism. Using a social cognitive approach and the inferential model of leadership perceptions, the study proposes and tests a moderated mediation model with multi-wave, multi-source data from 76 teams. The key contribution is uncovering how the same trait (narcissism) can lead to opposing follower perceptions and performance outcomes depending on perceived leader effectiveness.

title: Is the bottom line reached? An exploration of supervisor bottom-line mentality, team performance avoidance goal orientation and team performance

entries.rq_with_context: Supervisors who emphasize bottom-line outcomes at the expense of other priorities may inadvertently harm team performance, despite their focus on results. While prior research has linked bottom-line mentality (BLM) to unethical behaviors, its impact on actual performance remains unclear, with conflicting findings at the individual level. This study addresses this gap by examining team-level outcomes, drawing on social information processing theory. It proposes that supervisor BLM creates social cues that foster team performance avoidance goal orientation (TPVGO), which in turn reduces team performance. The study further tests whether performing tension—perceived contradictory demands—amplifies this effect. Using data from 258 teams in a Chinese food-chain company, the research aims to clarify the mechanisms through which supervisor BLM undermines team performance. The findings contribute to BLM literature by identifying TPVGO as a key mechanism and performing tension as a boundary condition.

title: A Wolf in Sheep’s Clothing: Exploring the Relationship Between Leader Humility and Unethical Behavior

entries.rq_with_context: Leader humility is widely viewed as beneficial for followers and organizational outcomes, yet little attention has been paid to its effects on leaders who display it. The paper identifies a gap in understanding whether such morally praiseworthy behavior might have unintended consequences for the leaders themselves, particularly through moral licensing. Drawing on moral licensing theory, the authors propose that leader humility increases moral credits, which may then justify unethical behaviors—either for the organization (pseudobeneficial) or toward it (detrimental). The study uses a survey of leader-follower dyads in Taiwan to test these relationships. It contributes by shifting focus from followers to leaders and identifying moral credits as a mechanism linking humility to unethical behavior, with relational accountability as a key moderator.

title: Serving to Help and Helping to Serve: Using Servant Leadership to Influence Beyond Supervisory Relationships

entries.rq_with_context: While servant leadership research has primarily focused on hierarchical, supervisory relationships, this study addresses a key gap by exploring how servant leadership operates in nonhierarchical contexts—specifically, when support managers (e.g., HR) influence line managers without formal authority. Existing theory suggests servant leadership spreads through social learning, but little is known about how or when it functions beyond direct supervision. The authors ask whether support managers’ servant leadership can initiate a trickle-around effect by shaping line managers’ leadership styles and, in turn, employee outcomes. Drawing on social learning and servant leadership theories, they propose a mediated model where line manager servant leadership transmits the influence of support managers. They further examine leadership self-efficacy as a boundary condition. The study contributes by demonstrating that servant leadership can be socially influential even without positional power, and that efficacy beliefs enhance its contagion.

title: Voice as a Signal of Human and Social Capital in Team Assembly Decisions

entries.rq_with_context: In today’s open talent economy, team membership is increasingly fluid, with individuals self-assembling into temporary teams based on perceived value. While prior research has focused on individual attributes in team assembly, less is known about how specific behaviors—particularly voice—signal an individual's potential contributions. This paper addresses that gap by investigating how two forms of voice—challenging and supportive—signal human and social capital, respectively, and thereby influence team formation. The authors test whether challenging voice leads to perceptions of quality work and personal reputation (human capital pathway), while supportive voice fosters friendship and trust (social capital pathway), both predicting team assembly. They use multiwave data from MBA programs and ERGMs to model relational choices. The key contribution is demonstrating that voice behaviors serve as critical signals beyond homophily, with social capital having a stronger effect on team selection than human capital.

title: How ‘matter matters’ for morality: The case of a stock exchange

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing interest in materiality in organization studies, organizational ethics is typically framed as individual, subjective, and disembodied. This creates a gap: the role of material artifacts and infrastructures in shaping moral orders remains underexplored. Drawing on science and technology studies (STS) and the social study of markets, this article investigates how moral norms are co-produced through sociomaterial arrangements. Using a historical sociology of the OFEX stock exchange, it analyzes how trading technologies like notebooks and electronic platforms generate distinct moral orders—such as 'the virtue of intervention' or 'the ethics of competition'. The study contributes to a 'new sociology of morality' by showing that moral orders are not just discursively constructed but materially embedded, temporary, and contested.

title: Peeking Inside the Black Box: Inventor Turnover and Patent Termination

entries.rq_with_context: Inventor mobility is known to transfer knowledge to destination firms, but less is understood about what happens to the knowledge assets—like patents—that inventors leave behind at their source firms. While firms own the intellectual property rights to these patents, they may lose access to the tacit knowledge that resides with the inventors, making future recombination and use of the patent difficult. This creates a gap in understanding how employee turnover impacts the strategic management of existing knowledge portfolios. The research asks: does inventor turnover increase the likelihood that firms will terminate their former inventors’ patents? Drawing on the knowledge-based view, the study argues that because tacit knowledge is critical for recombining explicit knowledge, its loss upon departure leads to higher termination rates. The analysis also considers how collaboration characteristics moderate this effect. Using longitudinal data from 102 pharmaceutical firms, the study finds that inventor turnover increases patent termination, especially when collaboration ties lack knowledge overlap, strength, or stability. The contribution lies in revealing how human capital and relational capital jointly shape knowledge portfolio decisions.

title: Extending organizational socialization theory: Empirical evidence from volunteer work for refugees in France and Australia

entries.rq_with_context: Volunteers are essential to nonprofits addressing complex societal issues like the refugee crisis, yet their socialization remains poorly understood. Existing research often treats organizational entry as a single phase and applies for-profit models to volunteering, missing the dynamic, emotionally charged reality of volunteer work. This study addresses this gap by exploring how volunteers helping refugees in France and Australia are socialized. Drawing on 42 interviews, 17 hours of observations, and document analysis, it investigates the socialization process, tactics used, and outcomes indicating progression. The authors identify a three-stage model—familiarizing with the role, bonding with the group, and embedding into the organization—that captures the volunteer experience more accurately than prior monolithic models.

title: Learning from the Past: How Prior Experience Impacts the Value of Innovation After Scientist Relocation

entries.rq_with_context: There is growing interest in studying the relocation of knowledge workers, yet we have limited understanding of how such moves disrupt scientists' innovation activities. Relocation may hinder coordination with prior collaborators and force work with new ones, potentially reducing innovation value. This study addresses this gap by investigating how a scientist’s research and development (R&D) experience influences innovation value after relocation. We develop a framework showing that R&D experience has a double-edged effect: it reduces innovation value before relocation due to rigidity but increases it afterward by helping adaptation and integration of new collaborators. Using longitudinal data from genomics scientists affected by the 1994 Northridge earthquake, we test these effects. Our contribution lies in revealing the shifting role of R&D experience across stable and disruptive contexts.

title: Talent management, identity construction and the burden of elitism: The case of management trainees in Hong Kong

entries.rq_with_context: Talent management (TM) is often framed as an organizational strategy to identify and develop high-potential employees, yet little is known about how early-career employees experience being labeled 'talented.' Most research adopts a managerial perspective, ignoring frontline voices. This study addresses that gap by exploring how management trainees in Hong Kong understand and respond to the identity of elitism conferred by TM programs. Drawing on Foucauldian disciplinary power and the 'principle of potentiality,' it investigates how organizations discursively construct elite identities, how these are internalized or resisted, and how legitimacy is negotiated. The research uses qualitative interviews with trainees and executives to uncover the subjective meanings and identity struggles tied to TM. Its key contribution is revealing the 'burden of elitism'—the psychological and social costs of being treated as a privileged future leader.

title: High Compensation and Unethical Reciprocity

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses a gap in social exchange theory by investigating how high compensation—typically seen as reducing workplace deviance—might instead trigger unethical reciprocity, where employees act unethically to benefit their employer. While existing research links low pay to retaliatory behaviors, less is known about the ethical risks of high pay. The authors propose that high-paid employees may feel obligated to reciprocate beyond work effort, leading to dishonesty or rule-breaking that harms third parties. Using experimental behavioral games and field data from police officers, the research tests whether high compensation increases such unethical reciprocity. The approach combines controlled lab experiments with archival analysis to establish causality and external validity. The key contribution is extending social exchange theory by showing that positive exchanges can produce ethically problematic outcomes, not just positive ones.

title: How leader and follower prototypical and antitypical attributes influence ratings of transformational leadership in an extreme context

entries.rq_with_context: Leadership ratings are influenced not only by leader behaviors but also by followers' personal attributes and the context in which leadership occurs. While prior research acknowledges follower attributes shape leadership perceptions, few studies have examined how the congruence between leader and follower attributes affects transformational leadership ratings, especially in extreme contexts where leadership demands are heightened. This study addresses this gap by investigating how alignment in affect (positive/negative), motivation (promotion/prevention focus), and cognition (relational/collective identity) between leaders and followers shapes transformational leadership evaluations among US Army soldiers in combat. Using leader categorization theory and implicit leadership theory, the study analyzes survey data from 1,587 soldiers across 262 units. The key contribution is demonstrating that follower-leader congruence in prototypical attributes amplifies transformational leadership ratings, particularly as deployment duration increases, thereby integrating personal and contextual factors into leadership attribution processes.

title: Ethical Leadership and Ethical Voice: The Mediating Mechanisms of Value Internalization and Integrity Identity

entries.rq_with_context: Ethical leadership is widely recognized for promoting positive employee behaviors, yet less is known about the underlying mechanisms—particularly those rooted in followers' self-concepts—through which it fosters ethical voice. While prior research has focused on proximal mechanisms like trust and social exchange, this paper addresses a gap by exploring more distal, follower-based processes: value internalization and personal identity. The authors argue that ethical leaders act as 'meaning makers' who signal organizational values, prompting employees to internalize them and activate ethics-related aspects of their self-concept, specifically integrity identity. The central research question is whether ethical value internalization and integrity identity mediate the link between ethical leadership and ethical voice. Drawing on self-concept and social information processing theories, the authors test a serial mediation model across three studies using time-lagged, multisource, and cross-lagged designs. The key contribution is identifying value internalization and integrity identity as novel psychological mechanisms explaining how ethical leadership translates into ethical voice behavior.

title: Pay Volatility and Employee Turnover in the Trucking Industry

entries.rq_with_context: Many organizations use pay systems that shift financial risk to employees by tying compensation to output or hours worked, leading to paycheck-to-paycheck fluctuations. While such systems offer employers cost flexibility, little is known about how employees respond behaviorally to these fluctuations. Existing research focuses on annual pay changes or intentions rather than objective turnover outcomes. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether pay volatility leads to higher voluntary turnover among truck drivers, using a large dataset of weekly pay and turnover records. Drawing on the Unfolding Model of Turnover, it proposes that fluctuating pay acts as a 'shock' that triggers exit thoughts. The study tests the direct effect of pay volatility on turnover and whether pay level and trajectory moderate this relationship. It contributes by linking dynamic pay patterns to actual turnover behavior in a high-volatility context.

title: To What Do I Owe This Visit? The Drawbacks and Benefits of In-Role and Non-Role Intrusions

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace intrusions—unexpected encounters initiated by others that interrupt an individual’s work—are typically viewed as negative experiences that deplete resources and increase strain. However, existing research has largely overlooked potential benefits and treated all intrusions as uniformly harmful. This paper addresses a gap by distinguishing between two types of intrusions: non-role (e.g., small talk) and in-role (e.g., project updates). The authors investigate how each type impacts daily work engagement and collaboration, and how these mechanisms indirectly influence task-focused and person-focused citizenship behaviors. Using a multistudy approach—including experimental experience sampling, a controlled experiment, and a longitudinal ESM study with R&D scientists—the research tests a theoretical model grounded in job demands theory. The key contribution is demonstrating that not all intrusions are detrimental: in-role intrusions can enhance engagement and collaboration, leading to positive extra-role behaviors.

title: Changing times for digitalization: The multiple roles of temporal shifts in enabling organizational change

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often attempt temporal shifts—deliberate changes in work rhythms or timing norms—to drive change, but these can backfire by creating speed traps or misalignment with external demands. While prior research highlights the importance of temporal shifts, it remains unclear when and how they successfully enable organizational change. This study addresses that gap by investigating how temporal shifts function in practice during a digitalization initiative at a design firm. The research asks: (i) What roles do temporal shifts play in enabling organizational change? and (ii) How are these shifts facilitated? The authors use an in-depth case study of a temporary organization implementing a new digital design approach, analyzing how a 'no-design time' regime reshaped temporal perceptions. The key contribution is identifying three complementary roles of temporal shifts—past-orienting, present-focusing, and future-directing—and showing how a 'temporal zone' established by the temporary organization enables and aligns these roles to foster change.

title: How does policy alienation develop? Exploring street-level bureaucrats’ agency in policy context shift in UK telehealthcare

entries.rq_with_context: Public policies often fail due to frontline staff feeling disconnected from policy goals—experiencing powerlessness or meaninglessness—a condition known as policy alienation. While current theory treats policy alienation as a static psychological state, this study identifies a gap in understanding how it develops dynamically over time, especially within group contexts. Drawing on an 8-year ethnographic study of UK telehealthcare policy, the authors investigate how shifting policy and organizational contexts generate episodes of misalignment that cumulatively contribute to policy alienation. Using a processual, relational approach grounded in participant observation and interviews with street-level bureaucrats, the study traces the evolution of alienation across multiple levels. The key contribution is reframing policy alienation as a temporal, group-level process rather than an individual state, thereby revealing how discretionary responses by frontline workers can either enhance or undermine implementation efforts.

title: Breaking the Chains: The Inverted-U-Shaped Relationship Between Action-State Orientation and Creativity Under Low Job Autonomy

entries.rq_with_context: Creativity is essential in modern organizations, yet it often occurs not only in supportive environments but also in constrained situations that conflict with employees' will. While prior research emphasizes high job autonomy as a key enabler of creativity, less is known about how people remain creative when autonomy is limited. This paper addresses this gap by investigating the role of action-state orientation—a personal tendency in how people respond to unwanted situations. The authors argue that neither strong action- nor state-orientation alone supports creativity under constraint; instead, a balanced integration of both enables creative synthesis. Using an interactionist perspective, they test whether the curvilinear effect of action-state orientation on creativity is strongest under low job autonomy. Their contribution lies in identifying a psychological mechanism that explains variability in creativity under constraint, advancing person-situation interaction theories in organizational behavior.

title: ‘And we gossip about my life as if I am not there’: An autoethnography on recovery from infidelity and silence in the academic workplace

entries.rq_with_context: The paper addresses the understudied impact of infidelity-induced betrayal trauma on academics, particularly within the high-pressure context of 'Fast Academia.' Despite the prevalence of workplace-related affairs and the known mental health consequences of betrayal, little research examines how betrayed partners navigate work and identity in academia. The author identifies a gap in understanding how silence functions—not just as stigma and isolation, but also as a potential space for recovery. The research question is how infidelity-related trauma interacts with academic identity and workplace dynamics, especially through forms of silence. Using autoethnography as both method and framework, the author analyzes personal and online recovery narratives through feminist and organizational lenses. The claimed contribution is illuminating the gendered, emotional, and structural challenges academics face when private trauma collides with professional expectations, and rethinking silence not only as oppression but also as care.

title: The Dynamics of Organizational Autonomy: Oscillations at Automobili Lamborghini

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational autonomy is a key design choice in multi-unit firms, yet existing research largely treats it as a static outcome determined by contingencies like performance or resource dependence. This study addresses a significant gap by asking how autonomy is dynamically renegotiated over time between a unit and its parent organization. While prior work explains settled levels of autonomy, it overlooks the ongoing process and agency of managers in creating fluctuations. Using a 21-year longitudinal case of Lamborghini under Audi, the authors develop a process model showing how dialectical tensions drive oscillations in autonomy. The study’s approach combines resource orchestration and organizational identity to explain these dynamics. The key contribution is a theory of autonomy as a dynamic, oscillating phenomenon sustained within a 'harmonic domain,' rather than a fixed state.

title: Searching for a Sign: CEO Successor Selection in the Wake of Corporate Misconduct

entries.rq_with_context: Following corporate misconduct, boards face pressure to restore ethical standards, yet they lack reliable information about candidates' moral principles. While prior research focuses on external signaling, this paper introduces image theory to explain how directors' internal cognitive images shift toward ethics after misconduct. The study investigates whether boards use a CEO candidate’s graduation from a religiously affiliated university as a cue for ethical leadership. It also tests whether such CEOs actually reduce future misconduct and how industry-level misconduct rates influence both selection and effectiveness. Using archival data on S&P 1500 firms and a policy-capturing study of real directors, the authors test these relationships. Their key contribution is shifting focus from external perceptions to directors’ internal decision-making processes in post-misconduct succession.

title: Beyond the Bottom Line: Don’t Forget to Consider the Role of the Family

entries.rq_with_context: Supervisor bottom-line mentality (SBLM)—a narrow focus on performance outcomes to the exclusion of other priorities—has been linked to negative workplace outcomes such as unethical behavior and poor leader-follower relationships. However, research has not explored how SBLM influences employees’ family lives or impacts their spouses. Given the increasing integration of work and family domains, this gap is significant. This study addresses it by investigating how SBLM affects employee and spouse organizational commitment through work-family conflict (WFC), family undermining, and spouse family-work conflict (FWC). Using conservation of resources (COR) theory, the authors test a model across three samples involving employee-spouse dyads. The key contribution is demonstrating that SBLM’s harmful effects extend beyond the workplace into family systems, influencing both partners’ work attitudes through spillover, crossover, and crossback mechanisms.

title: The Roller Coaster of Leader Affect: An Investigation of Observed Leader Affect Variability and Engagement

entries.rq_with_context: Work engagement fluctuates daily, and while prior research has focused on leaders’ behaviors as drivers of these fluctuations, recent scholarship suggests that leaders’ affective displays also play a critical role. However, existing studies typically treat daily observations of leader affect as isolated events, neglecting how the pattern of affect over time—its variability—might shape employee responses. This study addresses this gap by asking how observed leader affect variability moderates the impact of daily leader affect on employee work engagement via employee affect. Drawing on the emotion as social information (EASI) model and adaptation-level theory, the authors propose a cross-level moderated mediation model tested using experience sampling data from 75 employees over 10 days. The key contribution is demonstrating that affect variability matters: high variability weakens the positive effect of leader positive affect on engagement through reduced affective contagion.

title: Stigma Hierarchies: The Internal Dynamics of Stigmatization in the Sex Work Occupation

entries.rq_with_context: Stigmatized or 'dirty work' occupations are commonly understood as contexts where workers turn to one another for support against external stigma. However, this view assumes stigmatizers are only outside the occupation, ignoring possible internal dynamics of stigmatization. This study addresses a gap in the literature by exploring how stigma manifests within a stigmatized occupation. The authors investigate how and why stigmatization occurs internally among sex workers and what this means for their ability to find support and organize collectively. Based on a six-year qualitative study of sex work in Canada, the research uses interviews, observations, and social media data to trace the internal mechanisms of stigma. The core contribution is the discovery that sex workers create a 'stigma hierarchy' through ordering and detaching practices, undermining occupational unity and limiting social change.

title: The Org-B5: Development of a Short Work Frame-of-Reference Measure of the Big Five

entries.rq_with_context: Personality is widely studied in organizational research, but traditional noncontextualized measures may have limited predictive validity due to inconsistent respondent interpretation across life domains. Frame-of-reference (FOR) theory suggests that contextualizing personality items to the work domain improves measurement accuracy, yet existing FOR measures suffer from content validity issues, language difficulties, reliance on instructions alone, lack of access, or excessive length. This paper addresses these gaps by developing the ORG-B5, a 20-item work-FOR Big Five measure grounded in the knowledge-and-appraisal personality architecture (KAPA) theory. The research question is whether the ORG-B5 demonstrates superior psychometric properties, convergent and discriminant validity, and incremental predictive power over established measures like the Mini-IPIP and IPIP. The approach integrates KAPA theory with rigorous scale development procedures across eight samples in six studies, assessing reliability, validity, measurement invariance, and criterion prediction. The key claimed contribution is a freely available, psychometrically sound, short work-FOR personality measure that advances both theory and practice in organizational assessment.

title: Brokers in Disguise: The Joint Effect of Actual Brokerage and Socially Perceived Brokerage on Network Advantage

entries.rq_with_context: Individuals who span structural holes in their networks are thought to benefit from access to nonredundant information, which supports idea generation. However, a growing literature suggests that such brokers struggle to implement ideas because their unconnected contacts may distrust their motives. Most research focuses on either actual network structures or perceptual dynamics, but rarely both. This study addresses this gap by investigating how the interplay between actual brokerage and socially perceived brokerage affects innovation performance. It proposes that brokers achieve higher performance when colleagues perceive them to have closed rather than open networks, as this perception fosters trust. Using a multimethod approach—including a field study in a consulting firm and a preregistered experiment—the study tests this hypothesis and identifies trust as the underlying mechanism. The contribution lies in integrating structural and perceptual perspectives to explain variation in network advantage.

title: Feminism in women’s business networks: A freedom-centred perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Women’s business networks (WBNs) are often criticized for promoting a postfeminist view of freedom centered on individual self-realization, which undermines collective feminist efforts to dismantle structural inequalities. While existing research highlights this individualizing tendency, it tends to overlook the potential of WBNs as political arenas where shared concerns are debated and transformed. This study addresses that gap by asking how WBNs can help advance women’s freedom through claim-making practices. Drawing on Zerilli’s freedom-centred feminism, the authors analyze 1,529 blog posts from four WBNs using topic modeling and dialectical analysis. They identify three dialectics of freedom—conformity and imagination, performative care and relational care, and sameness and openness. The study contributes by reconceptualizing WBNs as sites of political plurality where feminist freedom is enacted through contested, uncertain, and fragile processes of world-building.

title: CEO Awards and Financial Misconduct

entries.rq_with_context: Financial misconduct by CEOs can destroy firm value and investor confidence, and prior research has focused on CEO characteristics as key determinants. However, less attention has been paid to how significant external events—such as being named a top business leader—might shift CEO attitudes and behaviors. This study addresses that gap by investigating whether winning a high-status CEO award triggers financial misconduct. We argue that such awards inflate a CEO’s sense of psychological entitlement, leading to rule-breaking behavior. Using a sample of Chinese-listed firms, we test this idea through difference-in-differences models and validate our theoretical mechanism with survey data. The study contributes by highlighting meaningful life events as critical antecedents of misconduct, beyond stable individual traits.

title: The extensification of managerial work in the digital age: Middle managers, spatio-temporal boundaries and control

entries.rq_with_context: The article investigates how middle managers' work experiences have transformed in the digital era, particularly regarding spatio-temporal boundaries. While existing research often frames these changes as deterministic outcomes of corporate restructuring and digital technology adoption, this study identifies a gap in understanding the agentic role of managers in shaping work practices. It asks how strategic and political choices contribute to both the extension and resistance of work extensification. Using a two-phase longitudinal interview study (2002–2006 and 2015–2019), the research analyzes how managers perceive shifts in when and where work occurs. The authors claim their contribution lies in advancing the concept of 'work extensification' and highlighting paradoxical trends where control mechanisms both expand and constrain managerial labor.

title: The Authenticity Paradox: Why the Returns to Authenticity on Audience Appeal Decrease in Popularity and Iconicity

entries.rq_with_context: While organizational authenticity is widely seen as enhancing audience appeal, less is known about its boundary conditions, especially when producers become popular or iconic. In markets where authenticity is prized, success may challenge audience perceptions of intrinsic motivation—a core component of authenticity—because popularity and iconicity signal commercial achievement, which can appear economically driven. This paper investigates whether the returns to authenticity decrease as producers gain popularity and iconicity. Using a social constructionist framework and data from the U.S. craft beer industry, the authors test how these factors interact. The key contribution is identifying the 'authenticity paradox': even though authenticity, popularity, and iconicity each boost appeal, popularity and iconicity reduce the added value of authenticity.

title: Professional boundaries in action: Using reflective spaces for boundary work to incorporate a new healthcare role

entries.rq_with_context: Introducing a new professional role into an established setting disrupts existing divisions of labor and triggers boundary negotiations among professionals. While prior research highlights the potential of reflective spaces to support such changes, there is limited understanding of the actual interactive processes occurring in these spaces. This study addresses that gap by analyzing naturally occurring interactions in work development meetings where a new hospitalist role was being incorporated in a university hospital. Using an ethnomethodological approach, the authors examine how professionals categorize the new role through talk-in-interaction. They identify different types of categorizations and explore how these shape boundary work. The study contributes by revealing how technical and contextual forms of practical reasoning either sustain stability or enable change in professional boundaries, offering a nuanced view of reflective spaces' transformative potential.

title: Can Supportive Coaching Behaviors Facilitate Boundary Spanning and Raise Job Satisfaction? An Indirect-Effects Model

entries.rq_with_context: As organizations face increasingly dynamic environments, team leaders are expected to adopt facilitative, coaching-oriented roles rather than directive ones. While prior research has linked supportive coaching to internal team processes, little is known about its impact on team members’ external activities—specifically boundary spanning, which involves building relationships with external stakeholders. There is also ambiguity in the literature regarding whether boundary-spanning behavior improves or harms individual job satisfaction due to potential role overload. This study addresses these gaps by testing an indirect-effects model in which supportive coaching of boundary spanning enhances team member boundary-spanning self-efficacy, leading to increased boundary-spanning behavior and higher job satisfaction. The authors use social cognitive theory and Hackman and Wageman’s team coaching framework to guide their hypotheses, analyzing survey data from 256 engineering employees. The primary contribution is clarifying the motivational pathway through which supportive coaching influences both external team behaviors and individual well-being.

title: Individual- and group-level consequences of divergence in perceived group affect

entries.rq_with_context: Work groups often develop shared affective states, but individuals may perceive these states differently. While prior research focuses on average levels of group affect, this study addresses the gap in understanding how divergence in these perceptions—both within individuals and across groups—affects outcomes. The authors ask whether misalignment in perceived group affect undermines individual social integration (commitment and proactive behavior) and weakens the link between group affect and performance. Drawing on EASI theory and the dispersion-composition model, they test these relationships in a field study of 1419 employees across 107 work groups in South Korea. They find that dissimilarity in perceived positive affect reduces commitment, and dispersion in positive affect weakens its positive effect on performance, contributing to theory on group affect dynamics.

title: Voice Quality and Ostracism

entries.rq_with_context: While voice research has traditionally focused on the quantity of employee suggestions, this paper highlights the importance of voice quality. Employees often fear the social consequences of speaking up, especially if their suggestions are judged as low quality. Existing research has not adequately explored how poor-quality suggestions affect peer relationships and social inclusion at work. This study asks: How does poor voice quality influence coworker-driven ostracism, and what are the downstream effects on the target employee’s self-perception and evaluations of others? Guided by sociometer theory, the authors use a six-week field study with employee-coworker dyads and two vignette experiments to test their model. The key contribution is revealing the 'dark side' of voice by showing that poor-quality suggestions trigger a cycle of social rejection and deteriorating voice behaviors.

title: Regulatory Spillover and Workplace Racial Inequality

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing normative support for racial equality in organizations, progress in workplace diversity—particularly for Black employees in managerial roles—has remained slow. Existing research attributes this to symbolic compliance or decoupling, but does not fully explain why some firms resist change. This study investigates whether state-level affirmative action bans, though legally limited to the public sector, create a normative spillover that legitimizes skepticism toward Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) practices among private-sector executives. The research question is whether these bans are associated with slower growth in Black managerial representation in private firms. Using a difference-in-differences design with EEO-1 data from 1985 to 2015, the study compares firms headquartered in states that adopted bans versus those that did not. It contributes by showing how regulations can exert influence beyond their legal scope through normative channels, particularly when organizational leaders hold ideologically aligned views.

title: People and the Place: Social Dominance Orientation Is Reciprocally Associated With Hierarchy-Enhancing Occupations Over Time

entries.rq_with_context: People’s sociopolitical beliefs, such as their preference for intergroup hierarchies (measured by social dominance orientation, or SDO), often align with the characteristics of their occupation. However, it remains unclear whether this alignment occurs because individuals sort into occupations matching their beliefs (occupational assortment), or because occupational environments shape individuals’ beliefs over time (occupational socialization), or both. Prior research has produced mixed findings, partly due to reliance on student samples and lack of large-scale longitudinal data across diverse occupations. This study addresses these gaps by analyzing longitudinal data from a national sample of adults already employed in either hierarchy-enhancing (HE) or hierarchy-attenuating (HA) occupations. Using cross-lagged panel models with 1-, 3-, and 5-year intervals, the authors test whether SDO predicts movement into HE occupations and whether HE occupations predict increases in SDO. The key contribution is demonstrating that both processes occur, but at different temporal scales—socialization effects appear within one year, while assortment effects emerge over three to five years.

title: Exploring the dynamics of slack in extreme contexts: A practice-based view

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations in extreme contexts must ensure resilience to maintain reliable operations, and slack is often cited as a key mechanism. However, most research treats slack as a structural resource, offering little insight into how actors actually produce and use slack in real time during crises. This study addresses that gap by asking how slack contributes to resilience in extreme contexts through micro-level practices. Using a practice-based perspective and 14 months of ethnographic fieldwork in a French Critical Care Unit, the authors analyze how medical staff gather, reconfigure, and deploy resources during shifting situations. They propose a dynamic model of 'slack practices' that connects situational changes with resource mobilization. The study’s key contribution is revealing how resilience is maintained not just through stored slack but through ongoing, situated practices that generate slack as needed.

title: CEOs’ Regulatory Focus and Risk-Taking When Firms Perform Below and Above the Bar

entries.rq_with_context: Managerial risk-taking is central to strategy research, with upper echelons theory emphasizing CEOs’ psychological traits and the behavioral theory of the firm (BTOF) focusing on organizational performance relative to aspirations. However, these theories offer conflicting predictions about when CEOs take risks. The paper addresses this contradiction by integrating both perspectives through regulatory focus theory (RFT). The research question is: How do CEO promotion and prevention foci interact with performance below and above aspirations to influence strategic risk-taking? Using a large sample of U.S. public firms, the authors test four hypothesized interactions. They contribute by showing that risk preferences are not fixed but depend on the fit between CEO disposition and performance context.

title: Encouraging or expecting flexibility? How small business leaders’ mastery goal orientation influences employee flexibility through different work climate perceptions

entries.rq_with_context: Flexible employees are crucial in uncertain environments, especially in small businesses that lack formal HRM systems to foster flexibility. While prior research links leadership to employee flexibility through learning climates, it overlooks how leaders might simultaneously create multiple climates. This study investigates how small business leaders’ mastery goal orientation (MGO) affects employee flexibility through two distinct work climates—mastery climate and adaptability climate. Using social learning theory and self-determination theory, it explores whether MGO promotes flexibility by encouraging learning, but potentially undermines it by creating normative expectations to be flexible. The study uses multi-wave, multi-level data from 141 Norwegian accounting firms and tests mediated relationships between leader MGO, employee climate perceptions, and leader-rated employee flexibility. It contributes by showing that a generally positive leadership trait (MGO) can have dual, opposing effects on employee behavior.

title: Careers advancement of women: Applying a multi-level relational perspective in the context of Turkish banking organisations

entries.rq_with_context: Despite increasing female participation in the Turkish banking sector, women remain underrepresented in managerial roles—a phenomenon not fully explained by existing Western-centric research. Prior studies have largely focused on single-level factors or Western contexts, leaving gaps in understanding how broader societal forces interact with organisational practices and individual experiences in hybrid cultural settings like Turkey. This article addresses this gap by exploring how national-level dynamics, such as religion-based social fragmentation, intersect with organisational cultures and individual perceptions across three distinct banking organisations (Turkish, Western, and Islamic). Using a multi-level relational framework based on Scott’s institutional pillars (regulative, normative, cultural-cognitive), the study investigates the interplay between macro-, meso-, and micro-level barriers. Its key contribution is revealing how organisational heterogeneity within a single national context shapes divergent career experiences for women, offering new insights into the contextual complexity of gender inequality.

title: The Epidemic of Mental Disorders in Business—How Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Spread across Organizations through Employee Mobility*

entries.rq_with_context: Mental disorders are rising globally and are a leading cause of long-term absence and work disability, making them a critical concern for organizations. While prior research focuses on internal workplace stressors as causes of mental disorders, this study addresses a gap by examining how these conditions may spread across organizational boundaries through employee mobility. It investigates whether employees leaving 'unhealthy' organizations (with high mental disorder prevalence) carry these disorders into new workplaces, acting as carriers even without formal diagnoses. Drawing on infectious disease epidemiology, the study uses longitudinal data on over 250,000 employees and 17,000 firms to test transmission patterns. It proposes that employee mobility serves as a pathway for organizational contagion, challenging the assumption that hiring from outside is universally beneficial.

title: Unpacking the Status-Leveling Burden for Women in Male-Dominated Occupations

entries.rq_with_context: Women in male-dominated occupations are known to face challenges from male colleagues and masculine workplace cultures, as well as from senior women who may not support their advancement. However, little research has examined how these women navigate collaborations with women in lower-status, female-dominated occupations—such as surgeons working with nurses. Despite their higher institutional status, women in these positions may face pressure from other women to be seen as equals, creating a novel challenge not addressed in prior work. This study investigates: What, if any, are the novel challenges and response strategies required of women in male-dominated occupations collaborating with women across occupational status hierarchies? Drawing on interviews with surgeons, the authors develop a grounded theory of the 'status-leveling burden'—the pressure women in high-status roles feel to downplay their authority when working with women in lower-status roles. The paper contributes to understanding how gender and occupational status intersect, revealing that shared gender can create as much tension as solidarity in cross-occupational settings.

title: How Do Employees React When Their CEO Speaks Out? Intra- and Extra-Firm Implications of CEO Sociopolitical Activism

entries.rq_with_context: CEO sociopolitical activism—when chief executives take public stands on contentious social or political issues—is becoming increasingly common, yet its effects on organizational stakeholders, particularly employees, remain poorly understood. Existing research has not adequately explored how such symbolic actions influence employee attitudes and behaviors, especially in relation to organizational commitment and ideological alignment. This study addresses that gap by investigating how CEO activism shapes employee responses, depending on whether the CEO’s ideological stance aligns with the prevailing values of the workforce. Drawing on stakeholder alignment theory and social identity theory, the authors examine the case of CEOs signing a public letter opposing North Carolina’s 2016 ‘bathroom bill’—a clear instance of liberal activism. They analyze differences between firms whose CEOs signed versus those who declined, using multi-source data. The study contributes to understanding the intra-firm (organizational commitment) and extra-firm (employee ideological support) consequences of CEO activism, highlighting the moderating roles of organizational ideology and CEO credibility.

title: The Two Blades of the Scissors: Performance Feedback and Intrinsic Attributes in Organizational Risk Taking

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational risk taking has been studied through two distinct theoretical lenses: the behavioral theory of the firm, which emphasizes performance feedback relative to aspirations, and prospect theory, which focuses on decision makers' evaluation of outcome magnitude and likelihood. However, prior research has typically examined only one of these 'blades of the scissors'—either context or content—despite the fact that real-world decisions depend on both. This creates a gap in understanding how these forces interact in organizational settings. The study addresses this gap by asking how performance feedback and intrinsic attributes of alternatives jointly determine risk-taking choices, and how deadline proximity and attainment discrepancy moderate this relationship. Drawing on both theoretical perspectives and testing predictions using 23,895 fourth-down decisions from the NFL, the authors analyze how decision makers weigh performance shortfalls and gains against the expected outcomes of risky actions. The study contributes by integrating decision context and decision content in explaining organizational risk taking, offering a more complete model than either theory alone.

title: Navigating turbulent waters: Crafting learning trajectories in a changing work context

entries.rq_with_context: Newcomers face challenges in accessing learning opportunities due to changes in work, such as outsourcing and automation, which often relegate them to low-level tasks like scutwork. Existing research acknowledges that power dynamics and structural arrangements in a community of practice can impede access, but little is known about how newcomers actively negotiate such access when it is not granted. This study investigates how merchant-navy cadets, denied access to critical navigation practices on ships, still manage to learn. It focuses on how they navigate constraints imposed by temporal schedules, spatial territories and hierarchical permissions. Using ethnographic data from five months of fieldwork, the authors analyze how cadets surreptitiously use structural arrangements to gain participation. The paper contributes by revealing how newcomers leverage structural elements through 'stealth work'—a blend of normative and counter-normative actions—to craft learning trajectories despite systemic barriers.

title: Managing liminal time in the fly-in fly-out work camp

entries.rq_with_context: Fly-in fly-out (FIFO) work camps are key organizational tools in resource extraction industries, serving as liminal spaces that manage the transitions of workers between remote worksites and distant homes. While existing research has focused on mobility and spatial dynamics, there is limited understanding of how time is experienced in these para-productive, permanently liminal sites. The gap lies in recognizing camp not just as a spatial container but as a temporal organizer that imposes rhythms disconnecting workers from their bodily, familial, and social time. This study investigates how FIFO workers experience this 'liminal time' and what strategies they use to cope with its disorienting effects. Drawing on qualitative fieldwork in Canada’s Athabasca Oil Sands, the authors analyze workers’ lived experiences of camp time and their temporal tactics. The research contributes to organizational studies by showing how workers’ temporal competence is crucial to sustaining the FIFO regime, revealing the human role in mediating institutional time.

title: Platform Governance Design in Platform Ecosystems: Implications for Complementors’ Multihoming Decision

entries.rq_with_context: Digital platform ecosystems involve complex interdependencies among producers, yet research has largely focused on direct governance behaviors of platform owners toward complementors. Less is known about how governance design indirectly creates costs for complementors through ecosystem complexity. This paper addresses the gap by asking how open governance, which grants autonomy to platform providers (e.g., smartphone makers), may increase ecosystem complexity and thereby deter complementors from multihoming. The authors propose that greater complexity raises customization costs, reducing multihoming likelihood. They test this using survival analysis on Health & Fitness apps in iOS and Android ecosystems. Their contribution lies in revealing unintended consequences of open governance and showing how complementor capabilities mitigate these frictions.

title: Neither timeless, nor placeless: Control of food delivery gig work via place-based working time regimes

entries.rq_with_context: Platform-based food delivery work is often framed as highly flexible and technologically controlled, with algorithms assigning tasks and monitoring performance. However, existing research largely overlooks how working time regimes function beyond mere allocation, particularly in their role in controlling labour. This study addresses the gap by asking how food delivery platforms design their working time regimes to ensure both efficient and reliable use of a self-employed, spatially distributed workforce. Drawing on labour process theory and a mixed-methods study of Deliveroo and Foodora in Germany, it investigates how these platforms combine algorithmic management with organisational control through working time. The article argues that such regimes do not simply coordinate work but actively shape worker behaviour by linking shift access to performance metrics. It claims to contribute by showing that platform control is hybrid—technological and organisational—and that it varies by local labour market conditions.

title: Disparate Safety Enforcement: Curvilinear Effects, Mechanisms, and Boundary Conditions of Supervisor-Rated Leader–Member Exchange

entries.rq_with_context: Despite decades of research on leader–member exchange (LMX), the leader's perspective on relationship quality and its impact on differential treatment remains underexamined, especially in safety-critical contexts. Most studies focus on employee perceptions of LMX and their outcomes, neglecting how leaders’ own assessments of these relationships affect their behavior toward subordinates. This gap is particularly consequential for safety enforcement, where inconsistent monitoring can lead to accidents. Drawing on relational leadership theory and affective events theory, we investigate whether supervisor-rated LMX (SLMX) predicts a curvilinear (U-shaped) relationship with safety enforcement. We test this across three studies—one in construction, one in hospitality, and an experimental study—while also examining leader safety commitment as a moderator and trust, consideration, and liking as mediating mechanisms. Our key contribution is a direct test of LMX theory’s core tenet: that leaders treat subordinates differently based on perceived relationship quality, with real implications for workplace safety.

title: Development as freedom? Insights from a farmer-led sustainable agriculture non-governmental organisation in the Philippines

entries.rq_with_context: Small-scale farmers in the Global South face intersecting agrarian and climate crises, worsened by dominant economic models promoting industrial agriculture. While Amartya Sen’s capability approach frames development as expanding individual freedoms (freedom to) and removing unfreedoms (freedom from), it does not adequately explain how these freedoms are relationally constituted or the role of non-human actors. This gap limits our understanding of how agency is formed in contexts of systemic vulnerability. Drawing on fieldwork with MASIPAG, a Filipino farmer-led NGO promoting agroecology, the study asks: how do agroecological work and grassroots organizational practices promote freedom for small-scale farmers under climate threat? Using a participatory action research approach, the authors analyze farmers’ practices through Sen’s framework while foregrounding relational and more-than-human entanglements. The paper contributes by identifying 'freedom with'—a novel form of freedom defined by relational, multi-actor capabilities that reframe agential becoming as co-constituted across humans, seeds, ecosystems, and climate.

title: Founders’ Prior Shared International Experience, Time to First Foreign Market Entry, and New Venture Performance

entries.rq_with_context: New ventures face pressure to internationalize early to survive and grow, yet they often lack the resources and experience needed for foreign market entry. While prior research has focused on founders’ independent international experience, less is known about the role of shared experience—when founders worked together in an international firm before starting their venture. This study investigates whether such shared experience reduces the time to first foreign market entry. It also examines two boundary conditions: whether founders’ diversity enhances the benefits of shared experience by enabling adaptation, and whether industry dynamism weakens it due to knowledge obsolescence. The study uses a sample of Swedish new ventures and finds support for all hypotheses. The contribution lies in showing that shared international experience accelerates early internationalization, but its value depends on team diversity and environmental stability.

title: The Influence of Nation-Level Institutions on Acquisition Premiums: A Cross-Country Comparative Study

entries.rq_with_context: Acquisition premiums—how much acquirers pay above a target’s market value—are critical to deal success, yet many studies overlook the role of national institutional environments. While prior research has focused on firm- and deal-level factors, this paper highlights that institutions differ across countries and significantly shape organizational behavior under uncertainty. The authors identify a gap in understanding how broader institutional contexts systematically affect premium decisions. Drawing on neo-institutional theory, they ask how cognitive, normative, and regulatory pillars at the country level influence domestic acquisition premiums. Using a sample of 21,304 deals across 34 countries from 1991–2017, they test hypotheses linking institutional forces to premium levels. The study contributes by showing that premiums are not just economically driven but are shaped by taken-for-granted practices, cultural norms, and legal disclosure rules.

title: To Buy Green or Not to Buy Green: Do Structural Dependencies Block Ecological Responsiveness?

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing interest in sustainable business practices, decisions about switching to environmentally friendlier input materials remain understudied. While prior research emphasizes external pressures like stakeholder demands and competitiveness as drivers of ecological responsiveness, less is known about internal organizational constraints that may inhibit such transitions. This paper addresses this gap by investigating why firms might resist adopting greener inputs even when they offer functional parity. The research question is: How do organizational structures—specifically product-input, process-inputs, and firm-intangibles dependencies—affect a firm’s willingness to substitute conventional inputs with more ecological alternatives? Using a conjoint experiment with 267 Finnish manufacturing firms, the study tests these effects. The key contribution is demonstrating that structural dependencies significantly condition ecological responsiveness, thereby extending theories of external influence by incorporating inertia rooted in organizational structure.

title: Storytelling as a Tool for Vicarious Learning among Air Medical Transport Crews

entries.rq_with_context: In knowledge-intensive work, direct observation and formal knowledge systems often fail to support vicarious learning due to high ambiguity and low observability of others’ work. This paper explores how storytelling serves as an alternative mechanism for vicarious learning, particularly when traditional methods are infeasible. Drawing on data from an air medical transport program, the study identifies a gap in understanding how storytelling functions as a dynamic, interpersonal process for learning from others’ task-relevant experiences. The research asks how storytelling helps flight nurses convert others’ experiences into actionable knowledge. Using ethnographic observations and interviews, the author builds an inductive model of storytelling as a multistage process—triggering, telling, and transforming—with implications for how learning occurs in dispersed, ambiguous work settings. The key contribution is a process model showing storytelling as a structured, contextually embedded tool for vicarious learning.

title: One-Hit Wonders versus Hit Makers: Sustaining Success in Creative Industries

entries.rq_with_context: Creative industries are characterized by fickle success, with most creators failing to repeat their initial hits (Lotka's Law). While creativity is presumed key to sustained success, prior research has focused on isolated creative acts rather than how past creativity shapes future opportunities. Existing work reveals a disconnect: novelty generally reduces the likelihood of market success, while variety increases it, but these findings treat each product as an independent event. This creates a gap in understanding how early creative choices affect long-term career trajectories. To address this, the author proposes a path dependence theory examining how the creativity in creators' portfolios at the time of their initial hit shapes their odds of sustaining success. Using archival data from the U.S. music industry (1959-2010) with over 3 million songs by 69,050 artists, the study tests whether early portfolio creativity predicts sustained success after initial success. The key claimed contribution is demonstrating that success in creative careers is path dependent, with early creativity shaping future opportunities through self-reinforcing mechanisms of learning and expectations.

title: When being oneself is socially rewarded: Social identification qualifies the effect of authentic behavior at work

entries.rq_with_context: While authenticity is often promoted as beneficial for well-being and performance, questions remain about its social consequences when individuals' values differ from their work environment. Prior research has not sufficiently explored how the social context qualifies the effects of authentic behavior. This paper addresses this gap by investigating whether social identification—reflecting alignment between individual and organizational values—determines whether authentic behavior reduces or exacerbates relationship conflict. Using an interactionist person–situation perspective and social identity theory, the authors propose a moderated mediation model in which social identification conditions the effect of authentic behavior on relationship conflict, which in turn affects task performance. The study contributes by showing that authenticity has positive interpersonal outcomes only when individuals are highly identified with their organization, clarifying when 'being yourself' is advantageous at work.

title: Employee proactive goal regulation and job performance: The role modeling and interacting effects of leader proactive goal regulation

entries.rq_with_context: Employees’ proactive motivational states—role breadth self-efficacy, psychological ownership, and activated positive affect—are known to support proactive goal regulation, which in turn drives proactive behaviors. However, less is known about how leaders’ own proactive goal regulation shapes these processes, particularly in relation to job performance. The gap lies in understanding leadership as a direct and moderating influence on employee goal regulation, beyond just shaping motivational antecedents. The research question is: how does leader proactive goal regulation affect the indirect relationship between employees’ motivational states and job performance via employee proactive goal regulation? The study uses a moderated mediation model grounded in social learning and self-regulation theory. The key claimed contribution is demonstrating both a role modeling effect and a compensatory moderating effect of leader proactive goal regulation in the goal regulation–performance linkage.

title: Manager or Politician? Effects of CEO Pay on the Performance of State-Controlled Chinese Listed Firms

entries.rq_with_context: State-controlled Chinese firms face dual objectives: maximizing financial returns for minority shareholders and fulfilling political goals like job creation for the state. Prior research emphasizes either principal-agent conflicts (PACs) or principal-principal conflicts (PPCs), but rarely integrates both. This gap limits understanding of how executives balance competing demands when incentivized by pay. The authors ask how CEO pay influences both financial and political performance in these firms, and under what conditions these effects are strengthened or weakened. Using agency theory and PPC perspectives, they analyze a sample of 230 firms from 2004–2014. They find that higher CEO pay improves both financial and political performance, but the strength of these relationships depends on structural factors related to the executive’s dual career incentives.

title: What’s It Like Inside the Hive? Managerial Discretion Drives TMT Gender Diversity of Women-Led Firms

entries.rq_with_context: Despite progress in workforce gender parity, women remain underrepresented in top management team (TMT) and CEO roles, raising questions about whether women leaders help advance other women. Two conflicting perspectives exist: the 'trickle-down effect' suggests diversity begets diversity, while the 'queen bee phenomenon' indicates senior women may distance themselves from junior women. Much research has focused on board-level influences, overlooking the unique role of the CEO. This paper investigates the CEO-TMT interface, arguing that women CEOs face distinct isolation and gender salience that may inhibit promoting other women. Using gender role theory and managerial discretion, the authors test how CEO power, board vigilance, and environmental munificence moderate this relationship. The study contributes by showing that structural discretion—not just individual bias—shapes gender diversity outcomes at the executive level.

title: Our Board, Our Rules: Nonconformity to Global Corporate Governance Norms

entries.rq_with_context: Despite widespread global norms promoting majority independent boards, many firms consistently deviate by either having too few or too many independent directors. While prior research has examined drivers of governance adoption, little is known about the conditions under which firms over- or underconform to these established norms, especially across different national contexts. This study addresses this gap by exploring how national institutional factors (such as shareholder and labor rights) and organizational conditions (like ownership structure and size) combine in complex configurations to produce nonconformity. Using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) on data from banks in OECD countries, the study identifies equifinal pathways to both over- and underconformity. The key contribution is demonstrating that nonconformity is not random but systematically produced by distinct power configurations among key actors, advancing understanding of how political processes shape corporate governance globally.

title: Alternativity as freedom: Exploring tactics of emergence in alternative forms of organizing

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses the limitations in existing research on alternative organization, which tends to define alternatives through fixed principles or practices, thereby overlooking their dynamic and relational nature. This approach fails to explain how alternatives interact with mainstream orders and often get co-opted despite their radical intentions. To address this gap, the article conceptualizes alternativity as a process of freedom rather than a stable form. It investigates how alternative organizing can maintain its liberating potential through emergent tactics that avoid full rejection or assimilation. The research question is: how do alternative forms of organizing create conditions for freedom, and what tactics enable the emergence of alternativity as freedom? Guided by a process view and critical theories of resistance (e.g., Foucault, Derrida), the authors draw on three empirical cases—sustainable fintech, mindfulness meditation, and an independent political party. Their key claimed contribution is identifying endurance, germination, and reiteration as central tactics that keep alternatives open and fluid, thereby redefining alternativity as freedom in process.

title: Shaping positive and negative ties to improve team effectiveness: The roles of leader humility and team helping norms

entries.rq_with_context: Effective team leadership requires managing both positive and negative relationships among members, yet research has focused mostly on how leaders promote positive ties while overlooking their role in reducing negative ones. Although social ledger theory suggests negative ties may have stronger effects than positive ones, it remains unclear how leaders shape these dual aspects of team networks or how such networks affect team outcomes. This study investigates how leader humility influences team effectiveness through its effects on friendship and hindrance tie density and subsequent team-helping norms. Drawing on social ledger theory and leader humility research, the authors propose a sequential mediation model. The key contribution is demonstrating how leader humility uniquely shapes both positive and negative network structures to enhance team performance and viability.

title: The (mostly) robust influence of initial trustworthiness beliefs on subsequent behaviors and perceptions

entries.rq_with_context: Initial trustworthiness beliefs are formed quickly, often with little information, and may influence individuals’ decisions to engage in risky or cooperative behaviors. While some trust theories suggest these beliefs are fleeting and replaced by direct experience, others propose they have lasting influence. This paper addresses the unresolved debate by testing whether initial trustworthiness beliefs continue to shape perceptions and behaviors after a trust violation or a two-week delay. Drawing on accessibility theory, the authors propose that initial beliefs remain influential by shaping how individuals interpret subsequent events. Using one longitudinal field study and two experiments, they examine how these beliefs affect future trust perceptions and cooperation. The authors claim their work demonstrates the mostly robust nature of initial trust beliefs and clarifies the conditions under which they persist or are overridden.

title: Collective sensemaking in the local response to a grand challenge: Recovery, alleviation and change-oriented responses to a refugee crisis

entries.rq_with_context: The refugee crisis on Lesbos presents a grand challenge involving extreme conditions, complexity due to diverse stakeholder involvement, and persistence over time. Existing research on collective sensemaking has largely focused on contained crises with formal, tightly coupled systems, leaving a gap in understanding how diverse actors make sense of and respond to ongoing, complex societal challenges like forced displacement. This study addresses how actors—locals, professionals, and volunteers—collectively interpret the crisis and shape their actions. Drawing on 71 interviews, the authors explore two research questions: (1) How do actors make sense of and position themselves in the local response to a grand challenge? (2) How do they enact the situation and impact the collective response? Using a constructivist and abductive approach, the study identifies patterns in collective sensemaking narratives. It contributes by showing how sensemaking in persistent, multi-stakeholder contexts leads to different action strategies and reveals the social and interactional basis of response dynamics.

title: Status–Authority Asymmetry between Professions: The Case of 911 Dispatchers and Police Officers

entries.rq_with_context: In many organizations, lower-status professionals (e.g., safety auditors, fact-checkers) are given functional authority over higher-status professionals (e.g., scientists, journalists) to ensure compliance with protocols. However, when status and authority are misaligned—a phenomenon called status–authority asymmetry—lower-status professionals face resistance and struggle to enforce compliance despite formal mandates. Prior research has examined relational accommodations or demographic overlap as potential solutions, but these often fail when demographics are consolidated and status hierarchies remain rigid. This study investigates how and when lower-status professionals can successfully elicit compliance in such contexts, using a 24-month ethnography of 911 dispatchers and police officers. It analyzes different relational styles—customizing, escalating, and publicizing—and their outcomes. The research finds that peer publicizing via a shared communication channel is most effective, revealing a novel mechanism of second-degree influence that bypasses direct confrontation.

title: Syncing Up: A Process Model of Emergent Interdependence in Dynamic Teams

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational teams increasingly form quickly and change frequently, breaking from traditional 'real' teams with stable membership and clear boundaries. While prior research has examined teamwork in more stable contexts, we know little about how dynamic teams—characterized by both temporary membership and fluid boundaries—can work interdependently rather than independently. A core challenge is that structural interdependence is ambiguous, and existing research presents conflicting views: one suggesting teams must alternate between internal and external work due to limited attention, and another proposing that teams can integrate peripheral members directly. This study addresses this gap by investigating how dynamic medical teams in a children’s hospital achieved interdependent work. Using observations and interviews, the author develops a process model showing how brief synchronous periods of internal and external teamwork—embedded within cycles of separate coordination—enabled emergent interdependence. The findings contribute to dynamic teams research by revealing how teams can look like 'real' teams despite instability, and extend external activities research by challenging the assumed trade-off between internal and external coordination.

title: Cracking the box or stretching its walls? Exploiting institutional plasticity in Iranian creative advertising

entries.rq_with_context: In highly institutionalized contexts, radical change is often infeasible, yet incremental shifts still occur. While existing research acknowledges grassroots, bottom-up change, it has not explained how challengers decide which institutional elements to target. Our study addresses this gap by investigating how actors identify and leverage institutional plasticity—the degree to which institutions can be 'stretched' without breaking. Drawing on a nine-month ethnography in an Iranian advertising agency, we examine how professionals challenged strict Islamic advertising regulations, particularly around the banned practice of celebrity endorsement. We trace how they navigated this conservative environment using strategic microprocesses. Our work contributes by revealing the mechanisms through which actors sense and exploit plasticity, offering a model of non-disruptive, incremental institutional change in coercively guarded settings.

title: The Task Bind: Explaining Gender Differences in Managerial Tasks and Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Women in management face persistent gender stereotypes that question their competence and commitment, leading to stereotype threat. While existing research shows stereotype threat can impair cognitive performance, less is known about how it shapes managers’ actual work behaviors and task allocation. This study identifies a novel mechanism—the task bind—where women managers, concerned about subordinates’ perceptions, focus disproportionately on visible, public tasks (like supervising on the floor) to prove their legitimacy, while neglecting private, planning-oriented tasks (like budgeting in the office). Using mixed methods in a grocery chain, the study asks how stereotype threat influences how women, compared to men, take up and perform managerial roles. The research combines interviews, observations, and archival data to test whether this task imbalance harms performance. It contributes by revealing how stereotype threat translates into behavioral tradeoffs with organizational consequences.

title: Delivering bad news fairly: The influence of core self-evaluations and anxiety for the enactment of interpersonal justice

entries.rq_with_context: Delivering bad news in a just manner is critical for workplace justice, yet managers often fail to treat recipients with dignity and respect. While prior research links actor characteristics to interpersonal justice, why these effects occur remains unclear. This paper asks: what motivates managers to deliver bad news fairly, and why do some fail?
