While such behavior is often seen as beneficial, little research has explored how peers in teams perceive and react to it in real time. Existing studies often rely on supervisor evaluations or retrospective self-reports, leaving a gap in understanding peer responses as dynamic, affective processes. This study asks: how do peers evaluate and respond to team member proactivity during the process, and how are these reactions shaped over time? Drawing on qualitative data from three agile teams observed over five months, the authors use a process model grounded in emotional episodes theory to trace peer reactions. The study’s main contribution is identifying four distinct pathways of peer response and showing how these evolve through cognitive, affective, and behavioral evaluations, thereby deepening understanding of proactivity as a social, negotiated process in teams.

title: To Change or Not to Change? Evidence on the Steadiness of More Hubristic CEOs

entries.rq_with_context: Research on CEO hubris has consistently shown that overconfident CEOs are drawn to challenging and consequential strategic actions, such as acquisitions and innovation. However, it remains unclear whether this disposition leads them to pursue broad changes in their firm’s overarching trajectory or to maintain stability despite engaging in bold initiatives. This gap arises because prior studies focus on discrete strategic activities rather than higher-order organizational change. The study addresses this by asking: does CEO hubris lead to greater strategic and TMT membership change, or does it induce steadiness? Using an upper echelons framework, the authors test competing hypotheses with panel data on S&P 1500 CEOs. Their key contribution is demonstrating that hubris is associated not with change, but with a preference for steadiness in both strategic orientation and leadership composition.

title: Official truth, applied deconstruction and post-inquiry sensemaking in the Mull of Kintyre helicopter crash

entries.rq_with_context: The Mull of Kintyre helicopter crash in 1994 killed all on board, and the Royal Air Force inquiry concluded the pilots were grossly negligent. This official version had significant consequences for the pilots' reputations and families, yet it did not resolve public uncertainty given the lack of physical evidence and multiple plausible explanations. While existing research focuses on sensemaking during crises or inquiries, there is limited understanding of post-inquiry processes when official conclusions are contested. This paper addresses that gap by analyzing how actors challenged the RAF’s finding over 17 years. Drawing on the sociology of science and knowledge, the authors use a case study approach to trace the mechanics of public contestation. They propose the concept of 'applied deconstruction' to explain how campaigns rebuild equivocality and open the 'black box' of official truth. The study contributes to understanding how and why some official versions are successfully overturned while others remain intact.

title: On ableism and anthropocentrism: A canine perspective on the workplace inclusion of disabled people

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing attention to both disability and non-human animals in organizations, no research has addressed the double marginalization that occurs when disabled people bring service animals to work. Existing studies separately explore ableism—the privileging of able-bodiedness—and anthropocentrism—the human-centered hierarchy over non-humans—but not their intersection. This study investigates how the spatial, discursive, and affective treatment of service dogs serves as a proxy for the inclusion or exclusion of employees with disabilities. Drawing on interviews and observations with eight service dog–human pairs in Belgium, the paper asks: how are service dogs in/excluded in the organizations under study, and with what effects for the in/exclusion of the disabled employee? The study uses a post-humanist, ableism-informed framework to analyze human–animal entanglement. It contributes by introducing the 'proxy' concept to explain peripheral inclusion, highlighting the role of affect in disablement, and taking animal labor more seriously.

title: Executive Board Chairs: Examining the Performance Consequences of a Corporate Governance Hybrid

entries.rq_with_context: The role of the board chair has traditionally been framed by agency theory as one of independent oversight, separate from strategic management. However, many firms have adopted a hybrid model—the executive board chair—who leads both governance and strategy. This innovation challenges theoretical assumptions about role separation but is increasingly common, with nearly a quarter of separate board chairs in the S&P 500 now designated as 'executive.' Despite its prevalence, little is known about the performance implications of this structure. The study addresses this gap by asking whether and under what conditions an executive board chair improves firm performance. Using a within-firm design across S&P 1500 companies from 2003–2017, the authors test how the presence of an executive board chair affects performance, moderated by CEO power, organizational complexity, and board leadership demands. The key contribution is providing empirical evidence that this hybrid governance form can enhance performance, while identifying boundary conditions that shape its effectiveness.

title: Dynamic relationships between leader–member exchange and employee role-making behaviours: The moderating role of employee emotional ambivalence

entries.rq_with_context: Leader–member exchange (LMX) is central to workplace relationships, yet little research has empirically tested its self-reinforcing nature over time—specifically, whether high-quality LMX leads to more role-making behaviours and whether those behaviours in turn improve LMX. Prior studies have largely focused on one-directional effects or static models, and have overlooked mixed emotional states like emotional ambivalence, which may interfere with this dynamic. This study addresses these gaps by examining reciprocal relationships between LMX and two forms of role-making: job-change negotiation and challenge-seeking. Using a three-wave longitudinal design with Chinese new graduates, the authors test whether these behaviours and LMX influence each other over time and whether emotional ambivalence moderates these effects. The approach integrates role-making theory with affective dynamics, providing a more nuanced understanding of LMX development.

title: The act of (de/re)growing: Prefiguring alternative organizational landscapes of socioecological transformations

entries.rq_with_context: The paper addresses how transformative socioecological change—specifically degrowth—emerges in practice. While degrowth is widely discussed as a macro-level policy agenda, there is little understanding of how such transformations are enacted at the personal and local level. The authors identify a gap in research on prefigurative organizing that includes nonhuman actors and their role in shaping alternative, post-growth ways of life. Drawing on 10 personal stories from the Nordics, the study explores how individuals initiate change by leaving growth-dependent systems and building new life-sustaining relations with nonhumans. Using a storytelling approach informed by more-than-human geography, it analyzes the processes through which degrowth is lived. The authors present their findings as an empirically grounded contribution to understanding how alternative organizational landscapes emerge through situated, everyday practices.

title: Age diversity and the monitoring role of corporate boards: Evidence from banks

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates how age diversity among corporate board members influences the monitoring role of boards, particularly in the banking sector. While prior research has largely focused on gender and ethnic diversity or the advisory role of boards, there is limited understanding of how age diversity affects monitoring functions like financial reporting quality. This gap is significant because banks' complex operations create information asymmetries that make effective board monitoring crucial. The paper asks: does greater age diversity on bank boards lead to higher-quality financial reporting, as indicated by reduced earnings management? The authors use a large U.S. bank dataset (N = 7005) and measure earnings management through discretionary loan loss provisions. Their approach employs fixed effects and propensity score matching to address endogeneity concerns. The key claimed contribution is providing first empirical evidence that age-diversified boards enhance monitoring performance in banks, contrary to mixed findings on age diversity in prior studies that focused on advisory outcomes.

title: Ventriloquial reflexivity: Exploring the communicative relationality of the ‘I’ and the ‘it’

entries.rq_with_context: Reflexivity is widely discussed in organizational research, yet the literature remains fragmented around four key tensions: the subject/object distinction, temporality, representation, and agency—each revolving around the interplay of an 'I' and an 'it'. Existing studies often treat reflexivity as an individual, retrospective, and representational practice, overlooking its interactional, emergent, and constitutive dimensions. This gap limits understanding of how reflexivity is actually accomplished in real-time organizational settings. This study addresses that gap by analyzing naturally occurring talk among practicing managers in a leadership development program. Using a communicative relationality approach grounded in CCO and ventriloquism theory, the authors explore how the 'I' and the 'it' are co-constituted through interaction. The research identifies three types of reflexive moments—bifurcating, conflating, and animating—as interactional forms of ventriloquial reflexivity, offering a processual, empirically grounded framework for understanding how reflexivity unfolds in organizational practice.

title: Gender Salience and Recategorization of New Directors: The Role of Political Ideology

entries.rq_with_context: Despite increasing gender diversity on corporate boards due to stakeholder and regulatory pressures, research shows mixed results regarding its benefits, and such diversity contradicts established demographic homophily patterns. This inconsistency raises questions about how boards manage the tension between symbolic compliance and actual decision-making dynamics. This paper investigates whether boards maintain value homophily by recategorizing female new directors based on shared political ideology—a deep-level value dimension that influences governance. Drawing on symbolic management and recategorization theories, the study tests whether the link between board and new director political ideology is stronger when appointing women. It uses a sample of 13,483 new director appointments in U.S. firms with fractional regression analysis. The key contribution is revealing that gender diversity may be offset by increased ideological conformity, challenging assumptions about the cognitive benefits of demographic diversity.

title: Walking the Tightrope: Coopetition Capability Construct and Its Role in Value Creation

entries.rq_with_context: Firms often engage in coopetition—simultaneous cooperation and competition—to create value, yet managing such relationships is challenging due to inherent paradoxical tensions. Prior research suggests that specialized capabilities, termed 'coopetition capability,' are needed to manage these tensions effectively. However, the construct lacks clarity in its definition and dimensions, and there is no validated scale to measure it—limiting theoretical development and empirical research. This study addresses these gaps by asking: (a) What unique features constitute coopetition capability? and (b) How is coopetition capability operationalized and measured? Drawing on paradox theory, the authors conceptualize coopetition capability as a multidimensional construct comprising mindset, analytical acumen, and executional skills. They develop and validate a 15-item scale using data from high-technology alliances and examine its nomological network. The study contributes to theory by providing construct clarity, a psychometrically valid measurement tool, and evidence of the capability’s role in enhancing value creation.

title: The Contingent Effects of Intrateam Abusive Behavior on Team Thriving and New Venture Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Abusive behavior within new venture teams (NVTs) is a common yet understudied phenomenon in entrepreneurship research, often portrayed in popular culture as part of the 'dark side' of startups. While prior research has focused on individual entrepreneurs’ antisocial traits, less is known about how hostile verbal interactions among NVT members impact firm growth. There is also limited understanding of why some ventures succeed despite such dysfunction. This study addresses this gap by investigating how intrateam abusive behavior relates to new venture performance through its effect on team thriving—defined as shared vitality and learning. Drawing on the socially embedded model of thriving at work, the authors propose that high perceived competitive intensity mitigates the negative indirect effects of abuse on performance. Using a national U.S. sample of NVTs, they test a moderated mediation model. The study contributes by shifting focus from individual-level dark traits to team-level abusive dynamics and identifying a contextual buffer that explains performance variability.

title: Cruel optimism as organizing strategy in USA Gymnastics: The threat of high-stakes organizations in precarious times

entries.rq_with_context: The case of USA Gymnastics and Larry Nassar reveals widespread sexual abuse within a youth sports organization, raising questions about how such violence could persist unchecked. Existing research often treats sexual violence as an individual phenomenon, but this paper argues for an organizational-level analysis. The gap lies in understanding how organizational strategies actively enable and normalize abuse. The research question is: What organizational processes engendered gymnasts' victimization by Larry Nassar? Using testimony from survivors, the study applies Berlant’s theory of cruel optimism to show how organizations use trauma as a strategy. The key contribution is identifying 'high-stakes organizations' as contexts where such violence becomes an intentional organizing tool.

title: Thinking outside Pandora’s box: Revealing differential effects of coping with physical and psychological menopause symptoms at work

entries.rq_with_context: Menopause is a significant yet often stigmatized aspect of gendered ageing at work, affecting many women during their mid- to later-career years. Despite growing awareness, organizations often lack adequate support structures, and prior research has largely treated menopause symptoms as a single category without distinguishing how different types might require different coping mechanisms. This study addresses the gap by exploring how women manage physical versus psychological menopause symptoms using the SOC framework and workplace social support. Drawing on two studies—one qualitative and one quantitative—the research asks how these strategies affect job performance and retention. It uses the life-span development model of Selection, Optimization, and Compensation to frame agentic behavioral strategies and examines how they interact with supervisory and female peer support. The key contribution is revealing that SOC strategies have opposing effects depending on symptom type: they improve performance for physical symptoms but harm it for psychological symptoms.

title: Rebooting One’s Professional Work: The Case of French Anesthesiologists Using Hypnosis

entries.rq_with_context: Professionals are typically resistant to adopting practices that contradict their field’s core tenets, especially when those beliefs are deeply internalized through training and culture. While prior research shows that external pressures like new technologies or regulations can force such changes—often with peers serving as guides—little is known about how professionals voluntarily break from established norms without such pressure. This paper explores the case of French anesthesiologists who adopted hypnosis, a technique many consider subjective and contrary to scientific rigor, thus challenging the foundational principle of evidence-based medicine. The research asks how these individuals justified such a shift internally and gained acceptance despite peer skepticism. Drawing on interviews and observations, the authors use a qualitative approach to trace the process of voluntary reinvention. They find that turning inward (to personal experiences with patients) and outward (to patient feedback and relationships), rather than to professional peers, enabled this change. The study contributes by identifying a novel pathway for individual professional reinvention that does not rely on external pressure or peer support.

title: Doing transgender ‘right’: Bodies, eroticism and spirituality in khwajasira work

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates how specialized work regimes affect the bodies and labor of khwajasiras in Pakistan, a marginalized transgender community. While existing research focuses on binary gender norms in standard workplaces, this study explores a unique context where transgender people occupy specialized roles—erotic dancing, spiritual toli work, and sex work—each with distinct bodily expectations. The authors identify a gap in understanding how these regimes, despite allowing transgression of gender binaries, reproduce their own forms of regulation and oppression. The research questions are: how do specialized transgender work regimes regulate bodies and work, and how do khwajasiras cope with these regimes? Using a case study of 47 khwajasiras, the authors analyze biographical narratives through the lens of gender performativity. They argue that differences in how khwajasiras enact transgenderness stem from tensions between audience expectations, community norms, and personal authenticity.

title: Employees’ Emotional and Behavioral Reactions to Corporate Social Irresponsibility

entries.rq_with_context: While research on employees’ reactions to corporate social responsibility (CSR) has expanded, little is known about how employees respond to corporate social irresponsibility (CSiR). This gap is critical because CSiR triggers stronger negative reactions than low CSR and can lead to damaging outcomes like reduced productivity and negative word-of-mouth. Existing literature lacks a consistent conceptualization of CSiR and overlooks employee behaviors beyond organizational punishment, such as compensating victims. Drawing on deonance theory, this paper defines CSiR through moral violation, harm, and intentionality, and explores how moral emotions mediate employee reactions. Using a multimethod design across two experiments and one field study, the authors test whether anger, sympathy, guilt, and pride explain punishing and compensating behaviors. The study contributes to micro-CSR research by offering a grounded definition of CSiR, demonstrating the role of multiple moral emotions, and highlighting compensating behavior as a novel response.

title: The Impact of Partner Organizational Structure on Innovation

entries.rq_with_context: Interorganizational partnerships are critical for innovation, yet knowledge flows within them often face friction. While prior research has focused on inter-firm dynamics, less is known about how a partner’s internal organizational structure shapes these frictions. This paper investigates how the centralization of decision rights in a partner firm influences both the breadth and rate at which startups can access its knowledge. The authors argue that centralized structures enhance access to a wider array of knowledge through integrated internal networks but reduce the speed of access due to bureaucratic complexity. Using data from corporate venture capital relationships in the pharmaceutical industry, they test conditions under which centralization becomes more beneficial—specifically when the incumbent has diverse knowledge, the startup needs varied expertise, or when social ties or proximity to authority help overcome delays. The study contributes by linking intraorganizational design to interorganizational innovation outcomes.

title: Bloody suffering and durability: How chefs forge embodied identities in elite kitchens

entries.rq_with_context: The article explores how suffering contributes to embodied identity construction among elite chefs, a phenomenon prevalent but undertheorized in organizational research. While existing studies acknowledge suffering as either disruptive or implicitly formative—such as in military or high-risk professions—it remains unclear how suffering is actively used by individuals to build and convey identity. Drawing on interviews with 62 chefs, the authors investigate how enduring physical and emotional hardship becomes central to who chefs are. They use a theoretical framework grounded in Merleau-Ponty’s notion of the body as a site of comprehension and identity, analyzing how chefs not only endure suffering but also perform and display it. The study’s key contribution is showing that suffering operates not just as a byproduct of work but as a deliberate form of embodied identity work—and that it carries an aesthetics that makes it culturally meaningful and identity-implicative.

title: Social courage promotes organizational identification via crafting social resources at work: A repeated-measures study

entries.rq_with_context: Employees’ identification with their employer organization is vital for motivation, well-being, and organizational success. While existing research highlights top-down factors like leadership and organizational support, less is known about how employees themselves can proactively shape their organizational identification (OI). This study addresses this gap by investigating whether workplace social courage—a personal resource—enables individuals to craft their social work environment, thereby promoting OI. Guided by conservation of resources (COR) theory, the study tests a longitudinal process where increases in social courage lead to increases in relational job crafting (crafting relationships and collaboration), which in turn boost social resources at work (meaningful relationships, relational identification, and social support), ultimately increasing OI. The study uses latent change score modeling with data from 2919 Finnish employees surveyed in 2019 and 2020. The findings contribute to OI literature by showing how bottom-up, employee-initiated behaviors drive identity formation.

title: Seeing others’ side to serve: Understanding how and when servant leadership impacts employee knowledge-hiding behaviors

entries.rq_with_context: Knowledge hiding—concealing or distorting requested knowledge—is recognized as a threat to organizational learning and trust. While prior research treats it as a unitary, unethical behavior, this study highlights its multidimensionality by distinguishing between evasive hiding, playing dumb, and rationalized hiding, the latter being ethically justified to protect confidential information. Existing studies overlook these differences, leading to incomplete understanding. Drawing on Social Information Processing theory, the authors investigate how servant leadership influences each form of hiding. They propose that servant leadership discourages deceptive hiding through fostering perspective taking, while encouraging rationalized hiding, particularly among employees high in justice orientation. The study uses time-lagged, two-source data to test these relationships, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of leadership’s role in shaping context-specific knowledge behaviors.

title: Burning up on Reentry: The Effect of Entrepreneurial Exit in the Hiring Context

entries.rq_with_context: While much research has focused on why entrepreneurs exit their ventures, little is known about how they are evaluated when attempting to re-enter the traditional workforce. It is commonly assumed that 'going back to work' is always an option, yet there is limited understanding of how recruiters perceive job applicants with entrepreneurial experience. The gap lies in identifying potential biases in initial screening processes and understanding the mechanisms behind them. Drawing on screening theory, attribution theory, and person-organization fit, this paper asks: How do recruiters evaluate former entrepreneurs compared to traditionally employed applicants, and what factors influence these evaluations? The authors use a mixed-methods approach across three studies involving experimental resume screenings, qualitative interviews with recruiters, and scenario-based assessments. Their key contribution is revealing systematic biases against former entrepreneurs during early hiring stages and uncovering the underlying assumptions driving these biases.

title: Defense in Competition: Multimarket and Structural Effects of Firm-Specific Competition on Risk Transfer

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the importance of defense in competition, research has largely focused on offensive actions, leaving defensive strategies like risk transfer underexplored. Existing studies often treat competition as a uniform industry trait, neglecting firm-specific variations in competitive interactions across multiple markets. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how firms adjust risk transfer in response to their specific multimarket contact and structural market conditions. Drawing on multimarket competition theory, we ask: How do multimarket contact, rivals’ risk transfer behavior, and egocentric industry concentration influence a firm’s risk transfer level? Using reinsurance data from the US property and casualty insurance industry, we model these relationships. The study contributes by introducing a firm-specific, multimarket perspective on competitive dynamics in risk management, revealing nuanced patterns that aggregate models miss.

title: Envy Influences Interpersonal Dynamics and Team Performance: Roles of Gender Congruence and Collective Team Identification

entries.rq_with_context: Envy is a common emotional response to upward social comparisons at work, yet little research has examined its dyadic interpersonal consequences and downstream effects on team performance. While prior studies have focused on either the envier’s or the envied’s reactions, this paper addresses a gap by simultaneously considering both parties’ behaviors—interpersonal deviance and advice seeking—and their collective impact. The authors ask: How does dyadic envy shape interpersonal dynamics, and when do these dynamics influence team performance? They draw on social comparison theory and social identity theory to propose that gender congruence amplifies these behavioral responses and that collective team identification buffers negative performance effects. The study uses time-lagged, multi-source data from 51 teams to test these ideas, offering a bottom-up model linking dyadic emotions to team outcomes.

title: Interactive Effects of Receiver Power and Generator Status on Endorsement of Creative Ideas

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often fail to capitalize on employee creativity not because of a lack of ideas, but due to insufficient endorsement by key stakeholders. While prior research has focused on how people recognize or perceive creative ideas, less is known about what drives actual endorsement—the willingness to support and implement them. This paper addresses that gap by investigating the role of receiver power in idea endorsement, drawing on associative evaluation theory. The authors propose that powerful individuals are more likely to endorse highly creative ideas because they have accumulated more positive associations with creativity. They further suggest that the idea generator’s status strengthens this effect. Using four studies across different contexts, the research tests these predictions through experimental and field methods. The key contribution is identifying receiver power as a critical factor in creative idea endorsement and demonstrating how it interacts with idea creativity and generator status.

title: Pulling Together While Falling Apart: A Relational View on Integration in Serial Acquirers

entries.rq_with_context: Serial acquirers face significant challenges in integrating multiple acquisitions, which strain managerial resources and organizational stability. While prior research highlights the importance of integration capabilities, it remains unclear how these capabilities evolve—or deteriorate—over time, especially in the context of frequent, overlapping integration efforts. This paper addresses this gap by exploring how relational dynamics influence integration capabilities in serial acquirers. Drawing on a longitudinal qualitative case study of a Scandinavian IT firm, the authors examine how successive integration processes disrupt existing relationships and hinder new relationship formation. The study uses a relational perspective to trace how these disruptions accumulate, ultimately depleting organizational capacity. The key contribution is revealing that the very processes intended to enhance integration—structural changes and integration initiatives—can erode the social fabric necessary for coordination and learning, leading to a downward spiral in integration capability.

title: Leaders’ Impulsive Versus Strategic Abuse, Goal Realization, and Subsequent Supportive Behaviors: A Self-Regulation Perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Abusive supervision is widely recognized as harmful, yet existing research presents conflicting views: some frame it as impulsive and dysregulated, while others suggest it can be strategic and goal-directed. However, prior studies typically treat abusive behaviors as driven by only one motive, neglecting the possibility that both impulses and strategic planning may coexist. This gap limits understanding of when and why such behaviors occur and what consequences they have for leaders themselves. The current research addresses this by differentiating between impulsive and strategic abuse using self-regulation theory. It asks whether these two forms of abuse differ in their effects on leaders’ goal realization and subsequent supportive behaviors. Using experience sampling data from two studies, the authors test a model in which goal realization mediates the relationship between abuse type and later supportiveness. The key contribution is demonstrating that abusive behaviors are not uniformly destructive from the leader’s perspective—strategic abuse can promote goal attainment and lead to increased support, especially when subordinates are competent.

title: Relational interdependencies and the intra-EU mobility of African European Citizens

entries.rq_with_context: The literature on intra-EU migration often assumes migrants are primarily from Eastern Europe and focused on skilled or middle-class mobility, overlooking the experiences of naturalized third-country nationals such as African European Citizens (AECs). Despite holding citizenship in EU countries with strong social protections, many AECs choose to relocate to the UK, a phenomenon that remains underexplored. This study addresses this gap by investigating how AECs leverage relational networks to overcome structural barriers such as discrimination and limited labor market access in their naturalized countries. Drawing on Elias’s figurational theory, it analyzes how ‘piblings networks’—informal, extended affiliations of putative relatives—function as relational capital to facilitate relocation and integration. The authors claim their contribution lies in re-conceptualizing integration and citizenship as relational and provisional, showing how transient interdependencies paradoxically support belonging and mobility.

title: Creating inclusivity through boundary work? Zooming in on low-wage service sector work

entries.rq_with_context: Workers in the low-wage service sector are sociodemographically diverse and vulnerable, yet inclusion research has largely ignored them. Dominant inclusion frameworks focus on professional, knowledge-based work and may not apply to precarious service work contexts. This study investigates inclusion dynamics in a Dutch aircraft cleaning company known for its diversity initiatives but marked by stark inequalities in working conditions. Through participant observation and interviews, the authors analyze everyday boundary work—how managers and workers include or exclude based on status, contract type, and identity—and its consequences. The research questions are: what inclusionary and exclusionary effects arise from this boundary work, and how do these modes interact to shape inclusivity? The authors argue that inclusion cannot be understood without examining co-constitutive exclusion processes and that decent working conditions form a 'silent foundation' for inclusivity.

title: ‘Getting a grip’? Phenomenological insights into handling work place in London’s Soho

entries.rq_with_context: The article investigates how iconic work settings like London’s Soho shape working lives and identities through deeply situated experiences. While existing research often treats place as a passive backdrop, this study identifies a gap in understanding how place and work dynamically co-constitute each other, especially in fluid, stigmatized, and historically layered locales. The authors ask how work identities are enacted through demonstrating a capacity to cope with such environments. Drawing on Merleau-Ponty’s phenomenological concept of ‘grip’, they analyze longitudinal interview data from workers in a hedge fund and sex shops in Soho. The study contributes to debates on work and place by showing that handling a distinctive locale—getting and maintaining an embodied, performative grip—is central to how working lives are experienced and understood.

title: Doing inclusion as counter-conduct: Navigating the paradoxes of organizing for refugee and migrant inclusion

entries.rq_with_context: Refugee and migrant inclusion initiatives often unintentionally reproduce hierarchies by constructing migrants as passive, dependent subjects in need of help—a phenomenon termed 'benevolent discrimination.' While critical diversity studies have identified these paradoxical effects, less is known about how organizations actively resist such dynamics on the ground. This article addresses that gap by investigating how civil society organizations (CSOs) navigate and resist the power relations inherent in national integration regimes. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork with three CSOs in Germany, the study explores how these organizations engage in 'counter-conduct' against the 'pastoral power' of state integration policies. It specifically analyzes everyday practices that challenge categorizations, hierarchical roles, and assimilationist goals. The authors argue that these practices allow for continuous critique and renegotiation of inclusion, contributing a Foucauldian perspective that shifts focus from discourse to micro-level resistance in organizing for inclusion.

title: Webs of oppression: An intersectional analysis of inequalities facing women activists in Palestine

entries.rq_with_context: Palestinian women activists operate within a complex context marked by settler-colonial domination, patriarchal structures, and authoritarian governance, which together shape their experiences of oppression. While feminist organizing literature often highlights gender-based marginalization, it frequently overlooks how intersecting factors like class, family background, and political positioning produce differentiated outcomes. Existing studies tend to treat women activists as a homogenous group, failing to account for the varying degrees of vulnerability and protection they experience. This study addresses that gap by asking: what are the multiple, intersecting layers of oppression that Palestinian women activists encounter, and how do these layers manifest themselves differently in activists’ everyday lives? Drawing on intersectionality theory and a patchwork institutions lens, the authors analyze in-depth interviews with 43 activists to uncover how systems of power interact across institutional, familial, and cultural domains. The study contributes by identifying forms of relative privilege—safeguarded, secured, and sheltered—that emerge from activists’ social positions, offering a more nuanced understanding of resistance and agency in oppressed contexts.

title: Financially insecure and less ethical: Understanding why and when financial insecurity inhibits ethical leadership

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses how supervisors' personal financial insecurity—a growing concern during global crises like the COVID-19 pandemic—influences their ethical leadership. While prior research has explored individual and organizational antecedents of ethical leadership, little attention has been paid to how leaders’ personal financial uncertainties may undermine their ethical behaviors. This paper fills that gap by drawing on uncertainty management theory (UMT) to examine anxiety as a psychological mechanism linking financial insecurity to reduced ethical leadership. The authors also introduce organizational pay fairness as a boundary condition. The study uses a multi-source, time-lagged design across two samples in China. The key contribution is demonstrating that even leaders in managerial roles may compromise ethical behaviors when facing financial insecurity, especially when they perceive pay as unfair.

title: Understanding meaningful work in the context of technostress, COVID-19, frustration, and corporate social responsibility

entries.rq_with_context: The digitalization of work and the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic have intensified employees' experiences of technostress and frustration, potentially undermining their sense of meaningful work. While meaningful work is known to depend on individual, organizational, and societal factors, there is limited understanding of how these interact in crisis and digitally invasive contexts. Existing research has theorized about digitalization’s impact on meaning at work but lacks empirical testing of mechanisms and boundary conditions. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether techno-invasion reduces meaningful work via frustration and whether perceived corporate social responsibility (CSR) can buffer this relationship. Using a four-wave longitudinal design during the first wave of the pandemic, the study applies the organizational frustration model and a holistic model of meaningful work. It contributes by empirically identifying frustration as a key mechanism and CSR as a boundary condition that shapes meaning-making under digital strain.

title: “Commit professional suicide or take up my pilgrim’s staff again?”: A cultural examination of how female managers resolve shock events in developing regions

entries.rq_with_context: Work–family conflict (WFC) research has largely focused on Western, developed contexts, overlooking how major WFC episodes unfold in developing regions where collectivistic values and low gender egalitarianism are prevalent. While existing theories, such as work–life shock events (Crawford et al., 2019), explain decision making in dual-earner couples in Western settings, they may not generalize to cultural contexts involving extended families and strong gender norms. This study addresses this gap by examining how female managers from Asia, Latin America, and sub-Saharan Africa navigate major WFC episodes in a male-dominated industry. Drawing on qualitative interviews with 50 women, the research asks: how do individualism/collectivism and gender egalitarianism shape WFC decision making during shock events? Using an episodic approach and the theoretical lens of shock events, it identifies decision-making patterns and reveals how cultural contexts reshape the interplay between rational assessment and identity-based action. The study contributes by contextualizing WFC decision making in understudied regions and proposing a culturally grounded framework.

title: Talking about disappointments: Identification work through multiple discourses at a prestigious university

entries.rq_with_context: Disappointment is common in contemporary academia due to tensions between traditional values and neoliberal managerialism, yet little is known about how individuals' talk about disappointment shapes their identification with organizations. While existing research suggests emotional discourse can limit identity options, this study addresses a gap by exploring how disappointment-talk might instead enable agency in identity work. Drawing on 104 narratives from academics at a prestigious British university, the research investigates how such talk functions as a discursive frame for navigating identification dilemmas. Using a narrative analysis approach, it focuses on how individuals engage with conflicting discourses—particularly prestige and academic neoliberalism—through their stories of disappointment. The study contributes by showing how emotion-talk can generate agency and reveals a novel discursive strategy—unravelling—through which individuals reconfigure conflicting discourses to manage organizational identification.

title: Coming from a Good Pond: The Influence of a New Venture’s Founding Ecosystem on Accelerator Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Startup accelerators aim to improve new ventures' strategies by providing resources and connections, yet most are concentrated in already successful entrepreneurial ecosystems like Silicon Valley rather than in underdeveloped regions where they might be most needed. While existing theories suggest accelerators are most impactful in resource-poor environments by filling critical gaps, this paper identifies a gap: little attention has been paid to how the characteristics of a startup’s founding environment shape the effectiveness of organizational sponsorship. The research question is whether accelerator impacts vary based on features of the startup’s pre-existing ecosystem, such as proximity to venture capitalists or networking opportunities. Using a regression discontinuity design with data from MassChallenge, the study compares admitted and non-admitted startups while holding perceived quality constant. The key contribution is demonstrating that accelerator benefits are not uniform but depend significantly on the richness of the startup’s founding environment, revealing mechanisms behind regional inequality in entrepreneurial outcomes.

title: Paying for Legitimacy: Autocracy, Nonmarket Strategy, and the Liability of Foreignness

entries.rq_with_context: Foreign firms often face economic barriers in host markets, known as the liability of foreignness, but the underlying causes—such as institutional distance, lack of social embeddedness, or discrimination—remain debated. This study investigates an underexplored driver: values-based ideological conflict between democratic and autocratic political systems. It asks whether foreign firms from autocratic regimes are charged higher lobbying fees in the U.S. due to perceived illegitimacy. Using transaction-level data on lobbying fees from 1998 to 2012, the authors test whether the fee premium persists and is higher in nationalist issue contexts. Their findings show that firms from autocratic countries pay significantly higher fees, which the authors attribute to reputational risk rather than service intensity. The study contributes to international business and organizational theory by identifying ideological conflict as a distinct source of the liability of foreignness.

title: Tedious Work: Developing Novel Outcomes with Digitization in the Arts and Sciences

entries.rq_with_context: Creative work is often portrayed as inspired and collaborative, yet a significant portion involves tedious, repetitive tasks that are essential but under-investigated. With the rise of digitization, opportunities for iteration and refinement have expanded, potentially increasing the burden of such labor. However, the consequences of this shift remain unclear. This paper explores how digitization shapes tedious work in two knowledge-intensive fields—systems biology and music production—and identifies the risks this work poses to creativity. The authors ask: How does tedious work emerge in the development of novel outcomes? Why does it become problematic? And what do actors do to reduce its negative effects? Drawing on comparative ethnography, they develop a model grounded in empirical observation. Their contribution lies in revealing the hidden, labor-intensive underpinnings of digital creativity and showing how actors actively manage the downsides of technological abundance.

title: Narrating Institutional Logics into Effect: Coherence Across Cognitive, Political, and Emotional Elements

entries.rq_with_context: Institutional logics are often treated as either deterministic forces or strategic tools, but how they operate in everyday interactions remains unclear. Existing research tends to reify logics or reduce them to outcomes without examining their unfolding in real-time interactions. This gap persists despite calls for micro-level studies of institutional dynamics. Drawing on an ethnographic study of a rape crisis center, the paper investigates how institutional logics—feminist, therapeutic, and administrative—are narrated into effect during board decision making. Through narrative analysis of storytelling interactions, it explores how people collectively shape and constrain the use of logics. The study reveals that decisions depend on coherence across cognitive (which logic is relevant), political (narrator’s subject position and interests), and emotional (roles and feelings) dimensions. Its contribution lies in showing that logics are neither imposed nor freely used but are locally instantiated through interactional processes limited by coherence.

title: Cleansing or Licensing? Corporate Social Responsibility Reconciles the Competing Effects of Unethical Pro-Organizational Behavior on Moral Self-Regulation

entries.rq_with_context: Employees sometimes engage in unethical pro-organizational behavior (UPB)—actions that benefit their organization but violate societal norms—such as lying to customers to protect company image. While prior research has explored what causes UPB, less is known about how employees behave afterward, with conflicting findings showing both increased helping and increased deviance. This gap persists because UPB has a morally paradoxical nature: it harms external stakeholders (triggering guilt) yet reflects loyalty to the organization (triggering entitlement). The authors propose that perceived CSR initiatives help resolve this ambiguity by shaping how employees interpret the morality of their UPB. Drawing on moral self-regulation theory, they test whether CSR strengthens moral cleansing (via increased moral deficit) and weakens moral licensing (via reduced psychological entitlement). Their multi-method approach across four studies tests this model, offering insight into when UPB leads to constructive versus destructive downstream behaviors.

title: Strategy by Doing and Product-Market Performance: A Contingency View

entries.rq_with_context: Strategy by doing emphasizes action over planning to generate organizational learning, especially in dynamic environments. However, existing research has largely assumed it is ineffective in stable settings and has not fully considered how different dimensions of environmental dynamism—market and technological—affect its efficacy. This creates a gap in understanding when and why strategy by doing improves performance across diverse contexts. The study addresses this by asking: How do market and technological dynamism jointly influence the relationship between product changes (as strategy by doing) and product-market performance? Using a large panel dataset of U.S. firms from 1996 to 2016, the authors test contingent effects through interaction models. They find that strategy by doing enhances performance in highly dynamic environments (with high levels of both dynamisms) and in stable environments (with low levels of both), but reduces performance in mixed environments. The contribution lies in challenging the assumption that strategy by doing only works in dynamic contexts and offering a more nuanced contingency model.

title: Not Always Helpful: Linking Intrateam Helping Types to Team Effectiveness From a Role Theory Perspective

entries.rq_with_context: While intrateam helping is generally viewed positively in teams research, this paper challenges that assumption by exploring potential downsides. The authors note that existing research often treats helping as a single, beneficial behavior, overlooking its possible negative consequences for team functioning. To address this gap, they distinguish between autonomous helping (which builds skills and independence) and dependent helping (which provides quick fixes without skill development). The research questions are: How do these two types of helping differentially affect team role-based functions and overall team effectiveness? And what team-level motivational factors—specifically team learning and performance goal orientations—drive each type of helping? Using a role theory perspective, the authors test a theoretical model across two studies involving student and manufacturing teams. Their key contribution is providing a more balanced view of intrateam helping by showing it can be both beneficial and harmful depending on its form and underlying motivations.

title: Coworker Injustices and Their Delegated Authority: Developing an Indirect Actor Model of Supervisor Justice

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace injustices are typically studied through a 'target similarity' lens, where victims respond directly to the offender's behavior. However, this approach overlooks how injustices by one party (e.g., a coworker) might influence perceptions of another (e.g., the supervisor). Given increasing team interdependence, coworker mistreatment may be seen as the supervisor’s responsibility—especially if the coworker acts on the supervisor’s behalf. The key gap is understanding when and why victims hold supervisors accountable for coworker injustices. This paper investigates the role of perceived intermediary delegation (PID)—when a coworker is seen as acting with the supervisor’s authority—and how victims’ relative status with the supervisor moderates this effect. Using fairness and role theory, the authors test a model in two studies. Their main contribution is identifying PID and relative status as boundary conditions shaping indirect accountability for coworker injustice.

title: Now It Makes More Sense: How Narratives Can Help Atypical Actors Increase Market Appeal

entries.rq_with_context: Atypical actors, such as those combining elements across categories, often face rejection due to audience confusion and perceived illegitimacy. While prior research has identified structural or reputational factors that mitigate this penalty, less is known about how actors themselves can strategically respond. This paper addresses this gap by examining whether atypical producers can use narrative language to improve audience evaluations. Drawing on processing fluency theory, the authors analyze over 78,000 Etsy crafters’ narratives to test how abstraction, cohesion, and conventionality in storytelling affect market appeal. They find that atypical producers who use more abstract, cohesive, and conventional narratives are better able to counteract evaluative discounts, suggesting narrative style is a key agentic tool in overcoming categorical penalties.

title: Shareholder Politics: The Influence of Investors’ Political Affiliations on Corporate Social Responsibility

entries.rq_with_context: Institutional investors are major political donors, yet little is known about how their political partisanship affects corporate decision-making. While prior research has explored how CEOs' and employees' political ideologies shape firm outcomes, the role of investor politics remains understudied. This paper addresses that gap by investigating how the political positions of institutional investors—measured through their donations—affect corporate social responsibility (CSR). The authors propose that liberal-leaning investors encourage greater CSR, but that this effect is mitigated when investors are politically dispersed and amplified when top managers are conservative. Using a dataset of political donations from 2,062 U.S. firms over 19 years, the study employs regression models with firm fixed effects and a quasi-natural experiment based on brokerage mergers. The findings contribute new evidence on shareholder politics and investor influence in corporate governance.

title: Rising Every Time We Fall: Organizational Fortitude and Response to Adversities

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational resilience has been widely studied in response to single, discrete adversities such as natural disasters or economic crises. However, organizations—especially long-standing ones—often face multiple, recurring adversities, a reality underexplored in current research. The episodic view of resilience fails to capture how firms build on past crises when confronting new ones, or what happens between adversities. This gap is especially critical in family firms, where the coupling of family and business systems intensifies stakes during crises. Drawing on a longitudinal case study of a UK family firm that endured four major adversities, this paper investigates how resilience unfolds across multiple events. Using qualitative data from interviews, archival sources, and observations, the authors analyze the processes enabling sustained resilience. They introduce the concept of organizational fortitude to explain how multilevel factors contribute to resilience over time. The study contributes by revealing the dynamic, cumulative nature of resilience and identifying mechanisms that help firms not only survive but thrive after repeated crises.

title: Employee Incentives and Family Firm Innovation: A Configurational Approach

entries.rq_with_context: Family firms often face a paradox between honoring tradition and pursuing innovation, yet some highly traditional firms remain innovative. While innovation depends on employee creativity, it remains unclear how family firms can configure HR incentives—such as pay, participation, or work–life balance—to overcome this tension. Prior research debates whether calculative (e.g., financial) or collaborative (e.g., participative) incentives are more effective, but has not examined how these interact with organizational culture. This study investigates how different configurations of incentives align with a family firm’s level of attachment to tradition to enable innovation. Using a qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) approach, the authors identify multiple pathways to innovation. They find that firms with high tradition rely more on collaborative incentives, while those with low tradition combine calculative and collaborative ones. The study contributes by showing that alignment between incentive systems and cultural context—not isolated practices—is key to unlocking innovation potential.

title: Loaded Down From Speaking Up: A Resource-Based Examination of Voicer Regret Following Supervisor Delegation

entries.rq_with_context: Employee voice is generally seen as beneficial for both organizations and employees, with supervisors typically responsible for enacting suggestions. However, supervisors often delegate enactment tasks back to the employees who voiced ideas, potentially imposing additional workload. This paper investigates how such delegation may unintentionally deter future voice by causing employee overload and subsequent regret—negative emotions arising from counterfactual thinking about avoidable work. Drawing on conservation of resources theory and counterfactual thinking, the authors propose a serial indirect effect where delegation increases overload, which fosters regret, ultimately reducing future voice. They also test whether supervisor consultation buffers this process. The research contributes by revealing a hidden cost of voice enactment and identifying regret as a key mechanism beyond fear or psychological safety.

title: The Effect of Incoming Board Interlocks With Public Firms on Private Firms’ Survival: Large-Scale Evidence From India

entries.rq_with_context: Private firms face distinct governance challenges, yet research on how board interlocks influence their survival remains limited. While prior work emphasizes board structure or director characteristics, little is known about the consequences of ties between private and public firms through shared directors. This paper addresses that gap by investigating whether incoming board interlocks—where public firm directors subsequently join a private firm’s board—improve private firm survival. Using data on over 28,000 Indian private firms from 1988 to 2017, the authors test for a nonlinear relationship between interlock count and exit risk. The study draws on agency theory and resource dependence, proposing that reputational risks motivate public directors to enhance monitoring at private firms. The key contribution is demonstrating that such interlocks have a curvilinear impact on survival, especially when linked to higher-governance public firms.

title: Relieving the Pressure: Team Familiarity Attenuates External Conformity Pressure on Team Member Decisions

entries.rq_with_context: Team members in organizations often face pressure from external parties to align their decisions with outside preferences—a phenomenon termed 'external conformity pressure.' While prior research has focused on within-group conformity (e.g., groupthink), less is known about how individuals resist pressure from outsiders. The authors argue that team familiarity—shared experience among members—may provide a sense of belonging that buffers against such external pressure. They test this idea using an archival dataset of NCAA football officiating crews and a laboratory experiment. Their approach integrates social belonging theory with team decision-making research. The key contribution is demonstrating that team familiarity can reduce conformity to external audiences, particularly under high-stakes conditions.

title: Not Like the Rest of Us? How CEO Celebrity Affects Quarterly Earnings Call Language

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing interest in CEO celebrity and its influence on organizational outcomes, limited research has explored how social evaluations like celebrity shape CEOs' language use in public communications. While prior studies show that language attributes affect stakeholder perceptions, little is known about how CEO characteristics—particularly celebrity—influence such language. This paper addresses this gap by investigating whether celebrity CEOs employ more positive, concrete, certain, and self-regarding language during earnings calls than noncelebrities, and whether these effects vary by degree of celebrity. Using a sample of 8,203 quarterly earnings call transcripts, the authors apply content analysis to test their hypotheses. The study contributes by linking CEO celebrity to specific language patterns, demonstrating that sociocognitive outcomes of celebrity—such as increased confidence and sense of authority—manifest in observable communication behaviors.

title: Identity-Consistent Self-Image Maintenance Following Leader Abuse: Integrating Self-Presentation and Self-Concept Orientation Perspectives

entries.rq_with_context: Abusive supervision negatively impacts employees, yet many remain in these relationships and actively manage how they are perceived by both their abusive leader and coworkers. While prior research has focused on emotional appraisals (e.g., guilt or shame) as drivers of self-image concerns, less is known about stable individual differences that explain why some employees feel compelled to protect their self-image while others do not. This study addresses this gap by investigating the role of relational self-concept—an orientation emphasizing interpersonal connections—as a key moderator. The research asks: under what conditions does abusive supervision trigger self-image maintenance behaviors? Using two field studies with Chinese professionals, the authors test a model integrating self-presentation and self-concept orientation theories. Their key contribution is identifying relational self-concept as a critical boundary condition that determines whether abuse leads to prosocial impression management toward coworkers (via relational reputation concerns) or the leader (via image preservation motives).

title: A Tale of Two Types of Standard Setting: Evidence From Artificial Intelligence in China

entries.rq_with_context: In emerging economies like China, standard setting often involves a hybrid system where both market actors and government institutions play key roles, reflecting different institutional logics. While prior research has focused on committee-based, market-driven standard setting in developed economies, less is known about how firms navigate these dual systems in emerging contexts. The gap lies in understanding how technologically advanced firms decide between participating in market-led or government-led standard-setting initiatives, given divergent goals and norms. This study addresses that gap by asking: How do firms with superior technological capability respond to market- versus government-led standard setting in China's AI sector? Using longitudinal data on 8,519 AI-active firms from 2010 to 2020, the authors analyze engagement patterns based on the identity of the chair organization in standard working groups. They find that technological capability increases participation in market-led but decreases it in government-led settings, with subfield diversity and state ownership moderating these effects.

title: Coworker Narcissism: Employee Emotional and Behavioral Reactions as Moderated by Bottom-Line Mentality and Trait Competitiveness

entries.rq_with_context: Working with narcissistic coworkers is commonly perceived as difficult, yet research has largely focused on leader narcissism or the narcissist’s own outcomes, leaving a gap in understanding how coworker narcissism affects others. This paper addresses that gap by examining how a coworker’s narcissistic rivalry—characterized by defensive competition and status protection—triggers negative emotions in focal employees. Drawing on social function of emotions theory, the authors propose that these emotions lead to different behavioral responses depending on individual differences: higher bottom-line mentality strengthens the link between negative emotions and defensive reactions like social undermining, while lower trait competitiveness strengthens the link to offensive reactions like work-goal progress. The approach uses three studies combining field and experimental data. The key contribution is clarifying when and why coworker narcissism motivates either dysfunctional or functional employee behaviors.

title: Better Safe Than Sorry: CEO Regulatory Focus and Workplace Safety

entries.rq_with_context: Research shows that CEO characteristics influence corporate strategies, including stakeholder engagement. While prior work links promotion-focused CEOs to broader stakeholder initiatives and prevention-focused CEOs to shareholder-oriented strategies, less is known about how these motivational orientations affect 'do no harm' initiatives like workplace safety. This study addresses this gap by investigating how CEO regulatory focus—promotion versus prevention—affects employee injury rates. The authors argue that prevention-focused CEOs, concerned with fulfilling obligations, will prioritize safety and reduce injuries, whereas promotion-focused CEOs, focused on growth, may impose aggressive workloads that increase injuries. They test this using S&P 500 data and OSHA injury records from 2002–2011. The study contributes by revealing the unintended consequences of CEO motivation on employee well-being, particularly in safety outcomes.

title: Green by Affiliation? Ownership Identity and Environmental Management System Adoption in Chinese Business Groups

entries.rq_with_context: Environmental management system (EMS) adoption has increased notably in China, yet research remains focused on standalone Western firms rather than the dominant business group structures in emerging economies. This creates a gap in understanding how ownership shapes EMS adoption in contexts like China, where business groups are central. Existing studies have largely neglected the role of ownership identity—particularly state, family, and foreign ownership—in influencing corporate environmental actions. This study addresses that gap by asking how these ownership types affect EMS adoption among Chinese business group affiliates. Drawing on resource dependence and ownership competence theories, the authors use logistic regression on data from listed Chinese firms (2008–2019) to test their hypotheses. The key contribution is revealing differential effects of ownership identity on EMS adoption within business groups, challenging assumptions of homogeneity among affiliated firms.

title: The Collective Candidate Experience: Theory and Business Unit Consequences

entries.rq_with_context: Despite widespread belief that candidate experiences impact organizational outcomes, academic research has largely focused on individual-level reactions to specific recruitment practices, leaving unclear whether these experiences influence broader business unit outcomes like collective turnover or customer satisfaction. This gap persists because prior research lacks a multidimensional, unit-level framework for understanding the overall candidate experience across the entire hiring process. This study addresses that gap by introducing the collective candidate experience as an aggregate of applicants’ cognitive and affective perceptions formed through interactions in business unit-specific social, structural, and physical contexts. Using signaling theory and insights from marketing’s customer experience literature, the authors propose and test a model linking collective candidate experience to collective new hire engagement, turnover intentions, turnover, and customer satisfaction in a multi-unit restaurant organization. The key contribution is demonstrating that candidate experience operates at the business unit level and has measurable downstream consequences.

title: Visible but Hidden: An Intersectional Examination of Identity Management Among Sexual Minority Employees

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing research on sexual minority employees' identity concealment at work, little attention has been paid to how other social identities—particularly race—shape these experiences. Existing studies often treat sexual orientation in isolation, ignoring the intersectional realities faced by employees with multiple stigmatized identities. This gap limits our understanding of how visible identities like race may influence decisions about managing invisible identities like sexual orientation. Drawing on intersectionality theory, this study investigates how racial and heterosexist harassment interact to predict identity concealment and suppression among White and Black LGBP employees. Using a two-wave survey design, the authors test competing models (additive, exacerbating, inuring) of how multiple forms of harassment combine. The primary contribution is demonstrating that the relationship between harassment and identity management depends on both type of harassment and employee race, highlighting the need for an intersectional approach in future research.

title: Contextual Inequality in the Performance Costs of Financial Precarity

entries.rq_with_context: A substantial proportion of workers experience financial precarity, defined as persistent concern about personal financial welfare, which research suggests harms work performance by depleting cognitive resources. However, this effect may not be uniform across workers. The paper identifies a gap in understanding how work contexts—particularly those disproportionately occupied by lower socioeconomic groups—shape the performance costs of financial precarity. The research question is whether low autonomy, high routinization, high interdependence, and low social support intensify or mitigate the negative relationship between financial precarity and daily work performance. Using experience sampling data over eight days from a nationally representative U.S. sample (N = 956), the authors test their hypotheses using multilevel logistic regression. They claim the study contributes by revealing contextual inequality in the performance costs of financial precarity, showing that structural features of jobs shape who bears these costs.

title: The Regulation of Religion by Secular Work Practice: Exploring Muslim Employees’ Performance of Religious Practice

entries.rq_with_context: Workplaces in the Global North are often shaped by secular norms that marginalize religious expressions, especially for Muslim employees who face both discursive Islamophobia and material constraints. While prior research focuses on discourse, this study highlights how everyday work practices—such as schedules, spaces, objects, and bodily norms—actively regulate religion. The authors ask: (1) How can work practice interfere with Muslim employees’ religious practice? and (2) How do Muslim employees negotiate these interferences? Using a practice lens and interviews with 30 Muslim employees in Belgium, the study analyzes non-discursive mechanisms of inequality. It contributes by showing how work practices reproduce secular order and how employees navigate them, offering a more embodied understanding of religious inclusion.

title: Reinforcing Political Inequality Through Diversity Initiatives: A Field-Level Perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Despite widespread investment in diversity initiatives to combat inequality, persistent disparities remain, particularly in politically charged contexts. Research has largely focused on economic inequality and organizational-level interventions, overlooking how broader sociopolitical systems shape diversity efforts. The role of the diversity field—comprising NGOs, government agencies, and consultants—in mediating between society and organizations remains underexplored, especially regarding political inequality. This study investigates whether and how diversity initiatives in Israel reproduce political inequality even as they address economic exclusion of Palestinian citizens. Using a 19-month field-level ethnography of the Israeli diversity field, the authors analyze practices, discourse, and symbolic representations across organizations. They find that while best practices improve economic inclusion, they simultaneously conceal political inequality through institutionalized silence on Palestinian identity and the dominance of Zionist symbols and language. The study contributes by revealing how field-level dynamics create a taken-for-granted separation between economic and political spheres, enabling false consciousness around inequality.

title: Too sleepy to be innovative? Ethical leadership and employee service innovation behavior: A dual-path model moderated by sleep quality

entries.rq_with_context: Ethical leadership is linked to various positive employee outcomes, yet its connection to service innovation behavior remains underexplored, especially the underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions. While prior research suggests ethical leadership can enhance innovation, little is known about how and when this occurs in service contexts. This study addresses this gap by proposing that ethical leadership boosts service innovation behavior through employees’ psychological ownership and creative self-efficacy, drawing on uncertainty reduction theory. Using two time-lagged studies with U.S. hospitality workers, the research tests a moderated mediation model. The key contribution is identifying both mediating mechanisms and the conditional role of sleep quality, offering new insight into the psychological processes linking ethical leadership to innovation.

title: Investigating the making of organizational social responsibility as a polyphony of voices: A ventriloquial analysis of practitioners’ interactions

entries.rq_with_context: While recent research conceptualizes corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a polyphonic and conflict-centered process shaped by multiple voices—including non-human elements like values, logos, and laws—little is known about which voices matter in practice and how they influence CSR decision-making. Existing work lacks empirical analysis of how tensions emerge from these voices in interaction and how practitioners navigate them. This study addresses these gaps by analyzing CSR discussions in a cooperative network through a ventriloquial lens, which reveals how elements of a situation are voiced through human interaction. It asks: (1) What elements make a difference in CSR discussions, how do they come to matter, and how does their polyphony affect participants? (2) What tensions emerge when these elements interact, and how do practitioners ethically respond? The authors use interaction analysis of recorded meetings to trace voice dynamics. Their contribution lies in showing how CSR is concretely shaped by inclusion and exclusion of voices, offering a nuanced understanding of ethical decision-making in practice.

title: The double-edged sword of negative supervisor gossip: When and why negative supervisor gossip promotes versus inhibits feedback seeking behavior among gossip targets

entries.rq_with_context: Negative supervisor gossip is a common yet understudied phenomenon that can convey evaluative information to employees, similar to formal feedback. While prior research highlights its detrimental effects, such as reduced well-being and social exclusion, it remains unclear how it influences employees’ proactive responses like feedback seeking behavior (FSB). The gap lies in understanding the dual mechanisms through which negative gossip may simultaneously encourage and discourage FSB. Drawing on feedback intervention theory (FIT), the authors propose that gossip triggers both task reflexivity (a constructive process) and negative affect (a dysfunctional reaction), which have opposing effects on FSB. Furthermore, they examine how individual differences in implicit theory of ability shape these pathways. The study uses an online scenario experiment and a multiwave field study to test this moderated mediation model. The key contribution is demonstrating that negative supervisor gossip acts as an unintended feedback source, with effects contingent on personal beliefs about ability development.

title: A woman’s got to be what a woman’s got to be? How managerial assessment centers perpetuate gender inequality

entries.rq_with_context: Managerial assessment centers (MACs) are presented as objective tools for leadership selection, yet they operate within gendered organizational contexts that disadvantage women. Prior research shows MACs favor masculine traits and organizational structures, yet paradoxically, women perform as well as or better than men in these settings. This study addresses the gap in understanding this 'Managerial Assessment Center Gender Paradox'—why women succeed despite systemic bias. Using interviews with MAC evaluators in a semi-military Israeli organization, we analyze how gender ideology shapes assessment practices. The research reveals that evaluators respond to women's presence with increased attention to gender conformity, creating what we term the 'benevolence effect'—a tendency to over-evaluate women who embody traditional feminine stereotypes. The study contributes by uncovering how seemingly favorable treatment of women actually reinforces patriarchal structures by advancing only those who conform to restrictive gender norms.

title: Understanding the negotiation and performance effects of idiosyncratic deals: Test of a moderated mediation model

entries.rq_with_context: Idiosyncratic deals (i-deals) are personalized work arrangements negotiated between employees and employers to meet unique individual needs, yet the mechanisms driving their formation and performance outcomes remain unclear. While prior research has identified individual and leadership factors as antecedents, little is known about the role of employee approach motive or supervisor political skill, nor how organizational context shapes these dynamics. Furthermore, although i-deals are linked to positive outcomes, the underlying mechanisms—particularly human capital development versus motivational explanations—are underexplored. This study addresses these gaps by proposing a moderated mediation model, drawing on social cognitive theory and resource-based perspective, to test how approach motive and supervisor political skill relate to i-deals, how i-deals foster personal skill development that enhances service creativity, and whether high-commitment HR systems condition these effects. The study contributes a more nuanced understanding of i-deals by identifying both dyadic antecedents and a skill-based mechanism, while highlighting contextual contingencies in their implementation.

title: Where the past meets the present: Upward mobility, environmental stimuli, and CEOs’ investment in corporate social responsibility

entries.rq_with_context: Despite early theorizing by Bowen (1953) on whether upwardly mobile managers are more socially conscious, it remains unclear how executives' social class origins influence their CSR decisions. While research shows that social class shapes values and behaviors, less is known about the dual influence of class origins and the experience of upward mobility. This study addresses this gap by focusing on CEOs from lower social classes—the most extreme cases of upward mobility—and testing how their background relates to CSR investments. Drawing on upper echelons and habitus theory, the authors propose that these CEOs develop competing internal dispositions: one shaped by early experiences of scarcity and interdependence, and another by the hardships of upward mobility that emphasize self-reliance. The research uses survey and archival data to test hypotheses about differential investment in community- versus employee-centric CSR. The key contribution is revealing the complex and sometimes contradictory ways in which upward mobility shapes executive decision making.

title: Ideas endorsed, credit claimed: Managerial credit claiming weakens the benefits of voice endorsement on future voice behavior through respect and work group identification

entries.rq_with_context: Employees often speak up with constructive ideas, and managerial endorsement is typically seen as beneficial for encouraging future voice.
