This gap is particularly significant in collaborations with deep sectoral differences, where conflicting interests may generate persistent tensions. Drawing on a qualitative case study of Action2020—a high-profile partnership between the World Business Council for Sustainable Development and the Stockholm Resilience Center—the study asks: How does paradox management shape the evolution of cross-sector goals? The analysis uses paradox theory to trace how conflicting demands around scientific independence and business survival influenced goal changes across three phases. The study contributes a process model that reveals how turning points, shifts in paradox poles, and intermediary roles shape cross-sector goal setting.

title: A Configurational Perspective on the Quality of Managers’ Counterfactual Reflections

entries.rq_with_context: Counterfactual reflection (CFR)—thinking about “what might have been”—can enhance learning, but only high-quality CFR yields benefits. While prior research has established a link between CFR quality and learning, little is known about why some experiences lead to high-quality CFR while others do not. Existing studies focus on isolated, linear effects of individual factors, yet managers reflect on experiences by considering multiple factors and their interdependencies. We suggest CFR quality is causally complex. Using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) on interviews with 129 managers reflecting on business-to-business negotiations, we identify configurations of negotiation factors linked to high- and low-quality CFR. We find that managers’ situation-specific ability to understand causal linkages and their motivation are key mechanisms: high-quality CFR occurs only when both ability and motivation are high. Our study contributes by revealing the underlying logic connecting experience to CFR quality, advancing the functional theory of counterfactual thinking.

title: Internal Control Weakness and Corporate Divestitures

entries.rq_with_context: Internal control weakness (ICW) disclosures under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) signal problems in financial reporting accuracy and organizational legitimacy, often stemming from high organizational complexity. While prior research has examined stakeholder reactions to ICW, there is limited understanding of how ICW affects firms' strategic responses, particularly corporate divestitures—a key tool for reducing complexity. This creates a gap in understanding what drives divestitures beyond economic efficiency motives. This study investigates whether firms use divestitures as a strategic response to remedy ICW after disclosure. It proposes that ICW disclosure increases the likelihood of divestitures, especially with newly appointed CEOs, but less so when ICW is common in the industry. It further examines dual performance outcomes: market reaction to the divestiture announcement and subsequent core business growth. The paper uses a panel of S&P 1500 firms (2003–2020) and fixed-effects Poisson and OLS models. The key contribution is revealing ICW as a novel antecedent to divestitures and demonstrating its nuanced performance consequences, advancing corporate strategy and internal control research.

title: Duality of Workload in Teams: A Daily Investigation of Team Workload and Team Functioning

entries.rq_with_context: Workload has traditionally been studied as a challenge stressor with motivational benefits, but recent research suggests it can elicit both positive and negative appraisals. While this duality has been recognized at the individual level, research on collective workload in teams remains limited. The gap lies in understanding how team-level workload impacts team functioning through both beneficial (e.g., enhanced team processes) and detrimental (e.g., increased member depletion) pathways, and under what conditions these effects occur. This study addresses this gap by applying job demands–resources (JD-R) theory to examine how daily team workload impacts team processes and team member depletion, which in turn affect team member satisfaction and team performance. The approach incorporates a daily diary design over five workdays with objective workload and performance data from 610 employees across 99 bank branches. The study claims to contribute by extending JD-R theory to the team level, offering a dual-pathway model of workload effects, and identifying boundary conditions related to perceived task significance and positive affect.

title: Tokens or Trailblazers: Identity Construction of Occupants of New Inclusion-Driven Roles

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly create inclusion-driven roles—such as chief diversity officer or lady officer—to signal commitment to diversity and inclusion. However, these roles are often ambiguous, with unclear expectations and competing demands to align with organizational norms while advocating for change. This ambiguity places a burden on occupants, especially when they belong to underrepresented groups, to define their roles and establish legitimacy. Prior research has studied identity construction in established roles or emerging occupations but has not addressed how occupants of newly created, inclusion-focused roles navigate ambiguity and societal tensions. This study asks how occupants of new inclusion-driven roles construct a role identity that legitimizes their work. Drawing on interviews with early lady officers in the Indian military, we use qualitative analysis to trace their identity work. Our contribution is an emergent theory showing how occupants initially emphasize professional identity to gain acceptance and later assert distinctive, inclusion-informed behaviors to reshape role expectations and build legitimacy.

title: Dare to Fight? How Activist Hedge Funds’ Hostile Tactics Influence Target Firm Resistance

entries.rq_with_context: Activist hedge funds increasingly influence corporate governance, yet little is known about how their engagement approaches—particularly the level of hostility in their tactics—affect target firm responses. While prior research focuses on financial outcomes or activist characteristics like reputation, the behavioral effects of tactical hostility remain unclear. We address this gap by investigating whether hostile tactics trigger psychological reactions in management and the board, leading to increased resistance. Drawing on cognitive and emotional responses such as ego threat and desire for control, we propose that hostile tactics paradoxically increase firm resistance. Using a sample of 731 activist campaigns from 2002 to 2015, we test this effect and examine boundary conditions. Our study contributes by revealing that hostility may backfire, challenging assumptions that aggressive tactics are effective in securing compliance.

title: Emotion Regulation During Hostile Interactions: Optimizing Regulation Profiles for Event Performance and Well-Being

entries.rq_with_context: Employees in many jobs must regulate their emotions when facing hostility from customers, clients, or students, which can harm well-being even as it supports performance. Prior research has mostly contrasted surface acting (suppression, faking expressions) and deep acting (reappraising feelings), suggesting deep acting benefits both performance and health. However, this dichotomy oversimplifies how people actually regulate emotions, particularly during intense hostility. No known research has simultaneously studied the use of multiple emotion regulation strategies at the event level or tested for trade-offs between real-time performance and well-being. The authors use a comprehensive six-strategy framework—suppression, distraction, situation selection, reappraisal, situation modification, and social support—and apply a person-centered approach to identify patterns. They examine how event intensity predicts profile use and whether certain profiles benefit event performance while others are better for well-being. The key contribution is revealing that performance and negative affect follow a trade-off: the most effective profiles for handling hostile events come at an emotional cost.

title: Managerial Human Capital and External Mobility: A Signaling Perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Managerial human capital is a critical resource for organizational success, yet it is difficult to assess in external labor markets due to information asymmetries. While internal labor markets can evaluate employees' managerial potential, external firms must rely on signals to infer capabilities. This study explores how two career-based signals—time to first managerial promotion and tenure in managerial roles—inform external mobility decisions. Prior research has treated firm-specific human capital as either a constraint or an enabler of mobility, but less is known about the temporal dynamics of such signals. Drawing on signaling theory, we propose that both signals exhibit inverted U-shaped relationships with external mobility due to opposing demand- and supply-side forces. Using a population-level dataset of 2,079 MLB scouts from 1988 to 2010, we test these predictions using logistic discrete-time event history analysis. The findings contribute to strategic human capital and mobility research by revealing the nuanced, non-linear role of career signals in managerial labor markets.

title: Grammatical Redundancy in Scales: Using the “ConGRe” Process to Create Better Measures

entries.rq_with_context: As organizational research models grow more complex, there is increasing pressure to use shorter scales to save time in data collection. However, shorter scales tend to be less reliable, and researchers often counteract this by using items that are grammatically redundant—nearly identical in wording—which inflates internal consistency but at the cost of domain coverage. This practice undermines content validity, a foundational aspect of measurement often overlooked. The paper addresses the gap in methods for quantifying and reducing grammatical redundancy during scale development. The research question is: How can researchers identify and reduce grammatical redundancy without sacrificing conceptual redundancy? The authors propose the ConGRe process, using natural language processing indices (TF-IDF and GloST) to guide item writing. The key contribution is a practical, pre-data-collection method for improving content validity in scales.

title: How narcissism, promotion criteria, and empowering leadership jointly influence creativity through diverse information searching: An expectancy perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Narcissism is typically viewed as a 'dark' personality trait linked to negative workplace behaviors, yet it may also carry potential benefits such as creativity. However, it remains unclear how to suppress its downsides while promoting its positive outcomes. Prior research presents conflicting findings on the narcissism–creativity link, suggesting context matters. This study addresses this gap by investigating how managerial practices—specifically promotions based on relative performance and empowering leadership—can channel narcissistic employees’ self-focus into productive behaviors. Drawing on expectancy theory, the authors propose that these practices shape valence, instrumentality, and expectancy, motivating narcissistic employees to engage in diverse information searching, which in turn enhances creativity. The research tests this model using multi-source, multi-time data from 462 employees across 88 teams.

title: Strategic, episodic and truncated orientations to planning in post-redundancy career transitions

entries.rq_with_context: The article investigates how workers in the Swedish steel industry navigate career transitions after redundancy, focusing on their orientations to planning. While career literature often assumes planning is an ongoing, lifelong process, this tendency is based largely on studies of managerial or professional workers. Less is known about how semi-skilled industrial workers—facing forced transitions—engage in planning over time. The study asks how post-redundancy experiences align with longer-term career planning processes. Drawing on working-life biographies collected several years after redundancy, the research uses qualitative interviews to explore the role of agency, structural constraint, and lived experience. It identifies three distinct planning orientations—strategic, episodic, and truncated—as ways people differentially engage with career planning. The contribution is to problematize the dominant assumption of ubiquitous lifelong planning by showing how planning varies meaningfully across working-life contexts and experiences.

title: Coping with personhood limbo: Personhood anchoring work among undocumented workers in Italy

entries.rq_with_context: Undocumented workers globally face 'personhood limbo'—a condition where socio-legal structures undermine their recognition and belonging, leaving them in a state of partial inclusion. While prior research has focused on how such limbo is created, little attention has been paid to how undocumented workers actively respond to it. This study addresses that gap by exploring how undocumented workers in Italy cope with personhood limbo through agentic practices. Drawing on interviews, the authors identify 'personhood anchoring work'—everyday strategies through which workers maintain fragments of their personhood. The study uses a relational and processual understanding of personhood to analyze these practices. The authors claim their work advances understanding of worker agency, personhood negotiation, and integration processes among marginalized migrants.

title: The pragmatic cycle of knowledge work: Unlocking cross-domain collaboration in open innovation spaces

entries.rq_with_context: Contemporary collaboration increasingly occurs in temporary spaces where actors from different domains and organizations work together despite having little shared knowledge. While research shows temporary spaces like hackathons can drive innovation, less is known about how actors overcome pragmatic challenges stemming from their situated knowledge. This study investigates how individuals address knowledge boundaries during open innovation events in the digital health sector. It draws on a pragmatic view of knowledge as localized, embedded, and invested in practice. By analyzing Hacking Health’s multi-event approach across cafes, workshops, hackathons, and bootcamps, the authors reveal how different temporary spaces orient distinct types of knowledge work. The key contribution is identifying a pragmatic cycle—exploring, complementing, mapping, and modeling—through which actors progressively build shared knowledge to sustain cross-domain collaboration.

title: Stigmatization by an Authoritarian Government: Russian NGOs Under the 2012 Foreign Agents Law

entries.rq_with_context: Most research on organizational stigma focuses on preexisting stigma or bottom-up processes, leaving unexplored how governments—especially authoritarian ones—actively stigmatize organizations. The dynamics between stigmatizer and stigmatized, as well as the role of state power in initiating and sustaining stigma, remain poorly understood. This paper addresses these gaps by investigating how the Russian government systematically stigmatized NGOs under the 2012 foreign agents law. Using an inductive qualitative approach with archival, online, and interview data, the study develops a three-phase process model: label emergence, enforcement and contestation, and propagation. The research contributes by revealing the mechanisms of state-led stigmatization, including the use of historical labels, evolving enforcement tactics, and the broadening of stigmatized categories beyond the original targets.

title: Harambee! A Triadic Perspective on Social Impact: Organizations, Evaluators, and Target Beneficiaries in Kenya

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often claim to create positive social impact through initiatives like corporate social responsibility (CSR), gaining legitimacy from evaluators such as donors, consumers, and funding agencies. However, research has shown these initiatives may produce limited or harmful outcomes for the very communities they aim to benefit, especially due to opacity—the difficulty evaluators have in verifying actual impacts. While scholars have studied the relationship between organizations and evaluators, target beneficiaries are typically viewed as passive recipients of these impacts, whether positive or negative. This study addresses a gap by asking: What role, if any, do target beneficiaries play in influencing the processes and outcomes of social impact creation? Drawing on a three-year qualitative study of a CSR project in Kenya involving a multinational corporation, its global audiences (evaluators), and local tea farming communities (target beneficiaries), the author examines how beneficiaries actively participated in the legitimation process. The study’s contribution lies in revealing how beneficiaries leveraged their corroboration of organizational claims to negotiate meaningful, context-specific changes—challenging the assumption that social impact is solely driven by organizations or compromised by decoupling.

title: Competition in Collaboration: The Problem of (Mis)Aligned Perception

entries.rq_with_context: Interorganizational collaborations frequently fail to meet expectations, even though firms are generally aware of competitive tensions that can affect cooperation. Prior research suggests such tension should be manageable, making it puzzling why collaborations still break down. This gap raises a key question: why does competitive tension continue to derail partnerships? The authors propose that the issue lies not in objective competition but in misaligned perceptions—when one partner views the other as a competitor while the reverse is not true. Using data from the U.S. software industry (1995–2012), they test whether this perceptual misalignment leads to mismatched expectations about behavior and performance, ultimately reducing the likelihood of collaboration renewal. They contribute by highlighting perceptual alignment as a critical factor shaping collaboration outcomes, thus advancing understanding of how cognition and social structure influence interfirm dynamics.

title: Wasted? The Downstream Effects of Social Movement–Backed Occupations

entries.rq_with_context: While existing research has focused on how social movements gain initial concessions from organizations (upstream processes), less is known about how movement priorities become institutionalized over time through downstream processes. A key gap concerns the role of formal occupations—such as recycling coordinators, diversity managers, or sustainability officers—created in response to movement pressure. These roles are tasked with embedding movement values, yet little is known about the challenges they face in advancing both movement goals and their own occupational standing. This study investigates how recycling coordinators in higher education navigated this dual mission over 25 years. Using longitudinal analysis of online forum discussions, it explores the tensions they faced and the strategies they used. The authors argue that despite successfully institutionalizing recycling and laying the groundwork for sustainability, the occupation itself declined when the environmental movement shifted focus. The study contributes to understanding the understudied downstream phase of movement impact by highlighting the central but precarious role of occupational actors in sustaining movement change.

title: Mechanisms of Organizational Imprinting: From Entrepreneur to Organization

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often retain core features shaped by their founders long after founding, even amid major disruptions. While imprinting theory explains this persistence, the processes by which individuals like entrepreneurs translate their beliefs into lasting organizational traits remain underexplored. Scholars have called for micro-level theories detailing how imprinting occurs, particularly through individual actions. This study addresses that gap by asking: how do entrepreneurs imprint organizations? Using a longitudinal historical case study of Carl Zeiss (1846–1990), the research analyzes how founder Carl Zeiss and partner Ernst Abbe instilled enduring practices, structures, and product orientations. The approach traces how their individual blueprints for high-precision manufacturing and science-based development were enacted. The study contributes by identifying specific mechanisms—early decisions, teaching, role modeling, and formalized rules—that explain how individual-level imprints persist across organizational dimensions.

title: Referral Triads

entries.rq_with_context: Referrals are central in professional service markets, where clients rely on intermediaries to navigate uncertainty by matching them with experts and building post-match trust. In healthcare, primary care physicians (PCPs) serve as key referrers who connect patients to specialists. However, existing research has not explored the potential tension between these two functions of referral: curating high-quality matches based on expertise and fostering trust through established relationships. The authors argue that this tension arises because strong ties between PCPs and specialists—while promoting trust—may lead to habitual referrals that limit exposure to more specialized providers. Using population-level medical claims data from Massachusetts, the study asks whether stronger PCP-specialist ties increase patient confidence in specialists and whether they reduce the fit between patients’ health conditions and specialists’ clinical experience. The analysis uses regression models with PCP-by-specialty fixed effects and instrumental variable strategies to account for endogeneity. Its core contribution is identifying a fundamental trade-off in referral systems: the same relationships that enhance trust can undermine match quality, suggesting a structural limitation in how intermediaries generate value in credence goods markets.

title: Give Peace a Chance? How Regulatory Foci Influence Organizational Conflict Events in Intractable Conflict Environments

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational conflict research typically assumes non-intractable contexts, but many organizations operate in intractable conflict environments (ICEs), where deep, unsolvable intergroup conflict shapes perceptions and behaviors. In such settings, potential conflict incidents are more likely to be perceived as threatening and emotionally intense, increasing conflict events. Prior work suggests promotion-framed interventions reduce conflict in benign environments by inducing a promotion focus, but these may not work in ICEs. This study asks: How can organizations address conflict ex ante in an ICE? The authors argue that an ICE induces a strong, salient prevention focus that overrides situational promotion framing. Using a field experiment in Ghanaian farming cooperatives, they test whether a prevention-framed intervention leads to fewer conflict events than a promotion-framed one. Their approach draws on regulatory fit theory, positing that matching the environment-induced prevention focus makes vigilant behavior feel 'right.' The study contributes by showing that the most effective conflict intervention in an ICE is the opposite of what is prescribed in typical organizational settings.

title: Lookism Climate in Organizations: Construct Development and Validation of a Scale

entries.rq_with_context: Research has consistently shown that physically attractive employees receive advantages in hiring, performance evaluations, and career advancement—a phenomenon known as the 'beauty premium.' However, existing studies are often context-poor, focusing on individual-level biases rather than organizational environments. A recent review calls for greater attention to organizational context in understanding when and why attractiveness influences workplace outcomes. This study addresses this gap by introducing the concept of 'lookism climate'—shared or individual perceptions that a workplace values physical attractiveness—and developing the Lookism Climate Scale (LCS) to measure it. Using eight samples of full-time employees from the U.S. and South Korea, the authors validate the scale’s psychometric properties and examine its nomological network. The study contributes a new contextual lens for studying appearance-based advantages, offering both theoretical insight and a practical measurement tool for future research and organizational assessment.

title: The Superstitious Heuristic in Strategic Decision Making

entries.rq_with_context: Strategic decision-making often involves heuristics due to bounded rationality, with existing research focusing on Western-centric types like fast-and-frugal rules or expert intuition. However, a distinct form—the superstitious heuristic, rooted in cultural beliefs about luck, fate, or paranormal forces—is widely used globally but overlooked in strategy literature, particularly because it is more prevalent in non-Western contexts. This gap limits our understanding of how executives make decisions under high uncertainty, where traditional heuristics may fail due to unrecognizable environmental cues. The study introduces the construct of the superstitious heuristic and investigates which executive characteristics (e.g., tenure, gender, functional background) are associated with its use, using data from Chinese executives. It employs survey methods and regression analysis to test main effects and moderation by institutional misalignment. The contribution lies in formally conceptualizing a new heuristic type and identifying contingent executive antecedents, thereby expanding the scope of upper echelons theory and heuristics research beyond Western assumptions.

title: Property Rights and Firm Scope

entries.rq_with_context: While much research on firm scope assumes a strong property rights regime, most countries have weak or evolving protections. This gap limits our understanding of how institutional changes shape corporate diversification. The authors address this by investigating how the strengthening of formal property rights affects firms’ horizontal and vertical scope decisions. They exploit China’s 2007 Property Law as a quasi-experiment, comparing private firms (treatment group) to state-owned enterprises (control group). Using difference-in-differences analysis, they test whether improved property rights lead firms to pursue more horizontally related and less vertically related diversification. A key contribution is showing how political connections moderate these effects, offering insight into the interplay between formal institutions and informal protections in shaping strategic choices.

title: Interactive Effects of CEOs’ Firm-Specific Experience and Versatile Experiences on Pursuit of New Growth Opportunity

entries.rq_with_context: Firms face a tension between leveraging existing resources through firm-specific knowledge and exploring new growth domains. While firm-specific experience is theorized to support path-dependent growth, it may also lead to cognitive entrenchment that limits innovation. Prior research offers conflicting predictions and mixed empirical results. This paper addresses this ambiguity by asking not whether firm-specific experience is good or bad, but under what conditions it supports opportunity pursuit. Drawing on Penrose’s theory of the growth of the firm, we examine how versatile managerial experiences—related-industry, international, and multifunctional—interact with firm-specific experience. Using data from U.S. food firms pursuing organic food opportunities (1997–2007), we test whether versatility moderates the impact of firm-specific tenure. Our key contribution is showing that firm-specific experience becomes beneficial only when complemented by versatile experience, reconciling opposing theoretical perspectives.

title: Once a job crafter, always a job crafter? Investigating job crafting in organizations as a reciprocal self-concordant process across time

entries.rq_with_context: While job crafting is widely seen as a beneficial, ongoing process, little is known about what sustains or undermines it over time. Existing research lacks longitudinal evidence on how the outcomes of job crafting feed back into future crafting efforts. This study investigates whether and how the attainment of self-concordant goals (e.g., fulfilling one’s calling) and organizational goals (e.g., increasing congregational attendance) influences subsequent job crafting. Drawing on self-concordance theory, the authors propose a reciprocal model in which self-concordant goal attainment reinforces further crafting, while organizational goal attainment may disrupt this cycle. Using longitudinal survey data from Church of England ministers across three waves over four years, the study tests these dynamics. The key contribution is advancing a temporal, self-concordant framework that clarifies how different types of goal attainment shape the sustainability of job crafting.

title: ‘Brazil must be a country for entrepreneurs and workers, not scoundrels’: Personal branding mechanisms underpinning CEO activism

entries.rq_with_context: CEO activism is increasingly common, yet little is known about how CEOs engage in activism through social media, especially in non-Western, right-wing contexts. While existing research focuses on the issues CEOs advocate for and how stakeholders respond, it overlooks the process of online identity construction. This study addresses that gap by analyzing how Luciano Hang, a conservative Brazilian CEO and activist, crafts his online identity on Instagram. Drawing on personal branding mechanisms—crafting a personal brand, content curation, conveying authenticity, connecting with audiences, and performativity—the study examines the strategic identity work behind his activism. Using critical visual analysis, the research reveals how Hang constructs a multifaceted online identity that aligns with right-wing ideologies. The contribution lies in uncovering the deliberate, strategic processes through which CEOs use personal branding to perform activism online, extending understanding beyond progressive, Western-focused studies.

title: Working with pride in the shadow of shame: Emotional dissonance and identity work during a corporate scandal

entries.rq_with_context: Corporate scandals generate public shaming and pressure on employees to express guilt and contrition, even when they are not personally responsible for the wrongdoing. Existing research assumes emotional dissonance—conflict between required and felt emotions—is something individuals seek to resolve. However, this study identifies a gap in understanding how emotional dissonance interacts with identity work in highly stigmatized organizational contexts. Drawing on ethnographic data from Danske Bank during its money-laundering scandal, the research asks: how do employees sustain emotional dissonance through ongoing identity work during corporate scandals? Using identity work theory (Watson, 2008) and an analysis of emotional labor, the study traces how employees manage conflicting emotions and social identities. It contributes by showing that emotional dissonance is not resolved but actively maintained through identity work to preserve a positive self-identity and organizational belonging.

title: Addressing durability in collaborative organising: Event atmospheres and polyrhythmic affectivity

entries.rq_with_context: Collaborative organizing often fails to sustain durability despite its reliance on passion, relationality, and creativity. While polycentric governance has been proposed as a relational principle to support lasting collaboration, existing research emphasizes institutional and communicative dimensions, largely overlooking affective dynamics. There is limited understanding of how affective atmospheres—especially those generated at events—can be cultivated to sustain collaborative work over time. Drawing on two ethnographic studies of an open-source software community and a network of impact entrepreneurs, this study asks: How are affective atmospheres generated at events contributing to durable processes of collaborative organising? The authors use an atmospheric and affective lens to trace the role of face-to-face events, analyzing how emergent and formalized events shape collaborative dynamics. They argue that durability is supported not through emotional stability, but through 'polyrhythmic affectivity'—an ongoing friction between togetherness, dissonance, and mutuality—which sustains emergent yet enduring order.

title: Corporate Scandals as Punctuating Events That Change Human Resource Roles

entries.rq_with_context: Corporate scandals disrupt organizational stability and create urgent demands for change, particularly in employee behaviors—central to the HR function’s domain. While HR role typologies suggest evolution toward external stakeholder responsiveness (e.g., Ulrich & Dulebohn’s Wave 4), empirical evidence on how such shifts occur during crises remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring how corporate scandals, conceptualized as event systems, trigger changes in HR roles. Using event systems theory (EST), the authors analyze five multinational case studies across pharmaceutical, chemical, and financial sectors. They ask how scandals alter HR’s responsibilities in compliance, risk, and cultural transformation. The study contributes by showing that HR role changes are not directly driven by external stakeholders but emerge from internal strategic recalibrations following scandals, challenging assumptions of linear HR role progression.

title: From Intent to Impact: A Proactive Event Approach for Amplifying Sustainability Across Time

entries.rq_with_context: There is growing concern about high levels of resource consumption in manufacturing, prompting firms to implement proactive sustainability initiatives. While event system theory (EST) has been used to understand unplanned events, less is known about how its propositions apply to strategically initiated proactive events. A key gap exists in understanding how event characteristics—such as duration, timing, and criticality—differ across lower-level units and influence both immediate and long-term outcomes. This study addresses that gap by examining a new sustainability monitoring system rollout across 87 manufacturing units of a Fortune 200 firm. Using a variant of discontinuous growth modeling (DGM), the authors test how event duration, timing, and managerial criticality behaviors relate to two phases of change: initial pre-post differences and longer-term post-event trajectories in energy consumption. The study contributes by extending EST to proactive events and demonstrating how DGM can be adapted for events with variable onset and duration.

title: Applying Event System Theory to Organizational Change: The Importance of Everyday Positive and Negative Events

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational change is typically studied as an organizational-level event, yet employees also experience 'everyday change events' as the change becomes embedded in their daily work. While research has explored reactions to large-scale change, less is known about how these macro-level evaluations interact with micro-level experiences over time. This paper addresses that gap by applying event system theory to examine how employees’ initial commitment to a merger influences their anticipatory perceptions, which in turn shape how they perceive everyday negative and positive change events. The authors investigate how these everyday events affect engagement, performance, fairness perceptions, and later commitment to the change. Using a longitudinal field design with pre-merger surveys, a daily diary study, and post-implementation surveys, they test top-down and bottom-up effects across levels. The study contributes by showing dynamic interplay between organizational and individual-level change experiences, highlighting both theoretical and practical implications for managing change through everyday events.

title: Resilience Within Constraints: An Event Oriented Approach to Crisis Response

entries.rq_with_context: Recent research on organizational and community resilience has highlighted the importance of collective responses to crises but has largely overlooked how institutional environments shape these responses. Crises like the COVID-19 pandemic unfold dynamically and are embedded within complex governance structures that constrain or enable local actors' ability to respond effectively. This paper addresses a critical gap by examining how macro-level decision-making configurations—specifically, the degree of autonomy granted to counties in healthcare decisions—affect local resilience outcomes. Using high-frequency U.S. county-level data, the authors investigate whether distributed (decentralized) decision-making leads to better pandemic outcomes compared to centralized models. They apply Event System Theory (EST) to account for the evolving nature of the crisis and test how structural and contextual factors moderate this relationship. The study contributes by showing that decision-making autonomy enhances resilience, particularly when communities have diverse healthcare systems and must adapt responses over time.

title: Event Space and Firm Value: Chinese Listed Firms in the US–China Trade War

entries.rq_with_context: While prior crisis management research emphasizes geographic proximity to physical events, this paper argues that events like trade wars impact firms through multidimensional 'event space' defined by product and geographic market directions. Existing studies overlook how non-geographic spatial proximities shape firm vulnerability during geopolitical crises. Drawing on event system theory, the authors investigate how Chinese firms were affected by the 2018 US-China trade war based on their membership in target industries (product market direction) and export activities to the US (geographic market direction), including spillover effects to related firms. The study also explores how stakeholder relationships—specifically state ownership and CSR—moderate these impacts. Using an event study method on a sample of 2,157 Chinese listed firms, the research tests hypotheses about spatial exposure and buffering effects. The key contribution is introducing a multidimensional model of event space that captures both intended and spillover effects of geopolitical shocks, advancing understanding beyond location-based risk assessment.

title: Creativity During Threat to Organizational Survival: The Influence of Employee Creativity on Downsizing Survival Selection

entries.rq_with_context: While employee creativity is generally seen as beneficial, less is known about how it affects the employees who demonstrate it, especially during organizational crises. Existing research offers mixed evidence on whether creative employees are rewarded or penalized, suggesting context matters. The authors identify a gap in understanding how high-stakes events, like threats to organizational survival, shape managerial evaluations of different types of creativity and subsequent downsizing decisions. Drawing on event system theory and threat rigidity theory, they propose that under such threats, managers favor incremental creativity (small improvements) over radical creativity (major changes) due to cognitive rigidity. The research question is: How do incremental and radical creativity influence downsizing survival selection via manager job performance evaluations when an organization faces a survival threat? The study uses a three-wave field study and two experiments to test this model. The key claimed contribution is revealing the differential impact of creativity types during organizational threats, advancing both creativity and downsizing literatures.

title: Managing Asymmetric Events With Anticipatory and Reactive Strategies

entries.rq_with_context: Information asymmetric negative events—damaging occurrences known to firm insiders before public disclosure—are critical moments that trigger impression management efforts. While prior research has studied anticipatory or reactive strategies in isolation, less is known about how these strategies are used together. This paper addresses that gap by investigating how a firm's use of anticipatory impression management (AIM) shapes its subsequent reactive impression management (RIM), how evaluators' reactions to AIM moderate that relationship, and the performance implications of different AIM-RIM combinations. Drawing on event-oriented and organizational impression management theories, the authors analyze 238 late-stage clinical trial terminations in the pharmaceutical industry. They find that specific AIM strategies predict particular RIM choices, that market reactions moderate some of these relationships, and that certain strategic pairings lead to better stock responses, thereby advancing understanding of coordinated impression management.

title: Reputation-Damaging Events Over a Long Time Horizon: An Event-System Model of Substantive Reputation Repair

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations face repeated reputation-damaging events (RDEs), yet often delay or avoid top-down substantive repair, responding instead only sporadically. Current discrete-event models assume a direct link between a single severe event and organizational response, failing to explain this asynchrony. This gap limits understanding of how chains of events over time shape strategic responses. Drawing on event system theory (EST), the authors investigate how 47 RDEs over a decade led to substantive repair in a multinational firm. They analyze how top managers interpret event patterns rather than individual incidents. The research asks: How do organizations manage reputation repair over long time horizons when responses are asynchronous with events? The study uses qualitative data including interviews, archival records, and observations. It contributes by proposing an event-system model that explains delayed repair through adaptive cycles and managerial purposeful avoidance.

title: A Summer of Protest: Using Event System Theory To Test an Intersectional Leadership Advantage

entries.rq_with_context: The Summer 2020 BLM protests in the U.S. represented high-strength, disruptive events tied to social identity threats, creating uncertainty about what constitutes effective leadership under such conditions. While research has separately examined race or gender in leadership, less is known about how their intersection shapes outcomes during mega-threats. The authors propose an intersectional leadership advantage (ILA), suggesting that Black women leaders, due to their unique social experiences, may be particularly effective in these contexts. Using event system theory and protest event analysis across 11,540 demonstrations, they test whether cities with Black women police chiefs experienced less violence. Their key contribution is identifying a synergistic effect of race and gender in real-world leadership effectiveness during societal crises.

title: Non-standard employment and underemployment at labor market entry and their impact on later wage trajectories

entries.rq_with_context: Non-standard employment (NSE) and underemployment have become widespread, especially among young workers, raising concerns about long-term labor market inequalities. While existing research has examined wage outcomes of NSE or underemployment separately, there is limited understanding of how their combined patterns in early careers shape future wages, particularly across gender. This study addresses this gap using Australian panel data from the HILDA Survey (2001–2020) to investigate how trajectories of NSE and underemployment in the first five years after education influence wage growth over the next decade. The authors employ multichannel sequence analysis followed by random effects panel models. They find that most combined patterns of NSE and underemployment are linked to significant initial wage penalties, though these diminish within 10 years, except for those primarily unemployed or inactive early on. The study's key contribution is demonstrating that it is the combination of employment instability and underemployment—not isolated experiences—that shapes early wage disadvantages, and that gender moderates these effects, with men facing steeper penalties.

title: Shape-shifting: How boundary objects affect meaning-making across visual, verbal, and embodied modes

entries.rq_with_context: Boundary objects are widely recognized as tools that help diverse collaborators create shared meaning, yet most research treats them as static artifacts despite their dynamic collaborative contexts. While prior studies acknowledge that boundary objects support coordination across differences, they under-theorize how the objects themselves change form during use. This gap is critical because meaning-making is processual and fragile, suggesting boundary objects must shift shape as collaboration evolves. We ask: How do boundary objects shape-shift across visual, verbal, and embodied modes, and how does this influence meaning-making? Drawing on a strong multimodal lens and longitudinal video ethnography of an interorganizational team, we analyze the shifting forms of a servitization roadmap. We show how its shape-shifting enables and constrains shared understanding, advancing theory by revealing the dynamic, relational nature of boundary objects.

title: There and back again: The roles of morning- and evening commute recovery experiences for daily resources across the commute-, work-, and home domain

entries.rq_with_context: While commuting is commonly studied for its costs, emerging research suggests it may also offer benefits through recovery experiences. However, little empirical work examines how daily commute-related recovery influences resource gains across life domains. This study addresses this gap by testing whether relaxation, mastery, and detachment during morning and evening commutes contribute to higher subjective vitality in work and home domains, drawing on the Work–Home Resources model and Conservation of Resources theory. Using a daily diary design across ten workdays, it models how morning commute recovery affects afternoon vitality, which then influences evening commute recovery and evening vitality at home. The study further investigates commute duration as a boundary condition, asking whether longer commutes impede or enhance the benefits of recovery experiences. The key contribution is providing empirical evidence for commuting as a source of daily resource gain rather than merely a cost, thereby shifting the dominant negative narrative on commuting in organizational research.

title: Bad apples and sour grapes: How fruit and vegetable wholesalers’ fantasy mediates experienced stigma

entries.rq_with_context: Fruit and vegetable wholesalers in France are widely stigmatised as 'thieves', 'bandits', and 'parasites' due to their intermediary role, leading to disintermediation efforts by retailers and producers. Despite persistent negative evaluations and marginalisation, these organisations have not rejected their stigmatised identity but instead embraced it. The gap lies in understanding how stigmatised organisations internally manage stigma without seeking legitimacy from external actors. This study addresses how internal dynamics—particularly fantasy and affective attachment—mediate the experience of organisational stigma. Using a qualitative case study of two French wholesalers, ORCHADE and POMA, the research analyses how members collectively maintain an idealised self-image of centrality. The authors contribute to stigma research by showing how fantasy enables stigmatised groups to resist change and sustain identity through self-idealisation.

title: Pay Premiums and Peer Spillovers: Unpacking the Value Proposition of Employing Stars as They Age

entries.rq_with_context: Star employees are known for creating substantial value through exceptional individual performance and indirect contributions to peers, yet concerns persist about whether organizations can capture sufficient value given stars' high pay and bargaining power. A critical gap exists in understanding how stars' value creation and capture evolve across their careers, particularly as aging may alter both their motivations and capacities. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how employee age influences the balance between stars' pay relative to individual performance (PRIP) and their indirect contributions to non-star performance. Drawing on cumulative advantage and career theories, the authors propose that stars increasingly capture value as they age due to growing bargaining power, while simultaneously enhancing their indirect value creation through peer spillovers. Using archival and survey data from a financial services firm, the study tests these dynamics and offers empirical insight into the shifting value proposition of stars over time.

title: To Toe the Party Line? The Impact of Firm and CEO Partisanship on Corporate Mass-Media Normative Legitimacy

entries.rq_with_context: Corporate political activity (CPA), especially partisan forms like PAC contributions, has traditionally been studied for its strategic value, with little attention to public legitimacy consequences. Despite growing concern about the societal implications of CPA and evidence that public opinion affects organizational legitimacy, research largely ignores how stakeholders view partisan CPA. This gap is critical because partisan political actions by firms and CEOs may conflict with public values, triggering normative backlash. This paper investigates the impact of firm- and CEO-level partisan PAC contributions on affective-based corporate legitimacy, proxied by media sentiment, using dynamic panel data models on S&P 500 firms from 2000–2020. It also explores post hoc whether firms adjust their CPA in response to legitimacy evaluations. The study contributes by being the first to systematically document the negative legitimacy effects of partisan CPA and showing how public sentiment can shape corporate behavior.

title: Competition and Constituents’ Polarization Online

entries.rq_with_context: Society is increasingly polarized, leading constituents to either identify with or disidentify from organizations based on conflicting identities. Competitive contests between organizations are identity-relevant events that can affirm or threaten these identities, potentially influencing how constituents engage online. While research suggests emotions drive online engagement, it remains unclear how polarized groups respond differently to organizational events. This study investigates how competitive outcomes—such as victories and losses—affect online engagement among identifying and disidentifying constituents, particularly focusing on the amplifying roles of close calls and unexpected outcomes. Using a mixed-method approach centered on NCAA football fans, the authors employ microeconometric analysis and a lab experiment. Their key contribution is revealing asymmetrical engagement patterns driven by identity rather than objective performance, showing that positive emotions more strongly drive engagement for identifying constituents.

title: Unpacking the Role of Job Insecurity for Employee Creativity: A Multidimensional Perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Modern organizations expect high employee creativity despite widespread job insecurity, yet research on the job insecurity–creativity link shows inconsistent results, often reporting near-zero overall effects. A key limitation is that both job insecurity and creativity are multidimensional constructs, but prior studies typically treat them as unidimensional. This paper addresses this gap by distinguishing between quantitative and qualitative job insecurity, and between radical and incremental creativity. The authors propose a conditional indirect-effects model in which career commitment mediates the relationship between quantitative job insecurity and radical creativity, while organizational identification mediates the link between qualitative job insecurity and incremental creativity. Turnover risk propensity and Confucian traditionality are tested as moderators. Using longitudinal and time-lagged multisource data from Chinese employees, the study aims to clarify when and why job insecurity harms specific forms of creativity, advancing a more nuanced theoretical understanding.

title: The Board Committee Chair Effect: How Much Does It Contribute to Firm Performance?

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research has established that strategic leaders such as CEOs and board chairs influence firm performance, little is known about the role of board committee chairs despite their critical responsibilities in monitoring and advising. Existing studies have largely overlooked this group, even though committees perform specialized tasks central to board functioning. This paper addresses this gap by asking: How much of the variance in firm performance can be explained by audit, compensation, and nominating committee chairs? Using variance decomposition analysis with multilevel modeling on a large sample of S&P 1500 firms from 1999–2017, the authors examine the magnitude of committee chair effects. They find that committee chairs collectively explain nearly 19% of performance variance—more than the board chair alone—and that these effects vary under CEO duality and across time periods, suggesting a need to reconsider their strategic importance.

title: Taking Charge as a Contextual Cue: How New CEO Regulatory Focus Influences Strategic Change

entries.rq_with_context: New CEOs face a sharp increase in job demands and vulnerability, creating a unique context that may alter how their psychological characteristics influence strategic decisions. While existing research suggests that promotion-focused CEOs are more likely to pursue strategic change, and prevention-focused CEOs are more risk-averse, this study challenges that assumption in the early tenure phase. We identify a gap in understanding how the transitional nature of becoming CEO interacts with regulatory focus to produce counter-normative behaviors. Our research question is: How does CEO regulatory focus influence strategic change during the initial years of tenure, and how is this relationship shaped by the heightened job demands and vulnerability of the new role? Using regulatory fit theory as our framework, we analyze a longitudinal dataset of over 800 public firms from 2001–2020. Our primary contribution is showing that the context of new CEO tenure shifts regulatory fit in ways that reverse traditional expectations—prevention-focused CEOs engage in more change, while promotion-focused CEOs engage in less.

title: Sustainability of Passion for Work? Change-Related Reciprocal Relationships Between Passion and Job Crafting

entries.rq_with_context: While passion for work is known to influence outcomes like performance and well-being, less is understood about how employees develop and sustain passion over time. Existing research often treats passion as a stable trait, overlooking its dynamic nature and the role of employee agency. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether and how passion evolves through proactive job crafting behaviors. Drawing on the self-concordance model, the authors propose that harmonious passion—autonomously internalized—promotes job crafting, which in turn strengthens subsequent passion, forming a self-reinforcing cycle. In contrast, obsessive passion—controlled and pressured—is expected to show weaker or no such reciprocal relationship. Using six-wave longitudinal data analyzed via latent change score modeling, the study tests these dynamics. The contribution lies in shifting the view of passion from static to dynamic, highlighting job crafting as a mechanism for sustaining passion.

title: Back From the Dead: Exploring the Tension Between Imagination and Custodianship in Revenant Organizations

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational actors increasingly seek to revive defunct or 'dead' firms—a process called reanimation—yet theory offers conflicting guidance on whether to leverage innovation or honor tradition. On one hand, failure suggests a need to move beyond the past; on the other, tradition may hold residual value worth preserving. This tension creates a critical gap in understanding how leaders successfully reanimate failed firms. The paper asks: How do organizational leaders successfully reanimate failed firms? Using a multiple-case study of six automotive companies, the authors identify a key tension between entrepreneurial imaginativeness and custodianship. Their analysis reveals that leaders who act as custodians—preserving core elements of the original organization—are more likely to achieve long-term survival than those who prioritize imaginative innovation.

title: Industry-Level Learning-by-Doing Rates and Corporate Development Activities

entries.rq_with_context: Firms engage in corporate development activities like acquisitions and alliances to access valuable knowledge, but such transactions involve exchange hazards. While prior research has examined these hazards separately, this paper investigates how industry-level learning-by-doing (LBD) rates—indicating how much knowledge is generated through own production experience—affect both ex ante (overpayment) and ex post (misappropriation) risks simultaneously. Existing literature largely treats LBD rates as proxies for cost advantages, neglecting their implications for knowledge characteristics and governance choices. This study fills that gap by theorizing that high LBD rates increase valuation uncertainty (raising overpayment risk) but reduce misappropriation risk due to low transferability. Using a sample of about 10,000 US manufacturing firm transactions from 1997–2006, the authors examine how LBD rates relate to the likelihood of any transaction, the choice between acquisitions and alliances, alliance governance (joint venture vs. contractual), and functional scope (inclusion of manufacturing). The contribution lies in integrating organizational learning with organizational economics to show how LBD intensity shapes transaction design through competing theoretical mechanisms.

title: Firm Formalization Strategy: The Interaction of Entrepreneurs and Government Officials in the Enforcement of Regulation

entries.rq_with_context: Entrepreneurs in early-stage market economies face complex decisions about complying with formal regulations, where institutional frameworks are weak and enforcement is inconsistent. While prior research often frames formalization as a binary economic choice or emphasizes government dominance in business–government relations, it underestimates entrepreneurs' agency in shaping their formality levels. There is limited understanding of how entrepreneurs strategically engage with enforcement officials to operate across a formality continuum. This study addresses the research questions: How do entrepreneurs decide their firm’s level of formality, and what strategic approaches do they use to engage with government officials responsible for regulatory enforcement? Drawing on qualitative data from Ethiopia, we analyze entrepreneurs’ interactions with officials using an inductive approach grounded in firm formalization and nonmarket strategy literatures. Our contribution lies in revealing how entrepreneurs actively shape their regulatory environment through strategic interaction, rather than passively responding to institutional pressures.

title: Strengthening Supervisor Bonds but Impairing Coworker Relations? The Divergent Effects of Voice Endorsement

entries.rq_with_context: Voice is essential for organizational improvement, yet research has largely focused on what leads supervisors to endorse employee suggestions rather than the consequences of such endorsement for the employees themselves. While endorsement is assumed to be beneficial, its emotional and relational effects on voicers remain unclear. This study investigates how voice endorsement influences both supportive voice toward supervisors and interpersonal conflict with coworkers, proposing divergent pathways through two forms of pride—authentic and hubristic—and examining the moderating role of narcissism. Drawing from appraisal theories of emotion, the authors test a model using multi-wave, multi-source data from a high-tech company. The study contributes by revealing that endorsement can simultaneously strengthen supervisor relationships and harm coworker relations depending on individual differences.

title: ‘Is it worth doing this or is it better to commit suicide?’: On ethical clearance at a university

entries.rq_with_context: The article investigates the ethical clearance (EC) process for social science research at a large university, focusing on how academics interpret and experience it. While EC is officially intended to uphold research ethics, existing literature suggests such systems often devolve into bureaucratic compliance rather than fostering ethical reflection. There is a gap in understanding how these processes are subjectively experienced and what meanings they generate among researchers. The research question is: what is the meaning and significance, from the point of view of people involved, of EC procedures in a university? The authors use a critical interpretive, reflexive case study approach based on interviews and observations. They argue that rather than promoting ethics, EC functions as a ritual of control that produces cynicism and undermines its own purpose.

title: Unlocking team performance: How shared mental models drive proactive problem-solving

entries.rq_with_context: Proactive problem-solving (PPS) is critical for organizational learning and continuous improvement, yet team-level factors that support it remain underexplored. While individual-level antecedents like job characteristics and leadership are well-documented, less is known about how team cognition—specifically shared mental models—affects PPS. Drawing on social identity theory, this study investigates whether shared taskwork and teamwork mental models promote PPS behaviors and coordination. Using multilevel path analysis with survey data from 266 individuals across 48 teams in manufacturing firms, the authors test how individual alignment with teammates’ mental models (individual level) and shared mental models (team level) influence PPS and team performance. The study contributes by linking shared cognition to proactivity and showing how team identity mechanisms facilitate both individual initiative and coordinated team problem-solving.

title: Living life ‘to the core’: Enacting a calling through configurations of multiple jobs

entries.rq_with_context: Many people believe they have a calling—a meaningful vocation they feel destined to pursue—but turning it into a career does not guarantee fulfillment. While prior research has examined calling sources, strength, and outcomes, it fails to explain the wide variation in how people enact their callings, especially through multiple jobs. This study addresses that gap by exploring how individuals’ self-determined conditions shape their enactment approaches. The research question is: how and why do people enact their callings in different ways, and how does that explain their experiences? Using qualitative interviews with 32 called individuals, we develop a core–periphery model grounded in calling conditions. The key contribution is revealing how conditionality, rather than passion alone, determines whether full-time or part-time enactment leads to meaningfulness.

title: Resisting by not resisting: Constructing inconsistencies to resist dual mandated changes

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often face multiple concurrent strategic changes, yet research has largely focused on single change initiatives. While we know that dual changes can interfere with each other—especially through perceived inconsistencies—the literature assumes these inconsistencies are passively detected rather than actively constructed. This paper addresses a critical gap: how such inconsistencies emerge and are used strategically in practice. The study investigates how employees in a Danish public school, facing two externally mandated changes—a working hour regulation and a school reform—progressively resist both by constructing discursive inconsistencies between them. It uses a longitudinal, practice-based case study to trace the processual dynamics of resistance. The authors propose that inconsistencies are not simply observed but deliberately built through specific practices over time. Their contribution lies in showing how resistance to mandated change can unfold stealthily by leveraging one change against the other, ultimately undermining the realization of both.

title: Place Iteration and Integration: How Digital Nomads Navigate the Mobile Worker Paradox

entries.rq_with_context: Digital nomads combine frequent geographic mobility with work, yet mobility typically undermines the sense of place needed for work effectiveness. This creates a paradox: mobility is essential to their lifestyle, but it threatens the stability required to perform well. While research suggests mobility and place are incompatible, digital nomads appear to resolve this tension, though how they do so remains unclear. This study examines how digital nomads navigate the mobile worker paradox—the conflict between needing mobility and needing place-based connections to work. Using a qualitative analysis of 73 interviews, we develop a model showing two distinct paths: place iteration and place integration. The key contribution is revealing how these workers reconcile mobility and place, challenging assumptions about their incompatibility and highlighting the role of individual differences like wanderlust.

title: Riding the Passion Wave or Fighting to Stay Afloat? A Theory of Differentiated Passion Contagion

entries.rq_with_context: Employees in high-passion teams are thought to benefit from the easy spread of passion, leading to improved performance and well-being. However, the observable and socially valued nature of passion may create informal norms and pressures for employees to feel more passionate, even when they don't naturally. This raises the question of whether the process of increasing one's passion through contagion—especially when driven by social expectations—comes at a psychological and relational cost. The authors propose a theory of differentiated passion contagion to distinguish between the benefits of feeling more passionate and the burdens of the effort required to get there. Using an experience-sampling study and a pre-registered experiment, they test whether passion contagion involves effortful regulation that offsets its advantages. The authors claim their work challenges the assumption that passion spreads costlessly and shifts understanding of when passion is beneficial versus detrimental.

title: Methodological Pluralism and Innovation in Data-Driven Organizations*

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly rely on data-driven innovation, but prior research presents a mixed view: while data analytics may boost firm-level sales, it may also suppress breakthrough innovations by favoring incremental, easily measurable improvements. This creates a theoretical tradeoff—data-driven processes may yield moderate successes but fewer high-impact hits. However, this perspective typically equates data-driven analysis solely with quantitative methods, overlooking the role of qualitative analysis. We argue that combining both methodologies may resolve this tradeoff. Our research question is: how does reliance on quantitative and qualitative analysis in an organization’s innovation process influence the commercial success of its new-product innovations? Drawing on a dataset of 3,,768 new-product launches from 55 consumer-packaged-goods firms and employee résumé data, we examine whether methodological pluralism—using both types of analysis substantially—leads to higher sales and more hits. Our findings show that neither method alone significantly affects sales, but together they have a complementary positive effect, especially on hit products and novelty.

title: A Little Help from My Friends? Navigating the Tension Between Social Capital and Meritocracy in the Job Search*

entries.rq_with_context: The job search is shaped by two conflicting cultural logics: social capital, which promotes using personal connections to find employment, and meritocracy, which emphasizes that jobs should be awarded based on qualifications rather than relationships. While prior research has shown the instrumental value of social ties in job finding, it does not explain how people reconcile the moral tension between benefiting from connections and upholding meritocratic principles. This study addresses that gap by exploring how young Spaniards justify or condemn the use of connections in their job searches. Drawing on interviews and a survey experiment, the authors identify a process they call 'situational alignment,' in which legitimacy is assessed based on whether the job seeker is qualified for the specific job and whether the help allowed for evaluation of suitability, such as through an interview. The key contribution is revealing a culturally embedded justification mechanism that allows people to embrace both logics simultaneously, while also perpetuating inequality.

title: Peer Influence in the Workplace: The Moderating Role of Task Structures Within Organizations*

entries.rq_with_context: Physicians’ decisions regarding delivery method—C-section versus vaginal—can have major health consequences, yet such decisions are influenced not only by medical factors but also by peers. While peer influence is recognized in organizational behavior, less is known about how formal organizational elements like task structures shape this influence. Existing research often treats formal structures and social dynamics separately, creating a gap in understanding how they interact. This study addresses that gap by investigating whether and how two features of task structure—task variety (the diversity of tasks a physician performs) and task similarity (the overlap between a physician’s tasks and those of peers)—moderate peer influence in a large sample of physicians across Brazilian hospitals. Using quasi-experimental variation in peer exposure, the authors employ regression models with rich controls to isolate peer effects. The study contributes by showing that peer influence in expert decision-making is not uniform but depends significantly on the formal configuration of work tasks.

title: Peer Response to Regulatory Enforcement: Lobbying by Non-Sanctioned Firms

entries.rq_with_context: Regulators rely on general deterrence—punishing one firm to encourage compliance by others—to enforce regulations under resource constraints. While existing research shows peer firms respond to sanctions with greater compliance, it is unknown whether they also engage in lobbying toward the sanctioning agency. This paper addresses that gap by asking: Do non-sanctioned peer firms increase their lobbying efforts targeting the regulator after a competitor is sanctioned? Using U.S. EPA violation data and a difference-in-differences design, the authors test this primary question and examine three motivational drivers. The study contributes by revealing a previously undocumented behavioral response—targeted lobbying—to general deterrence, expanding our understanding of firm responses beyond compliance.

title: Spoiled for Choice? When Work Flexibility Improves or Impairs Work–Life Outcomes

entries.rq_with_context: Work flexibility is widely seen as a resource that improves work-life balance, yet its benefits are inconsistent across employees. While existing research treats flexibility as uniformly positive, less attention has been paid to its potential drawbacks, such as decision fatigue or cognitive overload from managing increased discretion. This paper addresses the gap by exploring under what conditions flexibility enhances or undermines work-life outcomes. The authors propose that planning mediates the relationship between flexibility and outcomes like work-life balance effectiveness and exhaustion, with discontinuities (e.g., schedule instability or disruptions) and future temporal focus moderating this process. Using conservation of resources theory extended with dual-process models, they test a moderated mediation model across two studies with panel data. The key contribution is identifying boundary conditions under which flexibility helps or harms employees, shifting focus from organizational access to employee-level decision-making.

title: Narcissism at the CEO–TMT Interface: Measuring Executive Narcissism and Testing Its Effects on TMT Composition

entries.rq_with_context: Despite extensive research on CEO narcissism and its effects on firm outcomes, little is known about how CEO narcissism shapes the composition of the top management team (TMT), particularly through hiring and turnover. The interpersonal nature of narcissism suggests it may influence staffing decisions and team dynamics at the CEO–TMT interface, yet empirical research has been limited by a lack of measurement tools for non-CEO executives' narcissism. This paper addresses this gap by developing a novel measure of executive narcissism using LinkedIn profiles and testing three hypotheses. It asks: (1) Is CEO narcissism positively associated with the narcissism of newly hired TMT members? (2) Is CEO narcissism positively related to TMT turnover? (3) Does TMT narcissism moderate the effect of CEO narcissism on turnover? Using a large sample of S&P 1500 firms from 2015 to 2019, the authors employ instrumental variable and control function approaches to address endogeneity. Their key contribution is identifying CEO narcissism as a determinant of TMT composition and demonstrating interactive effects at the CEO–TMT interface.

title: More Than One Way to Pivot: The Case for Opportunity and Survival Pivots

entries.rq_with_context: Prior research characterizes entrepreneurial pivoting as a rapid and comprehensive strategic shift triggered by external opportunity-based information. However, this view may overlook important variation, particularly the role of internal threat-based signals and gradual change processes. The gap lies in the lack of theory explaining different pivot types and their triggers, especially survival-driven pivots not aligned with existing entrepreneurial learning perspectives. This study investigates whether there are distinct pivot types—specifically, those driven by opportunity versus survival motivations—and how they differ in process and antecedents. Using a two-study approach—first qualitative interviews, then an experimental vignette study with 1,945 entrepreneurs—it explores these variations. The key contribution is identifying two distinct pivot types and providing separate theoretical explanations: entrepreneurial learning for opportunity pivots and prospect theory for survival pivots.

title: Unraveling Mentors’ Positive and Negative Reactions to Protégés’ Taking Charge

entries.rq_with_context: Protégé proactivity, such as taking charge at work, is generally seen as beneficial for mentoring relationships. However, this research identifies a potential downside: when proactive protégés are perceived as less benevolent, mentors may feel threatened and react negatively. Existing studies have largely overlooked the adverse psychological responses mentors might experience when their protégés demonstrate high competence through proactive behaviors. This paper addresses that gap by investigating when and why mentors share or hide knowledge in response to taking-charge protégés. Drawing on social perception theory and envy subtypes theory, the authors propose a dual-path model where protégé benevolence determines whether mentors experience benign or malicious envy, which in turn affects knowledge sharing or hiding. The research uses two studies—one field survey with mentor–protégé dyads in China and one preregistered experiment in the U.S.—to test these predictions. The key contribution is uncovering the nuanced emotional mechanisms that explain divergent mentor reactions to proactive protégés.

title: Sharing the Spotlight: The Benefits of Having a Celebrity Competitor

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research has shown that high reputation and high status create stratified, negative outcomes for competitors, less is known about how celebrity—defined as audiences’ attention and positive emotive responses—affects those who compete with celebrities. Unlike reputation and status, celebrity is rooted in media narratives that generate excitement and emotional engagement. This paper identifies a gap in understanding how such narratives may extend benefits to secondary characters—noncelebrity competitors—through increased visibility and emotional resonance. The research question is: do noncelebrity competitors receive spillover benefits in media attention, emotive content, and earnings when they compete with a celebrity, and do these effects endure? Drawing on media routines and narrative theory, we test this using UFC fighter data over eight years. Our key contribution is demonstrating that celebrity generates positive spillovers for competitors in ways distinct from other social evaluations.

title: Type Diversity of Institutional Investors and Opportunistic Acquisitions

entries.rq_with_context: Institutional investors are known to influence firm strategic decisions, but research has largely overlooked how different types of institutional investors collectively affect these decisions. While prior work focuses on individual investor types, less is known about how diversity across legal types—such as pension funds, investment companies, and insurance firms—affects coordination and governance. This study investigates whether greater type diversity among institutional owners increases CEOs’ pursuit of opportunistic acquisitions by creating principal–principal conflicts that dilute collective monitoring. Using an entropy-based measure of legal type diversity and a sample of 2,106 U.S. firms, we analyze acquisition patterns linked to CEO stock sales post-announcement. Our approach draws on agency theory and social movement theory to explain how divergent investor interests hinder collective action. The study contributes by showing that diversity in investor legal types, not just ownership level, undermines governance effectiveness.

title: Interdependent Formation of Symbolic and Regulatory Boundaries: The Discursive Contestation Around the Home-Sharing Category

entries.rq_with_context: Category boundaries are crucial because they influence how products and producers are interpreted, valued, and regulated. While research has explored symbolic boundaries—how categories gain meaning—and regulatory boundaries—how laws demarcate markets—less is known about how symbolic distinctions translate into formal regulations.
