entries.rq_with_context: Work flexibility is commonly seen as a tool to reduce work–family conflict, but its effectiveness may depend on individual differences. Prior research shows that having both the ability and willingness to use flexible work arrangements helps reduce conflict, yet little is known about factors that might undermine this benefit. This study addresses the gap by introducing work flexibility-worry—the concern over negative evaluations or career penalties when using flexibility—as a key moderator. The research question is whether worry weakens the beneficial effect of willingness on the relationship between flexibility-ability and work–family conflict. Using a person–situation interaction framework, the study analyzes survey data from 924 Chinese employees through multivariate regression. It contributes by identifying conditions under which flexibility effectively reduces conflict, particularly highlighting the joint role of willingness and worry.

title: Linking leader humor to employee creativity: the roles of relational energy and traditionality

entries.rq_with_context: Leader humor has been shown to positively influence employee creativity, yet the mechanisms and boundary conditions of this relationship are not fully understood. While prior research has explored cognitive mediators like psychological capital, less attention has been paid to relational mechanisms grounded in resource dynamics. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether relational energy—a psychological resource gained through interactions with leaders—mediates the link between leader humor and employee creativity. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory, it further explores how employee traditionality, a cultural value emphasizing hierarchy and authority, shapes this process. Using data from employee–supervisor dyads in China, the study tests a moderated mediation model. It contributes by identifying relational energy as a key mediator and traditionality as a boundary condition, advancing understanding of when and how leader humor enhances creativity.

title: A resources gain perspective on family outcomes of proactive helping behavior

entries.rq_with_context: Employees’ daily work experiences can spill over into their family lives, yet most research on helping behavior has focused on its reactive forms and negative consequences, such as work-family conflict. This study addresses a gap by exploring the positive, distal effects of proactive helping behavior—voluntarily assisting others without being asked—on family relationship quality. Drawing on the work-home resources (W-HR) model, it investigates whether such behavior generates positive affect, which in turn promotes sharing of work experiences with spouses (work-family interpersonal capitalization), thereby enhancing family relationship quality. Using experience sampling data from 382 daily reports, multilevel modeling is applied to test these pathways. The study also examines independent self-construal as a boundary condition. The key contribution is identifying a positive ripple effect from proactive helping to family outcomes through an affective-behavioral mechanism and highlighting when this effect is stronger.

title: When does benevolent leadership inhibit silence? The joint moderating roles of perceived employee agreement and cultural value orientations

entries.rq_with_context: Employee silence—defined as the deliberate withholding of important information from leaders—is a widespread issue that can harm organizational functioning and employee well-being. While prior research highlights the role of supportive leadership in reducing silence, less attention has been paid to benevolent leadership, especially in Asian contexts where Confucian values emphasize benevolence. This study addresses this gap by examining whether benevolent leadership reduces employee silence, and under what conditions. Drawing on attribution theory and cultural values literature, the authors test whether perceived agreement among employees about their leader’s behaviors, along with individual power distance orientation and vertical individualism, moderate this relationship. The study contributes by identifying boundary conditions under which benevolent leadership is more or less effective in reducing silence.

title: The relationship between two dimensions of felt trust and promotive voice behaviour: the motivational mechanisms

entries.rq_with_context: Employees’ perceptions of being trusted (felt trust) may influence their willingness to speak up with suggestions (promotive voice behavior), but the underlying mechanisms and the distinct roles of felt trust dimensions remain unclear. Prior research has treated felt trust as unidimensional and focused more on trust than on felt trust, leaving gaps in understanding how and why employees engage in voice when they feel trusted. This study addresses this gap by differentiating between felt reliance (professional-based) and felt disclosure (relationally-based) and testing how they affect voice behavior through felt obligation and intrinsic motivation. Drawing on social exchange and self-determination theories, the authors use a two-wave survey of 269 employees and structural equation modeling to examine these mechanisms. The study contributes by clarifying the motivational pathways and showing that felt reliance, but not felt disclosure, directly promotes voice behavior.

title: Strengths use and work-related flow: an experience sampling study on implications for risk taking and attentional behaviors

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates how fluctuations in strengths use during daily work episodes relate to experiences of flow and subsequent behavioral outcomes. While prior research has connected strengths use and flow at a between-person level, less is known about within-person, momentary associations. Additionally, although flow is typically seen as beneficial, resource-based theories suggest it may deplete attention and energy, leading to potential downsides. This study addresses these gaps by testing whether episodic strengths use predicts flow, and whether flow is linked to risk taking and attentional performance using objective computerized tasks. The authors adopt an experience sampling method over five workdays with two daily assessments. Their main contribution is providing empirical evidence on the immediate behavioral consequences of flow at the micro-level.

title: More than just managerial self-efficacy: conceptualizing and predicting top managers' means efficacy about the organization under extreme events

entries.rq_with_context: Managers face growing environmental turbulence, including extreme events that test their ability to lead effectively. While past research emphasizes managerial self-efficacy—beliefs rooted in personal skills—this study highlights a gap in understanding external sources of efficacy, particularly the organization as a means to achieve goals. The authors argue that existing measures of 'managerial confidence' often conflate self-efficacy with beliefs about external supports. To address this, they introduce and test the concept of managerial means efficacy of the organization (MMEO). Using survey data from top U.S. transit agency managers, they examine how organizational slack, outsourcing, political fragmentation, and relationship management shape MMEO. The study contributes by distinguishing external from internal sources of managerial efficacy and identifying malleable organizational levers that influence it.

title: A dynamic process of different helping behavior: from the extended self-theory perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Helping behavior in organizations is typically categorized as proactive (self-initiated) or reactive (in response to requests), with most research focusing on their separate effects. While proactive helping is often seen as beneficial for helpers, reactive helping is frequently framed as depleting due to its imposed nature. However, this view overlooks the possibility that reactive helping might initiate a positive dynamic leading to future proactive behavior. This study addresses the gap by exploring whether and how reactive helping can lead to increased proactive helping over time. Drawing on extended self-theory, it proposes that responding to a request leads helpers to invest themselves in the task, expanding their sense of self to include it, which then motivates future proactive assistance. Using experience sampling data from 66 employees over ten days, the study tests a within-person mediated model. It contributes by showing how reactive helping may have underappreciated positive implications for the helper through self-investment.

title: How and when team reflexivity influences employee innovative behavior

entries.rq_with_context: Employee innovative behavior is critical for organizational survival and growth, yet the mechanisms linking team-level factors like team reflexivity to individual innovation remain underexplored. While prior research has linked team reflexivity to team-level outcomes, less is known about its cross-level influence on individual employees’ innovative behaviors, particularly through affective and attitudinal pathways. Drawing on affective events theory, this study explores how team reflexivity affects employee innovative behavior through the mediating roles of affective and normative commitment, and how benevolent leadership moderates these relationships. Using multilevel path analysis on survey data from 341 employees across 74 teams, the authors test a moderated mediation model. The study claims to extend understanding of the psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions through which team reflexivity fosters innovation at the individual level.

title: Hindering talented employees’ internal mobility: managers’ territorial response to stress

entries.rq_with_context: Managers may hinder talented employees' internal mobility due to psychological ownership, which creates a sense of possession over subordinates. While existing research links ownership to efforts preventing external mobility, less is known about its role in internal transfers. This study addresses the gap by testing whether managers’ psychological ownership of talent predicts use of persuasion and nurturing tactics to block internal moves. It further explores how job stress—defined as high role overload and low job social support—moderates these relationships. Using survey data from 116 managers, the study applies a time-lagged design and hierarchical regression to test hypotheses. The findings clarify boundary conditions under which ownership leads to hindering, extending theory on territoriality and talent management.

title: Is it my job? Leaders' family-supportive role perceptions

entries.rq_with_context: Despite extensive research on family-supportive supervisor behaviors (FSSB), it remains unclear whether supervisors view these actions as part of their formal job role or as discretionary, extra-role behaviors. This gap is critical because such perceptions may influence whether supervisors engage in FSSB. The study identifies a lack of research on individual-level, cognitive-motivational factors driving FSSB, particularly from the supervisor’s perspective. The research question is whether supervisors’ own work–family conflict and enrichment relate to their FSSB through their role perceptions (FSSB-RP), and whether reward systems moderate these relationships. The study uses role theory and a path analysis on survey data from 245 U.S. supervisors. It contributes by introducing FSSB-RP as a distinct construct and showing how personal and contextual factors shape these perceptions and behaviors.

title: Ethicality neutralization and amplification: a multilevel study of ethical leadership and unethical pro-organizational behavior

entries.rq_with_context: Ethical leadership (EL) is generally expected to reduce unethical behaviors, yet some studies suggest it may unintentionally increase unethical pro-organizational behavior (UPB), creating a paradox. This study addresses the gap in understanding why EL sometimes leads to UPB by distinguishing between individual-level EL (as a 'moral person') and group-level EL (as a 'moral manager'). The research question is: how do these two levels of EL differentially influence follower UPB willingness through distinct mechanisms? Using multilevel structural equation modeling on survey data from 423 Chinese employees across 81 groups, the study tests whether reciprocity beliefs mediate the individual-level effect and political climate mediates the group-level effect. The findings clarify the mixed results in prior literature by revealing dual pathways through which EL can either amplify or neutralize ethicality.

title: Health-oriented leadership as a job resource: can staff care buffer the effects of job demands on employee health and job satisfaction?

entries.rq_with_context: Job demands are known to impair employee health and satisfaction, and while leadership is recognized as a workplace resource, evidence for its buffering role is inconsistent. The job-demands resources (JD-R) and job demands-control-support (JDCS) models suggest that resources like leadership support can mitigate these negative effects, but empirical support is mixed, especially for health-specific outcomes. This study addresses the gap by focusing on staff care—a health-specific leadership behavior—within the health-oriented leadership (HoL) framework. The research asks whether staff care buffers the relationship between job demands and both health outcomes (strain, health complaints, general health) and job satisfaction. Using moderation analysis in two cross-sectional samples, it applies the JD-R and JDCS models to test this buffering effect. The study claims to clarify the inconsistent evidence on leadership’s protective role by using a more targeted, health-specific construct.

title: When does witnessing patient mistreatment hurt nurses' performance? Gauging the moderation roles of self-concern and other-orientation

entries.rq_with_context: Witnessing patient mistreatment is a common yet understudied stressor for nurses, with inconsistent findings on its impact compared to direct mistreatment. While existing research has focused on direct victims, less is known about how third-party nurses respond when observing colleagues being mistreated. This study addresses this gap by exploring emotional exhaustion as a key mechanism linking vicarious mistreatment to job performance. Grounded in stressor–strain appraisal theory, the authors propose that witnessing mistreatment leads to emotional exhaustion, which in turn reduces patient care behaviors and increases counterproductive work behaviors. The study further examines whether individual differences—specifically other-orientation and self-concern—moderate these relationships. The primary contribution is identifying other-orientation as a protective factor, showing that nurses high in other-orientation experience weaker negative effects when exposed to mistreatment.

title: The impact of support on employees' adaptive behavior: a moderated mediation model

entries.rq_with_context: Adaptive selling behavior is crucial in personal selling contexts where customer demands are diverse and unpredictable. While prior research has identified personal and job-related factors influencing adaptive behavior, less attention has been paid to intra-organizational support such as perceived organizational support (POS) and perceived supervisor support (PSS). This study addresses this gap by investigating how POS and PSS affect adaptive selling behavior through psychological empowerment, and whether customer orientation (CO) shapes these relationships. Drawing on social exchange theory, the authors propose a moderated mediation model tested with data from 200 Turkish salespeople. The study contributes by clarifying the psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions through which support influences adaptability in sales roles.

title: Passion in the pit: the effects of harmonious and obsessive passion on nurse burnout

entries.rq_with_context: Nurses have shown increased stress and burnout during the COVID-19 pandemic, yet many report high levels of passion for their work. While prior research has linked harmonious passion (HP) to positive outcomes and obsessive passion (OP) to mixed outcomes, few studies have examined how these forms of passion affect burnout through job stress, particularly using longitudinal data. There is also a need for more comprehensive measures of burnout beyond emotional exhaustion. This study addresses these gaps by testing a mediation model in which HP and OP indirectly affect disengagement and exhaustion through job stress, using data from nurses surveyed at three time points during the pandemic. The authors use Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and the Dualistic Model of Passion (DMP). Their main contribution is extending COR theory by conceptualizing both forms of passion as resources and offering a more complete model of burnout.

title: Driving for the unique opportunity for work: a qualitative study of nurses' motivation to commute to work

entries.rq_with_context: Nurses in rural regions face shortages and employment challenges, yet many choose to commute long distances to work in more urban healthcare settings. In Denmark, the region of Zealand experiences a significant net loss of nurses who commute to the capital region, exacerbating local staffing shortages. Despite existing theories on job motivation, there is limited qualitative understanding of why nurses make this choice, particularly from the perspective of motivation. This study addresses this gap by exploring the lived experiences of commuting nurses through semi-structured interviews. The research question is: what motivates rural nurses to commute to work in the capital region? The study uses a qualitative descriptive design with manifest and latent content analysis, framed by Herzberg’s Motivation–Hygiene Theory and Hackman and Oldham’s Job Characteristic Model. The key contribution is providing in-depth insight into how nurses perceive 'unique opportunities'—such as specialized roles, better management, and development possibilities—as central motivators, offering practical guidance for improving recruitment and retention in rural areas.

title: Gender, formal organizational status and humor use: perceptions of social acceptance

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace humor is recognized as a valuable managerial tool, yet research suggests it may be perceived differently based on the humorist’s gender. While humor can enhance leadership and relationships, women who use humor—especially assertive or targeted forms—may violate communal gender role expectations, leading to negative social evaluations. Prior studies show mixed findings: some indicate women using humor are seen as lower in status, while others suggest they gain leadership advantages with positive humor. A key gap is understanding how formal status and target gender condition these perceptions. This paper addresses that gap by exploring whether male and female humorists are judged differently when using aggressive or affiliative humor, depending on their status and the target’s gender. Using two scenario-based studies, the authors apply social role theory and expectancy violation theory to test their hypotheses. The study contributes by showing that audience perceptions of humorists are shaped by the intersection of gender, status, and target identity, revealing tighter behavioral constraints for women.

title: Interrupting the crossover effect of leader's role overload on employee's negative affect: the moderating role of self-concordance goal

entries.rq_with_context: The study explores how leaders' role overload may transmit to employees as negative affect, a phenomenon known as crossover. While prior research has established stress crossover from leaders to employees, direct empirical evidence linking leader role overload to employee negative affect remains limited, and little is known about boundary conditions. The study asks whether self-concordance goal—the degree to which employees pursue goals for autonomous rather than controlled reasons—buffers this effect. Drawing on self-determination theory, it uses a two-wave, paired survey of 51 leaders and 225 employees analyzed via cross-level modeling. The key contribution is identifying self-concordance goal as a moderating factor that can interrupt the negative emotional crossover from overburdened leaders to their subordinates.

title: Can you manage shocks? An investigation of career shocks on proactive career behavior: a COR theory perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Career shocks—unexpected positive or negative events outside an individual’s control—are increasingly relevant in modern career development, yet their relationship with proactive career behavior (PCB) remains underexplored. While prior research focuses on career planning and self-management, little is known about how employees respond to shocks, especially in high-pressure sectors like banking. This study addresses this gap by examining how career shocks directly and indirectly influence PCB through personal resources. Using COR theory, the authors propose that shocks either deplete or accumulate personal resources, which in turn affect proactive career efforts. The research tests this model empirically with a sample of 322 Pakistani banking employees. The primary contribution is establishing, for the first time, the mediating role of personal resources in connecting career shocks to proactive career behavior.

title: Non-work-related instant messaging in the workplace and daily task performance: complementarity between social and cognitive resources

entries.rq_with_context: Smartphones enable frequent non-work-related instant messaging (IM) during work hours, which may distract employees and impair task performance. While prior research emphasizes the distracting, resource-depleting effects of such behavior, this study addresses the gap by considering its potential social benefits. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory and positive spillover, the authors explore whether social support from personal contacts can offset the cognitive costs of non-work-related IM. Using experience sampling data from 75 employees over 10 workdays, they test a moderated mediation model. The key contribution is demonstrating that social support buffers the indirect negative effect of non-work-related IM on daily task performance through cognitive engagement.

title: Deep-level dissimilarity and leader–member exchange (LMX) quality: the role of status

entries.rq_with_context: Perceived dissimilarity in work-related attitudes and perspectives—referred to as deep-level dissimilarity—has been found to negatively affect the quality of leader–member exchange (LMX) relationships. However, existing research has largely overlooked how status influences this relationship. This study addresses a gap by examining whether the negative impact of deep-level dissimilarity on LMX quality depends on the demographic or positional status of the LMX partner. The authors test whether lower-status individuals (e.g., African-American women or organizational members) suffer a disproportionately negative effect when dissimilar to their leader. Using data from three studies and applying hierarchical linear regression and mixed-effects models, the research explores this moderating role. The study contributes by distinguishing between two types of status and analyzing their effects at the societal rather than relative level, offering new insight into when and for whom attitude dissimilarity harms LMX quality.

title: Why and when are silent employees less satisfied with their jobs? A conservation of resources perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Employee silence is a common workplace behavior that harms job satisfaction, but the underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions are poorly understood. Existing research confirms a negative relationship between silence and satisfaction, but lacks theoretical explanation of how this occurs or under what conditions it may be weaker. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory, this study investigates whether silence undermines satisfaction by depleting employees' vigor—an intrinsic energy resource. Using a time-lagged survey of 183 employees in Taiwan, the authors test a moderated mediation model. They find that vigor mediates the negative effect of silence on satisfaction, but only for employees with low positive affectivity. The study contributes by identifying vigor as a mechanism and positive affectivity as a buffer in the silence–satisfaction relationship.

title: When does presenteeism harm productivity the most? Employee motives as a key moderator of the presenteeism–productivity relationship

entries.rq_with_context: Presenteeism—attending work while unwell—is generally linked to lower productivity, especially among employees with chronic health conditions. However, existing research has overlooked how the reasons for presenteeism might influence this relationship. This study addresses that gap by investigating whether motives (approach or avoidance) alter the degree to which presenteeism harms productivity. Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory, the authors propose that approach motives may reduce productivity loss, while avoidance motives may worsen it. Using survey data from 327 dental hygienists with chronic illnesses, they test these moderating effects through moderated multiple regression. The study's contribution lies in showing that presenteeism is not uniformly harmful—motives matter in determining its productivity outcomes.

title: Challenge-hindrance stressors and career initiative: a moderated mediation model

entries.rq_with_context: With changing career patterns shifting responsibility for career development to individuals, understanding what drives employees to take career initiative is important. While prior research has examined personal and situational antecedents, little attention has been paid to how different types of job stressors—challenge versus hindrance—affect such proactive behavior. This study addresses this gap by exploring whether challenge stressors promote and hindrance stressors inhibit career initiative through employees’ positive affect. Using affective events theory and situational strength theory, the authors propose a moderated mediation model tested with two-wave survey data from 136 part-time MBA students. The key contribution is identifying positive affect as a mediating mechanism and job autonomy as a boundary condition in the stressor–career initiative relationship.

title: Above and beyond: helping behaviors among nurses in positive and negative reciprocity relationships

entries.rq_with_context: The study explores helping behaviors among nurses during the high-stress context of the COVID-19 pandemic, where resources are depleted and burnout is prevalent. Existing research suggests that social exchange theory (SET) and reciprocity norms predict helping, but it is unclear whether these norms hold when relationships cannot be terminated and stress is high. The paper investigates whether nurses still help despite low reciprocity, and what factors—such as perceived coworker efficacy or stress—better predict helping behaviors. Using a social exchange framework and random coefficient modeling on data from 155 nurses, the authors test how reciprocity, coworker efficacy, and stress relate to both person-focused and task-focused helping. The study contributes by showing that reciprocity norms may be suppressed in interdependent, high-pressure settings, and that perceptions of coworker ability matter more than reciprocal exchange.

title: Job experience as a buffer against incivility: a daily diary study

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace incivility is prevalent in healthcare and linked to negative employee outcomes, yet little is known about the mechanisms through which it operates or how job experience might protect workers. While prior research connects incivility to poor well-being, this study addresses gaps by examining sleep quality as a mediating mechanism and job tenure as a potential buffer. It also investigates inconsistencies in how incivility from different sources affects nurses. Using a daily diary design with 92 nurses, the study applies self-regulation and emotion regulation theories to test these relationships. The key contribution is identifying tenure and source-specific incivility as critical factors shaping the impact of workplace mistreatment on emotional and physiological outcomes.

title: Differential effects of rude coworkers and patients on nurses' safety performance: an emotional labor perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace incivility is a pervasive issue in healthcare, affecting nurses’ well-being and performance. While prior research has linked incivility to negative outcomes, little is known about how incivility from different sources—coworkers and patients—affects nurses’ safety behaviors. This study addresses that gap by exploring the differential impact of coworker and patient incivility on emotional labor (surface and deep acting), which may affect safety compliance and participation. Using a three-week longitudinal design with 187 nurses, the authors apply an emotional labor and ego-depletion framework to test these pathways. The key contribution is demonstrating that incivility from different sources triggers distinct emotional labor processes, with implications for nursing safety.

title: Losing compassion for patients? The implications of COVID-19 on compassion fatigue and event-related post-traumatic stress disorder in nurses

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates how the psychological impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on nurses leads to compassion fatigue and PTSD, focusing on the roles of perceived novelty, disruptiveness, and criticality of pandemic-related events. While existing research has documented high levels of psychological distress among nurses during the pandemic, it has largely overlooked the underlying psychological processes that link event characteristics to mental health outcomes. This paper addresses that gap by using event system theory (EST) to model how specific features of the pandemic trigger compassion fatigue, which then contributes to PTSD. The authors test a mediated model using survey data from 175 nurses collected during October and November 2020. Their main contribution is in extending EST by identifying compassion fatigue as a key mechanism linking strong events to adverse psychological outcomes in a high-stress caregiving context.

title: The impact of authoritarian leadership on employee creativity: the joint moderating roles of benevolent leadership and power distance

entries.rq_with_context: Authoritarian leadership, common in East Asia, has been linked to lower employee creativity, but findings are inconsistent and mechanisms unclear. While prior research has examined social exchange and stress-based mediators like fear and leader-member exchange, cognitive pathways such as self-concept remain underexplored. This study fills that gap by proposing creative self-efficacy as a mediating mechanism. Drawing on cultural self-representation theory, it examines how authoritarian leadership undermines employee creative self-efficacy, which in turn reduces creativity. It further tests whether benevolent leadership strengthens this negative effect due to psychological inconsistency and whether power distance conditions this moderation. The study uses survey data from 325 employees in Chinese firms and hierarchical regression analysis, claiming to offer new insight into the cognitive process and contingent effects of authoritarian leadership.

title: Gamifying an assessment method: what signals are organizations sending to applicants?

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly use gamified assessments in recruitment to attract talent, but little is known about how these methods shape applicant perceptions. While prior research shows gamification improves applicant reactions, the underlying mechanisms—particularly how applicants interpret the experience as a signal about the organization—are unclear. This study investigates whether the perceived enjoyment and flow from a gamified assessment lead applicants to infer an organization’s symbolic traits (innovativeness and competence), which then affect organizational attractiveness. Drawing on signaling theory, the authors test a mediated model using both a longitudinal study and an experimental design. The contribution lies in identifying the signaling mechanism through which gamified assessments influence employer image.

title: Resurrecting the evil genius: examining the relationship between unethical behavior and perceived competence

entries.rq_with_context: Prior research suggests unethical behavior lowers perceptions of competence, based on the stereotype content model (SCM) which links immoral actions to low trait warmth and, by extension, low competence. However, this link may not always hold, as the SCM treats warmth and competence as independent dimensions. The authors identify a gap in understanding when and why unethical behavior does not diminish perceived competence. They propose that act complexity—a dimension not previously examined—moderates this relationship. Using experimental scenarios, they test whether complex unethical behaviors (e.g., hacking) are perceived as indicators of competence unlike simple ones. Their contribution lies in identifying act complexity as a boundary condition that challenges the assumed negative link between unethicality and competence.

title: Daily supervisor support, engagement and prosocial behavior: how turnover intentions reduce the resources to pay it forward

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates how daily fluctuations in perceived supervisor support (PSS) relate to employees' job engagement and extra-role behaviors, specifically organizational citizenship behaviors (OCB). While prior research has established links between PSS, engagement, and OCB using static measures, this study addresses a gap by exploring within-person, day-to-day dynamics. The authors further examine how turnover intentions (TI) may act as a boundary condition, potentially weakening the motivational path from daily PSS to engagement and thus limiting citizenship behavior. Using conservation of resources (COR) and relational cohesion theories, the study employs a two-study design—daily surveys (Study 1) and a scenario experiment (Study 2)—to test these dynamic relationships. The key contribution is demonstrating that the positive, resource-based motivational process from daily support to engagement and OCB is significantly weaker when employees have high turnover intentions.

title: How leaders benefit from engaging in high-quality leader-member exchanges: a daily diary study

entries.rq_with_context: Leaders play a critical role in organizational functioning, yet research has predominantly focused on how leadership affects employee well-being rather than leaders' own well-being. While prior studies link leadership behaviors to leader outcomes, there is limited understanding of how leader-member exchange (LMX) behaviors—relationship-oriented actions aimed at building trust and mutual obligation—contribute to leaders’ daily job-related well-being. Drawing from conservation of resources (COR) theory and the success resource model (SRM), this study investigates whether engaging in LMX behaviors generates positive affect and perceived competence, which in turn enhance job satisfaction and psychological detachment. Using a daily diary design with 85 leaders over five workdays, multilevel path analyses were employed to separate within- and between-person effects. The authors aim to demonstrate that leaders benefit personally from high-quality exchanges with followers, contributing to a resource-gain spiral that supports their well-being.

title: Beliefs about job-seeking strategies: dimensionality, measurement and outcomes

entries.rq_with_context: Job-seekers vary in which strategies they use, and this study addresses what drives motivation for one strategy over another by focusing on job-seekers’ beliefs about strategies. While prior research has examined beliefs related to specific strategies (e.g., networking or internet job boards), less attention has been paid to beliefs that generalize across multiple strategies. This study identifies a set of salient, cross-strategy beliefs through focus groups, develops and validates a measure of these beliefs, and examines their relationships to strategy-specific motivation and behavior. Using data from three samples of job-seekers and an inductive approach guided by Ajzen (1991), the authors test for the factor structure, generalizability, and predictive validity of these beliefs. The key contribution is the first validated multidimensional measure of strategy beliefs generalizable across recruitment sources and the identification of specific beliefs most strongly linked to job-seeking motivation.

title: Trait affectivity and applicant reactions: a multiwave field study

entries.rq_with_context: Applicant reactions to selection procedures are shaped by perceptions of procedural justice, which have traditionally been explained through cognitive information processing models. However, gaps exist in understanding how dispositional affect—specifically trait positive affectivity (TPA) and trait negative affectivity (TNA)—influences these reactions. While organizational justice theory increasingly recognizes affective influences, few studies have tested how TPA and TNA impact justice perceptions and behavioral intentions in real hiring contexts. This study addresses this gap by investigating the role of TPA and TNA in shaping procedural justice perceptions and recommendation intentions across pre- and post-feedback stages in a field sample of police applicants. Using a three-wave design and affective justice theory, it tests whether these traits predict reactions and whether justice perceptions mediate the relationship. The findings contribute by integrating trait affectivity into applicant reactions research and clarifying its boundary conditions.

title: The intersectional effect of age and gender on the work–life balance of managers

entries.rq_with_context: Despite recognition of managerial role complexity, little research explores how age and gender jointly shape managers' work–life balance. Existing studies often overlook the intersectional effects of role identities, even though managerial expectations interact with life course shifts that differ for men and women. This study addresses this gap by testing whether age has a non-linear effect on work–life balance and whether this effect is moderated by gender. Drawing on social role theory and a gendered life course perspective, the authors use regression analysis with interaction terms on a sample of 421 U.S. managers. The study claims to offer one of the first empirical tests of non-linear intersectional effects of age and gender on managerial work–life balance.

title: How shared leadership affects team performance: examining sequential mediation model using MASEM

entries.rq_with_context: Shared leadership has been shown to positively affect team performance, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Prior research has largely examined single mediators—either team emergent states (like trust) or team processes (like learning)—but has not integrated both or considered their interrelationships. This study addresses the gap by proposing a sequential mediation model in which shared leadership enhances team trust (an emergent state), which in turn promotes team learning behavior (a process), ultimately improving team performance. Using meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) across 288 studies (N = 21,888 groups), the study tests this comprehensive pathway. The key contribution is revealing the sequential mediating role of team trust and team learning behavior, thereby advancing understanding of how shared leadership translates into performance through interconnected mechanisms.

title: Caring for yourself and for others: team health climate and self-care explain the relationship between health-oriented leadership and exhaustion

entries.rq_with_context: Health-oriented leadership is known to support employee well-being, but the underlying mechanisms are unclear. While prior research suggests self-care as a mediator, less is known about how team-level factors like team health climate contribute. This study addresses this gap by investigating both individual self-care and team health climate as mediators between health-oriented leadership and employee exhaustion. Using a time-lagged design with three measurement points, the authors test these mechanisms over time. The study contributes by identifying dual mediating pathways, emphasizing the role of team context alongside individual behavior.

title: Decent work and employee performance: a conservation of resources perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing interest in decent work (DW), little research has explored its impact on employee performance, particularly in organizational behavior contexts. While prior studies link DW to well-being and motivation, none have examined its effects on in-role performance (IRP) and organizational citizenship behavior toward the organization (OCBO). This study fills that gap by drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory to investigate whether career satisfaction (CS) mediates the relationship between DW and both types of performance, and whether supervisor ostracism (SO) moderates this process. Using two-wave survey data from 376 Chinese employees, the study tests a moderated mediation model. The findings contribute to DW research by demonstrating performance-related outcomes and identifying boundary conditions.

title: Understanding awe elicitors in the workplace: a qualitative inquiry

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the positive effects of awe on prosocial behavior, decision-making, and well-being, organizational research has largely overlooked awe, especially in workplace contexts. There is limited understanding of whether employees experience awe at work and what specifically might elicit this emotion in professional environments. This gap is particularly pronounced in cross-cultural research, where emotional experiences may differ due to cultural norms and values. To address this, the study explores the elicitors of awe at work through qualitative responses from 163 participants in the USA and Canada and 126 participants in China. Using grounded theory, the authors identify and compare awe-triggering experiences across these two cultural clusters. The research contributes by empirically identifying workplace-specific awe elicitors and highlighting both universal and culturally distinct sources of awe.

title: Double-edged sword of perceived mastery climate on evasive knowledge hiding: the mediating roles of perceived status and perceived social support

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses whether employees always disengage from knowledge hiding in a mastery climate, a question not fully answered in existing research. While prior studies suggest mastery climate reduces knowledge hiding, contradictory evidence shows employees may still hoard knowledge despite cooperative climates. This creates a gap in understanding the dual mechanisms through which mastery climate may simultaneously encourage and discourage evasive knowledge hiding. The research question is: how does perceived mastery climate influence evasive knowledge hiding through perceived status and perceived social support? Drawing on social exchange theory and social cognitive theory, the study proposes a dual-path model. The key contribution is revealing the paradoxical role of mastery climate by identifying two opposing mediating mechanisms and the moderating role of procedural justice.

title: Effect of workplace ostracism on employee initiative behaviour: a chained double mediation model

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace ostracism is a common negative work experience that may hinder employee initiative behaviour, which refers to self-starting actions that improve work conditions. While research has explored positive work factors that promote initiative, less attention has been paid to negative contextual factors like ostracism, especially in the Chinese organizational context where relational harmony is culturally significant. This study addresses the gap by investigating how ostracism undermines initiative through cognitive and affective mechanisms. Using cognitive appraisal theory, it proposes that ostracism reduces organisational identity (a cognitive response) and work well-being (an emotional response), which in turn reduce initiative. The key contribution is identifying a chained double mediation model that explains the psychological process linking a negative work event to reduced proactive behaviour.

title: Curvilinear relationship between ambidextrous leadership and employee silence: mediating effects of role stress and relational energy

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses inconsistent findings about ambidextrous leadership’s effects, which has been shown to both encourage and suppress employee voice or silence. While previous research typically assumed positive linear effects, recent studies suggest potential downsides, including increased cognitive strain and role stress. However, empirical evidence for a curvilinear (U-shaped) relationship remains scarce. This paper fills that gap by testing whether ambidextrous leadership first reduces, then increases employee silence at high levels. Using job demands-resources and social contagion theories, the authors propose and test a model where role stress and relational energy serve as mediating mechanisms, and power distance orientation as a moderator. The contribution lies in providing empirical support for the nonlinear influence of ambidextrous leadership on employee silence and uncovering dual cognitive-affective pathways.

title: Believe to achieve? Understanding how social class background impacts the effects of achievement striving on propensity to negotiate

entries.rq_with_context: Negotiation is critical for career success, yet individuals from lower social class backgrounds (SCBs) may be less likely to negotiate despite having strong achievement goals. While achievement striving is generally linked to proactive career behaviors, the authors argue that SCB shapes whether this motivation leads to negotiation. They identify a gap in understanding how structural factors like SCB condition the effectiveness of individual motivation. Drawing on social expectancy and self-regulation theories, the research asks: how does SCB moderate the effect of achievement striving on negotiation propensity via status-based identity uncertainty? The study uses a three-wave survey design with 460 U.S. participants to test this moderated mediation model. The authors claim the study reveals a mechanism through which economic inequality is reproduced in organizations.

title: Investigating the effects of high-involvement climate and public service motivation on engagement, performance, and meaningfulness in the public sector

entries.rq_with_context: Despite high levels of disengagement among public sector employees, much of the engagement research originates from the private sector and may not apply directly to public service contexts. Existing research has linked public service motivation to engagement, but little is known about how this translates into job performance and meaningfulness, or how contextual factors like high-involvement climate contribute. This study addresses these gaps by investigating whether public service motivation and high-involvement climate are associated with performance and meaningfulness through their impact on employee engagement. Using self-determination theory as a framework, the authors propose a mediated model tested with multi-source data across five days. The key contribution is demonstrating that both individual (public service motivation) and contextual (high-involvement climate) antecedents influence outcomes through engagement in a public sector setting.

title: The dark side of leave: how voluntary leave shapes preferences for male and female supervisors

entries.rq_with_context: Voluntary leave, such as community service or parental leave, is increasingly common in organizations and generally linked to positive outcomes. However, little is known about how taking such leave affects perceptions of supervisors, especially based on gender. Drawing on role congruity theory, the authors identify a gap in understanding how communal behaviors—like community service—may negatively affect men, who are expected to display agentic traits. The research asks whether community service leave reduces supervisor preference, particularly for male supervisors, due to perceived atypicality. Using experimental designs across two studies, the authors test this moderated mediation model. Their key contribution is revealing a previously understudied bias against men taking community service leave and showing that a simple informational intervention can reduce this bias.

title: What can I do for you? Line managers’ behaviors to support return to work for workers with common mental disorders

entries.rq_with_context: Sustainable return to work (RTW) remains challenging for workers returning after long-term sick leave due to common mental disorders (CMDs) such as stress, anxiety, and depression. While line managers play a key role in supporting these workers, little research has focused on their behaviors during the sustainable phase of RTW—after re-entry—where workers need ongoing support to prevent relapse. Existing studies have primarily examined earlier RTW phases and often overlooked line managers’ own perceptions of what enables or hinders their support. The study addresses this gap by exploring line managers’ supportive behaviors and the factors influencing them through longitudinal qualitative interviews. Using reflexive thematic analysis, the authors identify five key strategies and examine contextual influences. The contribution lies in being the first UK study to explicitly identify line manager behaviors in the sustainable phase and the individual and organizational factors shaping them.

title: Impact of supervisor developmental feedback on employee innovative behavior: roles of psychological safety and face orientation

entries.rq_with_context: Employee innovative behavior is critical for organizational competitiveness, yet the mechanisms through which leadership behaviors like feedback influence innovation remain unclear. While prior research has focused on leadership styles, this study addresses a gap by examining supervisor developmental feedback—an understudied but potentially important driver of innovation. It explores how psychological safety may transmit the effect of such feedback and how employees' face orientation (desire to gain face or fear of losing face) may condition this process, particularly in a high-context, collectivist culture like China. Drawing on social cognitive theory, the authors propose a moderated mediation model. The study’s contribution lies in identifying psychological safety as a key mechanism and differentiating between two culturally relevant aspects of face orientation as boundary conditions, thereby clarifying inconsistent findings in prior feedback research.

title: The effect of alcohol consumption on workplace aggression: What's love (and job insecurity) got to do with it?

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace aggression is a critical issue, and while alcohol use has been linked to aggression, its specific impact during work hours remains understudied. Prior research often focuses on general or post-work drinking, missing the proximal effects of in-work drinking, and overlooks how psychosocial factors might condition this relationship. This study addresses the gap by testing whether job insecurity and love of one’s job jointly moderate the alcohol-aggression link. Using a time-lagged survey of 325 employees, the authors analyze how these emotional states shape the drinking-aggression relationship. They find that alcohol use at work increases aggression, especially when employees both love their job and fear losing it. The contribution lies in identifying a high-risk psychological context—fearing the loss of a beloved job—that amplifies the effects of drinking on aggression.

title: Linking self-efficacy and organizational identification: a moderated mediation model based on a self-verification perspective

entries.rq_with_context: The paper explores how employees' self-efficacy, a dispositional trait reflecting confidence in personal capabilities, influences their identification with the organization. While prior research has focused on relational or collective factors as antecedents of organizational identification, less is known about how self-focused characteristics like self-efficacy contribute. The authors identify a gap in understanding the mechanisms and boundary conditions linking self-efficacy to organizational identification. Drawing on self-verification theory, they propose that employees with high self-efficacy engage in downward LMX social comparison to affirm their positive self-views, which in turn enhances organizational identification. They test a moderated mediation model using data from a field survey and a scenario-based experiment. The study contributes by revealing how and when self-efficacy leads to organizational identification through self-verification processes.

title: Leader failed humor and follower advice seeking

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research highlights the benefits of leader humor, less is known about what happens when leaders' attempts at humor fail despite benign intentions. The audience's evaluation of humor—whether it is perceived as successful or not—remains underexplored, especially its interpersonal consequences. This study addresses this gap by asking how follower perception of leader failed humor influences follower advice seeking. Drawing on benign violation theory, it proposes that failed humor reduces follower liking, which in turn decreases advice seeking, particularly when leaders and followers interact infrequently. Using a multimethod approach with two studies—one field study and one experiment—the research tests this moderated mediation model. The study contributes by introducing the concept of leader failed humor and revealing its negative downstream effects on follower behavior.

title: Working in times of COVID-19: investigating the effect of daily risk perception of COVID-19 infection on goal progress

entries.rq_with_context: The high transmission of COVID-19 has introduced unpredictable task setbacks that disrupt employees’ daily work goals, creating new stressors beyond health concerns. While prior research has focused on health-related anxiety during the pandemic, less is known about task-related anxiety and its effects on workplace outcomes. This study addresses that gap by exploring how perceived risk of infection leads to anxiety about task disruptions, which in turn affects daily goal progress. Drawing on the transactional theory of stress and coping, the authors argue that such anxiety may prompt problem-focused coping behaviors that enhance goal attainment. Using a daily diary design with multilevel analysis, the study further tests how individual conscientiousness and supervisor bottom-line mentality moderate these processes. The authors claim to advance understanding of stress appraisal and coping in the workplace during crises.

title: Occupational self-efficacy, job crafting and job satisfaction in newcomer socialization: a moderated mediation model

entries.rq_with_context: Newcomers often face misfit with their new jobs, and job crafting—proactively changing task, relational, and cognitive aspects of work—may help them adjust. While occupational self-efficacy (OSE) is known to relate to job satisfaction, the behavioral mechanisms, especially different forms of job crafting, remain unclear. This study addresses that gap by testing whether job crafting mediates the OSE–satisfaction link among newcomer media professionals in China. Drawing on social cognitive theory and job crafting theory, it also explores how hierarchical organizational culture shapes these relationships. Using a four-wave longitudinal design, the study tests a moderated mediation model. It claims to advance understanding by identifying cognitive crafting as a key mediator and revealing the conditional role of culture.

title: Energizing and depleting? The daily effects of organizationally focused citizenship behaviors

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational citizenship behaviors (OCB) benefit organizations, but their daily effects on employees—especially different types of organizationally focused OCB (OCBO)—are not well understood. Prior research has largely focused on helping behaviors or challenging behaviors like voice, leaving supportive OCBO such as advocacy participation understudied. It is also unclear how these behaviors affect employees through mechanisms like prosocial impact and ego depletion. This study addresses this gap by examining daily advocacy participation and voice using a dual-pathway model of proactivity. It tests whether these behaviors differentially influence job satisfaction and job stress through prosocial impact (energizing pathway) and ego depletion (depleting pathway). The study uses a daily-diary design with experience sampling to model within-person processes. The authors claim the study contributes by revealing distinct psychological mechanisms through which supportive and challenging OCBO affect employees on a daily basis.

title: Thinking of how you think of me: working cancer survivors' metaperceptions of competence and why they matter

entries.rq_with_context: Working cancer survivors often face 'Big C' stigma, including being perceived as low in competence, which can harm their employment outcomes. While research has documented discrimination against cancer survivors, less is known about how survivors internalize these perceptions and how such internalization affects their work attitudes and well-being. This study investigates how survivors’ competence metaperceptions—whether they believe others see them as competent—relate to turnover intentions and vigor at work. Drawing on the looking glass self and social cognitive theory, the authors propose that these metaperceptions influence outcomes via self-efficacy, with the need for emotional support as a boundary condition. The study uses survey data from 200 working survivors and a student vignette experiment. It contributes by showing how internalized stereotypes affect work motivation and highlighting self-efficacy as a psychological mechanism.

title: Political self-efficacy matters: an investigation of how and when leader political mentoring affects follower political behavior and promotability

entries.rq_with_context: Employees' career success often depends on their engagement in organizational politics, yet it remains unclear what situational factors drive political behavior while yielding positive outcomes like promotability. While mentoring has been linked to career advancement, little is known about how a specific form—leader political mentoring—affects followers' political actions and career prospects. This research addresses this gap by proposing political self-efficacy as a key motivational mechanism. Drawing on social cognitive theory, the study tests whether political mentoring enhances political self-efficacy, which in turn increases political behavior and promotability. The model further considers positive political perception as a boundary condition. The contribution lies in identifying a novel construct and clarifying the process and conditions under which political mentoring leads to constructive outcomes.

title: Co-worker undermining, emotional exhaustion and organisational commitment: the moderating role of servant leadership

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace mistreatment, particularly co-worker undermining, negatively impacts employee well-being and attitudes, yet little is known about the conditions under which these effects may be reduced. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether servant leadership can mitigate the negative consequences of co-worker undermining. Drawing on expectancy violation theory (EVT), the authors propose that servant leadership—by fulfilling employees’ expectations of supportive leadership—can buffer the relationship between co-worker undermining and emotional exhaustion, thereby preserving organisational commitment. Using two-wave, time-lagged data from 345 nurses in Malaysia and multilevel structural equation modelling, the study tests these relationships while controlling for transformational leadership. The key contribution is identifying servant leadership as a boundary condition that weakens the indirect link between co-worker undermining and organisational commitment via emotional exhaustion.

title: Engaging age-diverse workers with autonomy and feedback: the role of task variety

entries.rq_with_context: The aging workforce in developed countries calls for better understanding of how job design affects work engagement across age groups. While autonomy and feedback are known to enhance engagement, their effects on older versus younger workers remain unclear, with prior studies showing mixed results. This paper addresses the gap by exploring how task variety conditions the relationships between autonomy and engagement, and feedback and engagement, for different age groups. Drawing on socioemotional selectivity theory (SST) and selective optimization with compensation theory (SOC), the authors propose that these relationships depend on both age and task variety. Using a two-wave survey of 372 age-diverse employees, the study tests moderated moderation models. The authors claim their work advances lifespan perspectives on job design by identifying task variety as a key boundary condition shaping age-related differences in engagement.

title: Doing good or looking good: how socially responsible human resource management practices influence employees' CSR-specific performance

entries.rq_with_context: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has become essential for organizations, and employees play a central role in its success. However, little research has examined how to improve employees' CSR-specific performance—specifically their in-role and extra-role behaviors. While socially responsible human resource management (SRHRM) practices are increasingly adopted, their social impact remains understudied. This paper addresses this gap by exploring how SRHRM affects employees’ CSR performance through impression management and prosocial motivation, and how these processes depend on moral identity. Drawing on the multiple needs model of organizational justice and moral identity theory, the study uses survey data from 422 employees across 68 companies. It contributes by revealing the dual motivational mechanisms and boundary conditions through which SRHRM enhances employees' CSR performance.

title: Impact of leader aggressive humor on employee extra-role behaviors: opposite moderating effects of team identification and professional identification

entries.rq_with_context: Leader aggressive humor, defined as teasing or mocking subordinates to assert superiority, may harm employee extra-role behaviors such as proactivity and creativity. While prior research links this humor style to employee silence and reduced voice, less is known about its impact on proactive and creative behaviors. This study addresses that gap by testing feeling ostracized as a key psychological mechanism through which aggressive humor impairs these behaviors. Grounded in sociometer theory, it proposes that aggressive humor signals rejection, triggering ostracism and reducing risk-taking behaviors. Additionally, the study explores how team identification (amplifying the effect) and professional identification (attenuating it) condition this process. The authors claim the study extends understanding by identifying a novel mediating pathway and contrasting boundary conditions.

title: Using necessary condition analysis in managerial psychology research: introduction, empirical demonstration and methodological discussion

entries.rq_with_context: Managerial psychology research often expresses necessity statements—for example, that certain conditions are critical prerequisites for desired outcomes—but continues to rely on statistical methods that test sufficiency rather than necessity. This creates a theory-method mismatch, as traditional regression techniques cannot properly test whether a condition is necessary. The authors address this gap by introducing necessary condition analysis (NCA), a method designed to detect necessity relationships. Using a re-analysis of survey data from 506 Lithuanian soldiers, the study applies NCA to test whether autonomy, competence, and relatedness are necessary for work engagement, drawing on self-determination theory. The approach allows the authors to examine if low levels of any of these needs constrain high work engagement. The study’s contribution lies in demonstrating how NCA can empirically validate necessity claims that are theoretically implied but previously untested in the literature.

title: Avoiding the scenario of “The farmer and the snake”: the dark side of servant leadership and an intervention mechanism

entries.rq_with_context: Servant leadership is generally seen as beneficial, promoting positive follower attitudes and behaviors. However, this study questions whether such leadership can backfire when followers have negative traits like Machiavellianism, which may lead them to exploit their leaders' generosity. Existing research has overlooked how such dispositions might turn servant leadership into a source of psychological entitlement and deviance. The study addresses this gap by exploring whether high-Mach followers respond to servant leadership with entitled attitudes and harmful behaviors. Using self-evaluation theory and a three-wave survey of 344 employees, the research tests how leader negative feedback intervenes in this process. The key contribution is identifying a boundary condition and an actionable mechanism—negative feedback—that can prevent the 'dark side' of servant leadership.

title: Conscientiousness and leader emergence: the mediating role of functional behaviors

entries.rq_with_context: Despite strong evidence linking conscientiousness to leader emergence, the mechanisms through which this personality trait translates into leadership recognition remain unclear. Prior research has largely focused on single mediators, neglecting the possibility of multiple behavioral pathways. This study addresses that gap by investigating the parallel mediating roles of task-, relations-, and change-oriented behaviors in the conscientiousness–leader emergence link. Drawing on functional leadership theory and a trait–behavior–perception framework, the authors use a multi-study design combining field and experimental data with parallel mediation analysis. The key contribution is identifying which specific functional behaviors—task performance, helping behaviors, taking charge, and creativity—explain how conscientious employees become perceived as leaders.

title: The influence of multitasking on creative work involvement: a conservation of resources perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Multitasking is common in modern workplaces but may negatively impact employee creativity by depleting resources. While some studies highlight benefits of multitasking, less attention has been paid to its potential downsides, especially regarding creative work involvement. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether multitasking reduces creative work involvement through emotional exhaustion, using conservation of resources (COR) theory. It further examines whether employees’ regulatory focus—promotion or prevention—shapes their response to multitasking. The authors use a three-wave, two-source survey of 418 employees and 116 leaders, applying multilevel analysis. The key contribution is clarifying the mechanism and boundary conditions linking multitasking to creative work involvement.

title: Devote yourself to enjoy daily work: a diary study on flow experience and organizational identification

entries.rq_with_context: Employees in construction engineering projects face demanding and dynamic work environments that can affect their psychological states. While flow and organizational identification have been studied separately, little is known about how they relate to each other on a daily basis within individuals in this specific context. Existing research relies heavily on cross-sectional data, limiting causal inference. This study addresses this gap by investigating the temporal dynamics between daily flow and daily organizational identification using a diary design with 204 employees over 15 consecutive workdays. The authors use multilevel time-series cross-lagged path analysis to test directionality. They find that daily flow predicts same-day and next-day organizational identification, but not the reverse. The study contributes evidence of a unidirectional predictive pathway from flow to organizational identification at the within-person level in a high-demand work setting.

title: The effects of perceived overqualification on spouse undermining and support

entries.rq_with_context: Perceived overqualification (PO) is common due to rising education levels and limited job opportunities, yet research has largely focused on its workplace consequences, neglecting effects at home. It remains unclear whether PO leads to positive or negative family outcomes, and what mechanisms explain such spillover. Drawing on the work–home resources model, this study asks how and when PO influences spouse undermining and support via personal resources depletion. It uses a two-study dyadic survey design with employee–spouse pairs from China. The key contribution is demonstrating that work–family centrality determines the direction of PO’s spillover, revealing when overqualification drains or conserves personal resources in the home context.

title: Workplace incivility during organizational socialization: how new managers, varying in moral identity, perceive (mis)fit

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses how workplace incivility—low-intensity, ambiguous disrespectful behaviors—compromises organizational socialization among externally hired managers, particularly MBA graduates in Vietnam. While prior research has focused on positive socialization practices, less is known about how negative factors like incivility lead to socialization failure. Drawing on social identity theory, the authors propose that incivility harms new managers’ sense of fit with organizational values, reducing their affective commitment. They test whether perceived P-O misfit mediates the link between incivility and AOC, and whether moral identity strengthens this process. The study contributes by showing how value incongruence from incivility undermines integration, especially for individuals with strong moral identities.

title: Empowering and directive leadership and taking charge: a moderating role of employee intrinsic motivation

entries.rq_with_context: Employees’ proactive behaviors like taking charge—voluntary efforts to improve work processes—are critical in dynamic work environments. However, research on how leadership influences such behaviors has yielded mixed results, particularly regarding supportive leadership. This study addresses this gap by distinguishing between two specific leadership styles—empowering and directive—and their differential effects on taking charge. It further explores intrinsic motivation as a boundary condition using Person–Environment (P-E) fit theory. The research uses supervisor–employee matched data from South Korean organizations and hierarchical regression analysis. It contributes by showing that leadership style matters distinctly and that intrinsic motivation strengthens both the positive effect of empowering leadership and the negative effect of directive leadership on taking charge.

title: Employee engagement in corporate social responsibility: disentangling the effects of values vs prestige

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations invest heavily in external corporate social responsibility (ECSR), yet employee participation remains low, suggesting a gap in understanding what motivates engagement. While prior research links ECSR to positive employee outcomes, it is unclear whether these responses stem from employees’ alignment with organizational values (value congruence) or from pride in the company’s reputation (external prestige). This study addresses this gap by testing both mechanisms using social identity theory. It also examines how internal CSR (ICSR) moderates these effects. The research uses a longitudinal survey and structural equation modeling to assess the mediating roles of value congruence and prestige, and the moderating role of ICSR. The study claims to advance understanding of when and why ECSR leads to employee engagement in CSR behaviors.

title: Perceived innovation-oriented human resource system and innovative work behavior: the chain mediating role of innovative culture and intrinsic motivation

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses how individual perceptions of innovation-oriented HR systems (IHRS) affect employees' innovative work behavior (IWB), a topic understudied compared to firm-level HRM-innovation research. While prior work shows HR systems impact organizational innovation, less is known about how employee-level perceptions of specialized HR systems influence individual innovation. The research fills this gap by testing whether the IHRS-IWB relationship is explained through a chain of mechanisms: perceived innovative culture and intrinsic motivation. Using survey data from 481 Chinese employees across three organizations, the authors apply structural equation modeling to analyze the proposed sequential mediation. The study claims to contribute by linking individual HR perceptions to individual outcomes through combined cultural and motivational mechanisms.

title: Open-office noise and information processing

entries.rq_with_context: Open-office noise is a common concern in modern workplaces, yet its impact on cognitive performance remains unclear, with mixed evidence on its effects. While noise is generally seen as detrimental, some studies show neutral or even positive outcomes, suggesting that underlying processes like information processing styles may explain these inconsistencies. This study addresses this gap by testing how open-office noise influences task performance indirectly through changes in intuitive and analytical processing, and whether physiological and subjective arousal mediate these effects. Drawing on arousal-based models, the authors use a lab experiment with manipulated noise exposure and measures of cognitive processing during a Wisconsin Card Sorting Task. The contribution lies in identifying specific cognitive mechanisms—particularly urgent intuition and rational analysis—and the role of arousal in linking noise to performance.

title: How's the boss? Integration of the health-oriented leadership concept into the job demands-resources theory

entries.rq_with_context: Health-oriented leadership (HoL), particularly StaffCare—leaders’ health-related attitudes and behaviors toward employees—has been linked to better employee well-being, but research on its antecedents is limited and largely cross-sectional. Missing is an understanding of how within-person variability in leaders’ job conditions influences their StaffCare. This study addresses this gap by examining how weekly fluctuations in job resources (e.g., autonomy, social support) and demands (e.g., interruptions, role conflict) affect principals’ StaffCare over time. The authors propose a serial mediation model rooted in the job demands–resources (JD-R) framework, testing whether these job characteristics influence StaffCare via leaders’ SelfCare, work engagement, and emotional exhaustion. Using a weekly diary design with 234 school principals over five weeks, multilevel structural equation modeling is applied. The study contributes by integrating HoL into the JD-R model and highlighting SelfCare as a central mechanism in leaders’ motivational and strain processes.

title: When I see your pain: effects of observing workplace ostracism on turnover intention and task performance

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace ostracism is a widespread and harmful phenomenon, yet research has largely focused on direct victims rather than observers. There is limited understanding of how witnessing ostracism affects observers’ work-related outcomes and the psychological mechanisms involved. This study addresses this gap by examining whether observing ostracism increases turnover intention and reduces task performance through affective rumination. Drawing on the perseverative cognition framework, the authors propose and test a moderated mediation model using data from 218 employees in China. The study contributes by identifying affective rumination as a key cognitive mechanism and revealing that proactive personality intensifies the negative impact of observing ostracism.

title: Facades of conformity and cyberloafing: a moderated mediation model

entries.rq_with_context: Despite evidence linking facades of conformity (FOC) to negative emotional and attitudinal outcomes, little is known about its behavioral consequences, particularly in relation to counterproductive work behaviors like cyberloafing. There is a lack of understanding regarding the mechanisms through which FOC leads to such behaviors. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether and how FOC drives cyberloafing, using the job stress process model as a theoretical foundation. It proposes that FOC increases anxiety, which in turn increases cyberloafing, and that performance–avoidance goal orientation (PAGO) moderates this process. The study uses a two-wave survey of 185 Chinese employees to test these relationships, contributing to the literature by identifying FOC as a new antecedent of cyberloafing and clarifying the psychological pathway through which it operates.

title: The impact of knowledge brokering and role crafting on work engagement: a two-wave panel survey of older Japanese workers

entries.rq_with_context: With the global workforce aging, maintaining work engagement among older workers is a growing challenge. While job crafting has been studied as a mechanism for engagement, research on older workers has largely focused on task crafting (resource crafting), overlooking relational and cognitive dimensions (role crafting) and their alignment with aging theories like socioemotional selectivity (SST) and selection optimization and compensation (SOC).
