entries.rq_with_context: While prior research has focused on the negative effects of illegitimate tasks on recipients, little is known about how such tasks affect third-party observers. Existing findings on observers’ responses are mixed—some show increased helping, others show reduced prosocial behaviour—leaving unclear when and why observers help. This study addresses this gap by examining the underlying mechanism through which observed illegitimate tasks influence observer helping behaviour. Drawing on deservingness theory, it proposes that observers’ reactions depend on their judgement of whether the coworker deserves such treatment, which in turn affects sympathy and helping. The model is tested using a two-wave field study with 218 employees in China. The key contribution is identifying a serial cognitive-emotional mechanism and a critical boundary condition—interpersonal liking—that explains variability in observer responses.

title: Flexible paths to innovation: mitigating commuting’s impact on creative deviance

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses how long commutes may hinder employees' engagement in creative deviance—rule-breaking behaviors aimed at innovation—despite their potential benefits for organizations. While prior research has focused on individual and job-level factors influencing creative deviance, the impact of non-work factors like commuting remains unexplored. The authors identify a gap in understanding how daily stressors outside work affect innovative behaviors. They propose that commuting depletes resources, harming work–life balance, which in turn limits creative deviance. Using conservation of resources (COR) theory and an ethics of care perspective, they test a moderated mediation model. The study contributes by showing that commuting time is a novel contextual antecedent of creative deviance and that flexible work arrangements can buffer its indirect negative effects.

title: The effect of employee STARA awareness on job crafting: exploring the moderating role of positive stress mindset

entries.rq_with_context: As smart technologies, artificial intelligence, robotics, and algorithms (STARA) become widespread in organizations, employees are increasingly aware of how these technologies may affect their careers. This STARA awareness can act as a work stressor, prompting employees to engage in job crafting to adapt. However, little research has examined how STARA awareness leads to different types of job crafting—specifically approach (proactive improvement) versus avoidance (withdrawing from demands). Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, this study explores whether challenge and threat appraisals mediate the relationship between STARA awareness and the two forms of job crafting. It also tests whether a positive stress mindset strengthens the challenge pathway and weakens the threat pathway. Using survey data from 319 Chinese employees, the study applies regression and moderated mediation analysis to test these mechanisms. The findings clarify the psychological processes through which technological change influences employee behavior and highlight an individual-level factor that can shift responses toward more constructive outcomes.

title: Coping with interest incongruence: the joint roles of proactive personality and job crafting

entries.rq_with_context: Interest incongruence—when employees' vocational interests misalign with their work environment—is common and linked to negative outcomes like turnover and absenteeism. However, little is known about how employees respond behaviorally when they stay in such mismatched roles. The study addresses this gap by investigating cyberloafing as a potential coping behavior. Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, the authors propose that interest incongruence depletes psychological resources, leading employees to cyberloaf as a defensive strategy. They further suggest that proactive personality and job crafting toward interests may mitigate this effect. The research uses a three-wave survey of 429 Chinese employees to test a mediated moderation model. The key contribution is identifying personal resources and proactive behaviors that can reduce cyberloafing in the face of interest incongruence.

title: Linking leader boundary spanning to task performance and its boundary conditions: a conservation of resources perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Leader boundary spanning—leaders' efforts to build relationships with external parties—is increasingly important for organizational success, yet its impact on individual employee performance is not well understood. While prior research highlights the value of boundary spanning at the team level, less is known about how individual leaders’ external activities influence employee outcomes. This study addresses this gap by examining whether leader boundary spanning improves employee task performance, how self-efficacy mediates this relationship, and under what boundary conditions the effect is strongest. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory, the authors propose that leaders act as resource providers, enhancing employees’ self-efficacy, which in turn boosts performance. The study further tests whether abusive supervision (a situational factor) and emotional exhaustion (an individual factor) moderate this mediating process. The key contribution is identifying both a psychological mechanism and boundary conditions, offering a more nuanced understanding of when and how leader boundary spanning matters.

title: How do challenge and hindrance stressors differentially influence work-to-family enrichment? The roles of self-esteem and marital power

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates how different types of job stressors—challenge versus hindrance—affect employees' ability to transfer positive resources from work to family life (work-to-family enrichment, WFE). While prior research often treats job stressors as uniformly negative, inconsistent findings suggest that some stressors may actually promote WFE. The study addresses a gap in understanding the mechanisms and boundary conditions in this relationship. Drawing on the challenge-hindrance stressor framework and the work–home resources model, the research tests whether self-esteem mediates the effects of job stressors on WFE and whether marital power moderates this process. Using a three-wave survey of Chinese teachers, the authors employ path analysis to examine these relationships. The study claims to clarify how and when job stressors influence WFE by identifying self-esteem as a key personal resource mechanism and marital power as a family-contextual boundary condition.

title: Every coin has two sides: a self-determination perspective on the relationship between algorithmic management and gig workers’ job burnout

entries.rq_with_context: The gig economy has reshaped work through digital platforms that use algorithmic management to govern workers. While prior research has identified job burnout as a significant issue for gig workers, less is known about how specific features of algorithmic management contribute to or alleviate burnout. Existing studies often treat algorithmic management as a single construct, overlooking its multidimensional nature. This study addresses this gap by exploring three distinct aspects of algorithmic management—direction, evaluation, and discipline—and their varying effects on burnout among gig workers (e.g., food-delivery and ride-hailing drivers). Drawing on self-determination theory, the research models how each aspect influences the satisfaction of autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs, which in turn affect burnout. The approach uses survey data analyzed via structural equation modeling. The study's contribution lies in uncovering the dual role of algorithmic management: while some components reduce burnout by supporting psychological needs, others exacerbate it through controlling mechanisms.

title: Age diversity and team performance – the moderating roles of team LMX quality and differentiation

entries.rq_with_context: As age diversity becomes more common in teams due to demographic shifts, researchers and practitioners seek to understand when it enhances or harms team performance. Prior research suggests leadership can shape these outcomes, but most studies adopt a leader-focused perspective (e.g., transformational or empowering leadership), leaving a limited theoretical account of the relational dynamics between leaders and members. This study addresses that gap by examining how two aspects of team-level LMX—team LMX quality (the average quality of leader-member relationships) and team LMX differentiation (the degree of variation in those relationships)—moderate the link between age diversity and team performance. Drawing on social cognitive theory, the authors propose that leaders serve as role models whose relational behaviors influence team members' interactions. Using survey data from 64 hospital teams in Germany, they test these moderating effects. The study contributes by identifying specific relational leadership mechanisms that determine whether age diversity benefits or undermines team performance.

title: Beyond a buzzword: the agile mindset as a new research construct in organizational psychology

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research on agility has focused on external practices (e.g., Scrum), recent interest has turned to internal factors like the 'agile mindset'—defined as attitudes involving learning spirit, collaborative exchange, empowered self-guidance, and customer co-creation. However, it remains unclear whether this mindset is a distinct and useful construct or merely overlapping with established personality and motivational traits. This study addresses the gap by testing whether the agile mindset predicts key occupational outcomes—performance, innovative work behavior, vigor, and emotional exhaustion—above and beyond core self-evaluation, proactive personality, and prevention vs. promotion focus. Using a two-wave survey (N = 411) and structural equation modeling, the study evaluates the agile mindset’s factorial, discriminant, and incremental validity. The authors claim this provides critical validation for treating the agile mindset as a unique construct in organizational psychology.

title: Why do leaders reject employee voice: a job demands-resources and conservation of resources approach

entries.rq_with_context: Leaders often reject employee voice despite its importance for organizational improvement, yet the factors driving this response remain underexplored. While prior research has focused on leaders’ psychological threats or motivational states, this study addresses a gap by examining how job demands (role overload) and job resources (LLX) shape voice rejection through resource gain and depletion processes. Drawing on the job demands-resources (JD-R) model and conservation of resources (COR) theory, it asks how role overload and LLX affect voice rejection, and when LLX buffers the negative impact of overload. The study uses a three-wave, multi-source design with 205 leader–employee pairs to test a moderated mediation model. It contributes by revealing dual pathways—resource depletion (via emotional exhaustion) and resource gain (via change self-efficacy)—through which job characteristics influence leader behavior.

title: How does negative workplace gossip influence receivers’ interaction avoidance and willingness to cooperate? The role of attributed self-serving motives

entries.rq_with_context: Negative workplace gossip is common and often studied for its effects on targets, but less is known about how it affects the relationship between senders and receivers. While existing research highlights benefits for senders—such as emotional relief or enhanced influence—it overlooks how receivers interpret and respond to such gossip. The gap lies in understanding the psychological mechanisms that shape receiver behavior toward gossipy coworkers. This study addresses this by asking: how does negative workplace gossip influence receivers’ interaction avoidance and willingness to cooperate, and what role do attributions of self-serving motives play? Drawing on attribution theory and the warmth–competence framework, the authors propose a moderated mediation model in which these attributions shape judgments of senders. The key contribution is revealing when and how negative gossip backfires on senders by damaging relational and cooperative outcomes.

title: Linking creativity with unethical behaviors: investigating when and why creativity predicts unethical pro-organizational behavior

entries.rq_with_context: While creativity is generally seen as beneficial, recent research suggests it may have negative consequences, including unethical behaviors. This study addresses a gap by exploring whether creative behavior leads to unethical pro-organizational behavior (UPB), which is intended to help the organization but violates ethical norms. The authors propose that moral licensing—where past good deeds license future unethical ones—may explain this link. They specifically test whether moral credentials or moral credits mediate this relationship, and whether perceived organizational valuing of creativity (POVC) moderates the indirect effect. Using survey data from employees and supervisors, they apply moral licensing theory to identify the psychological mechanism and boundary condition in the creativity–UPB relationship. The study contributes by empirically linking creativity to UPB and clarifying the specific pathway—moral credentials—through which this occurs.

title: Coworkers’ self-leadership and employees’ knowledge sharing: a moderated chain mediation model

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses the interpersonal effects of self-leadership, which have been underexplored despite its recognized role in organizational dynamics. While self-leadership is known to enhance individual performance, less is known about how it influences peers' behaviors such as knowledge sharing. The authors identify a gap in understanding the psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions of this influence. Drawing on affective events theory, they propose that coworkers' self-leadership acts as an affective event that triggers admiration, leading to relationship desire and subsequently knowledge sharing. The model is tested using a two-wave survey. The research contributes by revealing the interpersonal pathway through which self-leadership affects knowledge sharing and identifying perceived competitive climate as a key moderator.

title: Authentic leadership and employee expediency: a moderated mediation framework

entries.rq_with_context: Employee expediency—unethical, self-serving shortcuts at work—is a growing concern, yet research on its prevention remains limited. While prior studies have explored leadership’s role in unethical behavior, insufficient attention has been paid to how authentic leadership may reduce expediency through internal motivational mechanisms. This study fills that gap by investigating whether self-verification striving, the tendency to align others' views with one’s self-concept, mediates the link between authentic leadership and expediency. Drawing on self-verification theory and using multi-level data from 502 employees across 96 teams in China, the authors test a moderated mediation model. They further examine whether leader–member exchange strengthens this process. The study contributes by identifying self-verification striving as a key psychological mechanism and highlighting leader–member exchange as a boundary condition.

title: Breaking the cycle of injustice: how leaders act justly under the double threat of higher-level injustice and low justice rewards

entries.rq_with_context: The phenomenon of trickle-down injustice suggests that unfair treatment by higher-level leaders tends to be replicated downward. However, it remains unclear why some lower-level leaders break this cycle by acting more justly after experiencing injustice. This study addresses the gap by exploring the psychological mechanisms that lead lower-level leaders to counteract injustice, particularly under conditions where fair behavior is not rewarded. Drawing on psychological reactance theory, the authors propose that injustice from supervisors triggers psychological disidentification, which motivates justice enactment. The research uses two scenario-based studies to test this model. The key contribution is identifying a reversal in the trickle-down process by showing how disidentification, especially in low justice reward contexts, drives lower-level leaders to act more justly.

title: Shelters from the storm: a daily investigation of customer sexual harassment and organizational resources as moderators

entries.rq_with_context: Customer sexual harassment (CSH)—customers' behaviors that are sexually harassing or based on sex/gender—poses a unique challenge in service workplaces, especially as it occurs frequently and targets employees outside organizational control. While prior research focuses on male-dominated settings, it remains unclear whether gender disparities in CSH persist in non-male-dominated industries like modern service jobs. Additionally, little is known about CSH's daily impacts on employee well-being or how organizations can help buffer these effects. This study addresses these gaps by investigating daily CSH among call center employees in South Korea using experience sampling. It asks: (1) Do women experience more daily CSH than men? (2) How is daily CSH linked to daily job satisfaction and work engagement? (3) Do organizational resources moderate these relationships? Guided by conservation of resources (COR) theory, the study tests perceived organizational support and effective customer-service training as buffers. The research contributes new evidence on gender disparities in CSH in female-majority contexts and identifies organizational supports that alleviate its daily harms.

title: Contextual cues matter: advancing personality research through the interactions of implicit and explicit personality with situations

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates how the combination of implicit (unconscious motives) and explicit (self-reported) aggression interacts with employees' perceptions of organizational justice—procedural, distributive, and interactional—to affect positive workplace behaviors like organizational citizenship behaviors (OCBs) and commendations. While prior research has explored implicit and explicit personality interactions, especially regarding counterproductive behaviors, little is known about how situational factors like justice perceptions shape positive outcomes for individuals with different aggression profiles. The study fills this gap by testing a three-way interaction model that integrates person-focused aggression traits with situational justice cues. Using survey data from 186 hospital employees and supervisor ratings, the authors employ moderated hierarchical multiple regression to analyze these complex interactions. The primary contribution lies in extending the implicit-explicit personality model to include contextual justice factors as moderators of positive, rather than negative, organizational behaviors.

title: Humanizing GenAI at work: bridging the gap between technological innovation and employee engagement

entries.rq_with_context: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in workplaces raises questions about its impact on employee performance, particularly regarding how employees perceive and adapt to this technology. While GenAI offers opportunities to enhance productivity and engagement, it also introduces uncertainties around job security and acceptance, creating a mixed perception among workers. Existing research lacks empirical evidence on managerial perspectives regarding employee engagement, trust, and attitudes during early stages of GenAI adoption. This study addresses that gap by exploring how these factors influence employee performance, using the S-O-R framework, TAM, and TRI models. It employs hierarchical regression and bootstrapping analysis on survey data from 251 managers in Spanish companies. The authors claim the study contributes to understanding the human side of GenAI implementation in organizational settings.

title: On the consequences of AI bias: when moral values supersede algorithm bias

entries.rq_with_context: AI bias poses significant risks to fairness and equity in human resource management, particularly in institutionally constrained regions with weak regulatory frameworks. While existing research has focused on technical solutions to algorithmic bias, there is limited understanding of the behavioural and social antecedents that drive managerial responses in such contexts. This study addresses this gap by investigating how organisational identity, procedural and distributive justice perceptions, and personal moral norms shape HR managers' reactions to AI bias in Ghana. Drawing on social identity theory, norm activation theory, and organisational justice theory, the study uses fsQCA to analyse survey data from 225 senior HR managers across multiple industries. The research contributes to the literature by identifying specific configurations of factors that lead to strong managerial responses to bias, emphasizing the role of subjective moral and organisational evaluations over purely technical assessments.

title: Unveiling the potential: exploring the adoption of GenAI and its impact on organizational outcomes

entries.rq_with_context: The study investigates the adoption of generative AI (GenAI) in the Indian retail industry, where rapid digitization and competitive pressures are shaping technology uptake. While prior research has examined general AI adoption, little is known about the specific drivers and outcomes of GenAI in emerging economies like India, particularly within the retail context. There is limited empirical evidence on how organizational factors such as top management support, openness to innovation, and competitive pressure affect GenAI adoption, and how this adoption translates into employee efficiency and firm performance. This study addresses these gaps by focusing on Indian retail employees and using PLS-SEM analysis on survey data from 188 respondents. It applies the TOE (Technological-Organizational-Environmental) framework and Resource-Based View (RBV) to model the adoption process. The study contributes by revealing the direct effects of antecedents on GenAI adoption, the mediating role of employee efficiency, and the moderating role of data-driven culture.

title: Technophobia and the manager’s intention to adopt generative AI: the impact of self-regulated learning and open organisational culture

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the potential benefits of generative AI in management, many business managers remain hesitant to adopt it, possibly due to technophobia—anxiety or fear toward new technologies. While prior research has explored technology adoption from a technical standpoint, there is limited understanding of the psychological and social factors shaping managers' decisions. This study addresses this gap by applying the cognitive-affective-normative (CAN) model to examine how technophobia, self-regulated learning (SRL), and organisational culture interact to influence managers’ adoption intentions. Using survey data from 528 Chinese managers, it tests whether SRL buffers the negative effect of technophobia and whether open organisational culture strengthens this buffering role. The study contributes by shifting focus from technology-centric views to a 'human-side' perspective on AI adoption.

title: Unmasking the silent threat: AI-induced human capital obsolescence and business failure

entries.rq_with_context: The paper addresses the growing threat of human capital obsolescence (HCO) in the context of rapid AI adoption, where employees' knowledge, skills, and abilities (KSAs) become misaligned with organizational demands. Despite increasing attention to AI's impact on work, there is limited scholarly understanding of how HCO unfolds differently across organizational types—particularly between state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and privately owned enterprises (POEs)—and how it leads to business failure. The research question is: how does AI shape the process of HCO in SOEs and POEs, and how do these contexts influence recognition, response, and failure outcomes? Drawing on human capital theory and a conceptual 2x2 framework, the study distinguishes between planned and unplanned HCO across these organizational forms. Its key contribution is advancing the concept of AI-induced HCO and linking it to distinct failure pathways in different institutional settings.

title: Emphasizing family as a source of social support: implications for work-family conflict and job satisfaction among hispanic professionals

entries.rq_with_context: Hispanics represent a growing segment of the US workforce, yet little research explores how their cultural values—particularly familism—affect workplace experiences like work-family conflict and job satisfaction. While familism has been linked to positive outcomes in education and mental health, its role in workplace dynamics remains unexamined. This study fills that gap by testing whether valuing family as a source of social support buffers against work interfering with family (WIF) and enhances job satisfaction among Hispanic professionals. Using survey data from 103 Hispanic professionals, the authors test a moderated mediation model grounded in theories of familism and work-family conflict. They find that family support reduces WIF, which in turn increases job satisfaction, and that these effects are stronger for women. The study contributes to the literature by being the first to empirically link family support values to workplace outcomes among Hispanics.

title: Discovering the (mis) alignment of the cultural values of African Americans and HR policies and practices

entries.rq_with_context: The US workforce is increasingly diverse, yet HR policies often reflect Anglo-American cultural values such as individualism and competitive achievement, potentially misaligning with the cultural values of African American employees. There is limited research on how well HR practices align with the work values of domestic minority groups like African Americans, despite evidence of higher turnover rates among them. This paper asks: What are the cultural values of African Americans, and to what extent do current HR policies and practices align with them? Using Hofstede’s (1980) cultural values framework, the authors analyze three dimensions—individualism/collectivism, power distance, and long-term/short-term orientation—to explore this alignment. The study contributes by identifying potential misalignment and proposing that better alignment could reduce turnover and improve job satisfaction among African American employees.

title: Muslim employees’ religious and intersectional identities as sources of discrimination: how deeper understanding can improve managerial practice

entries.rq_with_context: Muslim employees in Western Europe frequently face workplace discrimination, often attributed to religious identity, but less is known about how this intersects with gender, age, and ethnicity. Existing research tends to treat Muslim identity as monolithic, overlooking the layered discrimination resulting from multiple marginalized identities. This study addresses that gap by exploring how Muslim employees in Catalonia experience discrimination based on intersecting social categories. Using an intersectional lens, the authors analyze in-depth interviews with 39 diverse Muslim employees across service and non-service sectors. The research asks how these intersecting identities shape discrimination and what coping strategies individuals develop. The study contributes by highlighting the complexity of religious identity and the psychological toll of concealment, advocating for more nuanced HR practices.

title: Hispanic and Anglo Americans’ intentions to pursue IT careers

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the high demand and prestige of IT jobs, women and ethnic minorities like Hispanic Americans remain underrepresented in the field. While prior research has explored barriers for women and African Americans, there is limited understanding of the specific factors affecting Hispanics' career choices in IT. This study addresses this gap by validating a model that integrates cultural values (e.g., collectivism), self-efficacy, social influences, and stereotypes as predictors of career intentions. Using data from 90 Hispanics and 90 Anglos, the research employs regression and mediation analyses to test hypothesized relationships. The study contributes by identifying which factors significantly influence intentions to pursue IT careers among these groups, particularly shedding light on unexpected findings such as higher career intentions among Hispanics despite existing disparities.

title: Islamic religiosity: the influence of different forms of hijab on Saudi women’s experience of employment

entries.rq_with_context: Islamic religiosity, particularly through visible practices like the hijab, plays a significant role in shaping women's employment experiences in Muslim-majority societies such as Saudi Arabia. While existing research has explored religious discrimination in the workplace, few studies have examined how variations in hijab practices—such as wearing the headscarf versus the face veil (niqab)—impact career trajectories, especially amid modernization efforts like Saudi Vision 2030. There is limited understanding of how organizational practices and familial expectations interact with different forms of religious dress to create unique advantages or barriers for women. This study addresses that gap by asking how hijab practices rooted in Islamic religiosity influence hiring and career advancement for Saudi women. Using an interpretive qualitative approach with 50 employees in Riyadh, the research analyzes interviews through hybrid thematic analysis. It contributes by reframing the hijab as a spectrum of religious expression and highlighting how dress-based biases affect inclusion in a rapidly changing labor market.

title: A multi-method study of servant leadership and despotic leadership–work engagement nexus: the roles of identification with leader and political skill

entries.rq_with_context: Work engagement remains low globally, particularly in Pakistan, posing challenges for organizations. Leadership is a key factor that may influence employee engagement, yet the mechanisms through which positive (servant) and negative (despotic) leadership styles affect engagement are not fully understood. This study addresses this gap by examining identification with the leader as a mediating mechanism and employees’ political skill as a boundary condition. Using data from a three-wave survey (Study 1, n = 258) and two experimental studies (Study 2a and 2b) in Pakistan, the research tests a multi-method model grounded in social exchange theory and conservation of resources theory. The study contributes by identifying identification with the leader as a key mediating process and political skill as a moderator that can buffer the negative effects of despotic leadership and enhance the positive effects of servant leadership on work engagement.

title: Online interactions, offline behaviors: a study of social media feedback as an indirect predictor of prosocial behaviors at work

entries.rq_with_context: Social media has become a central part of daily life, yet research on its impact on workplace behaviors often focuses on usage patterns rather than interaction quality. While prior studies highlight negative outcomes like stress and boundary conflicts, less is known about how positive interpersonal exchanges on social media affect employees' workplace behaviors. This study fills that gap by examining whether favorable feedback—such as likes and written comments—triggers positive affect, which in turn boosts cognitive resources (energy, relational self-efficacy) and leads to prosocial behaviors like voice and helping. Drawing on the broaden-and-build theory, the authors use a weekly diary design with full-time employees to test indirect pathways over time. The study's main contribution is identifying social media feedback as a novel antecedent of workplace prosocial behaviors, emphasizing the unique role of written comments over likes.

title: Be cautious of your voice when boss is in shame: how manager shame shapes defensive reactions toward employee voice

entries.rq_with_context: Employee voice—employees expressing change-oriented ideas—is critical for organizational improvement, yet managers often react defensively. While prior research focuses on stable traits (e.g., low self-efficacy) that make managers defensive, less is known about how transient emotional states like shame affect these reactions. This study addresses the gap by exploring how feeling shame—a self-conscious emotion signaling a damaged self-image—moderates managers’ responses to voice. Using cognitive dissonance theory, the authors propose that shame increases ego threat from voice, leading to cognitive discounting of the voice and the voicer. The experimental study uses a 2x2 design with manipulated voice and shame conditions among Chinese managers. The key contribution is demonstrating that shame, as a temporary state, significantly shapes how managers evaluate voice and voicers, extending understanding beyond dispositional factors.

title: The negative consequences of team voice: an interaction of frequency and centralization

entries.rq_with_context: While team voice is generally seen as beneficial for team outcomes, empirical findings are mixed, with some studies showing negative consequences. A key gap is the lack of attention to how voice is distributed within teams, not just how much there is. Existing research often assumes voice is evenly distributed, but in reality, some members speak more than others. This study addresses that gap by investigating how team voice frequency and voice centralization interact to influence team decision-making effectiveness and subsequent team performance. Drawing on a team information-processing perspective, it proposes that high voice frequency may overwhelm teams when voice is widely distributed. The key contribution is showing that team voice can have negative effects under specific structural conditions, clarifying inconsistent findings in the literature.

title: LMX and recruiter incivility toward job seekers: a self-serving attribution perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Job seekers often face incivility during recruitment, yet the causes of such behavior by recruiters remain unclear. While high-quality LMX relationships are generally seen as beneficial, recent evidence suggests they may also lead to negative employee behaviors. This study addresses the gap by exploring how recruiters’ self-serving attributions—interpreting LMX quality as a result of personal merit—influence their sense of psychological entitlement and increase incivility toward job seekers. Using attribution theory, the authors propose a moderated mediation model tested with three-wave survey data from 320 recruiters. The key contribution is identifying a psychological mechanism through which positive leader-subordinate relationships may backfire in the recruitment context.

title: Allocation by effort or contribution? Differences in allocation preferences of the wealth-advantaged and wealth-disadvantaged under effort-contribution imbalance

entries.rq_with_context: When effort exerted and contribution made are not proportional—such as when some work hard but contribute little while others contribute greatly with little effort—organizations face a dilemma in deciding whether to reward based on effort or contribution. Existing research shows inconsistent findings: some studies report a preference for effort-based allocation, especially among lower-income individuals, while others find support for contribution-based allocation, often among higher-status groups. This study identifies wealth status as a key factor underlying these inconsistencies. It investigates how wealth-advantaged and wealth-disadvantaged individuals differ in their allocation preferences under effort-contribution imbalance, using experimental manipulations of wealth status and social cognition. The research employs a three-study design to test these effects and their underlying mechanisms. The authors claim this work reconciles contradictions in prior literature and reveals a new social cognition mechanism linked to competence and warmth perceptions.

title: A visionary future for sustainability: exploring how and when green visionary leadership promotes employee green innovation

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly emphasize environmental sustainability, and leadership plays a key role in driving green outcomes. While prior research has explored green leadership styles, direct evidence on how green visionary leadership (GVL) affects employee green innovation (GI) remains limited. A key unanswered question is the psychological mechanism through which GVL translates into GI, as well as the boundary conditions under which this process is stronger. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study investigates green passion (GP) as a mediating mechanism and green value orientation (GVO) as a moderating factor. Using multi-wave, supervisor-employee matched data from Chinese SMEs, the study tests a moderated mediation model. It contributes by identifying GP as a key motivational pathway and showing that GVO strengthens the impact of GVL on GI through GP.

title: How needs frustration and leader gender influence reactions to uncivil subordinates

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace incivility from subordinates is an understudied phenomenon, despite evidence that it can negatively affect leaders. While prior research has largely been correlational, this study uses an experimental design to test the causal impact of subordinate incivility on leader affective well-being. Drawing on self-determination theory, the authors investigate whether the effects of incivility are mediated by frustration of leaders’ need for competence and relatedness, and whether these mediation effects vary by leader gender. They test their hypotheses using a between-subjects experiment (N = 125) in which participants assume a leadership role and interact via email with a civil or uncivil subordinate. The study contributes causal evidence on the psychological mechanisms linking subordinate incivility to leader well-being, clarifying the role of gender in shaping these responses.

title: Focusing on the bottom line at the expense of creativity: the role of construal level in goal shielding

entries.rq_with_context: Many organizations emphasize meeting the bottom line, leading employees to adopt a narrow, result-focused mindset that may hinder creativity. While prior research has explored leader BLM's negative effects, less is known about how employees’ own BLM influences their creative outcomes. This study addresses this gap by investigating the cognitive mechanism—construal level—that links employee BLM to reduced creativity. Using goal shielding and construal level theories, the authors propose that BLM lowers employees’ construal levels, limiting abstract thinking essential for creativity. They also examine leader BLM as a boundary condition. The key contribution is identifying construal level as a mediating mechanism and showing how leader BLM amplifies these effects.

title: Exploring the nonlinear impact of emotional work demands and work passion on job satisfaction

entries.rq_with_context: Emotional work demands (EWDs) are central to occupational stress, especially in service professions like healthcare, yet their relationship with job satisfaction is not consistently linear. Some evidence suggests moderate EWDs may enhance satisfaction, while high demands often reduce it, indicating a potential curvilinear effect. However, it remains unclear how individual differences, particularly work passion, shape this relationship. This study addresses that gap by investigating how work passion moderates the nonlinear link between EWDs and job satisfaction. Using polynomial regression on longitudinal data from 267 nurses, the authors test for an inverted U-shape and a J-shape pattern depending on passion levels. The findings contribute by showing that work passion fundamentally alters how employees respond to emotional demands, challenging the assumption of uniform negative effects.

title: Two-faced employers? Employee psychological withdrawal reactions to employer signals during times of uncertainty

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates how employees respond psychologically when their employers manage uncertain situations like a pandemic. While prior research has focused on organizational signals to external stakeholders, this study addresses the gap in understanding internal signals during high-stress, uncertain contexts. The research asks how an employer’s handling of a pandemic influences employee psychological withdrawal and whether this relationship depends on employees’ general perceptions of organizational support. Drawing on signaling theory, the study proposes that inconsistent signals—between general support and crisis response—lead to perceptions of organizational hypocrisy, which in turn increase withdrawal. Using two field surveys and an experiment, the authors test whether perceived organizational support strengthens the effect of effective pandemic management on reducing withdrawal.

title: Bestowing roses, lingering fragrance: how mentor autonomy support influences the mentors’ thriving at work

entries.rq_with_context: While mentorship is often studied from the protégé’s perspective, less is known about how mentors themselves benefit, especially through high-quality interactions like autonomy support. Existing research has largely focused on protégé outcomes or negative experiences for mentors, leaving a gap in understanding the positive motivational mechanisms that drive mentor development. This study addresses this by exploring how mentor autonomy support affects the mentor’s thriving at work through the satisfaction of their basic psychological needs (relatedness, competence, autonomy). Using a three-wave study with 240 mentor-protégé pairs, the authors test a moderated mediation model grounded in Relationships Motivation Theory and Self-Expansion Theory. The key contribution is uncovering the internal motivational process and boundary conditions through which mentoring enhances the mentor's own growth.

title: Unpacking the black box of salesperson entrepreneurial behavior: the role of family motivation

entries.rq_with_context: Salespeople play a key role in corporate entrepreneurship by identifying and exploiting market opportunities, yet they face tension between short-term sales performance and long-term entrepreneurial efforts. While motivation is critical for driving such behaviors, family motivation—defined as the desire to benefit one’s family—has not been studied in this context. Although prior research shows family motivation increases work effort, it may also make employees more risk-averse. This study investigates how family motivation influences both opportunity recognition and exploitation among salespeople, using survey data from 280 Chinese sales employees. The authors test a moderated mediation model to understand when and how family motivation leads to incomplete entrepreneurial behavior. The study contributes by dissecting the dual role of family motivation in sales entrepreneurship and identifying gender as a boundary condition.

title: Achieving job performance through agility and innovativeness by strategizing learning ambidexterity

entries.rq_with_context: Personal agility and innovativeness are essential for high job performance, especially in dynamic work environments. While ambidextrous learning—balancing exploration and exploitation—is believed to foster these traits, little research has examined how both forms of learning simultaneously shape agility and innovativeness, nor how leadership may influence these relationships. This study addresses the gap by asking: (1) What factors simultaneously influence agility and innovativeness, thereby impacting job performance? (2) Are these effects moderated by knowledge-oriented leadership? Using ambidexterity theory and data from project managers in a high-tech firm, the study employs structural equation modeling and moderated regression. It claims to contribute by identifying the distinct mediating roles of agility and innovativeness and revealing the moderating effect of leadership on learning processes.

title: Pressured role modeling effect: a trickle-down model of leader OCB via citizenship pressure

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research assumes employees voluntarily imitate leader OCB, this study addresses a gap by exploring the controlled motivational mechanism—specifically, citizenship pressure—that may underlie this role modeling effect. It investigates when and why leader OCB might trigger pressure rather than voluntary engagement, particularly focusing on employees' individualism and collectivism as boundary conditions. The research question is: how does leader OCB influence employee OCB through citizenship pressure, and does this process vary by employees’ value orientations? Guided by social information processing (SIP) theory, the study proposes a moderated mediation model. The key contribution is revealing a 'pressured role modeling effect,' challenging the assumption of purely voluntary imitation and offering a more nuanced understanding of leader influence.

title: When it is relevant, I feel grateful: relevant organizational support drives employee customer orientation

entries.rq_with_context: In the service sector, customer orientation among front-line employees is critical for firm performance. Prior research shows that perceived organizational support (POS) can enhance employee customer orientation, but there is limited understanding of when and why this relationship holds. Existing studies have examined employee characteristics and contextual factors, yet overlooked how the personal relevance of support—whether employees see the support as aligned with their individual needs—influences its effectiveness. This study investigates the moderating role of support relevance and the mediating role of employee gratitude in the POS–customer orientation link. Using two studies (a survey and an experiment) with US-based front-line service workers, the authors test moderated mediation hypotheses. The key contribution is identifying personal relevance as a boundary condition that determines whether POS positively or negatively affects customer orientation, offering a more nuanced view of organizational support effectiveness.

title: The hidden pitfalls of flexibility: how work flexibility can promote strain and work–family conflict through telepressure

entries.rq_with_context: Work flexibility is often viewed as a resource that helps employees manage work and personal demands, reducing work–family conflict. However, emerging evidence suggests it may also lead to increased stress and work interference with family. This study addresses a gap in understanding the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which flexibility may produce negative outcomes. Drawing on job demands-resources (JDR) theory, it investigates whether telepressure—preoccupation with work-related messages—mediates the relationship between flexibility and strain outcomes like exhaustion and WIF, and whether future temporal focus moderates this process. Using a three-wave panel design with 266 employees, the study tests a moderated mediation model. It contributes by showing that flexibility can activate the health impairment pathway in JDR theory under certain individual conditions.

title: Can obsessive passion facilitate responses to job characteristics and help prevent psychological distress and turnover intention? A moderated mediation model

entries.rq_with_context: Although work passion is generally linked to positive outcomes, the role of obsessive work passion (OWP) remains ambiguous, with some evidence suggesting both negative and neutral effects. Existing research has focused mostly on behavioral outcomes or short-term effects, leaving unclear how OWP interacts with job characteristics over time to influence employee well-being. A key gap is understanding the psychological mechanisms—specifically, the frustration of basic psychological needs—that may explain these relationships. This study investigates how OWP moderates the link between job demands/resources and psychological distress and turnover intention via frustration of autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs. Using a longitudinal design with nurses, the authors apply the dualistic model of passion, job demands-resources model, and self-determination theory. The study contributes by identifying when and how OWP may buffer or exacerbate job-related stress.

title: Promoting well-being and performance in remote teams: the moderating effect of supportive leadership

entries.rq_with_context: Remote work has become widespread, but it introduces challenges such as reduced face-to-face interaction, increased isolation, and reliance on digital communication, which can exacerbate team conflict and harm employee well-being and collaboration. Existing research highlights the importance of leadership and communication in virtual teams, yet there is limited understanding of how conflict impacts well-being and trust in remote contexts, and whether supportive leadership can mitigate these effects. This study asks how team conflict influences burnout, psychological distress, trust and communication, and ultimately job performance in remote teams, and whether supportive leadership moderates these relationships. Using PLS-SEM analysis of survey data from 421 remote workers, the study tests a model grounded in COR, JD-R, and Social Exchange theories. It contributes by identifying supportive leadership as a key buffer against conflict-induced burnout and distress, while showing its limited effect on trust and communication.

title: Commitment is not enough: how and when occupational commitment influence employees' organizational turnover intention

entries.rq_with_context: While occupational commitment is generally linked to lower organizational turnover, recent research suggests this relationship is weaker than expected, indicating important boundary conditions. The paper identifies a gap in understanding the mechanism through which occupational commitment affects turnover intention, particularly when organizational context undermines employees’ agentic efforts. Drawing on Protean Career Theory, the authors propose that occupation-oriented job crafting serves as a key mechanism linking occupational commitment to reduced turnover, but that this process may fail when social faultlines block cross-group cooperation. They test how faultlines disrupt this mechanism and whether servant leadership can neutralize this disruption. The study uses a time-lagged survey (Study 1) and scenario experiment (Study 2) to validate the model. The contribution lies in revealing the conditional nature of occupational commitment’s effect on retention, especially when employees’ self-directed efforts are hindered by group divisions.

title: More to Lose: The Adverse Effect of High Performance Ranking on Employees’ Preimplementation Attitudes Toward the Integration of Powerful AI Aids

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the growing use of AI to augment employee work, algorithm aversion remains common, especially among high performers. While prior research focuses on individual, algorithmic, and task factors influencing this aversion, less is known about how social context—specifically one’s relative performance ranking—affects attitudes. This paper addresses that gap by investigating whether high performers resist AI integration not only due to confidence in their own abilities but also due to fears of losing their relative standing. Using a social comparison perspective, the research tests whether high performance ranking negatively impacts preimplementation AI attitudes through perceived potential loss of standing. The studies employ experimental designs across simulated and real job tasks to establish causality and mechanism. The key contribution is identifying a novel social-based mechanism that explains resistance to AI beyond existing ability-based explanations.

title: Attention Focus and New Opportunities: The Moderating Role of Managerial Attention to Alternative Issues

entries.rq_with_context: The strategy literature recognizes that managerial attention shapes how firms respond to industry change, but it often treats attention in isolation. This paper addresses a key gap by examining how the effect of attention to a new opportunity—here, a distributed electricity generation model—is shaped by other strategic issues managers attend to simultaneously. The authors argue that attention to a competing (legacy) model and broader strategic attention may hinder the translation of attention into action due to cognitive overload and organizational confusion. They test this using text analysis of earnings calls from 68 U.S. utilities (2003–2019). Their approach integrates attentional context and organizational capacity, showing that these constraints are stronger for smaller firms. The study contributes by contextualizing attention within a broader strategic agenda and identifying boundary conditions related to firm size.

title: Opportunistic Change During a Punctuation: How and When the Front Lines Can Drive Bursts of Incremental Change

entries.rq_with_context: Environmental jolts like the Covid-19 pandemic disrupt organizational stability and create conditions conducive to change, yet punctuated equilibrium theories focus primarily on top-down, radical change. Frontline staff possess valuable insights for improvement but are typically disadvantaged in getting their ideas adopted due to lack of power and entrenched stasis. This study addresses the gap in understanding how frontline-driven, incremental changes occur during such disruptions. Drawing on a two-year qualitative study at a hospital during the pandemic, the authors examine the trajectories of 33 pre-existing frontline change ideas to understand how and when these ideas were selected and retained. They use a process model informed by policy window theory and organizational opportunism. The key contribution is identifying a set of agentic practices that enable frontline staff to capitalize on transient windows of opportunity, revealing an alternative pathway for intentional organizational change.

title: CEO Initial Contract Duration and Corporate Acquisitions

entries.rq_with_context: The phenomenon under study is how CEO initial contract duration influences corporate acquisition strategies. While prior research has focused on financial aspects of CEO contracts like compensation, the nonfinancial aspect of contract duration remains understudied despite its increasing relevance in corporate governance reforms. This gap is important because shorter contracts are advocated for improved monitoring but may induce time pressure on new CEOs, shaping their strategic decisions. The research questions are: (1) whether shorter initial contract durations lead to more corporate acquisitions, and (2) whether such CEOs favor 'straightforward' M&A deals characterized by speed and lower risk. The authors use a theoretical framework based on time management theory and test their hypotheses using detailed SEC contract data from 1990–2017 and a quasi-natural experiment based on UK corporate governance reform. The key claimed contribution is demonstrating that contract duration—beyond financial incentives—affects CEO strategic behavior by inducing time-oriented decision-making.

title: Measure Twice, Cut Once: Unit Profitability, Scalability, and the Exceptional Growth of New Firms

entries.rq_with_context: The paper addresses a theoretical gap between research on new firm growth in entrepreneurship and mature firm growth in strategy literature. While existing work explains early-stage learning or late-stage scaling, it does not explain how new firms transition into mature ones. The authors identify a lack of clarity around 'premature scaling' and the role of unit profitability in this transition. Using three matched pairs of firms across nascent online fashion markets, they explore why some promising firms grow into mature, multiproduct organizations while others stall despite early success. The study uses a theory-building case method to trace firm trajectories over nearly a decade. Its key contribution is identifying a two-phase process—first focused learning about unit profitability, then capability-driven scaling—that enables exceptional growth.

title: The Double-Edged Sword of Exemplar Similarity

entries.rq_with_context: Firms often position themselves relative to category exemplars—outstanding, high-performing organizations—to gain legitimacy and recognition. Prior research highlights benefits of such positioning, including enhanced recognizability and better market outcomes. However, less is known about potential downsides, particularly when audiences compare similar firms directly. This study investigates how exemplar similarity differentially impacts two stages of analyst evaluation: screening (coverage decisions) and assessment (investment recommendations). Using a sample of 7,603 U.S. public firms from 1997–2022 and natural language processing to measure similarity, we test whether exemplar similarity has opposing effects across these stages. The key contribution is revealing the 'double-edged sword' nature of exemplar similarity, contingent on category characteristics and exemplar typicality.

title: The Effect of Financial Resources on Misconduct: Evidence from Lottery Ticket Sales

entries.rq_with_context: The relationship between financial resources and organizational misconduct remains unclear, with conflicting theoretical predictions—some suggesting poverty drives misconduct (strain theory), others that wealth enables it. Empirical studies face challenges including reverse causality, omitted variable bias, and measurement error. This paper examines whether increased financial resources reduce misconduct, using tobacco sales to minors as the outcome. Leveraging a difference-in-differences design based on lottery windfalls, the study isolates exogenous shocks to retailers’ financial resources. The approach helps address endogeneity concerns. The authors claim to provide plausibly causal evidence supporting strain theory, showing that sudden financial gains reduce misconduct in small retail firms.

title: How Mixed Performance Feedback Shapes Exploration: The Moderating Role of Self-Enhancement

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often use peer performance feedback to shape employee behavior, but it remains unclear how such feedback influences individual exploration decisions. Prior research suggests that relative performance comparisons affect learning and search, yet little is known about individual differences in interpreting this feedback. This paper investigates whether and how individuals’ tendency to self-enhance—defined as the motivation to maintain a positive self-image—moderates their response to peer performance information in an exploration-exploitation task. Using a preregistered experiment with manipulated peer feedback (high, low, or none), the authors test how self-enhancement shapes behavioral responses over time. Their key contribution is demonstrating that self-enhancement dampens exploration in the presence of upward social comparison, especially when mixed feedback creates interpretive flexibility.

title: Location-Specificity and Relocation Incentive Programs for Remote Workers

entries.rq_with_context: The rapid growth of remote work has enabled localities to compete for highly educated workers through relocation incentive programs, offering financial and social support to attract talent. However, these programs risk failure if remote workers—especially 'digital nomads'—collect incentives and leave quickly, undermining long-term economic benefits. Existing research has not clarified how localities can retain such mobile workers and generate lasting value. This paper addresses that gap by studying Tulsa Remote, a program that offers $10,000 and community integration services. The research question is: How can relocation incentive programs create and sustain value for localities by retaining remote workers? The authors use a mixed-methods approach, combining qualitative interviews with a difference-in-differences survey design comparing participants to 'near-treated' applicants. The key claimed contribution is demonstrating that location-specific mechanisms like community engagement enable value creation and retention.

title: The Relative Effects of a Scandal on Member Engagement in Rites of Integration and Rites of Passage: Evidence from a Child Abuse Scandal in the Catholic Archdiocese of Philadelphia

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational scandals are known to trigger negative stakeholder reactions, but little research explores whether these effects differ across types of member engagement. Existing studies often focus on aggregate outcomes, potentially overlooking important variations. This paper investigates how a scandal impacts two distinct forms of engagement—rites of integration, which strengthen community and identification, and rites of passage, which mark individual transitions. Using data from the Catholic Archdiocese of Philadelphia during a child abuse scandal, the authors test whether engagement declines more sharply in one type of rite than the other. They employ a longitudinal parish-level dataset from 1990 to 2010 and use seemingly unrelated regressions to compare standardized changes. The study contributes by showing that scandals affect engagement heterogeneously, with implications for understanding organizational resilience.

title: Regulation and Innovation Revisited: How Restrictive Environments Can Promote Destabilizing New Technologies

entries.rq_with_context: The relationship between regulatory restrictiveness and firm innovation has yielded conflicting findings: some studies show that restrictions reduce innovation by limiting available technological components, while others suggest they can stimulate innovation by prompting firms to search for new alternatives. This paper addresses the unresolved debate by examining two key contingencies—regulatory uncertainty and innovation type—that may explain these divergent results. The research asks how regulatory restrictiveness influences consolidating versus destabilizing innovation under varying levels of regulatory uncertainty. Using a novel dataset combining federal regulation texts and patent data from 1,242 U.S. firms (1994–2013), the authors apply a recombination-based framework to test their hypotheses. The study contributes by reconciling opposing views in the literature through empirical evidence showing that restrictiveness has differential effects depending on context.

title: Bridging the Chasm Between Intentions and Behaviors: Developing and Testing a Construal Level Theory of Internal Whistle-Blowing

entries.rq_with_context: Despite widespread corporate scandals and high reported intentions to report misconduct, actual internal whistleblowing remains low, revealing a persistent gap between intentions and behaviors. Existing theories like the Theory of Planned Behavior or Prosocial Organizational Behavior models fail to fully explain this disconnect, particularly how organizational factors influence each stage differently. This paper addresses that gap by proposing that employees think more abstractly when forming whistleblowing intentions and more concretely when deciding to act. The research question is: how do different ethical infrastructure systems—communication (abstract) versus surveillance, accountability, and retaliatory systems (concrete)—affect whistleblowing intentions and behaviors based on this shift in cognition? Using construal level theory, the authors test this framework across one field study and one experiment. Their key contribution is introducing a cognitive mechanism—processing fluency through construal fit—that explains when and why specific organizational systems are effective at bridging the intention-behavior gap.

title: Temporal Miscoupling: The Challenges and Consequences of Enacting a Practice in Decline

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often continue using practices even as broader institutional support for those practices declines, creating a lag between current conditions and organizational behavior. While research has explored how practices emerge or become entrenched, less is known about how people enact practices during decline, especially when legitimacy, familiarity, and supporting narratives fade. This paper addresses this gap by studying the challenges of performing a practice under conditions of 'temporal miscoupling'—when a practice persists despite being out of step with the contemporary institutional environment. Drawing on a field study of a labor strike in Canada, the authors examine how strikers coped with eroding political, legal, and cultural support, lack of experience, and minimal guidance. The study uses inhabited institutionalism and symbolic interactionism to analyze how people improvise local meanings and routines when traditional resources are absent. The key contribution is the concept of temporal miscoupling, which highlights how practice enactment in decline not only struggles to reproduce intended outcomes but also generates new, localized resources that may further undermine the practice’s historical meaning and future viability.

title: Do Investors Value Workforce Gender Diversity?

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing attention to workplace diversity, little is known about how investors react to disclosures of workforce gender composition. Prior research has largely focused on board-level diversity or used correlational designs that cannot establish causality. This paper addresses this gap by investigating whether investors respond to workforce gender diversity news as reflected in stock market reactions. The authors use event studies of U.S. technology and financial firms to test whether diversity disclosures trigger significant stock price changes. They also conduct randomized experiments with investors to examine psychological mechanisms. Their main finding is that investors react more positively when firms reveal relatively higher gender diversity. The key contribution is providing plausibly causal evidence that investors value workforce gender diversity, highlighting a new 'investor case' for diversity distinct from traditional productivity-based arguments.

title: Through the Narrows: The Meaning and Enactment of Interpersonal Holding

entries.rq_with_context: Individuals in organizations often face distress that not only stems from external circumstances but also triggers self-limiting internal responses, leaving them unable to fully access their agentic capacities. While existing research on organizational helping focuses on restoring role performance through instrumental or emotional support, it does not address how people become diminished in their sense of self. This gap is critical because traditional forms of help may fail when individuals are psychologically trapped in narrowed ways of being. The study asks: what are the behaviors that constitute interpersonal holding—a form of helping dedicated to surfacing, expanding, and integrating recessed aspects of the self? Drawing on in-depth interviews with professionals working in extreme caregiving contexts, the author uses grounded theory to identify a sequence of holding behaviors. The key contribution is a theoretical model of holding as a relational process that attends directly to the person (not just the role), offering new insight into how individuals can be supported to grow beyond self-imposed constraints during distress.

title: A Buddhist Mindfulness View of Paradox: Silence and Skepticism of Language to Dismantle Paradoxes

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations often face paradoxes involving contradictory demands, such as pursuing both economic and spiritual goals. While existing research focuses on cognitive and emotional strategies to manage tensions, this study explores how deep mindfulness practices may fundamentally alter the experience of paradox. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in three Korean Buddhist temples, where monks must reconcile spiritual ideals with business responsibilities, the paper identifies a gap in understanding how self-reflective practices like silence can dissolve rather than merely manage paradox. The research question is: how does Buddhist mindfulness—specifically silence and skepticism of language—help individuals dismantle paradox? Using an ethnographic approach and Yogācāra Buddhist philosophy as a theoretical lens, the study traces cognitive mechanisms that lead monks from differentiation to integration and ultimately to a nonexperience of paradox. The key contribution is proposing that mindfulness can eliminate paradox by undermining the linguistic categories that create it.

title: Organizational Selection of Innovation

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations face pressure to allocate limited resources to innovation projects, often relying on multiple decision makers to evaluate proposals. However, individual assessments are noisy, especially for unfamiliar projects, leading to suboptimal selection. Prior research has examined aggregation rules like voting and averaging in project approval contexts, but these do not account for budget-constrained portfolio selection that requires discrimination among alternatives. This paper addresses this gap by asking how different aggregation rules perform when organizations must select a subset of high-performing projects under resource limits. Using a simulation model based on Csaszar and Eggers (2013), the authors compare individual, delegation, voting, averaging, and ranking rules. Their key finding is that ranking—aggregating agents’ ranked lists via Borda count—often yields superior portfolio performance, particularly under tight budgets and uncertain expertise alignment.

title: Cultural Spawning: Founders Bringing Organizational Cultures to Their Startup

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational culture is foundational for startups, which lack formal structures and rely on culture for coordination. While genealogical effects—where new ventures inherit practices from prior employers—are documented, direct evidence of cultural transmission remains lacking due to culture's unobservable nature. This paper addresses the gap by asking whether and under what conditions founders bring elements of their former organization’s culture to their startups. The authors argue that cultural spawning occurs through cognitive learning, which depends on how long founders worked at the parent, how internally consistent the parent’s culture is, and how distinct it is from others. Using natural language processing on Glassdoor reviews of U.S. tech startups and matching methods, they test these predictions. The study contributes by providing empirical evidence of cultural spawning and identifying key contingencies related to learning and recognition in cultural transmission.

title: Improving Virtual Team Collaboration Paradox Management: A Field Experiment

entries.rq_with_context: Virtual teams are prevalent but face persistent collaboration challenges, particularly in balancing unity and diversity—the so-called team collaboration paradox. While paradox theory suggests that managing such tensions through a both/and approach could enhance performance, empirical evidence is scarce and scholars debate whether interventions can effectively improve paradox management. This study addresses this gap by testing whether team collaboration paradox management relates to team performance over time and whether it can be enhanced via a structured intervention. The authors use a field experiment with two waves of multisource data from 76 virtual teams across 37 organizations, comparing a control group with two intervention conditions: one with a single training session and another with an additional follow-up session. They find that only the intervention with a follow-up significantly improves paradox management and subsequent performance. The contribution lies in providing rare experimental evidence that paradox management can be improved and that follow-up sessions are critical for success.

title: The Indirect Effect of Entrepreneurship on Pay Dispersion: Entry Cost Reduction, Mobility Threat, and Wage Redistribution Within Incumbent Firms

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research has focused on the earnings of entrepreneurs themselves, this paper investigates how institutional changes that lower entrepreneurship costs indirectly affect compensation within established firms. The authors argue that existing studies overlook the strategic response of incumbent employers to heightened employee mobility threats, particularly the increased outside option value of starting a venture. They ask whether reduced entry costs lead to greater pay disparities among incumbent workers. Using a difference-in-differences design based on Portugal's 'On the Spot Firm' reform, they analyze how declining entrepreneurship costs influence wage distribution. Their key contribution is identifying mobility threat and bargaining power as mechanisms linking entrepreneurship policy to internal pay inequality.

title: Trailblazing Motivation and Marginalized Group Members: Changing Expectations to Pave the Way for Others

entries.rq_with_context: Employees from marginalized groups often face low performance expectations due to stereotypes, which can lead to negative outcomes like stereotype threat or more individual-focused responses like stereotype reactance. While past research emphasizes distancing from group identity to buffer these effects, less is known about when such expectations instead motivate people to improve opportunities for their entire group. This study addresses this gap by introducing 'trailblazing motivation'—a prosocial drive to break barriers for others. The research question is: when and how might a closer connection to one’s marginalized group drive people to increase opportunities for that broad group? Using a time-lagged survey and a preregistered experiment, the author tests a model integrating self-determination and regulatory focus theories. The key contribution is identifying a novel motivational response to low expectations that goes beyond self-focused coping and explains how belonging with one’s group can transform personal challenges into collective action.

title: Timing Is Everything: An Imprinting Framework for the Implications of Leader Emotional Expressions for Team Member Social Worth and Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Leader emotional expressions are known to influence team member performance by conveying information about social worth, such as respect and status. However, existing research largely overlooks how the timing of these expressions during a team’s lifecycle shapes their impact. While frequent positive or rare negative expressions are typically seen as beneficial, this paper questions whether early positive expressions may have enduring effects and whether later negative expressions might be interpreted differently depending on earlier emotional context. The research asks: How does the temporal sequence of leader emotional expressions—particularly positive ones early and negative ones mid-phase—affect individual performance through respect and status? The authors use an imprinting framework integrated with the social-functional approach to emotions, analyzing longitudinal data from consulting and sports teams. They argue that timing is a critical but underappreciated factor, and their key contribution is showing that early positivity imprints respect and enables later negativity to act as constructive 'jolts' rather than harmful signals.

title: Does a Theory-of-Value Add Value? Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial with Tanzanian Entrepreneurs

entries.rq_with_context: Entrepreneurs often face uncertainty when launching new ventures and are encouraged to use experimentation to validate their ideas. Two dominant approaches exist: an evidence-based approach emphasizing rapid hypothesis testing, and a theory-and-evidence–based approach that adds formal theory development before experimentation. While both methods promote learning, it remains unclear whether building a 'theory-of-value' provides additional benefits beyond experimentation alone. This gap is especially pertinent in developing economies where resources are scarce and training generalizability is uncertain. This study addresses these issues by conducting a randomized control trial with 151 Tanzanian agribusiness entrepreneurs assigned to either an evidence-based or theory-and-evidence–based training program. The research question asks whether the inclusion of theory development affects entrepreneurial outcomes. Using longitudinal data on business performance and model changes, the study compares revenue, profit, and termination rates. It finds that while both approaches similarly inform termination decisions, the theory-and-evidence–based approach leads to significantly higher economic performance.

title: Let Us Not Speak of Them, But Look and Pass? Organizational Responses to Online Reviews

entries.rq_with_context: Online reviews are increasingly influential in shaping organizational behavior, yet most research focuses only on public responses without examining actual offline actions. There is limited systematic evidence about how organizations integrate—or fail to integrate—online and offline reactions. This study addresses this gap by investigating when restaurants align their public promises with substantive changes and when they decouple them. Using a mixed-methods approach combining a lab-in-the-field experiment, archival data on TripAdvisor responses, and qualitative interviews with restaurant professionals in France, it analyzes factors that influence response coherence. The key contribution is identifying conditions under which organizations strategically separate rhetorical compliance from real change, advancing understanding of producer reactivity in digital evaluation contexts.

title: Female Entrepreneurs Targeting Women: Strategic Redirection Under Scientific Decision-Making

entries.rq_with_context: Female entrepreneurs who create value propositions targeting women may be constrained by their own user experiences, limiting their ability to assess broader market potential. While user entrepreneurship offers deep insight into needs, it can also lead to biased assumptions about commercial viability. Existing research has not adequately addressed how such entrepreneurs can overcome these cognitive limitations.
