This paper investigates how individual differences in cognitive reflection—the tendency to override intuitive responses with analytical thinking—affect decision accuracy in EBM contexts. It specifically compares active evidence collection versus passive presentation of evidence, and tests how cognitive and emotional load moderate these effects. Using three experimental studies, the authors examine when and how cognitive reflection enhances or fails to enhance decision-making accuracy. The key contribution is identifying boundary conditions for cognitive reflection in EBM, showing that its effectiveness depends on situational constraints and the mode of evidence access.

title: Participant Interactions with Artificial Intelligence: Using Large Language Models to Generate Research Materials for Surveys and Experiments

entries.rq_with_context: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT to create content for psychological studies, but clear guidance on valid and ethical implementation is lacking. Existing literature has explored LLM capabilities and biases, but there is no structured framework to guide organizational researchers in integrating LLMs into survey and experimental methods without compromising validity. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a decision-making framework with five use cases: LLM as research assistant, adaptive content creator, external resource, conversation partner, and research confederate. The authors also introduce QUAIL, an open-source tool that integrates LLM-generated content into Qualtrics. The research questions focus on when and how LLMs can be used effectively in research material creation, what technical steps support validity, and what ethical considerations must be addressed. The approach combines practical software development with a taxonomy of prompt design and a checklist for auditing validity.

title: Mind Your Own Business: Developing and Validating the Workplace Nosiness Scale

entries.rq_with_context: Although organizational privacy research has largely focused on formal monitoring technologies, little attention has been paid to informal interpersonal threats to privacy, such as intrusive information-seeking behaviors among employees. Despite the prevalence of everyday workplace communication, there is no established tool to measure whether certain information-seeking behaviors are perceived as nosy or intrusive. This study addresses this gap by developing and validating the Workplace Nosiness Scale. Using communication privacy management theory, the research examines how workplace nosiness—defined as intrusive attempts to gather private information—is influenced by factors like competitive climate and coworker liking, and how it relates to outcomes such as knowledge hiding and job stress. The key contribution is providing a valid, multidimensional scale that enables future research on informal privacy threats in organizations.

title: The Things I Do for You… and for Myself: Dyadic and Dynamic Effects of Social Support in Dual-Earner Couples

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the rise of dual-earner couples, gender norms may still shape how social support is provided and experienced at home, particularly under work-related stress. While prior research acknowledges the importance of spousal support, little is known about the day-to-day dynamics of support provision when both partners face job demands. The study addresses this gap by investigating how emotional exhaustion and work-to-family conflict influence daily support behaviors and well-being outcomes in couples. Using a daily diary design with an actor-partner interdependence model, the research examines both actor and partner effects, with attention to gender differences. It contributes by revealing asymmetric patterns in support dynamics—specifically, that women are more responsive to their husbands' distress, but men benefit more from being the provider—extending social role theory and social support resource theory.

title: Reducing Workplace Loneliness and Improving Well-Being of Full-Time Remote Workers: The Benefits of Sleep

entries.rq_with_context: With remote work becoming more common, workplace loneliness has emerged as a key concern for employee well-being. Although prior research suggests social interaction reduces loneliness, little is known about daily predictors of loneliness among fully remote workers, especially how personal resources like sleep may help. This study addresses this gap by testing whether sleep quality indirectly reduces daily workplace loneliness through greater vigor and coworker interactions. Using a within-person daily diary design across two samples—remote workers by choice (pre-pandemic) and by mandate (during COVID-19)—we apply Weiss’s (1973) model of loneliness and Quinn et al.’s (2012) model of human energy. The key contribution is identifying sleep as a modifiable daily resource that can mitigate loneliness, but only under certain remote work conditions.

title: How Charismatic Leadership Facilitates Unethical Pro‑supervisor Behavior: The Mediating Effect of Relational Energy

entries.rq_with_context: Charismatic leadership is widely associated with positive employee outcomes, yet its potential to trigger unethical behaviors—specifically unethical actions that benefit supervisors (UPSB)—remains underexplored. While prior research emphasizes the moral and motivational benefits of charisma, there is limited understanding of its unintended negative consequences. This study addresses this gap by investigating how charismatic leadership may lead to UPSB via the psychological resource of relational energy. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory, the authors propose that charismatic leaders energize employees, who then engage in UPSB to preserve these resource-generating relationships. The study further explores moral identity as a moderating factor, testing whether employees with strong moral self-concepts resist this pathway. Using multi-source, time-lagged data from 422 Chinese supervisor-subordinate dyads, it tests a moderated mediation model. The research contributes by revealing a previously overlooked mechanism through which charismatic leadership can inadvertently encourage unethical behavior, offering both theoretical refinement and managerial insight.

title: I Caught It, Now What Do I Do With It? Controlling For Insufficient Effort Responding

entries.rq_with_context: Self-report survey data are vulnerable to insufficient effort responding (IER), where participants provide inaccurate responses due to lack of attention, motivation, or effort. While numerous techniques exist to detect IER, the standard remedy—removing flagged respondents—risks reducing sample size, statistical power, and introducing sampling bias, especially since IER may be trait-like and related to demographics and personality. Existing alternatives, such as subgroup analyses or using IER scores as control variables, do not fully address the biasing influence of IER on substantive relationships. This study asks whether modeling IER as a directly measured latent method factor—a technique borrowed from common method variance research—can effectively detect and control for IER’s distorting effects on data. Using confirmatory factor analysis across two independent samples, the authors apply this method to examine how IER influences reliability and validity. They claim this approach offers a systematic, statistically sound alternative that retains more data while directly accounting for measurement error due to IER.

title: Balancing Accuracy and Acceptance of Algorithmic Hiring Decisions: Put the Human Touch into the Equation

entries.rq_with_context: Although algorithmic (mechanical) prediction is more valid than human (holistic) judgment in hiring decisions, it is rarely used because it restricts decision-makers’ autonomy, creating an 'autonomy-validity dilemma.' Prior research shows that allowing discretion—such as adjusting algorithmic outputs (clinical synthesis)—can increase acceptance but may compromise consistency and validity. This paper investigates two hybrid models—clinical and mechanical synthesis—to determine if they can improve predictive validity over holistic prediction while maintaining user acceptance. The authors test whether mechanical synthesis, which incorporates human judgment as a weighted input into an algorithm, offers a better trade-off than clinical synthesis, where humans adjust algorithmic outputs. The contribution lies in identifying mechanical synthesis as a method that enhances validity more than clinical synthesis and is perceived more positively in some aspects, thus offering a viable solution to the autonomy-validity trade-off.

title: Purity in Mire: Examining the Impact of Family Motivation on Employee Time Theft from an Impression Management Perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Time theft is a widespread and costly issue in organizations, yet research on individual-level factors like family motivation remains limited. While family motivation is known to drive work effort, its connection to unethical behaviors like time theft is unclear and potentially contradictory—some evidence suggests it may encourage deviance for family gain, while other reasoning implies it could discourage such behaviors to protect job stability. This study addresses this gap by exploring how family motivation is linked to different forms of time theft through the lens of impression management. Drawing on the idea that employees with strong family motivation are concerned with maintaining a positive professional image to secure long-term income, the research tests whether they are less likely to engage in observable or severely punished time theft. Using a three-wave survey and a scenario-based experiment, the study examines the mediating role of impression management motives and the moderating role of perceived workplace time theft norms.

title: When Less Is Not More: Incomplete Information in LinkedIn Assessments and the Moderating Role of Applicants’ Résumé

entries.rq_with_context: Recruiters increasingly use LinkedIn and other social media to assess job candidates, but profiles often contain incomplete or inconsistent information, creating ambiguity in hiring decisions. While prior research shows decision-makers prefer complete information, it is unclear how this 'incomplete information bias' operates in digital contexts like LinkedIn assessments. This paper investigates how varying levels of LinkedIn information affect hireability ratings and explores the underlying mechanisms (e.g., trustworthiness, professionalism). The authors test this across two contexts: when LinkedIn is the sole source (active sourcing) and when it supplements a full résumé (background check). Using experimental and interview methods, they find that incomplete profiles reduce hireability in active sourcing but not when a résumé is available. The study contributes by adapting the traditional incomplete information paradigm to digital selection and showing how context moderates its effects.

title: Stroke My Ego, I Will Scratch Your Back: Employee Narcissism and Supervisor Supplication on LMX and OCB

entries.rq_with_context: Employee narcissism is typically linked to poor interpersonal relationships and lower-quality social exchanges in organizations, often resulting in reduced leader–member exchange (LMX) and organizational citizenship behaviors (OCB). While prior research has focused on the direct negative effects of narcissism, less is known about managerial strategies that might mitigate these outcomes. This study addresses a gap by investigating whether supervisor supplication—a tactic involving feigned incompetence or need for help—can alter how narcissistic employees perceive LMX. Drawing on social exchange theory, the authors argue that narcissists, who desire recognition and superiority, may interpret supplication as a valuable relational resource, leading to improved LMX perceptions and subsequent OCB. The research uses both an experimental study (N = 163) and a field study (N = 376 dyads) to test a moderated mediation model. The key contribution is showing that a managerial impression management tactic can positively influence workplace outcomes for narcissistic employees, shifting focus from narcissism's inherent downsides to contextual strategies that can improve relational dynamics.

title: The Roles of Workplace Ostracism and Perceived Power in Predicting Abusive Supervision

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational research has established that abusive supervision is often triggered by threats supervisors experience from superiors or subordinates. However, little attention has been paid to how threats from peer coworkers—equally important sources of workplace social connection—might contribute to abusive behaviors. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether workplace ostracism by peer coworkers provokes abusive supervision as a form of displaced reactance. Drawing on reactance theory, the authors propose that being ostracized thwarts supervisors’ sense of control, leading them to restore it through abuse toward subordinates. They further suggest that this mediation is stronger when supervisors perceive lower levels of power. Using an experimental design (Study 1) and a field survey in South Korea (Study 2), the study tests this moderated mediation model. The authors claim this work advances understanding of abusive supervision by identifying peer-level ostracism as a novel antecedent and highlighting the psychological mechanism and boundary condition involved.

title: The Downside of Ethical Convictions: Why and When Employees Reduce Ethical Voice in Response to Perceived Supervisor Ethical Conviction

entries.rq_with_context: Employees face ethical challenges in organizations and are encouraged to use ethical voice to address unethical practices. However, little research explores why they might withhold such voice, especially in response to supervisors' ethical stances. While ethical voice is promoted, supervisors with strong ethical convictions may unintentionally suppress it by appearing rigid and controlling. This study fills that gap by examining how perceived supervisor ethical conviction negatively affects employee ethical voice through diminished self-perceived status and moral ownership, drawing on the group engagement model. Using time-lagged data from 281 employees in China, the research finds that these psychological mechanisms explain the suppression of ethical voice, especially when supervisors are seen as hypocritical. The study contributes by identifying a downside to strong ethical convictions and revealing the serial mediating process through which they inhibit voice.

title: How and When Team Mindfulness Enables Us to Navigate Adversity: Survey and Field Experimental Evidence

entries.rq_with_context: Teams frequently face adversity, yet little is known about how team mindfulness helps them cope and recover. While mindfulness has been linked to individual resilience, its role at the team level—especially during organizational crises—is unclear. Additionally, it remains unknown under what conditions (e.g., task structures) team mindfulness is most effective. This study addresses these gaps by investigating how team mindfulness fosters team resilience through emotional support and information sharing, and how team task interdependence strengthens these relationships. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory and team dynamics literature, the authors test a moderated mediation model using data from manufacturing and sales teams undergoing business transformation. The research contributes by identifying interpersonal mechanisms and boundary conditions that clarify when and how team mindfulness supports resilience.

title: Developmental Interactions Between Employees with Visual Impairments and Their Sighted Managers: A Process Theory

entries.rq_with_context: Despite technological advances, people with visual impairments remain underemployed in administrative roles due to a 'bilateral hesitation'—managers are reluctant to assign tasks, and employees wait for vision-free work. Prior research identifies attitudes and beliefs (e.g., implicit person theory) but fails to explain how these attitudes evolve over time or how to transform problematic interactions. This study aims to develop a process theory that reveals how attitudes combine, form, and lead to specific outcomes in developmental interactions. Using grounded theory analysis of 24 participants in Japan, the research investigates the sequence of interactions between employees and managers. Its contribution lies in offering a dynamic, stage-based model that explains when and how inclusion or exclusion unfolds, moving beyond static findings to actionable process insights.

title: Towards a Psychometrically Sound and Culturally Invariant Measure of Propensity to Trust

entries.rq_with_context: Propensity to trust is a well-established construct in organizational and psychological research, defined as a stable trait reflecting one’s general willingness to trust others. However, existing measures—including the widely used Mayer and Davis (1999) scale—have shown low reliability (e.g., Cronbach’s alpha below 0.70), questionable validity due to use of the word 'trust' in items and reverse-coded items, and lack of evidence for cross-cultural invariance. This gap limits the validity of international trust research. The current study addresses these issues by developing and validating a new propensity to trust scale through three studies. The research question is whether a new scale can be created that is reliable, valid, and invariant across cultures. Using data from 2,786 working adults across 30 countries, the authors test the scale’s psychometric properties and invariance across GLOBE clusters and tightness-looseness cultural dimensions. The key claimed contribution is the first culturally invariant measure of propensity to trust, enabling more robust cross-cultural research.

title: Improving Advisor Systems: Algorithms that Explain Themselves

entries.rq_with_context: Algorithms often outperform human judgment in decision-making tasks like hiring, yet people resist using them, partly because algorithmic advice lacks the explanations typically provided by human advisors. Prior research shows that transparency about algorithm design does not always increase trust or use. This study tests whether brief, case-by-case narrative explanations from an algorithm—linking its rating to specific applicant data—can improve decision makers’ trust, advice use, and judgment outcomes. Using a hiring simulation with real assessment data, the authors compare narrative versus numeric advice, narrative versus descriptive algorithm introductions, and default settings. They find that narrative explanations slightly increase trust, perceived human interaction, intention to use, judgment consistency, and accuracy when advice is not the default, suggesting that 'explaining itself' makes algorithms feel more human and usable.

title: Leadership Dynamics in Teams: The Reciprocity of Shared and Empowering Leadership

entries.rq_with_context: Leadership is increasingly seen as a dynamic, reciprocal process rather than a unidirectional influence from formal leaders. While prior research has focused on how formal leaders foster shared leadership, less is known about how followers' collective leadership efforts shape formal leaders' behaviors. This study addresses that gap by investigating how shared leadership at the team level influences empowering leadership over time. The authors propose that when teams engage in shared leadership, formal leaders respond by trusting their team more, which then encourages them to exhibit more empowering leadership. They further hypothesize that this indirect relationship is moderated by leader self-efficacy—leaders with higher confidence may be more responsive to shared leadership. Using a three-wave longitudinal design with Bayesian cross-lagged panel modeling, the study tests these dynamics. The key contribution is advancing understanding of leadership as co-constructed through mutual influence, highlighting trust as a mechanism linking informal team behavior to formal leadership change.

title: Staying in a Stressful Job? The Role of Job Embeddedness for Truck Drivers’ Well-Being and Turnover Intentions

entries.rq_with_context: Truck drivers face high levels of work stress due to time pressure, situational constraints, and electronic surveillance, contributing to high turnover in an already strained industry. While prior research shows job embeddedness reduces turnover intentions, it remains unclear how organizational and community embeddedness interact with different types of stressors to influence well-being and turnover. This study investigates whether being embedded in the organization or community buffers the adverse effects of these stressors among local truck drivers—a blue-collar group often underrepresented in research. Using conservation of resources (COR) theory, the authors test if embeddedness serves as a resource pool that mitigates stressor-outcome relationships. The key contribution is demonstrating that community embeddedness can both buffer and exacerbate outcomes depending on the stressor type, challenging assumptions about its uniformly beneficial role.

title: “When I Have the Advantage, I Prefer AI!” The Influence of an Applicant’s Relative Advantage on the Preference for Artificial Intelligence Decision-making

entries.rq_with_context: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in human resource management, yet applicants' responses to AI decision-making remain inconsistent across studies. While some perceive AI as fair and objective, others view it as opaque and biased. This paper addresses the gap in understanding why applicants differ in their preferences by investigating the role of relative advantage—applicants’ perception of their competitiveness compared to others. Drawing on prospect theory, the authors propose that applicants who are at an advantage prefer AI decision-making because they seek consistency to maintain their favorable position, whereas disadvantaged applicants prefer human decision-makers for greater variability and risk. The study uses survey and experimental data across multiple HR scenarios to test this idea. Its key contribution is revealing how applicant heterogeneity shapes AI acceptance, clarifying conflicting findings in the literature.

title: From Strengths Mindset to Knowledge Sharing: Roles of Self-Efficacy and Strengths-based Human Resource System

entries.rq_with_context: Knowledge sharing is essential for organizational learning and innovation, yet the psychological antecedents that drive such behavior remain incompletely understood. While prior research has focused on situational and personality-based factors, the role of employee mindset—specifically, a strengths mindset—has received limited attention. This study addresses this gap by investigating how a strengths mindset affects knowledge sharing among employees. Drawing on social cognitive theory and person-situation interactionism, we propose that strengths mindset enhances self-efficacy, which in turn promotes knowledge sharing, and that this mediated relationship is stronger when employees perceive their organization as having a strengths-based HR system. Using a two-study design with three-wave data from Chinese employees in different industries, we test a moderated mediation model. Our findings clarify the psychological mechanism and contextual boundary condition that explain when and how strengths mindset contributes to knowledge sharing.

title: Advancing Organizational Science Through Synthetic Data: A Path to Enhanced Data Sharing and Collaboration

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational science faces persistent challenges in data sharing due to privacy, proprietary concerns, and ethical restrictions, limiting transparency and reproducibility. While open science initiatives encourage data availability, actual sharing rates remain low. Synthetic data—artificially generated data that mimics the statistical properties of real data without containing actual individual records—offers a potential solution. This study addresses two key questions: (1) How well do synthetic datasets replicate analytic results from original data (substitutability)? (2) How effectively do they prevent overlap or re-identification (security)? Using generative adversarial networks (GANs), the authors apply a systematic framework to two empirical datasets. Their approach includes generating synthetic data and evaluating it through basic and use-specific tests. The contribution lies in introducing a practical framework tailored to organizational researchers unfamiliar with machine learning methods, thereby supporting broader adoption of synthetic data as a tool for enhancing data sharing.

title: The Scholarly Impact of Industrial-Organizational Psychologists in Academia: Normative Data and Construct Validity

entries.rq_with_context: Scholarly impact is a key criterion in academic evaluation, especially for promotion and tenure, yet there is limited field-specific normative data to interpret what counts as strong impact. While bibliometric indicators like the h-index are widely used, their interpretation often lacks standardized benchmarks, particularly within subfields like industrial-organizational (I-O) psychology. Existing studies provide broad norms across psychology or collapse data across departments and career stages, limiting their utility. This study addresses this gap by generating normative data specifically for I-O psychologists in research-focused academic positions (N = 1075) who are members of SIOP. The research questions are: (1) What are the normative levels of scholarly impact across multiple metrics? (2) How do various bibliometric indicators relate, testing their construct validity? (3) How does impact vary by department, rank, and fellow status? (4) How well do individual rankings based on textbook citations converge with standard bibliometric metrics? The study uses descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, nonparametric ANOVAs, and exploratory factor analysis. Its main contribution is providing field-specific norms and evidence on the validity and differentiation of impact metrics.

title: Guilty When Proven Innocent? The Lingering Negative Effects of False Accusations on Trust and Organizational Decision-Making

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational hiring decisions heavily rely on reputational information, which can be inaccurate due to false accusations. While research has explored how reputations influence trust, less is known about whether exonerating evidence can fully restore trust after a false accusation. This study addresses that gap by testing whether false accusations continue to harm trust and hiring outcomes even after being disproven, particularly focusing on the difference between competence- versus integrity-based accusations. Using four experimental studies with working adults in hiring manager roles, the authors examine how trust and hiring decisions evolve after a refutation. The key contribution is demonstrating that refuted false accusations concerning integrity—unlike those concerning competence—continue to undermine trust and hiring, not because trust is harder to repair, but because the initial erosion is greater.

title: Selective Incivility Toward Black Employees Fuels Social Pain Minimization and Defensive Silence

entries.rq_with_context: Workplace incivility disproportionately impacts Black employees and can lead to employee silence, where individuals withhold information due to fear of mistreatment. While prior research has linked incivility to negative outcomes, less is known about the psychological mechanisms connecting incivility to silence, especially among Black employees. This paper addresses that gap by testing whether social pain minimization—defined as the invalidation of emotional distress when seeking support—mediates the effect of incivility on defensive silence. Using three studies with multi-wave and experimental designs, the authors examine this process specifically among Black employees. They find consistent evidence that incivility predicts social pain minimization, which then increases defensive silence. The work contributes by identifying a key socioemotional mechanism linking incivility to organizational withdrawal behaviors in marginalized groups.

title: Sustainable Leadership for Employee Performance and the Moderating Roles of Family-Work Conflict and Work Pressure: The Job Demands–Resources Perspective

entries.rq_with_context: Sustainable leadership is increasingly recognized for its role in promoting long-term organizational and societal development, yet its impact on employee-level performance remains underexplored. While some organizations worry that sustainable practices may harm employee performance, evidence suggests it could enhance motivation and outcomes. However, the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which sustainable leadership influences performance—particularly via work engagement—and how job demands like family–work conflict and work pressure shape these relationships are not well understood. Drawing on the job demands–resources (JD–R) theory, this study investigates whether work engagement mediates the link between sustainable leadership and employee in- and extra-role performance, and whether family–work conflict and work pressure act as moderating factors. Using a multilevel approach across two studies—one in a high-risk industry (coal mining) and another in diverse general industries—the study tests these relationships at both between- and within-person levels. The findings contribute to clarifying when and how sustainable leadership improves employee performance by identifying the motivational process and contextual contingencies that determine its effectiveness.

title: Intersectional Penalties for Perceived Interpersonal Justice Violations among Black and Hispanic Male Leaders in the Workplace

entries.rq_with_context: Despite growing awareness of racial inequities, Black and Hispanic men continue to face workplace disadvantages linked to stereotypes portraying them as aggressive and dangerous—stereotypes historically tied to systemic racism in criminal justice. While prior research has explored barriers to leadership for underrepresented groups, less attention has been paid to how these leaders are judged once in position, especially when displaying behaviors seen as agentic or aggressive. This paper investigates whether Black and Hispanic male leaders suffer harsher evaluations and relational consequences for interpersonal injustice compared to White male leaders and Black or Hispanic female leaders. Drawing on the MOSAIC model of intersectional stereotyping and organizational justice theory, the authors use two field studies with employee-subordinate dyads to test their hypotheses. They find that subordinates react more negatively to interpersonal injustice from Black or Hispanic male leaders, not because of greater fear, but because such actions are seen as violating societal norms about how these men 'ought' to behave.

title: Reconsidering the Trade-off Between Speed and Accuracy: The Role of Perceived Goal Progress Velocity

entries.rq_with_context: The speed-accuracy trade-off is well-established: faster task completion typically leads to more mistakes. However, prior research has not considered how subjective perceptions of speed—specifically, feeling slow—impact accuracy. This study addresses the gap by investigating whether slow perceived progress velocity, even when actual speed is constant, can hinder accuracy through increased frustration. Drawing on Carver and Scheier’s control theory, the authors test the idea that falling below a desired rate of progress (velocity referent) triggers frustration, which narrows attention and harms accuracy. The experiment manipulates perceived velocity by varying practice trial speed while holding actual task speed constant. The research contributes by showing that subjective speed perceptions, not just objective speed, influence accuracy—adding nuance to traditional trade-off models.

title: The Impact of Inclusive Leadership on Team Innovation: A Moderated Chain Mediation Model

entries.rq_with_context: Team innovation is critical for organizational success, especially in diverse and competitive environments. While previous research has linked various leadership styles to innovation, inclusive leadership uniquely addresses both belongingness and uniqueness of team members—key prerequisites for innovation. However, the mechanisms through which inclusive leadership enhances innovation by integrating team diversity remain unclear. This study addresses this gap by investigating the mediating roles of team diversity climate and team reflexivity, drawing on Team Regulation Theory (TRT), which suggests that environmental factors like leadership dynamically regulate team cognitions and actions. The study also examines team career calling as a boundary condition that may strengthen the link between diversity climate and reflexivity. Using a four-wave time-lagged survey of 119 teams, the research employs path analysis and bootstrapping to test a moderated chain mediation model. The key contribution is clarifying the process through which inclusive leadership leverages diversity resources to foster innovation, thereby enriching understanding of team regulation and diversity outcomes.

title: Effects of Racial Demographics, Ideology, and Economic Threat on Majority Group Discrimination Claims

entries.rq_with_context: As the U.S. becomes more racially diverse, some White Americans express concerns about anti-White discrimination, particularly when they perceive threats to their social or economic status. While prior research has explored individual attitudes about White victimhood, little is known about how community-level factors relate to actual discrimination claiming behavior. This study investigates whether the proportion of people of color in a county predicts the prevalence of formal anti-White discrimination claims, and whether political conservatism and White unemployment moderate this relationship. Using geocoded EEOC data linked to county-level demographic and economic data, the authors test these associations across U.S. counties. They claim their work provides the first large-scale evidence linking macro-level social contexts to behavioral manifestations of majority group status concerns.

title: Following the Rules to Drive Innovation: A Resource Conservation and Allocation Model of Work Standardization and Innovation

entries.rq_with_context: Despite the widespread use of work standardization for efficiency and reliability, its effect on team innovation remains unclear, with prior research showing both positive and negative outcomes. A key gap is the lack of distinction between creative idea generation and their implementation, and how resource-related mechanisms and motivational factors jointly shape innovation outcomes. This study addresses this by proposing that standardization conserves resources that can be used for idea implementation, but only when teams are incentivized to allocate those resources toward innovation. The research question is: How do work standardization and rewards for innovation jointly moderate the relationship between team creativity and innovation? The study uses a resource conservation and allocation framework, integrating expectancy theory, and tests this via a multilevel field study and a controlled experiment. The authors claim the study clarifies the ambiguous role of standardization by identifying when and how it supports innovation.

title: Why Do Applicants (Dis)Like Selection Methods? The Role of Stimulus and Response Format for Need Satisfaction

entries.rq_with_context: Applicants often react more positively to interviews than to personality inventories, but it is unclear which specific features of selection methods drive these reactions. Prior research compares whole instruments but does not isolate methodological features or explain the underlying psychological mechanisms. This study addresses this gap by examining two method factors—stimulus format and response format—and their impact on applicant reactions through the lens of self-determination theory. Using a 2×2 experimental design with personality assessments that vary only in format, the study asks how these method factors affect perceptions of interpersonal warmth and opportunity to perform, and whether need satisfaction mediates these relationships. The approach allows for isolating format effects while holding content constant. The authors claim this contributes to both applicant reaction research and personnel selection design by identifying specific levers for improving applicant experiences.

title: Servant Leadership and Cooperation: The Moderating Role of Leader Group Prototypicality

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research has established that servant leadership promotes follower cooperation, less is known about the conditions under which this effect holds. This study addresses the gap by investigating leader group prototypicality—whether followers see the leader as 'one of us'—as a boundary condition. The research question is whether servant leadership is more strongly related to cooperation when leaders are perceived as prototypical of the group. Drawing on social identity theory, the study uses a multi-study design including cross-sectional and longitudinal surveys to test this moderation effect and the mediating role of group identification. The key claimed contribution is clarifying when and through what mechanism servant leadership fosters cooperation, emphasizing prototypicality as a critical yet overlooked boundary condition.

title: From Emotional Rollercoasters to Spock Strategists: A Person-Centric Approach to Unravelling the Coping Profiles of Entrepreneurs for Enhanced Well-being

entries.rq_with_context: Entrepreneurs face high levels of stress yet often report greater well-being than waged workers, a phenomenon potentially explained by their coping strategies. While past research has examined individual coping strategies in isolation—typically problem-focused versus emotion-focused—this approach overlooks how people combine strategies in practice. The authors address this gap by identifying distinct coping profiles among the self-employed using a person-centric approach. They use Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) to uncover common configurations of coping strategies, examine how these profiles relate to well-being outcomes, compare profile distributions between self-employed and waged workers, and explore determinants such as personality and education. The study's contribution lies in moving beyond single-strategy analyses to reveal nuanced patterns in how entrepreneurs cope and thrive.

title: Parent–Adolescent Transmission of Emotional Exhaustion: Testing a Social-Cognitive Spillover and Crossover Model

entries.rq_with_context: Emotional exhaustion among working parents is a growing concern with implications extending beyond the workplace into family life and adolescent well-being. While prior research has shown that work-related stress can spill over into the home domain and crossover to family members, less is known about the specific mechanisms through which emotional exhaustion is transmitted to adolescents. The authors identify a gap in understanding how emotional labor—specifically surface acting—serves as a behavioral mechanism in this transmission process. Drawing on social cognitive theory, they propose that adolescents learn emotion regulation strategies by observing their parents. The study investigates whether parents' emotional exhaustion leads to increased surface acting at home, which in turn is adopted by adolescents at school, resulting in emotional exhaustion. Using a four-wave longitudinal design with 256 Chinese families, the study tests this spillover-crossover model and examines parent-adolescent relationship quality as a potential moderator. The research contributes to the literature by identifying a novel social learning pathway for the intergenerational transmission of emotional exhaustion.

title: The Mixed Blessing of Dancing with Star Employees: A Social-Comparison-Based Analysis of the Effects of Star Employees on Non-Stars

entries.rq_with_context: Star employees are recognized for their high performance, visibility, and social capital, yet their presence can have mixed effects on non-star colleagues—ranging from inspiration to resentment. While existing research highlights both positive and negative impacts, there is limited integrative understanding of the psychological mechanisms behind these dual effects. This study addresses the gap by asking: under what conditions do non-stars respond positively or negatively to star employees? Drawing on upward social comparison theory and the pain-driven dual envy (PaDE) framework, the authors propose that non-stars’ expected future similarity with stars determines whether they experience benign or malicious envy. The research uses a scenario-based experiment (Study 1) and a multi-wave field survey (Study 2) to test this model. The key contribution is identifying expected future similarity as a boundary condition that explains when star employees inspire emulation versus incite harmful gossip.

title: Performing for Status: A Hierometer Approach to Follower Narcissism and the Impact of Leader-Member Exchange on Follower Performance

entries.rq_with_context: The paper investigates why some followers improve their job performance in response to high-quality Leader-Member Exchange (LMX) relationships while others do not. While LMX theory suggests that mutual trust and respect motivate performance through fulfilling a need to belong, prior research shows inconsistent support—particularly among individuals high in traits like extraversion or agreeableness that reflect strong belongingness needs. This raises questions about alternative motivational drivers. The authors propose that status fulfillment, rather than belongingness, may better explain performance reciprocation in LMX relationships. Drawing on hierometer theory, they argue that individuals sensitive to status—such as those high in grandiose narcissism—are more likely to increase performance when they experience high LMX, especially if they perceive their leader as holding high organizational status or feel envied by coworkers. Using latent change regression analysis of performance appraisals over one year in two field studies (N = 198 and 282), the study tests whether narcissism and status-related cues moderate the LMX-performance link. The research contributes by challenging the dominant sociometer-based interpretation of LMX and offering status-driven mechanisms to explain when and for whom LMX translates into performance gains.

title: Sick of Leading? Supervisory Responsibility and Its Consequences for Sickness Absenteeism and Sickness Presenteeism

entries.rq_with_context: Leadership positions are often seen as demanding and potentially harmful to health, contributing to organizational difficulties in filling such roles. However, research on the direct health consequences of supervisory responsibility remains mixed and often overlooks specific behaviors like sickness absenteeism and presenteeism. This study addresses this gap by investigating how holding a leadership role with supervisory responsibility impacts two key labor-market health behaviors: taking sick leave (absenteeism) and working while sick (presenteeism). Drawing on the job demands-resources (JD-R) model, it proposes that supervisory responsibility acts both as a job resource and a challenge demand, reducing absenteeism but increasing presenteeism. The analysis uses German employer-employee data to test these relationships, with permanent availability and time pressure posited as mediating mechanisms. The study contributes by clarifying the dual health implications of leadership roles and identifying specific job characteristics that drive these outcomes.

title: Here’s Looking at You: Does Eye Contact in Video Interviews Affect How Applicants are Perceived and Evaluated?

entries.rq_with_context: Video interviews are increasingly used in hiring, but prior research suggests applicants are often rated lower than in face-to-face interviews, with impaired eye contact proposed as a key reason. However, no experimental studies have tested this claim directly. This paper addresses that gap by examining how vertical and horizontal eye contact deviations—common in video setups—affect applicant perceptions. Using two experiments with recorded asynchronous video interviews, the authors test whether such deviations reduce interview performance ratings, hirability, warmth, competence, and social presence. They apply social presence theory and media richness theory to frame eye contact as a driver of perceived connection. The key contribution is providing causal evidence on whether and how eye contact impacts applicant evaluation in technology-mediated interviews.

title: The Dual Processes of Leader-Member Exchange Social Comparison

entries.rq_with_context: Leader-member exchange social comparison (LMXSC)—employees’ comparisons of their leader relationships with those of peers—is often viewed as beneficial for employee performance. However, this perspective overlooks potential downsides, particularly for certain individuals. This study addresses a gap in research by asking for whom and why LMXSC may be beneficial or harmful. Drawing on social information processing and social comparison theories, the authors propose a dual-process model: LMXSC can enhance perceptions of distributive, procedural, and interactional justice for employees high in psychological entitlement, boosting job performance. Conversely, for employees with high interdependent self-construal, LMXSC can trigger concerns about social-relational threats (CSRT), reducing job performance while increasing OCBI as a compensatory behavior. The study uses a multi-wave field design with supervisor-subordinate-coworker triads in China to test these ideas. It contributes by challenging the uniformly positive view of LMXSC and identifying individual differences that determine its mixed effects.

title: The More Contextualized, the More Valid: Effects of Contextualization Strategies on Forced-choice Measurement

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research shows that contextualizing personality measures (e.g., framing items around work) improves their criterion-related validity in single-statement formats, it remains unknown whether similar benefits apply to forced-choice (FC) measures, which are designed to reduce response biases and faking. The response processes in FC formats differ fundamentally from single-statement formats due to comparative judgments, raising uncertainty about the generalizability of contextualization effects. This study addresses this gap by experimentally testing three forms of contextualization—instructional, statement-based (tagged/complete), and combined—on two FC personality measures. Using a between-subjects design, it evaluates how these strategies affect reliability, criterion-related validity (for work and non-work outcomes), and discriminant validity. The key contribution is providing the first empirical evidence on how contextualization impacts FC measurement, offering guidance for optimizing their validity in personnel selection contexts.

title: Supporting Academic Parents: The Effects of Dependent Care Policies on Research Productivity Trends

entries.rq_with_context: Academic parents, particularly women, face challenges maintaining research productivity after childbirth due to increased family responsibilities. Despite calls to support faculty caregivers, little research has examined whether work-family policies like paid parental leave and childcare benefits effectively sustain long-term productivity. This study addresses that gap by testing how policy availability and use relate to objective research productivity trends—measured via top publications and h-index trajectories—using data from 386 business professors across 108 universities. Drawing on the work-home resources model, it examines whether these policies buffer productivity declines post-childbirth and whether effects vary by gender and birth order. The study contributes an objective, longitudinal analysis of policy impacts, offering clearer evidence than prior studies relying on subjective performance measures.

title: Recovery and Recidivism: The Aftermath of Helping the Organization Unethically

entries.rq_with_context: Unethical pro-organizational behavior (UPB), though intended to benefit the organization, violates ethical norms and creates moral tension for employees. While prior research has explored why UPB occurs, less is known about its aftermath, particularly the cognitive responses of perpetrators. Existing studies focus on affective reactions or short-term compensatory behaviors, but fail to account for the potential escalation of UPB over time. This study addresses this gap by investigating two opposing cognitive pathways following UPB: one leading to moral recovery and another to recidivism. Drawing on moral self-regulation and moral disengagement theories, it asks how UPB influences subsequent behaviors through perceived loss of moral credits and moral disengagement. The approach uses a dual-path model tested across an experimental (Study 1) and a longitudinal field study (Study 2) with service employees. The research contributes by revealing that UPB can simultaneously trigger constructive and destructive behavioral tendencies, offering a more nuanced understanding of post-UPB dynamics.

title: Examining Retaliation Intentions Among Stuck Employees

entries.rq_with_context: Employees who want to leave but feel unable to do so—termed 'stuck employees' or 'reluctant stayers'—represent a growing and understudied segment of the workforce. Research on employee retaliation has largely overlooked this group, despite evidence suggesting they may be more prone to counterproductive behaviors. The study addresses a gap by investigating how and when an employer's decision to compromise employee safety affects retaliation intentions, particularly through the lens of perceived organizational support. Using social exchange theory, the authors examine whether high levels of general organizational support typically reduce retaliation, but may instead increase it for stuck employees. They test a moderated mediation model using survey data from 327 U.S. workers exposed to vignettes about employer decisions regarding safety. The key contribution is identifying preexisting turnover intentions and perceived ease of leaving as boundary conditions that reverse the expected protective effect of organizational support.

title: An Unmet goal? A Scale Development and Model test of the role of Inclusive Leadership

entries.rq_with_context: Despite widespread advocacy for inclusive leadership (IL) as a solution to workplace inequity, there is limited empirical evidence on whether IL actually supports members of historically marginalized groups. Additionally, existing IL measures lack alignment with contemporary inclusion theory, particularly the dual components of belongingness and uniqueness. This study addresses these gaps by first developing and validating a new 10-item IL scale grounded in Randel et al.'s (2018) framework, then testing a model of how IL influences both interpersonal inclusion behaviors (allyship, antiracism) and personal experiences of inclusion (workgroup inclusion, authenticity). The study further investigates whether IL indirectly reduces emotional exhaustion and increases empowerment through these pathways. Using a multi-wave design with a diverse sample, the research applies social information processing and social learning theories to explain mechanisms. The primary contribution is providing empirically grounded evidence on IL’s role in supporting marginalized employees, offering both a practical measure and insights into its broader psychological impacts.

title: The Positive Spillover of Managers’ Ally Work: Perceptions of Manager Liberalism and Its Effect on Employee Volunteering

entries.rq_with_context: Managers’ ally work—actions to support less-advantaged social groups—has been studied primarily for its antecedents, especially how political ideology influences such behaviors. However, less is known about the downstream effects of managers’ ally work on observing employees. This paper shifts focus to explore the positive spillover of managers’ self ally work, defined as behaviors aimed at personal transformation to become a better ally. Drawing on the theory of political ideology-as-motivated cognition, the authors argue that employees perceive such behavior as signaling managerial liberalism, which in turn motivates politically aligned (liberal) employees to comply with volunteering requests. They propose that this spillover effect is limited to discretionary, politically resonant behaviors like volunteering and does not extend to more formally expected work behaviors. The study uses six empirical studies (field and experimental) to test these predictions, with positive appraisal of the volunteering request examined as an additional mechanism. The key contribution is identifying a novel spillover effect of ally work—on employee volunteering—while highlighting its ideological boundaries.

title: How to Frame the Frame of Reference: A Comparison of Contextualization Methods

entries.rq_with_context: Personality assessments are widely used in employment settings, yet their predictive power for job performance remains weaker than cognitive ability tests. Contextualization—modifying personality measures to reflect a specific frame of reference like work—has shown promise in improving validity. While prior research supports contextualization overall, few studies have directly compared its most common forms: instruction-level (modifying test instructions) and tag-level (adding 'at work' tags to items). One prior direct comparison yielded inconsistent results, and existing evidence is limited by cross-sectional designs and methodological variability. This study addresses that gap by directly comparing instruction- and tag-level contextualization using a rigorous within-person, time-lagged design with a working sample (N = 399). It evaluates both methods across multiple work-relevant criteria linked to each of the Big Five traits. The approach includes correlation comparisons, hierarchical regression, and relative weights analysis to assess incremental and relative predictive validity. The study aims to provide clear guidance on which method—tags or instructions—more effectively enhances personality assessment validity in organizational contexts.

title: To Add or to Multiply? Gender, Sexual Minority Status, and Sexual Harassment in the Norwegian Police Service

entries.rq_with_context: Sexual harassment remains a persistent issue in organizations, yet research often overlooks the role of sexual orientation. While both gender and sexual minority status are theorized to influence harassment risk, it is unclear how they interact—whether their effects are additive or multiplicative. In the context of the Norwegian Police Service—a setting with high gender equality and formal protections for sexual minorities—this study investigates if being a sexual minority heightens harassment risk similarly across genders. Using survey data from 4,386 employees, the authors test competing hypotheses about additive versus interactive effects. They find support for additive effects: both women and sexual minorities face higher odds of harassment independently. The key contribution is clarifying that sexual minority status elevates risk for both women and men, with sexual minority women facing the highest overall risk, even in a progressive national and organizational context.

title: Overqualified Employees’ Actual Turnover: The Role of Growth Dissatisfaction and the Contextual Effects of Age and Pay

entries.rq_with_context: Perceived overqualification is common and linked to higher turnover, but existing theories focusing on external comparisons (e.g., relative deprivation) may not fully explain why these employees leave, especially when such comparisons are favorable. This study addresses a gap by exploring internal motivations, specifically unfulfilled aspirations for personal growth, as a key driver of turnover among overqualified workers. The research question is: does growth dissatisfaction mediate the effect of perceived overqualification on actual turnover, and do age and pay moderate this relationship? Drawing on self-determination theory, the study uses three-year longitudinal data from South Korea (N = 2473). It contributes by identifying an internal psychological mechanism—growth satisfaction—that explains turnover beyond traditional external cognitive models.

title: Paternalism in the Performance Context: Evaluators Who Feel Social Pressure to Avoid Exhibiting Prejudice Deliver More Inflated Performance Feedback to Women

entries.rq_with_context: Performance feedback is essential for employee development, but research suggests women often receive less developmental feedback than men. While some studies show women receive more favorable qualitative feedback, the reasons behind this inflation remain unclear. This paper identifies a potential mechanism: feedback providers who feel social pressure to avoid appearing prejudiced may overcorrect by exhibiting protective paternalism, leading them to soften feedback for women. The authors test whether this external motivation to avoid prejudice increases protective paternalism, which in turn predicts more inflated feedback. Using both field and experimental data, the study examines this moderated mediation model to explain how well-intentioned bias can undermine feedback accuracy and perpetuate gender inequity.

title: How Virtual are We? Introducing the Team Perceived Virtuality Scale

entries.rq_with_context: With the rise of remote and hybrid work, understanding how team virtuality affects collaboration has become critical. However, existing research relies heavily on structural indicators (e.g., frequency of technology use, geographic dispersion), which fail to explain inconsistent findings about virtual team effectiveness. This gap suggests that subjective experiences of virtuality may matter more than objective conditions. The study addresses this by developing and validating a scale for Team Perceived Virtuality (TPV), defined as a shared emergent state reflecting collectively-experienced distance and information deficits. Using five studies across diverse samples, the authors test the construct’s structural, discriminant, and criterion validity. The key contribution is a psychometrically sound, theory-grounded instrument that captures how virtuality is experienced, offering a new way to assess team dynamics beyond structural metrics.

title: When Words Matter: Communal and Agentic Language on Men and Women’s Resumes

entries.rq_with_context: Despite progress toward gender equality, women remain underrepresented in leadership and STEM fields, partly due to gender stereotypes that disadvantage them in hiring. Prior research shows others describe female applicants in more communal and less agentic terms, which harms their evaluations. However, little is known about how men and women describe themselves on actual resumes. This study fills that gap by analyzing real and experimentally generated resumes to determine whether gender differences in self-presentation exist and what consequences they have. The research asks: (1) Do women use more communal and less agentic language than men on their resumes across job types? (2) Does communal language reduce perceived leadership ability and hireability, especially for women applying to masculine-typed jobs? The study uses linguistic content analysis (LIWC) across three studies—archival resume analysis, experimental resume writing, and experimental evaluation—to test these questions. The authors claim the work advances understanding of how self-perceptions of gender norms shape applicant behavior and contribute to workplace disparities.

title: The Influence of Working from Home vs. Working at the Office on Job Performance in a Hybrid Work Arrangement: A Diary Study

entries.rq_with_context: The shift to hybrid work has made it important to understand how working from home (WFH) versus working at the office (WATO) impacts job performance on a daily level. Prior research shows a positive correlation between remote work and performance but lacks understanding of the underlying mechanisms, especially using within-person designs. This study addresses that gap by investigating the mediating roles of daily concentration, social isolation, work engagement, and tension. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) theory, it proposes both motivational and health-impairment pathways. Using an 8-day diary study with 203 employees in a public organization, the research applies multilevel SEM to test indirect effects. The main contribution is identifying specific daily processes—both beneficial and detrimental—through which WFH influences performance.

title: Promoting Voice: The Interplay of Job Reflective Learning, Risk-taking Climate, and Age

entries.rq_with_context: Employees' reflective learning is increasingly seen as important for organizational adaptation, but less is known about its effects on specific proactive behaviors like promotive voice—voicing new ideas to improve work processes. While social cognitive theory suggests that reflection can lead to proactive behavior, the role of organizational context and individual differences in this process remains unclear. Existing research has not sufficiently examined how environmental factors like risk-taking climate or personal characteristics like age might shape the impact of reflective learning on voice. This study addresses this gap by exploring how RTC and age moderate the relationship between job reflective learning and promotive voice. Using data from South Korean employees, it applies hierarchical regression to test a three-way interaction. The key contribution is showing that the effect of reflective learning on voice is not uniform—it depends on both organizational climate and employee age.

title: Bringing Self-Determination Theory to the Forefront: Examining How Human Resource Practices Motivate Employees of All Ages to Succeed

entries.rq_with_context: Despite widespread use of self-determination theory (SDT) in HR research, there is limited empirical evidence establishing the full mediational pathway—HR practices leading to basic psychological need satisfaction, which then enhances autonomous motivation and improves work outcomes. Prior studies often invoke SDT without measuring all components simultaneously, leaving theoretical gaps. This study addresses this by testing a complete SDT-based model using longitudinal data from 818 employees. The authors examine how perceptions of HR practices affect performance, thriving, commitment, and turnover intentions via need satisfaction and motivation. They also explore age as a moderator, responding to calls for age-inclusive HR frameworks. The approach uses multilevel structural equation modeling to assess mediation and moderated mediation, offering a more rigorous test of SDT in HR contexts than prior work.

title: The Influence of Employment Quality on Employee Health Complaints: A Parallel Mediation Model

entries.rq_with_context: Employment quality is recognized as a social determinant of employee health, yet little is known about the underlying psychological mechanisms linking them. While prior research shows that high-quality employment (e.g., permanent, full-time, higher salary) is associated with better health, most studies have not explored how or why this occurs. This study addresses this gap by investigating two potential mediators: work engagement (a positive motivational state) and affective job insecurity (an emotional stress response). Using a time-lagged design with three measurement points, the authors test a parallel mediation model across 247 employees. The approach is grounded in the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) theory, which suggests both motivational and health-impairment pathways. The study contributes to understanding the mechanisms behind employment quality’s impact on health, offering insights for both theory and policy.

title: Interest Gaps in the Labor Market: Comparing People’s Vocational Interests with National Job Demands

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses a gap in vocational research by investigating the match between people's vocational interests and actual job demands in the labor market. While prior research has focused on how interests predict career choices and job outcomes, little is known about how well the supply of interests aligns with national job demands. Using a national dataset of 1.21 million U.S. residents and occupational data from O*NET and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the study examines whether interest supply matches demand across RIASEC categories (Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional) in 2014, 2019, and projected 2029. It also explores how these gaps differ across education levels. The key contribution is providing empirical evidence of large and persistent mismatches between popular interests and available jobs, particularly showing surpluses of artistic interest supply versus demand and shortages in conventional interest alignment.

title: The Joint Fluctuations of LMX and Relative LMX Predict Follower Work Effort: A Dual-Dynamic Perspective

entries.rq_with_context: While prior research has established links between leader-member exchange (LMX) and employee work outcomes, less is known about how changes in LMX and relative LMX (RLMX) over time jointly affect work effort. Existing studies often treat LMX as static and overlook the dynamic interplay between absolute and relative changes in leader-follower relationships. This study addresses this gap by investigating how concurrent fluctuations in LMX and RLMX predict follower effort in a dynamic team context. Drawing on self-regulation theory, it proposes a dual-dynamic perspective to examine how these changes serve as feedback on goal attainability. The research uses multi-wave, multisource data from an insurance call center to test these relationships. It contributes by integrating time and social comparison into LMX research, offering a more nuanced understanding of when and why employees increase their work effort.

title: Linking Organizational Political Diversity with Satisfaction and Performance: The Implications of Presidential Elections

entries.rq_with_context: In politically polarizing times, organizations may experience tensions due to political diversity among employees. While prior research focuses on perceived political similarity and individual-level outcomes, it remains unclear whether objective, aggregated political diversity affects organizational-level outcomes like culture and value satisfaction. The study addresses this gap by investigating the longitudinal relationship between political diversity and organizational effectiveness across 15 years of data. The authors argue that political diversity may harm culture and value satisfaction, particularly when political identities are made salient by national events like presidential elections. Using archival data from S&P 100 firms, they test this hypothesis with multilevel and time-varying effect modeling. The study contributes by shifting focus from political leaning to political diversity and showing how temporal context shapes its impact.

title: Why Do Employees Perform Better Under Paradoxical Leaders? The Mediating Role of Group Harmony

entries.rq_with_context: As organizations face increasing complexity and competing demands, paradoxical leadership—where leaders manage seemingly contradictory needs simultaneously—has gained attention. While prior research links this leadership style to positive employee outcomes, it remains unclear how it affects multiple performance dimensions at both team and individual levels, especially through team-level mechanisms. This study addresses that gap by investigating whether paradoxical leadership influences team performance, organizational citizenship behavior (OCB), and counterproductive work behavior (CWB) via group harmony. Drawing on paradox theory, the authors propose a multilevel model tested with data from 195 bank employees and their managers. The key contribution is identifying group harmony as a mediating mechanism that explains how paradoxical leadership fosters positive outcomes and curbs negative ones.

title: The Dynamic Influence of Personality on Psychological Contract Evaluations: a 2-Study Investigation of Approach/Avoidance Goals and Emotion Regulation Strategies

entries.rq_with_context: Psychological contract breach (PCB) and violation feelings are subjective employee responses to perceived employer obligations not being met, with significant negative consequences for workplace attitudes and behaviors. While personality traits like neuroticism and conscientiousness have been linked to PCB, most research focuses on stable between-person differences and neglects dynamic within-person mechanisms. This paper addresses the gap by exploring how short-term fluctuations in state neuroticism and state conscientiousness relate to PCB and violation feelings through mediating mechanisms (approach/avoidance goals) and moderating factors (emotion regulation strategies). The research uses an experience sampling method across two studies to test time-lagged within-person relationships. The key contribution is a dynamic model that explains how self-regulatory processes shape the personality–PCB link, offering both theoretical refinement and practical insights for managing employee reactions.

title: Validation and Measurement Invariance of the German and Spanish Gender Bias Scale for Women Leaders

entries.rq_with_context: Gender bias remains a key barrier to women's representation in leadership, yet most measurement tools were developed in North American contexts. The Gender Bias Scale for Women Leaders (GBSWL) was designed to assess multifaceted gender bias but has not been validated outside the U.S. To enable cross-cultural research, this study tests the factorial validity and measurement invariance of the GBSWL in Germany and Spain—two countries with high gender egalitarian values but persistent inequality in leadership. The authors test three research questions: (1) Does the original factor structure replicate in German and Spanish samples? (2) Are the German and Spanish versions measurement equivalent across cultures? (3) Does the scale function similarly for women with and without leadership roles? Using confirmatory factor analysis across four samples (N = 870), the study evaluates model fit and invariance. The main contribution is providing a psychometrically sound, cross-culturally applicable version of the GBSWL for use in European organizational research.

title: Navigating Through the Digital Workplace: Measuring Leader Digital Competence

entries.rq_with_context: As organizations increasingly rely on digital tools for communication and collaboration, leaders face new challenges in guiding teams effectively in virtual settings. Despite the growing importance of digital leadership, there is no consensus on the core competencies required or a psychometrically sound instrument to measure them. Existing frameworks are either too broad, industry-specific, or conflate technological skills with general leadership abilities. This study addresses this gap by proposing a new construct—Leader Digital Competence (LDC)—comprising three dimensions: digital interaction, digital openness, and digital role modeling. Using four independent samples, the authors develop and validate a 10-item scale to assess LDC from an employee perspective. The key contribution is a reliable and valid measurement tool that enables future research on how leaders' digital competencies influence team and organizational outcomes in digital workplaces.

title: Revisiting the Inhibitory Effect of General Mental Ability on Counterproductive Work Behavior: The Case for GMA-Personality Interaction

entries.rq_with_context: Counterproductive work behavior (CWB) is a significant concern for organizations due to its detrimental effects on performance and financial outcomes. While prior research has theorized that general mental ability (GMA) negatively predicts CWB, empirical support has been inconsistent, with some studies finding no relationship. This inconsistency may stem from treating the GMA-CWB relationship as a main effect rather than considering moderating factors. The paper proposes that the meta-trait stability—comprised of conscientiousness, agreeableness, and emotional stability—moderates this relationship, such that GMA only inhibits CWB among individuals low in stability. Using two large samples of full-time employees, the study applies moderated multiple regression to test this conditional inhibitory effect. The findings support the hypothesis and suggest that incorporating interaction effects between GMA and stability can clarify previous mixed findings, offering a more nuanced understanding of how cognitive ability influences workplace deviance.

title: Observing Interviewees’ Inner Self: How Authenticity Cues in Job Interviews Relate to Interview and Job Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Job interviews are a central part of hiring, and candidates are often advised to 'be themselves,' yet little is known about which observable behaviors actually signal authenticity to interviewers. While prior research links perceived authenticity to more favorable evaluations, it does not clarify what behavioral cues drive those perceptions or whether such cues are related to actual job performance. This gap raises concerns about potential bias—if authenticity cues improve interview scores but do not reflect job-relevant skills, they could undermine selection validity. Drawing on person perception theory, particularly the realistic accuracy model, this study identifies and observes verbal, paraverbal, and nonverbal authenticity cues in mock interviews. It tests how these cues relate to (a) raters’ perceptions of authenticity, (b) interviewer ratings of interview performance, and (c) supervisor ratings of actual job performance. The authors also examine whether effects hold beyond first impressions and verbal cognitive ability. The primary contribution is introducing and validating the concept of authenticity cues as distinct behavioral indicators that differentially predict interview and job outcomes.

title: Ask, but You Might not Receive: Unanswered Supervisor Support Scale Development and a Daily Diary Study

entries.rq_with_context: Employees may actively seek support from supervisors but not receive it—an experience termed unanswered supervisor support (USS). While supervisor support is well-studied, existing research tends to focus on either the availability of support or employees’ proactive efforts to seek it, overlooking situations where requests go unanswered. This gap limits understanding of the distinct consequences of unmet support requests. The study addresses this by developing a USS measure and examining its daily impact using a diary method with 199 employees over five workdays. Drawing on self-determination theory, it investigates whether USS affects outcomes through need satisfaction and need frustration. The research contributes by introducing a validated USS scale, demonstrating its unique daily effects, and showing that need frustration—particularly competence and relatedness frustration—mediates the link between USS and emotional exhaustion.

title: How (if at All) do Perceptions of Supervisor’s Listening Differ from General Relationship Quality?: Psychometric Analysis

entries.rq_with_context: Employees who perceive their supervisors as good listeners report better well-being, job satisfaction, and psychological safety. However, concerns exist about whether these benefits stem uniquely from listening or from overlapping constructs like trust, respect, or humility. Prior research shows high correlations between listening and relationship quality, but it remains unclear whether they are distinct constructs or part of a broader relational network. This study investigates the convergent and divergent validity of four perceived listening measures against 16 relationship behavior and relationship quality constructs using data from 2,038 subordinates. The authors apply psychometric techniques including disattenuated correlations, profile similarity, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and exploratory graph analysis (EGA). They find strong evidence for convergent validity among listening measures but limited divergent validity, suggesting that perceived listening is highly intertwined with other relational constructs.

title: Further evaluation of the performance diagnostic checklist 1.1: Outcome agreement between supervisors and employees

entries.rq_with_context: The Performance Diagnostic Checklist-Human Services (PDC-HS) is a tool used to identify variables contributing to employee performance concerns in human service settings. While prior research has evaluated its validity and reliability using analog methods like video vignettes, little is known about the agreement between supervisors and the employees themselves when completing the PDC-HS in real-world settings. Existing studies that have included both perspectives either used different versions of the checklist or did not report outcomes by respondent, limiting direct comparison. This study addresses that gap by comparing PDC-HS 1.1 outcomes between BCBAs and their SBAs regarding inconsistent procedural fidelity reporting. The researchers used the PDC-HS 1.1 to assess domain-level concerns and compared rankings using visual analysis and Kendall rank-order correlations. The study contributes data on inter-rater agreement between supervisors and employees, which informs whether self-assessment with the PDC-HS may be a viable alternative to supervisor assessment in organizational behavior management.

title: An analysis of interactive computer training on staff acquisition of MSWO preference assessment implementation

entries.rq_with_context: Interactive computer training (ICT) is increasingly used to teach job-related skills in behavioral health settings, offering advantages like consistency and reduced training resources. However, prior studies show mixed results regarding whether ICT alone leads to mastery, with many participants requiring additional feedback or in-person coaching. This study addresses the gap by evaluating whether an ICT program in Articulate Rise 360 can train both inexperienced and experienced staff to implement the MSWO preference assessment with fidelity. The study uses a multiple baseline design across participants and systematically adds behavioral skills training (BST) components if ICT alone is insufficient.
