The key contribution is identifying that ICT alone was effective for only one of nine participants, highlighting the need for supplemental training elements to achieve mastery.

title: Participatory approach to selecting technologies for instruction delivery at an electric heater manufacturing plant

entries.rq_with_context: Large industrial settings often implement technology to improve efficiency, but costly or poorly adopted solutions can be abandoned or fail to deliver expected benefits. Management-driven technology choices may overlook worker needs, leading to low morale or resistance. This field study addresses the gap in understanding how worker involvement influences technology selection for instruction delivery in manufacturing. Using a participatory approach, frontline workers at an electric heater plant tested and selected between ruggedized tablets and AR glasses. The research question is: which technology do workers prefer for accessing assembly instructions, and how does participation influence adoption? The study applied a descriptive, field-report approach using survey data from all 21 line workers. The contribution is demonstrating that participatory methods lead to sustainable, worker-supported technology adoption even when it differs from management’s initial preference.

title: When less is more: Exploring the relation between delay discounting rates in a personal and organizational context

entries.rq_with_context: Many work decisions involve trade-offs between immediate and delayed rewards, and prior research suggests workers prefer immediate outcomes due to organizational uncertainty. However, it remains unclear whether this preference stems from environmental factors alone or is also shaped by an individual's reinforcement history. This study explores differences in delay discounting between personal and organizational contexts using a standardized task with employees from a private security corporation. It specifically investigates whether discounting rates differ by context, whether job position (manager vs. operative) influences discounting, and whether personal discounting predicts organizational choices. The study uses a behavioral economics framework and direct choice tasks, contributing to understanding how context and individual history jointly shape decision-making at work.

title: Behavior-based safety with paramedics

entries.rq_with_context: Paramedics face high occupational risks due to the dynamic and unpredictable environments in which they work, and accident rates among German Red Cross (DRK) paramedics have been rising since 2011. While Behavior-Based Safety (BBS) has proven effective in many industries, it has rarely been applied in healthcare settings, especially emergency medical services. There is a gap in understanding how BBS can be adapted to the unique context of paramedics’ work. This study investigates whether BBS practices—specifically behavioral observation and feedback—can improve safety behavior among paramedics. A multiple baseline design across two rescue stations was used to evaluate changes in safety compliance. The authors suggest the study contributes to demonstrating the feasibility and transferability of BBS in emergency healthcare contexts.

title: Variations of the Dependent Group Contingency and Effects on Employee Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Employee performance problems in human service settings can negatively impact client care, and managers often face challenges in implementing efficient, effective interventions. When performance issues occur across multiple staff and are linked to weak consequences, group contingencies offer a practical solution. Dependent group contingencies—in which one individual’s performance determines a group reward—have been used in educational settings but are understudied with adult employees, especially regarding how variations in implementation affect outcomes. This study addresses a gap in understanding how making the 'hero' known versus anonymous influences performance. The research evaluates two variations of a dependent group contingency on weekly graph completion by direct care staff using a combination withdrawal and alternating treatments design. Its contribution lies in comparing these two practical variations to identify which more effectively improves compliance with documentation tasks.

title: An analysis of research designs in theJournal of Organizational Behavior Management(2000–2022)

entries.rq_with_context: Organizational Behavior Management (OBM) research has historically relied on single-case experimental designs, as shown in studies covering publications up to 2009. However, recent trends in research design usage in the Journal of Organizational Behavior Management (JOBM) are unknown. There is a need to understand whether the field has maintained its preference for single-case methods or if there has been a shift toward group or other designs. This study fills that gap by analyzing all empirical articles in JOBM from 2000 to 2022. The research question is: What types of research designs have been used in JOBM during this period, and how do they compare in frequency? The authors systematically coded each empirical article by design type, including single-case, group, quasi-experimental, and others, and further classified specific designs and statistical tests. The key contribution is providing an updated, quantitative overview of methodological trends in OBM research to inform training and practice.

title: Behavioral Safety in a Dental Surgery Facility

entries.rq_with_context: Dental professionals face numerous occupational hazards, including biological, chemical, physical, and ergonomic risks, which contribute to high rates of occupational diseases such as skin conditions and musculoskeletal disorders. Despite known risks, research on safety interventions in dental settings is limited, particularly regarding behavior-based safety (BBS), which has been widely applied in industrial contexts but rarely studied in dentistry. There is a gap in understanding how BBS strategies—such as feedback and goal setting—can be implemented in small dental practices to improve safety behaviors. This study addresses that gap by implementing a BBS intervention in a dental surgery facility with seven employees. Using a changing criterion design, the researchers examined whether task clarification, verbal and graphical feedback, goal setting, and reinforcement could increase the percentage of safe behaviors. The study contributes preliminary evidence that BBS methods can be adapted to dental environments and lead to measurable improvements in safety behavior.

title: Exploring the Relationship Between Evaluation Frequency and Monthly Fidelity Score on Provider Retention: A Longitudinal Study

entries.rq_with_context: Provider turnover in applied behavior analysis (ABA) is high, with rates as high as 75% annually, driven by factors like burnout, pay, and supervisory support. While prior research has identified supervisory support as a key factor, most studies have been survey-based and have not examined applied, observable supervision practices such as procedural fidelity data collection. This study addresses a gap by investigating whether the frequency of fidelity evaluations and monthly fidelity scores are linked to provider retention. Using a longitudinal design, the authors analyzed data from 1,586 participant months across 19 ABA organizations, tracking evaluation frequency, fidelity scores, and retention three months later. The key contribution is providing empirical evidence on how objective supervision practices relate to retention, offering a feasible, data-driven approach to reduce turnover.

title: Gender and Geographic Affiliation of Editors of theJournal of Organizational Behavior Management(2000–2022)

entries.rq_with_context: There is a well-documented history of underrepresentation of women and non-U.S. scholars in academic publishing, particularly in behavior analysis. Prior studies have shown declining participation by women as roles become more prestigious—a pattern described as a 'glass ceiling'—and a strong dominance of U.S.-based scholars. While some research has examined authorship trends in the Journal of Organizational Behavior Management (JOBM), little is known about the gender and geographic makeup of its editorial leadership over time. This study fills that gap by analyzing the presumed gender (based on pronouns) and geographic affiliation of JOBM’s editorial staff from 2000 to 2022. Using descriptive analysis of publicly available data from journal issues, faculty websites, and direct contact, the authors quantify representation across editorial roles. The study contributes a longitudinal perspective on diversity in JOBM’s leadership and highlights persistent imbalances in gender and geography.

title: An Evaluation of a Staff Management Strategy to Minimize Reactivity in Procedural Fidelity of Intervention Implementers

entries.rq_with_context: Reactivity—where staff perform better when they know they are being observed—threatens the validity of procedural fidelity assessments in behavior analytic interventions. While feedback is known to improve staff performance, it typically occurs during observed sessions, potentially reinforcing reactivity rather than genuine skill maintenance. A key gap is how to maintain high procedural fidelity when supervisors are absent, especially since most intervention time occurs without direct observation. This study addresses that gap by evaluating whether providing feedback following observer-absent sessions increases procedural fidelity in unobserved conditions. Using a multiple baseline design across participants, the researchers applied behavioral skills training followed by feedback only after covert observations. The key contribution is demonstrating a practical staff management strategy that may minimize reactivity and support more accurate assessment of true implementation fidelity.

title: The Effects of Performance Improvement on Feedback Accuracy and Omission

entries.rq_with_context: Feedback is a core component of organizational behavior management, but its effectiveness depends on accurate measurement and consistent delivery. Prior research shows that when recipients react negatively to feedback, providers are less accurate in their observations and more likely to omit feedback. This study addresses a gap by testing whether observed improvement in the recipient's behavior—despite negative reactions—can counteract these effects. The research question is whether behavioral improvement acts as a reinforcing consequence for feedback providers, sustaining accuracy and delivery. Using a mixed AB group design with a simulated safety observation task, the study compares a control group (no behavior change) to a progressive improvement group (10% increase in safe behavior per session). The authors claim this identifies a variable that may help maintain feedback integrity even when reactions are negative.

title: An Evaluation of Staff Reactivity Following Performance Feedback and Self-Monitoring Procedures in a Group Home Setting

entries.rq_with_context: Staff often fail to implement behavior intervention plans with fidelity when supervisors are not present, threatening treatment integrity and client outcomes. While performance feedback and self-monitoring have been shown to improve staff adherence during supervision, it remains unclear whether these improvements persist when staff are unaware they are being observed—a phenomenon known as reactivity. Prior studies present mixed findings: some show improvements only when observers are present, while others suggest self-monitoring may sustain performance. This study addresses this gap by evaluating staff reactivity in a group home using both conspicuous and inconspicuous observation conditions. The research uses a multiple baseline and alternating treatments design to assess the effects of behavioral skills training (BST), performance feedback, and self-monitoring on treatment integrity. The authors aim to determine whether self-monitoring can increase performance in the absence of an observer, thereby reducing reactivity and improving real-world implementation.

title: Behavioral Skills Training for Active Shooter Scenarios Among Human Service Staff

entries.rq_with_context: Mass shootings are increasingly common in schools and healthcare settings, yet there is little research on training staff who must protect both themselves and clients with disabilities during such incidents. Previous studies suggest 75% of people freeze during emergencies, highlighting the need for effective training. This study addresses the gap by evaluating whether Behavioral Skills Training (BST) can teach Registered Behavior Technicians® to correctly perform run, hide, and fight behaviors in active shooter scenarios. Using a concurrent multiple-baseline design, the researchers assessed skill acquisition, generalization to novel stimuli, and maintenance over time. The study contributes evidence that BST is an effective method for teaching complex, safety-critical behaviors to human service staff.

title: The Use of a Treatment Package to Increase Timely Submission of State Regulated Medication Administration Documentation

entries.rq_with_context: Regulatory compliance in human service settings is critical for health and safety, yet supervisors often find it burdensome and time-consuming. Despite existing research on performance management strategies like feedback and task clarification, there is limited evidence on how these can be embedded into current organizational systems—particularly using in-house supervisors—to improve compliance with state-mandated documentation. This study addresses this gap by evaluating a treatment package consisting of a checklist and bi-weekly feedback meetings to increase timely submission of medication administration records. Using a multiple baseline design across participants, the approach applies Organizational Behavior Management (OBM) principles within existing supervisory frameworks. The authors claim the study contributes to OBM literature by demonstrating how simple, low-cost interventions can be integrated into routine supervision to improve regulatory compliance.

title: In-Person and Telehealth Behavioral Skills Training to Reduce Child Restraint System Misuse

entries.rq_with_context: Child restraint system (CRS) misuse remains a serious public health issue, with high rates persisting despite existing education efforts by certified Child Passenger Safety Technicians (CPSTs). Traditional didactic training improves knowledge but often fails to ensure correct and lasting CRS use. This study addresses the gap in effective, scalable, and sustainable training methods by evaluating Behavior Skills Training (BST)—a method involving instruction, modeling, rehearsal, and feedback—delivered both in-person and via telehealth. The research questions are whether BST reduces CRS misuse more effectively than traditional training, and whether telehealth delivery is as effective as in-person BST. Using a longitudinal quasi-experimental design with a 37-step task analysis, the study compares misuse rates before and after training and at 9-month follow-up. The authors claim the study contributes by validating BST as a scalable, long-term solution that can be delivered remotely to improve child passenger safety.

title: An Evaluation of Magnitude in Monetary Incentives

entries.rq_with_context: Monetary incentives are commonly used in organizational behavior management (OBM) to improve employee performance, but there is little systematic research on what magnitude of incentive is effective. Existing studies use idiosyncratic incentive amounts without clear justification, often based on availability or intuition rather than empirical evaluation. This lack of guidance makes it difficult for practitioners to design cost-effective incentive programs. To address this gap, the study first identifies the minimum effective incentive magnitude through a progressive decrease procedure (Study 1), then tests whether $2.11 consistently increases performance when delivered repeatedly (Study 2). The research uses a multiple baseline design across participants and a simulated filing task in a real workplace. It claims to provide initial data on the magnitude of monetary incentives that can maintain increased responding in administrative staff.

title: A Graduate-Level Course in Organizational Behavior Management

entries.rq_with_context: The fifth edition of the BACB® Task List (2017) increased required training in Personnel Supervision and Management from 10 to 30 hours, necessitating a dedicated OBM course in graduate programs. While many behavior analysis programs exist, few offer structured, verified coursework in OBM. This paper addresses the gap by describing a long-standing, BACB®-verified graduate course at Missouri State University. The research question is how to design and implement a graduate-level OBM course that meets accreditation standards while providing practical, hands-on learning. The course uses the Daniels and Bailey (2014) textbook as a foundation and adds supplemental readings and a performance management project. The authors claim the contribution is a detailed, replicable model for training future behavior analysts in organizational applications.

title: Instructional Activities to Enhance Teaching Organizational Behavior Management

entries.rq_with_context: The demand for Organizational Behavior Management (OBM) training is growing due to upcoming changes in certification requirements by the Behavior Analyst Certification Board (BACB), including new content on personnel supervision and a required OBM course for trainees. Despite increasing interest, there is a shortage of instructors with OBM expertise and limited published resources on effective teaching methods or classroom assignments for OBM. Existing models like the consultation workshop provide some guidance but lack detailed, classroom-based project examples. This paper addresses this gap by presenting instructional activities that promote experiential learning in OBM courses. It outlines multiple assignments used in undergraduate and graduate classes, each aligned with core OBM topics. The primary research question is how these activities can enhance student learning of OBM concepts and skills. The approach involves describing each assignment’s structure, context, and integration into course units. The authors claim the contribution is offering practical, ready-to-implement teaching tools for OBM educators.

title: Practitioners’ Views on Essential Coursework, Skills, and Fieldwork in Organizational Behavior Management Graduate Training Programs

entries.rq_with_context: While there are recommendations for content in a single OBM course, no formal guidelines exist for OBM graduate training programs. This gap is increasingly relevant as the Behavior Analyst Certification Board now requires OBM coursework for certification, likely increasing demand for structured training. Existing OBM programs vary in coursework and structure, potentially leading to inconsistencies in graduate preparedness. To address this, the authors surveyed OBM practitioners to identify what they view as essential coursework, critical skills, and the role of fieldwork in graduate training. The study uses survey data from 43 practitioners to inform curriculum development. The authors suggest this information can help standardize core components of OBM training programs.

title: Continuous Performance Feedback: Investigating the Effects of Feedback Content and Feedback Sources on Performance, Motivation to Improve Performance and Task Engagement

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations are increasingly adopting continuous performance feedback to improve employee performance, motivation, and engagement, moving away from traditional performance ratings. However, there is limited empirical evidence on how specific characteristics of feedback—such as content (quantitative vs. qualitative) and source (computer-mediated vs. person-mediated)—influence these outcomes. While prior research highlights mixed results on feedback effectiveness, little is known about the relative impact of these two dimensions in a continuous feedback setting. This study addresses this gap by experimentally testing how feedback content and source affect performance, motivation to improve, and task engagement using a task-based experiment. The authors use a mixed 2×3 factorial design with a cognitive n-back task and measure behavioral and psychophysiological responses. The key contribution is providing empirical evidence on which feedback characteristics yield better performance and motivational outcomes in continuous feedback systems.

title: Effects of Feedback Statements on Staff Procedural Integrity

entries.rq_with_context: Supervisor feedback is known to improve employee performance, but there is limited research on the essential components of effective feedback, particularly in real-world organizational settings. Previous studies have largely used simulated tasks with undergraduate participants, limiting generalizability. This study addresses a gap by testing uniform feedback sequences—two or three corrective or positive statements—on Registered Behavior Technicians implementing a complex, real-world task (DTT with children with ASD). The research question is: How do the amount and type of feedback statements affect procedural fidelity? Using a multielement design within a multiple baseline framework, the study evaluates performance changes across feedback conditions. The authors claim the study provides applied evidence on feedback structure in naturalistic work environments.

title: Using Web-Based Behavioral Skills Training to Teach Online Interview Skills to College Students

entries.rq_with_context: Interviews are a critical part of job and graduate school admissions, yet many college students struggle to effectively communicate their skills. Behavioral Skills Training (BST) has been shown to improve in-person interview skills, but no research has evaluated its use for training virtual interview skills, which present unique challenges like technological barriers and reduced social cues. This study extends prior research by testing the effectiveness of BST delivered in a synchronous web-based format to teach online interview skills to college students. Using a multiple baseline design, the study evaluates whether BST improves targeted vocal and non-vocal interview behaviors. The authors aim to demonstrate that BST can be successfully adapted to online contexts, maintaining its effectiveness in skill acquisition.

title: Effects of Feedback Timing on Accuracy of Functional Analysis Implementation

entries.rq_with_context: Functional analysis (FA) implementation is a complex skill requiring precise responses to client behaviors, particularly when procedures are individualized. While feedback is known to support training in such skills, little is known about how the timing of feedback—specifically when it is delivered relative to performance—affects learning outcomes. Prior studies on feedback timing show mixed results, often focusing on simple tasks or general skills. This study addresses a gap by evaluating feedback timing in the context of complex, individualized FA procedures. Using an adapted alternating treatment design within a multiple baseline framework, the authors compare three feedback arrangements: all feedback after performance, all before, and corrective feedback before with positive feedback after. The primary contribution is identifying how different temporal placements of feedback impact accuracy in FA implementation among adult learners.

title: Managerial Behavioral Training For Functional Leadership: A Randomized Controlled Trial

entries.rq_with_context: Leadership training is widely used, yet high-quality evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in naturalistic settings remains scarce. While goal setting, performance feedback, value-based feedback, and consequential listening are theorized to support effective leadership, there is limited causal evidence showing that training in these behaviors leads to measurable improvements. This study fills that gap by testing a manualized Managerial Behavioral Training (MBT) program grounded in behavioral principles. Using an RCT design with pre- and post-training employee ratings, the study asks whether MBT improves managers’ functional leadership behaviors and, in turn, leadership performance. The approach integrates performance analysis, participative goal setting, instruction, practice with feedback, and homework. The authors claim this study provides rigorous causal evidence on how behavioral training improves leadership in real-world organizational settings.

title: Using Behavioral Skills Training to Teach Peer Support Workers to Respond to Ethical Scenarios

entries.rq_with_context: Peer support workers use lived experience to support others in recovery, but must also navigate ethical challenges like boundary crossings—such as being asked for money or personal information. While ethical codes exist, training on how to respond in the moment is often lacking. Previous research has not evaluated whether behavioral skills training (BST) can teach these real-time ethical responses. This study asked whether a remote, group-based BST program could teach peer support workers to set boundaries during simulated ethical scenarios. The training used a task analysis with specific steps: orient, restate needs, set a boundary, redirect, and repeat as needed. The study contributes preliminary evidence that BST with supplemental feedback can improve boundary-setting skills in this population.

title: Intervening to Prevent Unwanted Touching of Museum Displays: Incorporating an Observing Response with Three Prompting Conditions

entries.rq_with_context: Museums face ongoing challenges with visitors touching art displays, which can cause irreversible damage due to skin oils and physical contact. Despite common use of signs and barriers, no prior empirical study has measured the frequency of display touching or evaluated the effectiveness of sign interventions. This study addresses that gap by testing three sign types—Directive, Rationale, and Rationale-plus-Graphic—in a real-world museum setting using behavioral observation. It also introduces an observing response (visitors moving to the back of a double-sided sign to read the message) to assess whether engaging with the sign leads to greater compliance. Using an alternating treatments design, the study compares sign conditions and a baseline (No-Sign) condition. The authors claim the study is the first to empirically evaluate antecedent prompts for reducing harmful visitor behavior in museums, contributing practical, cost-effective strategies to protect valuable art.

title: An Evaluation of Daily Stress and Procedural Fidelity Among Direct Care Staff

entries.rq_with_context: Direct care staff play a critical role in implementing behavior intervention plans with procedural fidelity, which is essential for positive client outcomes. While factors like training and intervention complexity are known to influence fidelity, little is known about how acute daily stressors—short-lived, infrequent events—impact staff performance. Existing research on acute stress and job performance shows mixed results, with some studies showing enhanced performance under stress and others showing impairment. This study addresses this gap by examining the relationship between perceived daily stress and procedural fidelity among eight direct care staff members. Using repeated measures and nonparametric analyses, the study assesses stress via the Daily Stress Inventory and fidelity through direct observation. The authors suggest that understanding this relationship could inform strategies to support staff and improve client care.

title: The Effect of Social Comparison Feedback and Value Statements in a Clinic

entries.rq_with_context: The study addresses the challenge of improving performance among low-performing employees in workplace settings, specifically focusing on behavior technicians in an autism clinic who were completing few end-of-shift cleaning tasks. While performance feedback is a well-established organizational behavior tool, there is limited understanding of how social comparison feedback (SCF) affects low-performers, especially given concerns that ranking-based comparisons may harm motivation. The research gap lies in whether non-ranking forms of SCF—such as graphic and verbal comparisons to top performers—can effectively improve performance without negative side effects. The research question is whether graphic and verbal SCF increases the number of cleaning tasks completed by low-performers. The study uses a concurrent multiple baseline design across three participants, delivering private SCF that includes performance graphs and value statements. The authors claim this approach demonstrates that SCF can be effective for low-performers when applied through non-ranking, less competitive formats.

title: Using the Performance Diagnostic Checklist-Human Services (PDC-HS) to Enhance Data Collection Procedures in Residential Treatment Settings for Clients with Significant Behavioral Challenges

entries.rq_with_context: In residential treatment settings for individuals with developmental disabilities and severe behavioral challenges, accurate and consistent data collection by direct care staff is critical for effective treatment planning, yet it is often incomplete or inaccurate. Prior training and modeling efforts have failed to ensure reliable data recording, suggesting a need for targeted, function-based interventions. The current study addresses this problem by using the Performance Diagnostic Checklist-Human Services (PDC-HS) to identify specific performance deficits among staff across three residential homes. Based on PDC-HS findings, a prompting intervention was implemented via text messages to staff near the end of their shifts. Using a multiple baseline design across settings, the study evaluates whether this low-effort, antecedent-based strategy improves correspondence between narrative logs and formal behavior data forms. The authors claim the study contributes to organizational behavior management by demonstrating how function-based assessments can guide efficient, effective interventions to enhance data collection practices.

title: Increasing Warehouse Worker Performance Using Voice Technology that Provided Immediate Feedback: Personal Performance Productivity Prompt

entries.rq_with_context: In large industrial warehouses, maintaining productivity is critical, yet traditional paper-based or delayed feedback systems often fail to support real-time performance improvement. While voice-directed systems already provide hands-free task guidance, they typically do not deliver personalized, immediate feedback on individual performance. This creates a gap between goal setting and performance awareness. This study investigates whether integrating a personal performance productivity prompt—delivering audio feedback of units per hour after each completed assignment—improves selector productivity in a distribution center. Using a nonconcurrent multiple baseline design across three warehouse zones, the study evaluates performance changes after implementing the prompt. The contribution is demonstrating how a simple technological enhancement grounded in Organizational Behavior Management principles can effectively improve worker performance in real-world settings.

title: Teaching Supervisory Skills to Behavior Analysts and Improving Therapist-Delivered Discrete Trial Teaching

entries.rq_with_context: Effective supervision in Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) is critical for ensuring high-quality service delivery, yet there is limited empirical research on how to train supervisors to improve their practice. While the Behavior Analyst Certification Board (BACB) has provided guidelines for supervisor qualifications and training, few studies have tested systematic methods for improving supervisory skills. This study addresses this gap by evaluating a BST-based training protocol for BCBAs who supervise therapists implementing DTT. The research question is whether this structured training improves supervisors’ ability to provide feedback and support, and whether those changes subsequently improve therapist performance. Using a concurrent multiple baseline design across five supervisors, the study implemented a competency-based training protocol grounded in BST principles—consisting of instruction, modeling, rehearsal, and feedback. The key contribution is demonstrating an empirically supported method for training supervisors that leads to measurable improvements in both supervisor and therapist performance.

title: Behavioral Assessment in Virtual Reality: An Evaluation of Multi-User Simulations in Healthcare Education

entries.rq_with_context: Medical error is a leading cause of death in the U.S., with faulty communication during patient handoffs identified as a key contributor. The TeamSTEPPS® framework has been adopted to improve teamwork and communication, but objective measurement of these skills remains limited. While VR offers a promising platform for high-fidelity, measurable simulations, its use in healthcare education lacks validation against established direct simulation methods. This study evaluates the convergent validity of multi-user VR simulations by comparing them to in-person simulations in assessing communication accuracy and situational awareness among healthcare students. Using a pre/post design, it measures performance across both modalities before and after training. The authors claim this work contributes to validating VR as an objective behavioral assessment tool in medical education.

title: The Use of a Pictorially Enhanced Self-Instruction Packet to Improve Weekly Time Sheet Completion in an ABA Clinic

entries.rq_with_context: In ABA clinics, accurate and complete timesheet completion is essential for correct insurance billing and ethical compliance, yet incomplete or incorrect documentation remains a common issue. Existing research has applied organizational behavior management (OBM) interventions to improve clinical documentation such as session notes, often using feedback-dependent methods that require supervisor time. While self-instruction (SI) procedures have been used to teach ABA skills, no studies have tested SI for improving timesheet completion, nor used preintervention assessments like the Performance Diagnostic Checklist-Human Services (PDC-HS) to guide intervention selection. This study asks whether a PDC-HS-guided pictorially enhanced self-instruction (PESI) packet improves weekly timesheet completion among five technicians. The study uses a concurrent multiple baseline design across participants. It contributes a low-resource, scalable intervention that does not rely on ongoing supervisor involvement.

title: An Investigation of Behavioral Contrast in a Simulated Workplace

entries.rq_with_context: Behavioral contrast, well-documented in non-human animals, refers to an increase in responding in one component when a second component is placed on extinction. While some studies have shown this effect with humans, there is limited consistency and adherence to basic research standards in organizational behavior management (OBM) applications. Existing research lacks consistent replication under controlled conditions that account for rule-governed behavior and reinforcement schedules. This study investigates whether positive molar behavioral contrast can be observed in college students performing a typing task under variable interval and extinction schedules, following strict experimental analysis of behavior guidelines. Using an ABA reversal design across two experiments, the authors test if behavioral contrast occurs and whether procedural changes (e.g., longer sessions, explicit rules) improve its likelihood. The contribution lies in assessing the feasibility of translating basic behavioral principles into OBM-relevant contexts.

title: The Effects of Remote Instructions, Rehearsal, and Feedback on Preference Assessment Implementation

entries.rq_with_context: The shift to telehealth during the COVID-19 pandemic has necessitated changes in staff training procedures within applied behavior analysis (ABA). While behavioral skills training (BST) is effective, its full protocol may not be efficient or feasible remotely. Feedback has been identified as a potentially sufficient component for skill acquisition. This study addresses the gap in understanding how remote delivery of feedback—following written instructions and remote rehearsal—affects staff ability to accurately implement MSWO preference assessments. Using a concurrent multiple baseline design, the authors evaluate whether remote feedback increases implementation accuracy. The key contribution is demonstrating that remote feedback alone can effectively train a critical ABA skill, supporting more scalable and accessible training models.

title: A preliminary investigation of procedural refinements to the performance diagnostic checklist - human services

entries.rq_with_context: The PDC-HS is a functional assessment tool used in Organizational Behavior Management (OBM) to identify causes of employee performance problems and guide interventions. However, the current method for selecting interventions—often based on the category with the highest 'no' responses—lacks clear guidelines, leading to inconsistent use, especially among novice practitioners. This ambiguity can result in inefficient or inappropriate intervention choices. The study addresses this gap by evaluating two proposed refinements: a 50% cutoff threshold to identify problematic categories and decision-making models (DMMs) to select a single intervention focus when multiple categories exceed the threshold. Using a between-groups design with vignettes based on published cases, the research tests whether access to these refinements improves alignment with evidence-based intervention selections. The key contribution is preliminary validation of structured tools that could enhance objectivity and utility of the PDC-HS in real-world settings.

title: Behavior-based safety 2022: today’s evidence

entries.rq_with_context: Behavior-based safety (BBS) has been widely adopted since the 1980s to reduce workplace injuries, yet there is limited empirical guidance on which design elements make BBS most effective. While prior research has examined observation and feedback frequency, few studies have analyzed the relative impact of key BBS components such as who conducts observations, how often, and how they are trained. This paper addresses this gap using a large dataset from 88 international organizations implementing DEKRA’s BAPP® system, with over 1.3 million observational data points. The research asks which BBS design factors—such as contact rate, observer participation levels, observer tenure, area of observation, and use of structured comments—are most strongly associated with injury reductions. The analysis uses regression modeling and longitudinal injury data to test these relationships. The authors claim this provides evidence-based guidelines for optimizing BBS design, challenging prevailing recommendations that emphasize high participation and frequent observations.

title: The Use of Task Clarification and Self-Monitoring to Increase Affirmative to Constructive Feedback Ratios in Supervisory Relationships

entries.rq_with_context: Supervisory relationships are critical for employee performance and satisfaction, and prior research suggests that a 4:1 ratio of affirmative to constructive feedback is ideal, similar to findings in marital relationships. However, little research has examined practical methods to help supervisors reach this ratio. This study addresses that gap by evaluating the effectiveness of task clarification and self-monitoring in increasing feedback ratios among supervisors of direct care staff in an autism intervention clinic. Using a behavioral intervention framework, the researchers applied a concurrent multiple baseline design across supervisor-staff dyads. The key contribution is demonstrating a feasible, low-cost method to improve supervisory interaction quality in human service settings.

title: Changing driver yielding behavior on a city-wide basis

entries.rq_with_context: Pedestrian fatalities have been rising in the U.S., and low driver yielding at crosswalks is a contributing factor. While prior studies show that enforcement and engineering treatments can increase yielding, it is unclear whether these effects can be achieved on a city-wide scale, especially in larger cities within sprawling metropolitan areas. This study evaluates a multi-component program—including high-visibility enforcement, public feedback signs showing weekly yielding rates, low-cost in-street signs, and community outreach—in two cities (Ann Arbor, MI, and Saint Paul, MN) to determine its effectiveness in changing driver behavior across both treatment and untreated sites. Using a non-concurrent multiple baseline design, the researchers measured yielding during staged and natural pedestrian crossings. The key contribution claimed is demonstrating that city-wide behavioral change in driver yielding is possible using applied behavior analysis principles, even in large urban environments.

title: The Efficacy of Variations of Observation and Data Recording on Trainee Performance

entries.rq_with_context: The observer effect—where trainees improve their performance after observing and recording others' behavior—has been shown to enhance skill implementation in some settings, but prior studies often require experimenter feedback to achieve high integrity. This paper identifies a gap in understanding which variations of observation and data recording might reduce reliance on feedback while still improving trainee performance. The research questions ask whether video-based observation with data recording, peer observation with feedback, or requiring accurate data recording can improve guided compliance integrity. The authors use a nonconcurrent multiple baseline design across three experiments to test these variations. They claim the study contributes by evaluating practical modifications that could make training more resource-efficient without sacrificing effectiveness.

title: An Examination of Variables that Predict Turnover, Staff and Caregiver Satisfaction in Behavior-analytic Organizations

entries.rq_with_context: Staff turnover is a significant issue in human service organizations, particularly in Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) due to high training costs and intensive job demands. Despite high reported turnover rates in ABA (around 50%), there is limited empirical data identifying specific predictors. This study uses accreditation data from the Behavioral Health Center of Excellence® (BHCOE®) across 100+ U.S. ABA organizations to identify predictors of turnover and satisfaction. The research questions focus on how factors like pay, staff and caregiver satisfaction, supervisor turnover, and organizational quality predict technician and supervisor turnover, as well as staff and caregiver satisfaction. Using multiple regression analyses on existing organizational data, the study tests these relationships. The authors claim the work contributes by identifying key, measurable predictors within real-world ABA settings using large-scale data, offering practical insights for reducing turnover and improving satisfaction.

title: Comparing Video Modeling and Computer-Based Instruction to Teach Preference Assessment Implementation

entries.rq_with_context: Staff in applied behavior analysis must accurately implement skills like paired-stimulus preference assessments (PSAs), which are critical for identifying effective reinforcers for individuals with autism and developmental disabilities. Current gold-standard training (behavioral skills training) is effective but time-intensive and requires trainer presence, making it difficult to scale. Asynchronous methods like video modeling (VM) and computer-based instruction (CBI) offer scalable alternatives, but their comparative effectiveness is unknown. This study addresses the gap by comparing VM and CBI for teaching PSA implementation to trainees with little prior experience. The research uses a randomized pre-post design to evaluate treatment integrity, errors, duration, and social validity. It contributes evidence on which asynchronous method may be more effective and acceptable for training staff in real-world settings.

title: A comparison of the effects of various performance feedback presentations on typing accuracy and speed

entries.rq_with_context: Performance feedback is widely used in organizational settings to improve task performance, but there is inconsistency in the literature about which combinations—such as feedback with goal setting or praise—are most effective. Prior reviews suggest that combining feedback with antecedent or consequence-based procedures enhances its impact, yet no clear consensus exists on the optimal combination. This study addresses that gap by experimentally comparing the effects of performance feedback alone, feedback with goals, and feedback with praise on typing accuracy and speed in a controlled laboratory setting. Using a mixed factorial design, it also examines whether feedback focused on accuracy, speed, or both influences outcomes differently. The central contribution is testing, under controlled conditions, whether additive components like goals or praise enhance feedback’s effectiveness beyond feedback type alone.

title: The Use of a Brief Treatment Package to Increase Session Note Completion in an ABA Agency

entries.rq_with_context: Behavior technicians in applied behavior analysis (ABA) agencies are required to complete detailed session notes for insurance documentation, care coordination, and treatment tracking. Despite their importance, little research has examined how to improve the completeness of these notes. Luna and Rapp (2019) explored using checklists in simulated settings but noted limitations including lack of experimental control, no use of feedback, and absence of real-world generalization. To address these gaps, this study evaluates a treatment package—consisting of a sample note, self-monitoring checklist, and written/verbal feedback—on actual note completion during in-clinic sessions. Using a multiple baseline design across six technicians, the research asks whether this package increases the number of correctly completed items on session notes. The approach builds on organizational behavior management principles to support staff performance. The authors claim the study contributes by demonstrating an effective, socially valid, and easily implemented intervention in a real-world ABA setting.

title: Computerized Immediate Feedback on Food Safety Quality Control and In-Process Inspections at a Food Manufacturing Plant

entries.rq_with_context: Food manufacturing companies face significant challenges in ensuring product safety, particularly in executing timely and accurate product recalls. Despite regulatory requirements under the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA), many manufacturers still rely on manual, paper-based systems that hinder rapid traceability. The host company in this study consistently failed to meet the industry standard of 100% data retrieval accuracy within two hours during mock recalls. To address this gap, the authors implemented a computerized system using tablets for in-process inspections with immediate visual and audio feedback. The research question is whether this intervention improves the speed and accuracy of retrieving quality control data during mock recalls. The study uses a field experiment with an AB design comparing paper-based versus computerized systems. The authors claim the study contributes by demonstrating how integrating technology into in-process inspections can enhance consumer safety through faster, more accurate recall capabilities.

title: An Evaluation of Feedback-Based Interventions on Promoting Use of Personal Protective Equipment in a School

entries.rq_with_context: Employees in human service settings, especially those working with individuals who exhibit severe problem behaviors, face high rates of on-the-job injuries. Despite safety guidelines and prescribed personal protective equipment (PPE), staff often fail to use PPE consistently. Existing research has used the PDC-Safety to identify barriers to safe behavior, but no studies have examined whether PDC-Safety-informed interventions can generate tailored solutions across different groups or whether increased PPE use reduces actual injuries. This study addresses these gaps by implementing individualized, feedback-based interventions in three classrooms based on PDC-Safety results. The research question is whether these interventions increase PPE adherence and reduce injury rates. The approach uses a modified consecutive case series design with direct observation and injury data. The authors claim the study demonstrates both improved safety behavior and reduced injuries, supporting the utility of the PDC-Safety in real-world settings.

title: The Effects of Feedback Accuracy and Trainer Rules on Performance during an Analogue Task

entries.rq_with_context: Feedback is a core intervention in Organizational Behavior Management (OBM), often assumed to be most effective when accurate. Recent research suggests that awareness of feedback inaccuracy can reduce its effectiveness, and that verbal rules (e.g., rumors) in organizations may independently affect performance. However, no prior study has examined how rules provided during training about potential feedback inaccuracy interact with actual feedback accuracy. This study fills that gap by testing the effects of two variables: (1) the level of actual feedback accuracy (one-third, accurate, or tripled), and (2) the description of feedback accuracy given by a trainer during training. Using an analogue banking transfer task, the study employs a between-groups experimental design to assess performance across nine conditions. The key contribution is examining the interaction between experiential feedback and verbally transmitted rules—a novel combination in OBM research.

title: Teaching Appropriate Feedback Reception Skills Using Computer-based Instruction: A Systematic Replication

entries.rq_with_context: Feedback is commonly used in organizational settings to address performance issues, but most research focuses on how it is delivered rather than how it is received. Since feedback effectiveness likely depends on recipient behavior, there is a gap in understanding how to train individuals to receive feedback appropriately. This study investigates the efficacy of computer-based instruction (CBI) in teaching feedback reception skills—such as eye contact, active listening, and commitment to change—using a systematic replication of prior research. The approach uses a non-concurrent multiple baseline design across participants to assess changes in both feedback reception and job task performance. The study contributes by extending CBI to a complex social skill and examining its potential impact on work outcomes.

title: Consumer behavior analysis and the marketing firm: measures of performance

entries.rq_with_context: The paper addresses the need to evaluate firm performance through the lens of consumer behavior, using principles from consumer behavior analysis—an interdisciplinary field integrating behavioral economics and marketing. Prior research has identified systematic patterns in consumer buying behavior, such as brand loyalty and market penetration, but less attention has been paid to how these behaviors are influenced by the types of reinforcement they produce. The authors argue that firm strategies should be informed by measures of consumer behavior grounded in the Behavioral Perspective Model (BPM), which distinguishes between utilitarian and informational consequences of consumption. The central research question is: How do consumer behavior patterns—shaped by reinforcement type, package size, price promotions, and setting openness—relate to both consumer choice and organizational performance? The study uses consumer panel data and behavioral economic models to analyze these relationships. Its main contribution is the integration of consumer-level behavioral measures with firm-level outcomes to assess marketing effectiveness.

title: Increasing Productivity in a Manufacturing Setting using Daily Process Walks

entries.rq_with_context: Manufacturing productivity is critical for meeting customer demand and increasing revenue, and both Lean Manufacturing and Organizational Behavior Management (OBM) offer strategies to improve performance. While Lean provides systematic process analysis tools like Gemba walks, it often lacks focus on individual behavior change, which OBM can support through goal setting and feedback. The study addresses a gap in how frequently applied, behaviorally-informed process walks impact daily productivity. It evaluates whether daily process walks (DPWs), incorporating goal setting and feedback, can improve casting output in a metal manufacturing plant. Using an ABCDC design, the study tests the incremental effects of enhanced DPWs that include frontline communication and posted feedback. The authors claim this integration offers a practical way to institutionalize OBM practices within routine management activities.

title: Using Adaptive Computer-based Instruction to Teach Staff to Implement a Social Skills Intervention

entries.rq_with_context: Staff training in behavioral interventions often relies on Behavior Skills Training (BST), which is effective but time-consuming and requires skilled trainers, making it difficult to scale in large or geographically dispersed organizations. Existing alternatives like video modeling or telehealth reduce some in-person requirements but still depend on trainer-provided feedback. This study addresses the gap in scalable, independent training methods by evaluating Train-to-Code (TTC), an internet-based program that uses video coding to teach intervention steps without live trainers. The research question is whether TTC can effectively teach staff to implement a social skills intervention with fidelity in role-play probes. The study uses a multiple probe across participants design, comparing pre- and post-training performance. The contribution is demonstrating that a computer-based system alone can lead to skill acquisition in two out of three participants, suggesting potential for distance training in applied settings.

title: Evaluating a Consultant-Delivered Behavioral Skills Training and Self-Assessment Checklist Package used in the Czech Republic

entries.rq_with_context: In the Czech Republic, applied behavior analysis (ABA) services are expanding, but practitioners operate with limited oversight, mentorship, and access to professional development, often working in isolation and facing ethical challenges. Existing BST models typically focus on discrete, observable skills rather than the complex, interlocking behavior chains required of supervisory-level practitioners. This creates a gap in sustainable, generalizable training approaches for independent practitioners in underserved regions. To address this, the study piloted a consultant-delivered, extended-format BST series incorporating modular content, practitioner-driven topics, and a self-assessment checklist. The research question is whether this adapted BST package is socially valid—perceived as acceptable and meaningful—and supports skill application beyond training sessions. The approach uses a mixed-methods design combining BST with self-assessment data collected over time. The authors claim this model offers a feasible framework for professional development in emerging ABA markets.

title: A comparison of the feedback sandwich, constructive-positive feedback, and within session feedback for training preference assessment implementation

entries.rq_with_context: Feedback is widely used to improve employee performance, and while both positive and constructive comments are considered important, the sequence in which they are delivered—such as the commonly used feedback sandwich—remains debated. Despite its popularity, the feedback sandwich has been criticized for potentially diluting constructive criticism, reducing discriminability between behaviors, and possibly functioning as an aversive stimulus over time. However, empirical evidence comparing feedback sequences is limited, especially in the context of training new skills rather than improving existing ones. This study addresses this gap by comparing the feedback sandwich, constructive-positive feedback, and within-session feedback in training participants to implement a multiple stimulus without replacement (MSWO) preference assessment. Using an experimental design with repeated role-plays, the study tests whether feedback sequence affects implementation fidelity, training satisfaction, and feedback satisfaction. The primary contribution is extending prior research by evaluating feedback sequences in a skill acquisition context while approximating real-world training practices, such as varying feedback amount based on performance.

title: A Component Analysis of an Electronic Data Collection Package

entries.rq_with_context: Accurate data collection is critical in behavior analysis, but human error—especially delayed recording—can compromise data quality and lead to poor treatment decisions. Electronic data collection (EDC) systems offer promise by providing automated prompts and feedback, potentially replacing supervisory oversight. However, little research has examined which specific components of such systems are effective. This study fills that gap by conducting a component analysis of an EDC system to identify how automated prompts and different types of feedback influence data collection timeliness among caregivers working independently. Using a single-case design, the authors test each component individually. They claim the study contributes to understanding how technology can support data fidelity in real-world, unsupervised settings.

title: Further Evaluation of the Validity and Reliability of the Performance Diagnostic Checklist-Human Services

entries.rq_with_context: The Performance Diagnostic Checklist-Human Services (PDC-HS) is an informant-based tool used by consultants to identify variables affecting employee performance in human service organizations. While prior research demonstrated its validity and reliability using scripted video vignettes, those scenarios may lack real-world applicability. This study addresses that gap by using transcribed interviews from actual PDC-HS consultations to create more authentic video scenarios. The research question is whether the PDC-HS remains valid and reliable when assessed with these realistic vignettes. Using a repeated-measures design with three videos indicating one, two, or three problematic domains, the study evaluates validity through scoring accuracy and reliability via test–retest and interrater agreement. The key contribution is providing further evidence of the tool’s psychometric properties under conditions closer to actual practice.

title: Utilizing the Performance Diagnostic Checklist – Human Services to Assess and Improve Employee Performance on Mand Training: A Replication

entries.rq_with_context: In human service settings like applied behavior analysis (ABA), frontline staff often fail to implement key procedures such as contriving opportunities for mand training, which is critical for client learning. While tools exist to diagnose causes of poor performance, there is limited research applying these tools to complex, clinically significant behaviors in community-based settings. The study uses the PDC-HS to assess why three behavior instructors perform poorly on mand training and whether the recommended intervention—behavioral skills training (BST)—improves their performance. Using a multiple baseline design across participants, the authors evaluate BST’s effectiveness. The study claims to replicate and extend prior findings by demonstrating the utility of the PDC-HS in real-world, home-based ABA services.

title: An Application of Pay-for-Performance in a Human Services Setting

entries.rq_with_context: Human services organizations often struggle with financial sustainability, yet pay-for-performance (PFP) systems—where compensation is tied directly to output—have been rarely studied in this sector despite their demonstrated effectiveness in other fields. Existing research shows PFP can improve performance, but gaps remain regarding its feasibility and effects in service-based, non-profit settings where work outputs are harder to quantify. This paper addresses that gap by implementing and evaluating a PFP system in a behavioral health clinic’s consultation department staffed by behavior analysts. The research question is whether transitioning from conventional fixed pay to a PFP model increases billable service hours and improves net profit. The study uses an A-B-C design across three phases: baseline (standard pay), process intervention, and PFP. The contribution lies in demonstrating a practical application of PFP in a human services context, including financial modeling, implementation steps, and social validity data.

title: Using Prompts and Feedback to Reduce Illegal Parking in a University Parking Lot

entries.rq_with_context: Illegal parking on university campuses is a persistent problem that contributes to student frustration and has been linked to attrition, especially among first-generation and non-traditional students. While universities commonly use citations to deter illegal parking, these punitive measures may increase negative feelings toward the institution without fully addressing the underlying causes, such as confusion about parking rules. Prior research shows that informational signs and citizen-led warnings can reduce illegal parking, but few studies have combined direct performance feedback with enforcement. This study investigates whether adding performance feedback—via sticky notes placed on illegally parked vehicles—reduces illegal parking more effectively than citations alone. Using a reversal design across four semesters, the authors measure changes in illegal parking rates during baseline, treatment, and reversal phases. The study contributes by demonstrating a low-cost, behavior-analytic intervention that complements traditional enforcement.

title: Examining the Effects of Feedback Accuracy and Timing on Skill Acquisition

entries.rq_with_context: Feedback is widely used to improve performance in organizational settings, but less is known about how specific dimensions like accuracy and timing influence its effectiveness. While prior research shows accurate feedback improves performance and immediate feedback is generally better than delayed feedback, no study has examined how accuracy and timing interact. This study addresses that gap by testing the combined effects of feedback accuracy (100%, 80%, 20%) and timing (trial-by-trial vs. block feedback) on skill acquisition using a computerized match-to-sample task with undergraduate students. The authors use a 2 × 3 factorial design to compare performance across conditions. They find that accuracy significantly affects performance, while timing does not, and there is no interaction between the two.

title: Teaching Employees How to Receive Feedback: A Preliminary Investigation

entries.rq_with_context: While extensive research exists on delivering feedback to improve workplace performance, little to no empirical attention has been paid to how employees receive feedback, despite anecdotal evidence that employee behavior during feedback sessions may influence its effectiveness. Existing nonempirical sources suggest certain behaviors—like active listening and acknowledging mistakes—may help, but these have not been systematically tested or taught using behavioral methods. This study addresses this gap by developing a set of observable feedback-receiving skills and testing whether they can be taught using behavioral skills training (BST). Using a nonconcurrent multiple-baseline design across three participants, the researchers evaluated skill acquisition and maintenance. The primary contribution claimed is the initial development and preliminary evaluation of a teachable repertoire for receiving feedback, representing a novel direction in organizational behavior management.

title: The Role of Effort in Shifting Preference for Feedback Stimuli

entries.rq_with_context: Feedback and praise are commonly used in organizational behavior management, and while research has examined employee preferences for feedback format, little is known about how those preferences change over time. Existing studies typically assess preference at a single point, ignoring potential shifts due to repeated exposure. This study addresses the gap by evaluating whether preference for feedback-related stimuli changes after repeated exposure to high- and low-effort tasks. Drawing on the basic literature on within-trial contrast, it asks whether stimuli signaling work become less preferred and whether praise stimuli following work become more preferred—especially after higher-effort tasks. Using a simulated work task with an FR1 vs. FR20 schedule, the study measures changes in preference through repeated paired-stimulus assessments. It contributes to OBM by exploring how the timing and effort context of feedback delivery may shape employee preferences over time.

title: Effects of Accurate and Inaccurate Feedback on Work Performance: The Role of the Awareness of Inaccuracy

entries.rq_with_context: Feedback is a widely used tool in organizational behavior management, and it is generally assumed that feedback must be accurate to improve performance. However, in practice, supervisors may provide inaccurate feedback—either due to lack of monitoring or intentional bias—and workers may or may not detect this inaccuracy. Prior research suggests that when workers are unaware of inaccuracy, inaccurate feedback may still be effective, but when they are aware, it may undermine performance. This study investigates the role of awareness by manipulating whether participants can visibly see the outcomes of their work. It asks: does inaccurate feedback affect performance differently when performance outcomes are visible versus non-visible? Using a simulated task with a 2x2 experimental design, the study tests performance under accurate/inaccurate feedback and visible/non-visible conditions. The contribution is empirical evidence that visibility of performance outcomes (as a proxy for awareness) moderates the effectiveness of feedback accuracy.

title: Increasing Following Headway in a Driving Simulator and Transfer to Real World Driving

entries.rq_with_context: Tailgating, or following too closely, is a major contributor to rear-end crashes, yet many drivers misestimate their following headway and fail to maintain safe distances. Prior research has shown interventions can improve following headway in simulators, but effects often do not maintain. This study fills a gap by evaluating a comprehensive package intervention—including self-monitoring and education—aimed at increasing following headway among young drivers in a simulator, assessing maintenance during a reversal phase, and testing whether gains transfer to real-world driving. The study uses a non-concurrent multiple baseline design with three participants. The authors claim the study contributes by demonstrating both maintenance and real-world transfer of improved following headway using a behavioral intervention.

title: Using a Consultant Workshop Model to Improve Performance Management in Chinese Autism Agencies: A Preliminary Study

entries.rq_with_context: Educational services for children with autism in China vary in quality, and organizational behavior management (OBM) and performance management (PM) practices remain underdeveloped in this context. Despite evidence supporting PM components like training, monitoring, and feedback in Western settings, these methods have not been systematically introduced or evaluated in Chinese autism agencies. The study investigates whether using a consultant workshop model—training managers to implement a structured PM system—can improve teacher performance across multiple domains of ABA instruction. The approach follows a preliminary quasi-experimental A-B design across four agencies, measuring changes in teaching fidelity. The authors claim the study offers initial evidence for the cross-cultural applicability of OBM methods in improving service delivery in non-Western, resource-limited contexts.

title: A Preliminary Laboratory Evaluation: Effects of Consequence Quality and Ratio-Schedule Arrangements on Staff Performance

entries.rq_with_context: In organizational settings, time-based pay systems often lack contingency between performance and reinforcement, leading to lower productivity and job satisfaction. Contingent-pay systems may improve performance, but questions remain about how best to structure them—specifically, whether using high-preference versus varied reinforcers and fixed-ratio (FR) versus variable-ratio (VR) schedules affects outcomes. Prior research shows mixed results regarding varied reinforcers and schedule types, with some evidence favoring high-preference and VR schedules. This study addresses gaps by examining the effects of both consequence quality and schedule type on performance and preference in a laboratory setting. Using a reversal design with a multielement component and concurrent-chains preference assessment, the authors evaluate responding under four conditions: FR/HiP, VR/HiP, FR/Varied, and VR/Varied. The contribution is a preliminary comparison of how these combined parameters influence performance and choice in a simulated workplace task.

title: Hiring Behavior Analysts: Free Gifts at a Booth Increase Verbal Contacts with a Recruiter, but Not Serious Job Inquiries

entries.rq_with_context: The demand for certified behavior analysts has risen sharply, creating challenges for organizations trying to hire qualified staff. While employers commonly use exhibit booths at conferences and career fairs—and often provide small free gifts—there is no published evidence on whether such giveaways actually influence recruitment outcomes. Existing literature recommends these practices, but their empirical effects are unknown. This study addresses that gap by asking: Does providing free items at a recruitment booth increase the number of attendees who verbally contact a recruiter or leave an email for follow-up? Using an alternating-treatments design across three events, the researchers compared conditions with and without giveaways. They found that giveaways significantly increased verbal contacts but did not significantly increase email sign-ups, suggesting they attract attention but may not boost serious job interest.

title: Using Virtual Simulations to Assess Situational Awareness and Communication in Medical and Nursing Education: A Technical Feasibility Study

entries.rq_with_context: Communication and situational awareness are critical skills in high-reliability organizations like healthcare, yet objective methods for assessing them remain limited. While TeamSTEPPS® is widely used to improve these skills, there is little empirical assessment of its impact using precise behavioral measures. This study addresses this gap by using virtual reality (VR) simulations combined with verbal coding and eye-tracking to assess the effects of TeamSTEPPS® training on communication accuracy and observing responses among medical and nursing students. A pre/post design was used with a VR emergency simulation involving an eclamptic seizure scenario. The study contributes a technical feasibility demonstration of integrating VR with behavioral measurement tools to objectively evaluate training outcomes.

title: The Impact of Authority Relations and Feedback Delivery Method on Performance

entries.rq_with_context: Organizations increasingly use technology to deliver feedback, but the effectiveness of different methods may depend on social dynamics like authority relations. While feedback is known to improve performance, less is known about how its impact varies based on who delivers it and how, especially when considering established authority relationships. This study addresses this gap by testing performance under four feedback conditions: authority face-to-face, authority email, non-authority face-to-face, and non-authority email. Using a simulated work task with 120 participants, the authors compare performance across these conditions. They find that both feedback methods work well with authority figures, but only face-to-face feedback is effective with non-authority figures. The study contributes by showing that the social relationship between provider and recipient moderates the effectiveness of feedback delivery method.

title: Contracting to (dis)incentivize? An integrative transaction-cost approach on how contracts govern specific investments

entries.rq_with_context: Buyer–supplier collaborations face multiple frictions—haggling, non-contractible adaptation, and the risk that suppliers may appropriate the buyer’s preexisting resources through specific investment. While transaction cost economics (TCE) has traditionally studied these frictions in isolation, less is known about how contracts govern investment when all three interact. This paper addresses the gap by asking how contract form (closed vs. open price) affects the level of supplier-specific investment and when such contracts are chosen to incentivize or disincentivize investment. Using an integrative TCE model and empirical data on 155 procurement contracts, the study analyzes how the tradeoff between adaptation benefits and haggling costs, moderated by appropriation concerns, shapes governance. The key contribution is showing that contracts do not always aim to maximize investment—sometimes they are designed to suppress it to protect the buyer’s proprietary resources.

title: Mutualism and the dynamics of new platform creation: A study of Cisco and fog computing

entries.rq_with_context: Established firms often struggle to regain leadership when left behind by dominant platforms like cloud computing, facing a strategic dilemma between joining the existing ecosystem as a complementor or attempting to displace it with a new platform. However, joining risks marginalization, while direct competition risks failure and loss of existing relationships. This study examines how Cisco, a networking hardware incumbent playing a peripheral role in the cloud ecosystem, responded to this challenge by creating Fog computing—an adjacent platform addressing unmet needs in IoT data processing. The research investigates how firms can simultaneously pursue legitimacy in both the dominant and emerging platform ecosystems. Using a longitudinal case study, the authors develop a process model showing how dynamic material, symbolic, and institutional strategies enabled Cisco to introduce its new platform first through symbiosis with cloud computing, then through partial competition. The study contributes a mutualistic 'rising tide lifts all boats' strategy, contrasting with prevailing 'winner takes all' narratives in platform competition.

title: Multilevel optimal distinctiveness: Examining the impact of within- and between-organization distinctiveness of product design on market performance

entries.rq_with_context: Multiproduct organizations face competing pressures to balance design consistency within their product lines and differentiation from competitors. While optimal distinctiveness (OD) research has traditionally focused on organizational-level distinctiveness, little attention has been paid to how distinctiveness operates within organizations. This study identifies a gap in understanding how distinctiveness at multiple levels—within and between organizations—affects performance. It proposes that within-organization distinctiveness harms market performance by reducing brand coherence, while between-organization distinctiveness improves performance by enhancing competitive positioning. Furthermore, it hypothesizes that high between-organization distinctiveness weakens the negative impact of within-organization distinctiveness. The authors test these ideas using a multilevel framework applied to automobile design data from 2001 to 2016. Their key contribution is advancing OD theory by framing it as a multilevel construct influenced by contextual interactions.

title: Long-tenured independent directors and firm performance

entries.rq_with_context: Many firms have a long-tenured independent director (LTID), yet research on board tenure yields inconsistent results, possibly because it focuses on average board tenure rather than individual director characteristics. The agency perspective suggests LTIDs may become CEO cronies and impair monitoring, but the authors theorize LTIDs may instead add value through firm-specific knowledge, status, and motivation to act as strategic partners. The research question is whether the presence of an LTID is positively associated with firm performance. The study uses 15 years of S&P 1,500 data and an instrumental variable approach based on director age at hire. The main contribution is providing causal evidence that LTIDs enhance firm performance, contrary to agency-based concerns about long tenure.

title: Dynamic resource redeployment in global semiconductor firms

entries.rq_with_context: Diversified firms must decide how to reallocate resources across businesses to maximize value. While prior research focuses on resource redeployment via new business entry or complete exit, this study examines temporary redeployment among incumbent businesses—retrenchment and deepening—within the global semiconductor industry. It highlights gaps in understanding how such redeployment occurs without full entry or exit, how it may be driven not only by underutilized resources (supply-driven) but also by resource demands from expanding businesses (demand-driven), and how resource characteristics shape these patterns. Using product-level data from 2001–2016, the study investigates these dynamics across fabless and integrated device manufacturers (IDMs). It applies resource-based theory, particularly Anand et al.'s (2016) framework on resource fungibility, scalability, and decomposability, to explain differences in redeployment behavior. The study contributes by revealing that temporary internal redeployment is more common than entry or exit, identifying demand-driven reallocation, and showing how firm-level resource characteristics condition redeployment flexibility.

title: Platform governance matters: How platform gatekeeping affects knowledge sharing among complementors
